title: Comment from Walsh, Marce

text:
Subject: Protect Our Wildlife—Do Not Weaken the Endangered Species Act

To Secretary Doug Burgum and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service,

We, the undersigned concerned citizens, urge you to maintain the Endangered Species Act (ESA) exactly as it is written and to reject the currently proposed amendments that threaten to dismantle America’s most effective wildlife protection law. For over 50 years, the ESA has prevented the extinction of 99% of the species under its care. We ask that you stand by science and conservation, rather than corporate interests, to ensure this legacy continues.

We staunchly oppose the following proposed changes to the ESA:

Removing the “Blanket Rule” for Threatened Species: We oppose ending the automatic protections for species listed as “threatened.” forcing them to wait for species-specific rules leaves them vulnerable to exploitation and hunting when they need help the most.
Prioritizing Profit Over Extinction: We reject the proposal to allow economic impacts to be weighed when deciding if a species should be listed. A species’ right to exist should be determined by biological science, not by the cost to industry.
Redefining “Harm” to Exclude Habitat Destruction: We oppose the proposal to rescind the definition of “harm” that includes habitat degradation. Destroying a wild animal’s home is the same as destroying the animal itself.
Limiting Critical Habitat Designations: We oppose rules that make it easier to exclude areas from “critical habitat” protection based on economic or national security claims, which will shrink the safe havens our wildlife desperately needs.
These changes will have devastating, real-world consequences for California’s iconic species:

Tope Sharks: Conservation groups recently secured a legal agreement requiring a protection decision for these sharks by August 2025. However, if the ESA is weakened, the Tope shark could be listed as “threatened” but denied actual protection due to the removal of the “blanket rule,” allowing the soupfin trade and bycatch to continue driving them toward extinction.
Southern Sea Otters: These otters rely entirely on healthy kelp forests. If the definition of “harm” is changed to exclude habitat modification, industries could pollute or destroy these vital kelp ecosystems without violating the ESA, effectively evicting otters from the only home they have.
Humpback Whales: While recovering, humpbacks still face threats from entanglement and climate-driven shifts in food sources. Inserting economic cost-benefit analyses into the ESA could delay necessary restrictions on fishing gear or shipping lanes, prioritizing short-term profits over the survival of these majestic giants.
We call on you to uphold your duty to steward our nation’s natural heritage. Please keep the Endangered Species Act strong, science-based, and free from economic loopholes.

Signed,

Kenedy Witherow, Westerville OH

I'm not an expert but even Chat GPT agrees we need to protect our animal relatives.
A strong reason for keeping the Endangered Species Act (ESA) is that it protects ecosystems that humans depend on.

When a species disappears, it often disrupts food webs, pollination, water quality, and other natural processes. The ESA helps keep these systems intact by preventing the loss of key species. In practice, that means:

Preserving biodiversity, which increases ecosystem resilience to climate change, disease, and natural disasters.

title: Comment from Reddy, Nadia

text:
I am submitting this comment in strong opposition to the proposed rule that seeks to reinstate the definitions of “effects of the action” and the “environmental baseline” found in the 2019 consultation framework. While the proposal cites adherence to statutory text following the Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo decision, the practical effect of these reinstated definitions will be to weaken environmental protection and fundamentally undermine the protective intent of the Endangered Species Act (ESA).
The Problem of Baseline Erosion
The core failing of the 2019 environmental baseline definition is that it contributes to baseline erosion. By establishing the baseline using the current, already degraded state of the environment—and by excluding certain ongoing, non-federal harms from the assessment—the regulations allow the acceptable level of environmental impact to continuously decline.
This approach means that every new federal action is measured against a diminished status quo, enabling incremental environmental degradation – not preservation - for imperiled species. Projects that would have been unacceptable in a healthier ecosystem are deemed compliant simply because the regulatory reference point has shifted downward. This makes effective conservation and species recovery virtually impossible. This is especially concerning in a time when biodiversity is shrinking at alarming rates nationwide.
Ignoring Foreseeable and Cumulative Harm
The proposed reinstatement narrowly defines the “effects of the action,” which limits the ability of the FWS to properly consider the full scope of a project’s impact.
1.Exclusion of Cumulative Effects: The narrow scope risks ignoring how a specific federal action interacts with other concurrent private or state activities, which are likely to occur. This shields projects from accountability for their combined, cumulative damage to sensitive habitats.
2.Failure to Account for Climate Change: Climate change is arguably the most significant foreseeable threat to endangered species. By limiting the scope of analysis to direct or immediate effects, the reinstated framework will make it exceedingly difficult for the Services to fulfill their mandate to use the "best scientific and commercial data available" when assessing how a proposed action will exacerbate future, climate-driven stressors (such as ocean acidification or extreme weather) on a species.
Undermining the Protective Intent of the ESA
The ESA's ultimate purpose is to provide a comprehensive scheme for the conservation and recovery of imperiled species. Regulations that unduly constrain the ability of agency experts to assess and mitigate complex, compounding threats and fails to serve the American people.
I urge the FWS to reject the reinstatement of the 2019 definitions and instead adopt a framework that enables robust, forward-looking regulations that fully account for all foreseeable, cumulative environmental impacts to truly meet the statutory requirements of conservation and protection.

title: Comment from Mulligan, Elise

text:
I'm writing to express my strong opposition to the revisions that threaten to undermine the scientifically grounded protections embodied in the Endangered Species Act. While increased efficiency and regulatory clarity are cited as aims, the proposed rule poses serious risks to species recovery and thereby to the biodiversity we leave for future generations - our own kids, in other words.

First, the proposed elimination of the default protections for species listed as “threatened” removes a crucial early intervention mechanism. Evidence in conservation science shows that rapid response, even before full species-specific regulations are developed, increases the probability of recovery and reduces extinction risk. Delaying safeguards until rules are drafted leaves at-risk populations exposed during critical windows of vulnerability.

Second, the proposal to allow non-biological factors—such as economic or national-security considerations—to override biological data when designating critical habitat dilutes the ESA’s scientific integrity. Habitat loss and degradation consistently top the list of threats to imperiled species and are central to the ESA’s analysis of listing decisions. By introducing trade-offs that bypass rigorous ecological assessment, the rule would weaken one of the most effective tools for species recovery.

Third, narrowing the definition of “harm” or “take” to exclude significant habitat modification would be a major step backward. Habitat modification is quantitatively one of the principal drivers of species decline; omitting it from the definition of harm undermines the ESA’s ability to address root causes of extinction. Science supports the need to preserve the entirety of ecosystem functions, not just direct mortality of individuals.

This proposed rule risks eroding the scientifically robust framework that has made the ESA a cornerstone of U.S. biodiversity conservation. If adopted, it could compromise not only species currently in crises, but also our capacity to hand down a resilient natural heritage to our kids. I urge you to withdraw this proposal and retain the full scientific integrity of the ESA’s protections.

Thank you for your time and consideration.
title: Comment from Fennessy, Christine

text: I strongly oppose the proposed rule revising the regulations at 50 CFR part 402, which implements Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Although the Service intends to restore clarity by replacing most 2024 provisions with those from 2019, the specific revisions concerning the "environmental baseline" and the "reasonably certain to occur" standard risk weakening the effectiveness of the consultation process.The rule proposes reinstating $\S 402.17$, which governs the "reasonably certain to occur" standard. New factors proposed for $\S 402.17(\mathrm{~b})$ formalize a restrictive proximate causation test by focusing on the action agency's "ability to prevent the consequence due to its limited statutory authority" and whether the consequence would occur "regardless of whether the proposed action goes forward." Incorporating this strict test into the regulations may be misused by Federal agencies to dismiss effects that are foreseeable and causally related to their action. This risks allowing the incremental degradation of protected species and habitat by separating a single Federal action from its aggregate consequences.Furthermore, the proposal seeks to rescind the 2024 amendments that facilitated "offsetting" Reasonable and Prudent Measures (RPMs)—measures intended to compensate for incidental take. Removing language that supports compensatory RPMs limits the flexibility of the Services to require meaningful conservation actions that ensure the overall negative effect of a project is minimized. This reduces the available tools for achieving conservation goals in complex consultation scenarios.Finally, the proposed revision to the definition of "environmental baseline" in $\S 402.02$ adds the phrase "as they would be reasonably expected to occur." Injecting this forward-looking forecast into the definition of the baseline—which should be a snapshot of current conditions without the action's effects—introduces ambiguity and confuses the roles of the baseline and the "effects of the action" analysis. These proposed revisions threaten to inappropriately narrow the scope of Section 7 consultation, reduce the Services' capacity for requiring effective mitigation, and ultimately compromise the long-term conservation mandate of the ESA. I urge the Services to withdraw these proposed changes and maintain strong, clear regulatory standards.

title: Comment from Callahan, Eamon

text:
Topline

Dramatically expands FWS’s ability to exclude areas from critical habitat, especially when there are economic objections, energy-development concerns, or federal land users pushing for exclusion.

Summary

Proposed to revise portions of regulations for section 4 of the Endangered Species Act of 1973. Currently, the section of the ESA requires economic impact, the impact on national security, and any other relevant impact of designating any particular area as critical habitat and authorizes the exclusion of areas from critical habitat if the benefits of excluding the area outweigh the benefits of designating it as critical habitat. The proposed revisions articulate when and how we determine whether the benefits of excluding an area outweigh the benefits of designating the area as critical habitat.

Talking Points

Altering portions of Section 4(b)(2) of the Endangered Species Act of 1973 (ESA) would have serious negative implications for Gray Wolves.

Removing key provisions that would protect critical habitats from development, or other uses, greatly reduces the available habitats for Gray Wolves that help them thrive.

These critical habitats provide essential prey, shelter, and space for packs to grow, away from human activity and development that often threaten their survival.

As a keystone species, gray wolves play a crucial role in maintaining health, balance, and structure of our nation’s natural ecosystems.

text:
I am submitting this comment because biodiversity and healthy ecosystems matter deeply to me. As someone who lives in Michigan with 483 threatened and endangered species, I am concerned about weakening protections for these species in my own state, but many others around our great country. The Endangered Species Act works because it centers science and the public interest—not political pressure or economic influence. Science can tell us what species need to survive; values determine whether we choose to protect them. These rules shift decision-making away from both. The proposed changes would allow industry considerations to outweigh both biological need and scientific reality.

Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4): Removing automatic protections from newly listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed.
Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)): Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide.
Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)): Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening ecosystem health. If economic interests weigh more than essential habitat, entire ecosystems are at risk, not just wildlife species.
Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7): Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife. 

Federal oversight is often the only check on state wildlife systems that are already heavily shaped by industry interests.

Please strengthen, not weaken, federal safeguards so states and industry cannot sidestep responsibility to protect imperiled wildlife. I urge the agency to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s strong, science-based protections so that future generations may know how amazing these species are.

text:
"To Secretary Doug Burgum and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service,
We, the undersigned concerned citizens, urge you to maintain the Endangered Species Act (ESA) exactly as it is written and to reject the currently proposed amendments that threaten to dismantle America’s most effective wildlife protection law. For over 50 years, the ESA has prevented the extinction of 99% of the species under its care. We ask that you stand by science and conservation, rather than corporate interests, to ensure this legacy continues.
We staunchly oppose the following proposed changes to the ESA:
Removing the “Blanket Rule” for Threatened Species: We oppose ending the automatic protections for species listed as “threatened.” forcing them to wait for species-specific rules leaves them vulnerable to exploitation and hunting when they need help the most.
Prioritizing Profit Over Extinction: We reject the proposal to allow economic impacts to be weighed when deciding if a species should be listed. A species’ right to exist should be determined by biological science, not by the cost to industry.
Redefining “Harm” to Exclude Habitat Destruction: We oppose the proposal to rescind the definition of “harm” that includes habitat degradation. Destroying a wild animal’s home is the same as destroying the animal itself.
Limiting Critical Habitat Designations: We oppose rules that make it easier to exclude areas from “critical habitat” protection based on economic or national security claims, which will shrink the safe havens our wildlife desperately needs.
These changes will have devastating, real-world consequences for California’s iconic species:
Tope Sharks: Conservation groups recently secured a legal agreement requiring a protection decision for these sharks by August 2025. However, if the ESA is weakened, the Tope shark could be listed as “threatened” but denied actual protection due to the removal of the “blanket rule,” allowing the soupfin trade and bycatch to continue driving them toward extinction.
Southern Sea Otters: These otters rely entirely on healthy kelp forests. If the definition of “harm” is changed to exclude habitat modification, industries could pollute or destroy these vital kelp ecosystems without violating the ESA, effectively evicting otters from the only home they have.
Humpback Whales: While recovering, humpbacks still face threats from entanglement and climate-driven shifts in food sources. Inserting economic cost-benefit analyses into the ESA could delay necessary restrictions on fishing gear or shipping lanes, prioritizing short-term profits over the survival of these majestic giants.
We call on you to uphold your duty to steward our nation’s natural heritage. Please keep the Endangered Species Act strong, science-based, and free from economic loopholes.
Signed,
Tena Rohr

I am commenting on this matter because I have always been an animal lover. Wildlife and all forms of biodiversity make this planet worth living on and they are worth fighting for. Besides their intrinsic value, they also provide us incredibly rich ecosystem services that we need to survive. The Endangered Species Act, which has protected so many species over the decades, works because it centers science and the public interest- not political pressure or economic influence. The proposed changes would allow industry considerations to outweigh both biological need and scientific reality.

If you limit federal review of agency actions, so many issues could go undetected until it’s too late.

How can we be the most beautiful and best country in the world if we allow these types of actions to take place against any creature who lives here?!
I urge you to withdraw these proposals and strengthen, not weaken, federal safeguards that protect America’s great wildlife.

text:
* I am submitting this comment because biodiversity and healthy ecosystems matter deeply to me.
* As someone who lives in North Carolina and regularly sees the effects of habitat loss, I am concerned about weakening protections for imperiled species.
* I care about science-informed stewardship of the wildlife in this country.
* The Endangered Species Act works because it centers science and the public interest—not political pressure or economic influence.
* Science can tell us what species need to survive; values determine whether we choose to protect them. These rules shift decision-making away from both.
* The proposed changes would allow industry considerations to outweigh both biological need and scientific reality.
* Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4):Removing automatic protections from newly listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed.
* Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)):Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide.
* Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)):Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening ecosystem health. If economic interests weigh more than essential habitat, entire ecosystems are at risk, not just wildlife species.
* Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7):Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife. 
* Federal oversight is often the only check on state wildlife systems that are already heavily shaped by industry interests.
* These rollbacks reduce public accountability at a time when most Americans support stronger environmental conservation protections.
* A democratic, science-based process requires transparency and meaningful review.
* I urge the agency to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s strong, science-based protections.
* Please strengthen, not weaken, federal safeguards so states and industry cannot sidestep responsibility to protect imperiled wildlife.
* I ask you to uphold the intent of the ESA: preventing extinction and ensuring future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems.

text:
Nov 22, 2025

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Interior’s proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

These proposed changes try to redefine harm, add more weight to economic considerations, narrow critical habitat protections, and weaken protections for threatened species.

I care because I love nature, wildlife, and people. I am fortunate that my property backs up to local woods in Annapolis, MD that I can access easily. It brings me tremendous joy to walk and see life all around me. I also care deeply about human health and understand that there is a direct relationship between biodiversity, a healthy ecosystem, and human well-being. I believe these changes are short-sided and move us in the wrong direction both now and for future generations.

Since 1970, there is an alarming decrease in biodiversity and wildlife populations having decreased by 73% since 1970 (Living Planet Report).

Additionally, extinction risk is rising. The Red List Index that tracks the conservation status of species shows a decline across all major species groups. They are threatened by habitat loss (due to deforestation, agriculture, resource extraction), climate change, over exploitation, pollution, and disease.

Often federal oversight is the only safeguard against unchecked industry influence. Rolling back these protections will further erode public accountability at a time when a vast majority of Americans support stronger conservation measures. A democratic, science-based process demands transparency, rigorous review, and meaningful public participation.

Delaying biodiversity action is costly both environmentally and economically. Investing in biodiversity (conservation, restoration, and sustainability) can unlock trillions in economic value and create hundreds of millions of jobs.

This matters because humans rely on healthy ecosystems. Ecosystems provide free services to us in the form of clean water, food systems via pollination and soil health, and mitigating climate change via carbon sequestration. Degrading habitats due to unchecked development and resource extraction will create long-term cascading negative effects on those free services.

A livable planet is not optional. Please choose to strengthen, not undermine, the ESA protections that safeguard it.
Thank you,
Megan Forrester

text: Hello, I am using my voice as an American and a passionate environmentalist to show my opposition to the proposal to roll back the 2024 Endangered Species Act regulations. As someone who loves spending time outdoors, it breaks my heart to see how quickly natural spaces I once enjoyed are being replaced by warehouses and new developments. These changes have a huge impact on local wildlife including habitat loss and reduced biodiversity, making it harder for them to survive. Hence, the Endangered Species Act is very important to me, and weakening its ability to protect threatened and endangered species is never something I will be onboard for. These proposed changes to the Act concern me because climate change and other anthropogenic impacts on the planet are already a huge deal, and species are disappearing at rates 10 to 1,000 times faster than the normal 'background' rate of extinction. Rolling back the Endangered Species Act would only speed up this process by weakening requirements for protecting critical habitat and making delisting easier, even when recovery criteria have not been fully met. The 2024 rules were designed to better reflect modern ecological realities, such as species needing future habitat as climate conditions shift. The proposed rollback would force agencies to ignore the best available science on foreseeable risks, long-term population trends, and habitat needs. It also favors development interests over conservation, which takes away from the whole point of the Act being created. Many people are "short-term" thinkers, meaning, they only worry about the present. Well, if we use up all our natural resources and strip the planet of life today, there won't be any tomorrow. We are in the middle of an environmental crisis, and the last thing we need is weakening our laws protecting wildlife at risk of going extinct. Humans may be innovative, but triggering an ecological collapse is not something that can be resolved overnight. We need to do our part now to protect our wildlife, before it is too late. I urge for the withdrawal of this proposed rule and for the 2024 regulations to be retained.

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to firmly oppose the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. Each of these changes would significantly weaken the ESA's capacity to prevent extinction, foster species recovery, and preserve ecosystems vital to wildlife and human communities.

1. Repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule
The ESA's purpose is to act before species reach crisis levels. The 4(d) rule has historically demonstrated that early protections reduce recovery costs and prevent further declines. Eliminating default protections for threatened species would cause unnecessary delays and expose vulnerable species to harm, contrary to the ESA’s intent and resulting in higher ecological and financial costs.

2. Economic considerations in listing decisions
The ESA mandates that listing decisions rely solely on the best scientific data, not economic impacts. Allowing economic factors would undermine scientific integrity and delay protections until species face extinction risks. Weakening future-threat criteria would make timely listing less probable, increasing preventable extinctions.

3. Reduction of critical habitat protections
Habitat loss is a major driver of biodiversity decline. Narrowing critical habitat designations and redefining “harm” would undermine recovery planning and reverse scientific and legal precedent. This would weaken inter-agency consultations and increase ecological risks.

4. New loopholes for bypassing ESA protections
Creating mechanisms for agencies to override ESA protections would conflict with the ESA's purpose, reducing transparency and minimizing science-based decision-making. This would disproportionately impact imperiled species, accelerating declines.

The collective impact of these proposals would weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation, delay protections, reduce habitat conservation, heighten extinction risk, undermine cooperation, and increase recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has successfully prevented 99% of listed species from extinction. It is a critical law because of its grounding in science and early action. These proposed changes oppose those principles.

In light of the global biodiversity crisis, the U.S. should enhance—not weaken—its most effective wildlife protection law.

Request

For these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw the proposed rule changes and maintain the current regulatory framework, rooted in science and precedent.

Thank you for considering this comment.

Simon
title: Comment from Drabbe, Simon

text:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to firmly oppose all four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently under review. Each proposal—whether viewed separately or together—would greatly undermine the ESA’s capacity to prevent extinction, aid species recovery, and conserve ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. **Eliminating Default Protections for Threatened Species (Repeal of the Blanket 4(d) Rule)**

The ESA was crafted to take action before species reach critical levels. The long-standing 4(d) rule is based on decades of scientific evidence showing that early, precautionary protections decrease recovery costs and prevent further decline. Removing default protections for threatened species would lead to unnecessary delays, require case-by-case rulemaking for protections that are currently automatic, and expose vulnerable species to avoidable harm. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive intent and will result in higher ecological and financial costs over time.

2. **Listing Species: Economic Considerations and Weakening Future-Threat Analysis**

The ESA mandates that listing decisions rely solely on the best available scientific data, not economic impacts. Introducing economic considerations—either directly or indirectly—would contradict statutory language, compromise scientific objectivity, and risk deferring protections until species are near extinction. Additionally, limiting the use of projected threats overlooks current conservation science, which indicates that pressures like habitat loss, warming temperatures, and shifting ranges pose risks long before population declines are evident. Weakening future-threat criteria diminishes the likelihood of timely listings and raises the chance of preventable extinctions.

3. **Reducing Critical Habitat Protections and Narrowing the Definition of “Harm”**

Habitat loss is a leading cause of biodiversity decline worldwide and in the U.S. Reducing critical habitat designations, especially unoccupied or climate-refugia areas essential for recovery, undermines recovery planning. Similarly, restricting the definition of “harm” so that habitat degradation is excluded would overturn decades of legal and scientific precedent. Habitat destruction often indirectly kills wildlife, a fact long recognized by law. Weakening these definitions would render inter-agency consultations less effective, increase biological risk, and contradict the ESA’s recovery mandate.

4. **Introducing Loopholes for Bypassing ESA Protections**

Creating or expanding mechanisms that allow agencies to circumvent ESA protections, even when extinction is a plausible outcome, conflicts with the core purpose of the ESA. Such loopholes would encourage project-specific exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decision-making away from science-based analysis. This would disproportionately impact wide-ranging and imperiled species such as Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves, potentially accelerating declines in already pressured species.

**The Cumulative Impact of These Proposals**

Individually troubling, these proposals collectively would:
- Weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation,
- Delay or block protections for species in need,
- Reduce habitat conservation amid accelerating climate change,
- Increase extinction risk for both domestic and international species,
- Undermine inter-agency cooperation, and
- Elevate long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has successfully prevented 99% of listed species from extinction, largely because it is rooted in science, precaution, and early action. These proposals contradict those principles.

At a time of unprecedented global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should be reinforcing—not weakening—its most effective wildlife protection law.

**Request**

For these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed rule changes completely and maintain the existing regulatory framework, which is grounded in science, legal precedent, and decades of successful implementation.

Thank you for considering this comment.

text:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to strongly oppose the four proposed amendments to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations under review. Each of these changes, both individually and collectively, threatens to weaken the ESA’s capacity to prevent extinctions, aid species recovery, and preserve ecosystems vital to wildlife and human communities alike.

1. **Repealing Default Protections for Threatened Species (Removal of the Blanket 4(d) Rule)**

The ESA is designed to act before species escalate to critical levels. The longstanding 4(d) rule is based on decades of scientific evidence showing that early, precautionary measures lower recovery costs and avert further declines. Eliminating default protections for threatened species would lead to unnecessary delays, demanding case-by-case rulemaking for protections that are currently automatic, thus exposing vulnerable species to preventable harm. This contradicts the preventive intent of the ESA and will lead to increased ecological and financial costs over time.

2. **Incorporating Economic Considerations and Weakening Future-Threat Analysis for Species Listing**

The ESA mandates that listing decisions rely solely on the best available scientific data, not economic factors. Introducing economic considerations contradicts the legal language, undermines scientific objectivity, and risks delaying protections until species face imminent extinction. Furthermore, restricting future-threat analysis disregards current conservation science that shows gradual pressures like habitat loss and climate change already pose significant risks to species before population declines become visible. Weakening these criteria reduces the likelihood of timely listings and raises the risk of preventable extinctions.

3. **Reducing Critical Habitat Protections and Limiting the Definition of “Harm”**

Habitat loss is the foremost driver of biodiversity decline globally and in the U.S. Reducing critical habitat designations, especially those crucial for long-term recovery, undermines effective planning. Additionally, narrowing the definition of “harm” to exclude habitat degradation contradicts established legal and scientific precedent, as such degradation often leads indirectly to wildlife mortality. Weakening these definitions will make inter-agency consultations less effective, increase biological risks, and conflict with the ESA’s recovery goals.

4. **Creating Loopholes Allowing Agencies or Committees to Bypass ESA Protections**

Establishing mechanisms for agencies to override ESA protections, even when extinction is foreseeable, undermines the ESA’s primary purpose. I am compelled to voice my firm opposition to the four suggested amendments to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently under review. These changes would collectively and individually undermine the ESA’s effectiveness in preventing extinction, aiding species recovery, and conserving ecosystems vital for both wildlife and human communities.

1. Removing automatic protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)

The ESA aims to intervene before species reach critical levels. The existing 4(d) rule is supported by decades of scientific research, showing that early, precautionary measures reduce recovery costs and prevent further decline. Ending these automatic protections would lead to unnecessary delays, necessitate individual rulemaking for protections that are now automatic, and expose vulnerable species to needless risks. This undermines the ESA’s preventive intentions and would lead to greater ecological and financial costs over time.

2. Making it tougher to list species by incorporating economic factors and weakening future-threat analysis

The ESA dictates that listing decisions must rely solely on the best scientific data, free from economic influences. Including economic considerations contradicts this directive, risks delaying protections until species face extinction, and undermines scientific rigor. Moreover, ignoring projected or climate-related threats dismisses current conservation science, which underscores that habitat loss, climate change, and other pressures already jeopardize species long before population declines are evident. Weakening these criteria reduces the likelihood of timely protection, increasing preventable extinction risks.

3. Diminishing critical habitat protections and narrowing the definition of “harm”

Habitat loss is the leading cause of biodiversity decline globally and nationally. Reducing critical habitat designations—particularly those crucial for long-term recovery—compromises recovery plans. Similarly, redefining “harm” to exclude habitat degradation undermines legal and scientific precedent. Habitat loss often leads to indirect wildlife harm, a fact long recognized by the law. Weakening these definitions would hamper effective inter-agency consultations, heighten biological risks, and conflict with the ESA’s recovery focus.

4. Creating new loopholes for agencies or committees to bypass ESA protections

Creating or expanding pathways for agencies to bypass ESA safeguards, even when extinction is a foreseeable consequence, contradicts the ESA’s core mission. Such loopholes would encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decisions away from science-based assessments. This would disproportionately impact vulnerable species like Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves, potentially accelerating declines for many species already under severe pressure.

Cumulative impact of these proposals

Individually troubling, together these proposals would:
- Erode the ESA’s scientific underpinnings,
- Hinder protections for at-risk species,
- Reduce habitat conservation amid accelerating climate change,
- Raise extinction risks for both domestic and international species,
- Undermine inter-agency collaboration, and
- Escalate long-term recovery expenses for taxpayers.

The ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from extinction and stands as one of the most successful conservation laws due to its foundation in science, precaution, and proactive measures. These proposed changes contradict these principles.

In this time of unprecedented global biodiversity loss, the United States should fortify—not weaken—its most effective wildlife protection legislation.

Request

For these reasons, I strongly urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed changes and maintain the current regulatory framework, which is grounded in scientific evidence, legal precedent, and decades of proven success.

Thank you for considering this perspective.

text:
As a citizen who is very alarmed by the threats to our precious wildlife that are already creating an extinction crisis, I implore you NOT to weaken the ESA under any of the 4 proposed "revisions." A recent poll by the Outdoor Recreation Roundtable found that roughly four out of five (81%) Americans are concerned about the state of the environment, the welfare of animals, and conservation.For more than half a century, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has stood as one of the most important and successful conservation laws ever passed in the United States—if not in the world.
It saved the bald eagle, peregrine falcon, and wild turkey from extinction in the lower 48 states, kept grizzlies on the map in the northern Rockies, brought wolves back to Yellowstone and the Southwest, facilitated a spectacular rebound of American alligator populations, and shielded hundreds of lesser-known plants and animals whose survival stitched together the ecological fabric of the nation’s public lands.These changes are particularly jarring given the scale of environmental pressures facing the nation’s wildlife. Rising temperatures, megadroughts, intensifying wildfires, invasive species, ocean acidification, and habitat fragmentation are accelerating extinction risks way faster than at any time in modern history.

text:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently under review. Each of these proposals—individually and collectively—would significantly weaken the ESA’s ability to prevent extinction, support species recovery, and protect ecosystems that are vital to both wildlife and human well-being.

1. Repeal of the Blanket 4(d) Rule: Eliminating Default Protections for Threatened Species
The ESA was designed to take proactive measures before species reach critical endangerment. The long-standing 4(d) rule reflects decades of scientific consensus that early, precautionary protections reduce recovery costs and prevent further decline. Eliminating these default safeguards would introduce unnecessary delays, require burdensome case-by-case rulemaking, and expose vulnerable species to avoidable harm. This change contradicts the ESA’s preventive intent and would likely result in greater ecological and financial costs over time.

2. Incorporating Economic Considerations and Weakening Future-Threat Analysis in Listing Decisions
The ESA clearly mandates that listing decisions be based solely on the best available scientific data, NOT economic impacts. Introducing economic considerations would undermine the statute’s integrity, compromise scientific objectivity, and risk delaying protections until species are on the brink of extinction. Furthermore, restricting the use of projected threats ignores current conservation science, which shows that factors such as habitat loss, climate change, and shifting species ranges pose significant risks well before population declines are observable. Weakening these criteria would reduce the likelihood of timely listings and increase the risk of preventable extinctions.

3. Reducing Critical Habitat Protections and Narrowing the Definition of “Harm”
Habitat loss remains one of the primary drivers of biodiversity decline. Curtailing critical habitat designations, particularly for unoccupied or climate-resilient areas essential for recovery would severely hinder conservation efforts. Likewise, narrowing the definition of “harm” to exclude habitat degradation would overturn decades of legal and scientific precedent. Habitat destruction often results in indirect mortality, a fact long recognized in ESA implementation. These changes would weaken inter-agency consultations, elevate biological risks, and undermine the ESA’s recovery objectives.

4. Creating Loopholes That Undermine ESA Protections
Expanding mechanisms that allow agencies to bypass ESA protections, even in cases where extinction is a plausible outcome, runs counter to the Act’s core purpose. Such loopholes would encourage project-specific exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decision-making away from science-based analysis. This would disproportionately affect wide-ranging and imperiled species such as the Monarch Butterfly, Rusty Patched Bumblebee, Florida panther, grizzly bear, and gray wolf, potentially accelerating their decline.

Cumulative Impact of the Proposed Changes
While each of these proposals is concerning on its own, their combined effect would:

Undermine the ESA’s scientific foundation,
Delay or obstruct protections for at-risk species,
Weaken habitat conservation amid accelerating climate change,
Increase extinction risks for both domestic and international species,
Erode inter-agency collaboration, and
Raise long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.
The ESA has prevented the extinction of 99% of listed species, largely due to its foundation in science, precaution, and early intervention. These proposed changes are inconsistent with those principles.

At a time of unprecedented global biodiversity loss, the United States should be strengthening, NOT weakening, its most effective wildlife protection law.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed rule changes and retain the current regulatory framework, which is grounded in science, legal precedent, and decades of proven success.

Thank you for your consideration.

I care deeply about this wildlife and healthy ecosystems. Our country and our communities depend on the Endangered Species Act to ensure federal actions don’t push species closer to extinction.

The consultation process is one of our most important protections against irreversible harm. I’m concerned that narrowing the Section 7 reviews process will allow damaging projects to advance without fully assessing their impacts. Many species already face rapid habitat loss and other stresses. Weakening the science-based review process could allow projects causing permanent environmental damage to be greenlit.

The existing consultation process is also vital for transparency and accountability. State wildlife decisions are often influenced by political and industry pressures, and robust federal oversight helps keep decisions grounded in science and the public interest.

I urge the agency to withdraw this proposal and preserve strong Section 7 consultation requirements. Wildlife deserves careful, science-based review before federal actions move forward.

text: I STRONGLY disagree with this proposal. I’m writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed changes under dockets FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, and FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048. The Endangered Species Act has been one of the most effective conservation tools we have, and it continues to be essential for protecting vulnerable wildlife and the ecosystems they rely on.

I’m deeply concerned about any changes that weaken how species are listed or reclassified, narrow the use of the best available science, or make it harder to designate and protect critical habitat. Species like the Hawaiian monk seal, Guadalupe fur seal, and southern sea otter are still with us today because these protections were applied fully and responsibly.

I’m also worried about the proposed revisions to the inter-agency consultation process under Section 7. Weakening how federal agencies evaluate the 'effects of the action,' the environmental baseline, or what is considered 'reasonably certain to occur' could allow more federal projects to move forward without fully assessing their impact on endangered species or their habitat. The ESA only works when agencies are required to look at the full picture, and these changes appear to shift the balance away from science-based protection.

Additionally, the proposal to expand when areas can be excluded from critical habitat designation would tilt decisions toward short-term economic interests instead of long-term ecological health. Critical habitat is the backbone of species recovery, and carving out more exceptions would undermine that purpose.

I urge the agencies to keep the ESA strong, maintain clear and science-driven safeguards, and reject these rollbacks. Healthy, resilient ecosystems benefit all of us, and protecting them should remain a priority.

title: Comment from Vlasopolos, Anca

text:
I am submitting this comment regarding the proposed revisions to ESA Section 7 regulations governing interagency consultation. My comments focus on the importance of maintaining comprehensive, science-based assessments of action impacts—direct, indirect, and cumulative—to support species recovery and to ensure that federal actions avoid unintended environmental and community risks.

1.Science-based listings support stability
The ESA’s requirement to rely on “the best scientific and commercial data available” provides a consistent framework for evaluating biological status. Retaining this basis helps avoid uncertainty and litigation. Communities, landowners, and businesses depend on regulatory predictability, so listings should remain grounded in biological evidence rather than economic or political considerations.

Recommendation: Ensure listings rely solely on scientific data for long-term decision-making.

2.Critical habitat supports species and people
Protections maintain watershed health, reduce flood risks, sustain fisheries, and stabilize ecosystems supporting rural economies and recreation. Broadening non-designation or exclusion criteria may weaken these benefits.

Recommendation: Apply a precautionary, science-informed approach to maintain ecological functions supporting human well-being.

3.Comprehensive analysis anticipates risks
Section 7 consultations ensure federal actions consider biological impacts. Narrowing “effects of the action” or “environmental baseline” could limit consideration of cumulative or long-term changes—like altered water flow, wildfire frequency, or shifting species distributions—affecting ecosystems and communities.

Recommendation: Retain definitions allowing agencies to incorporate the best available science on cumulative and long-term effects.

4.Timely protections reduce costs and risks
Immediate protections stabilize populations early, when recovery is more achievable and less expensive. Requiring species-specific 4(d) rules for every threatened listing risks gaps during critical periods.

Recommendation: Maintain a default level of protection to ensure continuity and reduce costlier recovery measures later.

5.Economic impacts must not override recovery
Transparency and statutory consistency build public trust. While economic and social factors matter, they must be balanced with the ESA’s core purpose: preventing extinction and ensuring recovery. Over-reliance on exclusions may undermine ecosystem services such as pollination, erosion control, clean water, and recreation.

Recommendation: Ensure exclusions do not compromise species needs or ecosystem services that support communities.

The ESA has a nearly 50-year record of safeguarding species, supporting sustainable land management, and preserving ecosystems that communities depend on. Revisions should maintain its effectiveness as a science-driven, prevention-oriented tool serving both wildlife and people.

I respectfully urge the agencies to adopt final rules that preserve the ESA’s effectiveness in safeguarding wildlife and environmental systems critical to human communities.
Thank you for considering these comments.

title: Comment from Kohler, Lisa

text:
To whom it may concern,

I'm writing to strongly oppose the four proposed amendments to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently being evaluated. These changes, both individually and collectively, would significantly undermine the ESA’s capacity to avert extinction, assist in species recovery, and preserve the ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. **Removing default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)**

The ESA is designed to act before species reach critical levels. The long-established 4(d) rule is based on decades of scientific evidence showing that early, precautionary measures lower recovery costs and prevent further declines. Eliminating default safeguards for threatened species would cause unnecessary delays, mandate case-by-case rulemaking for protections currently automatic, and expose at-risk species to avoidable harm or death. This opposes the preventive aim of the ESA and will lead to higher ecological and financial costs in the long run.

2. **Making it harder to list species by allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis**

The ESA clearly states that listing decisions should be based solely on the best available scientific data, not economic impacts. Including economic considerations would contradict statutory language, compromise scientific objectivity, and risk delaying protections until species are in dire straits. Furthermore, limiting the use of projected or climate-driven threats ignores current conservation science, which shows that pressures like habitat loss and climate change already place species at risk long before declines are visible in population counts. Weakening future-threat criteria reduces the likelihood of timely listings and increases preventable extinction risks.

3. **Reducing critical habitat protections and limiting the definition of “harm”**

Habitat loss is the primary driver of biodiversity decline globally and in the United States. Reducing critical habitat designation—especially for unoccupied or climate-refugia habitat crucial for recovery—undermines recovery planning. Similarly, narrowing the definition of “harm” so habitat degradation isn’t considered would reverse decades of legal and scientific precedent. Habitat destruction often indirectly harms wildlife, and the law has long recognized this. Weakening these definitions would make inter-agency consultations less effective, heighten biological risk, and contradict the ESA’s recovery mandate.

4. **Opening new loopholes that allow agencies or special committees to bypass ESA protections**

Creating or expanding ways for agencies to bypass ESA protections, even when extinction is foreseeable, conflicts with the ESA’s core purpose. Such loopholes would promote project-specific exemptions, reduce transparency, and move decision-making away from science-based analysis. This would disproportionately affect wide-ranging and imperiled species like Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves, potentially hastening declines in species already under significant stress.

The collective impact of these proposals

While concerning individually, together these changes would weaken the ESA's scientific foundation, delay or block needed protections, reduce habitat conservation, increase the extinction risk for both domestic and international species, undermine inter-agency cooperation, and heighten long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct, making it one of the most successful conservation laws in history because it is rooted in science, precaution, and early action. These proposed changes challenge those principles.

In a time of unprecedented global biodiversity loss, the United States should be bolstering—not weakening—its most effective wildlife protection law.

For these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed rule changes completely and maintain the current regulatory framework, which is based on science, legal precedent, and a history of successful implementation.

Thank you for considering this comment.
title: Comment from Filardo, Alex

text: I am submitting this comment because biodiversity and healthy ecosystems matter deeply to me, and because I care profoundly about the future of Alaska—its brown bears, wild salmon, and the irreplaceable habitats that sustain them. I love Alaska for its vast, intact landscapes and the powerful ecological relationships that define its identity. As someone who lived in Homer and regularly witnessed the effects of habitat loss, I am deeply concerned about weakening protections for imperiled species. I believe strongly in science-informed stewardship of the wildlife in this country. The Endangered Species Act works because it centers science and the public interest, not political pressure or economic influence. Science can tell us what species need to survive; values determine whether we choose to protect them. These proposed rules shift decision-making away from both. The proposed Classification Rule would remove automatic protections from newly listed species, placing vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule would create inconsistent protections and slow recovery for threatened wildlife at a time when they need the fullest safeguards we can offer. Narrowing the criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override ecological necessity, putting entire ecosystems—not just species—at risk. Likewise, weakening the Section 7 consultation process would make it easier for harmful projects to proceed without fully assessing their impacts. Federal oversight is often the only check on state wildlife systems heavily influenced by industry pressure. These rollbacks would reduce public accountability at a time when Americans overwhelmingly support stronger wildlife protection. A democratic, science-based process requires transparency and rigorous review. I urge the agency to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s strong, science-driven foundation. Please strengthen, not weaken, federal safeguards so neither states nor industry can sidestep responsibility for protecting imperiled wildlife. I ask you to uphold the intent of the ESA: preventing extinction and ensuring that future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems.

title: Comment from Duffy, Kate

text:
I submit this comment as a citizen deeply concerned about the ecological integrity and economic stability of our nation’s landscapes in light of the proposed rule by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) and the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) to revise the inter-agency cooperation regulations under §7 of the Endangered Species Act of 1973 (ESA) via Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044. While I recognize the intent to increase regulatory predictability for stakeholders, the proposal substantially weakens the mechanisms designed to ensure timely and science-based species conservation efforts. For instance, the proposed rule adjusts the definitions of “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and alters the standard for reasonable and prudent measures under §7. In doing so, it opens the door for federal actions to proceed with less rigorous oversight of potential harms to listed species and their critical habitats, which undermines the core purpose of the ESA.
From an ecological standpoint, these changes are troubling. The proposed rule reverts to earlier, more permissive regulatory frameworks — specifically the 2019 version — which were already challenged for offering less robust protection. By narrowing the “environmental baseline” and loosening definitions, federal agencies may effectively ignore cumulative stresses from habitat fragmentation, climate change, and other threats. That means key species could face increased risks of extinction before listing or protection sufficiently responds. Moreover, healthy ecosystems provide essential services — such as clean water, pollination, and flood mitigation — whose degradation imposes real costs on agriculture, energy, and municipal infrastructure. Rolling back protections may save short-term regulatory effort but will likely create long-term ecological debt.
Economically, the assumption that this rule will impose minimal burdens on small entities and governmental actors overlooks the downstream costs of delayed species protections and degraded ecological services. The Agencies certify that this rule will not have significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. However, by weakening §7 consultation pathways and increasing uncertainty around interagency obligations, the rule may trigger litigation, costly project delays, and retroactive restoration obligations — all of which increase risks for land managers, local governments, and private developers. Additionally, by failing to proactively conserve species and habitats, we shift costs onto future stakeholders — the taxpayers, property owners, and industries who will bear the brunt of remediation and lost ecosystem function. For these reasons, I strongly urge FWS and NMFS to withdraw or significantly revise the proposed rule, retain the stronger 2024 framework (or build even more robust consultation standards), and commit to long-term conservation that aligns ecological integrity with sustainable economic outcomes.

I strongly oppose the alterations to weaken the Endangered Species Act.

As someone who lived in China and now a citizen of the United States, I saw the difference between how these governments treat their nations’ treasure: nature and wildlife. The disregard for the intricacies of natural ecosystems and human hubris for so-called development has severely undermined china’s biodiversity, to the point where seeing wildlife and naturally grown trees is rare in most cities.

I’ve always appreciated how much the US government protects our land through crucial legislation like the Endangered Species Act, establishment of national parks, and strong enforcement of these laws. This is what real development look like, because without nature and other species we co-inhabit this earth with, we cannot thrive or survive. Real development is taking responsibility and treating wildlife with respect instead of hubris.

This starts from protecting their habitat, increasing measures to safeguard at risk species, using a science-based approach, and ensuring proper federal review to enforce these laws. It’s disheartening and disappointing to see the government attempting to reverse these measures, which makes the younger generation feel more grim about the future.

Please listen to the people’s pleas and do what’s best for all species on earth, our future generations, not corporate giants who only have myopic interests in mind.

Nature belongs to us all, and it’s our responsibility to safeguard it as we would our children, because without nature, there’s no future. Thank you.

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service,

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed revisions to the interagency cooperation regulations under Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

As a citizen deeply concerned about biodiversity, environmental health, and the future stability of our ecosystems, I strongly urge the Services to ensure that any regulatory changes strengthen—not weaken—protections for threatened and endangered species.

The ESA remains one of the most successful conservation laws in the world precisely because it requires federal agencies to carefully evaluate how their actions affect vulnerable species and their habitats. Section 7 is a critical safeguard that prevents avoidable harm and ensures science-based decision-making.

I respectfully request that the final rule:

1. Maintains strong scientific integrity.

Biological evaluations and consultations must rely on the best available science, including up-to-date climate data, ecosystem modeling, and cumulative impact analysis.

2. Ensures that interagency cooperation remains transparent and enforceable.

The process should not allow shortcuts that could sidestep meaningful review or limit public oversight.

3. Prioritizes habitat protection.

Habitat loss remains the leading driver of species decline. The regulatory revisions must explicitly protect critical habitat and prevent fragmentation, degradation, and encroachment.

4. Addresses climate and ecosystem stressors.

Wildlife today faces unprecedented pressures from climate change, habitat alteration, and pollution. Section 7 consultations must account for these compounding factors to ensure long-term viability of listed species.

5. Avoids any language that could weaken agency accountability.

Federal agencies must remain fully responsible for evaluating and mitigating impacts to listed species before undertaking any action that may affect them.

Protecting threatened and endangered species is both a scientific responsibility and a moral one. I urge the Services to finalize a rule that strengthens the ESA’s core mission and ensures that interagency cooperation continues to uphold the highest standards of conservation, transparency, and ecological stewardship.

Thank you for considering this comment.

Respectfully submitted
Dr.Joyce Liy

To whom it may concern,

I am writing to firmly oppose the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently being considered. These changes, both individually and collectively, would greatly weaken the ESA’s capability to prevent extinctions, support species recovery, and conserve the ecosystems vital to wildlife and human communities alike.

1. Removing Default Protections for Threatened Species

The ESA's design is to act before species reach critical levels. The existing 4(d) rule embodies years of scientific evidence showing early protections lower recovery costs and prevent declines. Eliminating automatic protections would cause unnecessary delays, require individualized rulemaking, and expose vulnerable species to preventable harm, contradicting the ESA's preventive goals and increasing long-term ecological and financial costs.

2. Economic Factors and Weakening Future-Threat Analysis

The ESA mandates that listing decisions rely solely on the best scientific data, not economic impacts. Including economic considerations would oppose statutory language, compromise scientific objectivity, and risk delaying protections until species face extinction. Dismissing projected or climate-driven threats neglects conservation science, which indicates that factors like habitat loss and warming temperatures pose significant risks long before population declines are evident. Weakening future-threat criteria reduces timely listings and heightens the likelihood of preventable extinctions.

3. Reducing Critical Habitat Protections and Narrowing “Harm” Definition

Habitat loss is the primary cause of biodiversity decline. Limiting critical habitat designation directly hinders recovery planning. Redefining “harm” to exclude habitat degradation reverses decades of legal and scientific precedent, ignoring that habitat destruction can indirectly kill wildlife. Weakening these definitions reduces inter-agency consultation effectiveness, increases biological risk, and conflicts with the ESA’s recovery mandate.

4. Allowing Agencies to Bypass ESA Protections

Expanding mechanisms that let agencies override ESA protections, even when extinction is foreseeable, contradicts the ESA’s core mission. These loopholes promote exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decision-making away from science-based analysis, disproportionately affecting species like Florida panthers and gray wolves, accelerating declines in already pressured species.

The Combined Impact

• weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation,
• delay or block necessary protections,
• reduce habitat conservation amid climate change,
• increase extinction risks for species globally,
• undermine inter-agency cooperation,
• and escalate long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has successfully prevented 99% of listed species from extinction due to its foundation in science, precaution, and proactive measures. These proposed changes conflict with these principles. In an era of unprecedented biodiversity loss, the U.S. should reinforce, not weaken, this vital conservation law.

Request

For these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed rule changes and maintain the current regulatory framework, which is grounded in science, legal precedent, and decades of successful implementation.

text:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am reaching out to express my firm opposition to the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently under review. Each proposal, both individually and collectively, poses a significant threat to the ESA’s mission to prevent extinctions, aid in species recovery, and safeguard the ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. Eliminating Automatic Protections for Threatened Species (Repeal of the Blanket 4(d) Rule)

The ESA is designed to act before species reach critical levels. The long-standing 4(d) rule is backed by decades of scientific evidence showing that early, precautionary measures lower overall recovery costs and stop further declines. Ending automatic protections would lead to unnecessary delays, require case-by-case rulemaking, and expose vulnerable species to avoidable risks. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive purpose and will result in higher ecological and financial costs in the future.

2. Increasing Difficulty in Listing Species by Considering Economic Factors and Weakening Future-Threat Analysis

The ESA mandates that listing decisions be based solely on the best available scientific data, not economic impacts. Introducing economic factors—either directly or indirectly—would undermine scientific objectivity and delay protections until species are critically endangered. Restricting the use of projected or climate-driven threats ignores current conservation science, showing that slow-acting pressures like habitat loss and climate change already endanger species long before visible population declines. Weakening future-threat criteria reduces timely listings and raises the risk of preventable extinctions.

3. Weakening Critical Habitat Protections and Narrowing the Definition of “Harm”

Habitat loss is the leading cause of biodiversity decline globally and in the U.S. Reducing the designation of critical habitats, especially those critical for long-term recovery, directly undermines recovery planning. Similarly, narrowing the definition of “harm” to exclude habitat degradation reverses decades of legal and scientific precedent. Habitat destruction often indirectly harms wildlife, a fact long recognized by the law. Weakening these definitions would make inter-agency consultations less effective, increase biological risks, and conflict with the ESA’s recovery goals.

4. Creating New Loopholes Allowing Agencies or Committees to Bypass ESA Protections

Establishing or expanding mechanisms for agencies to override ESA protections—even when extinction is a foreseeable outcome—conflicts with the ESA’s core purpose. These loopholes would encourage project-specific exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decision-making away from science-based analysis, disproportionately affecting imperiled species like Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves.

The Combined Impact of These Proposals

While each proposal is concerning, collectively these rules would:
• Weaken the scientific basis of the ESA,
• Delay or block protections for species in need,
• Reduce habitat conservation amidst accelerating climate change,
• Increase extinction risk for both domestic and international species,
• Undermine inter-agency cooperation, and
• Raise long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has successfully prevented 99% of listed species from extinction. It is one of the most effective conservation laws, grounded in science, caution, and early action. These proposed changes are contrary to these principles.

Amidst unprecedented global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should be strengthening, not weakening, its most effective wildlife protection law.

Request

Given the reasons above, I urge the agencies to retract all four proposed changes and maintain the current regulatory framework, which is scientifically grounded, legally sound, and has proven successful over decades.

Thank you for considering this comment.

text:
The proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act threaten to undermine one of the most successful and widely supported conservation laws in U.S. history. Since its passage in 1973, the ESA has prevented more than 99% of listed species from going extinct, demonstrating that strong, science-based protections are effective when fully implemented. Weakening the Act now would reverse decades of progress and expose vulnerable species to irreversible harm.

First, limiting the role of science in listing decisions or allowing economic factors to influence whether a species deserves protection fundamentally contradicts the core purpose of the ESA. Decisions about whether a species is at risk of extinction should be based on biological status alone—not short-term economic interests or political pressure. Allowing economics to override biology opens the door to development projects that could push struggling species past the point of recovery.

Second, proposals that restrict the designation of critical habitat jeopardize the ecosystems species depend on to survive. Habitat loss remains the leading driver of extinction. Without strong, proactive habitat protections, recovery becomes significantly more difficult and costly. Diluting the rules for identifying and protecting critical habitat will allow fragmentation to continue unchecked, ultimately making restoration efforts less effective and more expensive.

Third, weakening protections for “threatened” species removes an essential preventative tool. The ESA’s existing “threatened” category allows conservation measures to begin before a species becomes critically endangered. Eliminating or reducing automatic protections for threatened species would force wildlife managers into reactive, emergency-mode conservation only after species have reached the brink—when recovery is harder and far more expensive.

Finally, Americans overwhelmingly support the ESA and its science-based approach to protecting wildlife. The Act is not only an environmental safeguard but also an ethical commitment to stewardship and biodiversity. Proposed changes prioritize short-term economic gains over long-term ecological stability, undermining a law that has proven both effective and adaptable.

In an era of rapid habitat loss, climate disruption, and biodiversity decline, the United States should be strengthening the Endangered Species Act—not weakening it. Maintaining robust protections is essential to ensuring that future generations inherit functioning ecosystems and the wildlife that depends on them.

text:
I submit this comment on docket FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044 regarding revisions to the regulations
implementing section 7 of the Endangered Species Act (ESA). I focus on the definition and
use of the environmental baseline, the risk of shifting baselines, the need to account for
long-term cumulative effects and fragmentation, and the danger that a narrowed notion of
“foreseeable” will undermine the requirement that federal agencies insure their actions do
not jeopardize listed species or destroy or adversely modify critical habitat.

Section 7(a)(2) requires agencies, in consultation with the Services, to insure that
actions they authorize, fund, or carry out are not likely to jeopardize listed species or
destroy or adversely modify critical habitat. Biological opinions implement this by
analyzing the status of the species, the environmental baseline, the effects of the
action, and cumulative effects. Any change that narrows the baseline or truncates the
scope of “effects” weakens this core protection.

The environmental baseline must be grounded in the best scientific and commercial data
available. Modern ecology warns of “shifting baseline syndrome”: each generation
unconsciously accepts degraded conditions as “normal,” underestimating the magnitude of
decline. If the baseline is treated as a simple snapshot of conditions when an action is
proposed, rather than as the present state evaluated against historically viable
conditions, the Services will underestimate risk and overestimate the sufficiency of
remaining habitat. The rule should make clear that the baseline is not a momentary
photograph; it must describe current conditions in relation to an ecologically meaningful
reference period when self-sustaining populations and functional ecosystems existed. A
severely depleted but “stable” state is degraded and precarious, not benign.

The best available science shows that habitat loss and fragmentation are major drivers of
extinction risk. Long-term fragmentation experiments and global syntheses demonstrate that
fragmented habitats lose much of their biodiversity, and that small, isolated patches are
far less effective at sustaining populations than large, connected areas. For many species
with large home ranges, seasonal migrations, or metapopulation dynamics, habitat patches
may be temporarily unoccupied during surveys yet still be essential for movement,
dispersal, and demographic “rescue.” Section 7 analyses must therefore treat fragmentation
and connectivity as central components of both the baseline and the effects of the action
and should not treat temporarily unoccupied habitat fragments as unimportant.

The proposed language that the environmental baseline refers to conditions that “would
reasonably be expected to occur without the action” risks importing a narrow notion of
“foreseeable” that is inconsistent with the ESA and conservation science. Section 7 cannot
“insure” against jeopardy if consultations ignore or discount impacts that science shows
will almost certainly occur over the life of the action simply because they lie beyond a
short project or budget cycle. Contemporary extinction-risk analyses show that species’
fates over coming decades depend strongly on projected climate and land-use trajectories
and that ignoring future global change systematically underestimates risk. Any
interpretation of “reasonably be expected to occur without the action” that, in practice,
caps the temporal scope of baseline and effects analysis at a short horizon is
inconsistent with section 7 and the best-available-science mandate.

After the Supreme Court’s decision in Loper Bright, courts will no longer defer
automatically to agency interpretations of ambiguous terms. They will ask whether these
regulations implement ESA section 7 as written. A framework that narrows the environmental
baseline, truncates the temporal scope of effects analysis, or discounts well-documented
fragmentation and climate-driven threats would be vulnerable as contrary to law and
arbitrary and capricious.

For these reasons, I respectfully request that the Services:

Reaffirm an environmental baseline that incorporates past and present anthropogenic
impacts and evaluates current conditions against historically viable states; • Recognize
shifting baseline syndrome and use historical reference conditions and long data series
wherever available;

Clarify that fragmentation, connectivity, and long-term cumulative
effects are key components of the baseline and the effects of the action, especially for
wide-ranging and migratory species; and

Make clear that the temporal scope of “reasonably be expected to occur without the action”
and “effects of the action” covers the full period over which threats and responses can be
reliably projected using the best available science.

Sincerely,
James A Rader
