text:
I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under the Endangered Species Act - section 7. Robust consultation is one of the ESA’s most critical safeguards, and these changes would dangerously weaken it at a time when listed species are already facing unprecedented pressures.

By narrowing core definitions—such as the “environmental baseline” and what effects are “reasonably certain to occur”—the proposal would allow agencies to ignore cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are widely recognized in the scientific literature. For many species, especially those already stressed by habitat loss and climate change, these impacts are not secondary concerns but primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from analysis undermines the ESA’s purpose and violates the requirement to rely on the best available science.

The proposal’s elimination of offsetting measures further erodes protections. When harm cannot be fully avoided, offsets have been a critical tool for limiting long-term damage and preventing incremental losses from pushing populations closer to collapse. Removing this tool will allow repeated, unmitigated impacts to accumulate over time.

The ESA is a conservation statute designed to promote recovery, not merely to delay extinction. These revisions abandon that mandate and put listed species at even greater risk. I urge the Fish and Wildlife Service to withdraw this proposal immediately and commit to strengthening—rather than dismantling—the consultation process that species depend on for survival.

title: Comment from Grant, Kiara

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule changes to Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Section 7 is one of the most critical safeguards in the ESA, ensuring that federal agencies do not take actions that jeopardize the survival and recovery of endangered or threatened species or destroy or adversely modify their critical habitat.

The proposed regulations would significantly weaken the interagency consultation process by raising the burden of proof for the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) and the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS). By limiting the scope of impacts that can be considered, these changes would exclude indirect, cumulative, and climate-driven effects—despite overwhelming scientific evidence that such impacts are among the greatest threats to imperiled species today.

Federal actions rarely affect species in isolation or through immediate impacts alone. Habitat fragmentation, water withdrawals, pollution, and climate-related stressors compound over time and across landscapes. Preventing USFWS and NMFS from fully considering these effects undermines the best available science and contradicts the intent of the ESA, which is to prevent extinction and promote recovery—not merely to avoid immediate harm.

Weakening Section 7 consultation would shift risk away from federal agencies and onto vulnerable species and ecosystems that cannot withstand further degradation. This proposal threatens to erode accountability, reduce transparency, and allow harmful projects to move forward without adequate environmental review.

I urge the agency to withdraw this proposal and maintain a robust, science-based Section 7 consultation process that fully considers all direct, indirect, cumulative, and climate-related impacts on listed species and their critical habitats. Our natural heritage, biodiversity, and ecological resilience depend on strong enforcement of the Endangered Species Act.

text:

The Services should not insert 402.17(b)(4) or 402.17(b)(5). 402.17(b)(4) as written could have the effect of absolving the Services of their obligation to protect listed species if there is a cumulative effect of the agency's action plus some other action that is outside their limited statutory authority. The Services should not put on blinders and pretend that actions happen in isolation and do not affect or are not affected by other consequences with which consequences of the Services' actions may interact. 402.17(b)(5) similarly may remove the Services' obligations consistent with the purposes of the Act if the consequence of a proposed action is cumulative with other, ongoing consequences from other sources. For example, if the Services' action contributes to climate change, habitat loss, disease transmission, noise disturbance or other impact that is larger scale and potentially ongoing from other sources, the Service should still consider the consequences of their proposed action even if the consequence might continue to happen due to other sources if the Service did not take their proposed action.

text:
1. “Section 2 of the Act [also] makes explicit that it is the policy of Congress that all Federal agencies and departments seek to conserve endangered and threatened species and use their authorities to further the purposes of the Act (16 U.S.C. 1531(c))”. Why wouldn’t Services have at least some discretionary of authority over all Federal activities and facilities?
2. In considering “[i]f the consequence would occur regardless of whether the proposed action goes forward.” – it would be important to acknowledge the quantity and quality of the impact in both cases. Assuming there would be some loss or damage to habitat that is inevitable - it’s unlikely to be the exact same amount or would necessarily have the exact same effect.
3. Offsets work well both for conservation and for economic advancement. I’ve seen it help conserve parcels of environmentally sensitive land and, at another time, moved a small wetland with a unique endangered plant species from an area where an airport was being expanded. It is the mandate of the ESA for Services to do all that they can to conserve and protect endangered and threatened species. This environmental/business partnership can certainly be part of the solution. I don’t understand why you would remove this as an option.. “Offset” and “Mitigation” may not be mentioned in the ESA statutory texts – but they certainly can be very useful tools to help to save listed species… the actual goal and intent of the ESA.
4. It is stated that “an agency's action cannot be considered a cause of an environmental effect when the agency has no authority to prevent the effect.” This logic is faulty. In this situation, the effect caused by the agency’s action could certainly lead to the degradation of a critical habitat or harm to the listed species… and therefor be the primary cause of the environmental effect causing harm. Maybe the agency cannot do anything about the harm it is causing – but with the mandate by the ESA to do all things possible to protect and conserve listed species, I believe all of these situations, where the agency cannot prevent the effect of its actions, are prime opportunities for the possibility of review, mitigation and using offsets in order to do all things possible to protect and conserve listed species. I do not believe that the logic of it-does-not-count-because-the-effect-cannot-be-prevented is valid, and leads to continued injury and the likelihood of further extinctions. Denial does not make the harm disappear – it should be faced and dealt with through review, mitigation when possible, and the use of offsets to continue required conservation efforts as much as possible. Your statement is on the wrong track and undermines any possible solutions and efforts to meet the obligations of the ESA.
Thank you for your consideration.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I am reaching out as a deep appreciator of the wildlife and ecosystems of the United States to advocate that the Endangered Species Act (ESA) not be changed.

The Endangered Species Act was developed to protect endangered and threatened species. It is based on scientific research and overwhelming public interest in the survival of one of our country's most precious resources - our wildlife. It has continued to prove its value in this role. The US Fish & Wildlife Service website states "Throughout its history, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has proven to be incredibly effective in stabilizing populations of species at risk, preventing the extinction of many others, and conserving the habitats upon which they depend." (https://www.fws.gov/program/endangered-species)

The rule would roll back regulations and re-adopt a weaker framework. It also narrows how effects on species and habitat can be analyzed. There are numerous issues with the i) elimination of the use of “offsets” in Reasonable and Prudent Measures (RPMs) under Section 7 consultations; ii) narrowing of the definition of “environmental baseline”; and iii) tightening of what counts as an impact “reasonably certain to occur”. One issue is that it raises the evidentiary threshold and excludes many indirect, cumulative, or climate-driven effects. It also limits what background impacts can be considered during consultation. It makes it harder to evaluate cumulative and landscape-scale harms from federal actions. Plus, it directly weakens how Section 7 operates, which is the mechanism that prevents harmful federal projects (grazing permits, oil and gas drilling, dams, pipelines, timber sales) from further endangering wildlife.

Section 7 is the backbone of the ESA: it prevents federal agencies from approving projects that would jeopardize species or destroy critical habitat. These revisions would: i) make it easier for federal agencies to overlook harmful impacts from pipelines, dams, mining approvals, grazing permits, and other federal actions; ii) reduce the ability of scientists to consider real-world risks such as climate impacts, cumulative habitat fragmentation, and landscape-scale stressors; and iii) weaken the consultation process by limiting what counts as an effect, especially long-term or geographically dispersed ones.

Section 7 consultation is the heart of the ESA; any weakening puts species survival at risk. Raising the threshold for “reasonably certain to occur” effects will erase legitimate scientific evidence and allow harmful actions to proceed without full review. The rollback reinstates 2019 rules that courts and scientists criticized as inconsistent with the ESA’s conservation mandate. Climate impacts, cumulative habitat loss, and landscape-scale consequences must be included in consultations as they are essential to understanding jeopardy. The rule should be withdrawn; the Service should restore the stronger 2024 protections instead of narrowing them.

I strongly urge you to withdraw these proposed rules to maintain the strength and success of the ESA, as one of the only set of protections afforded to our country’s wildlife.

text:
I oppose reinstating regulatory text or interpretive changes that reduce clarity around the biological standards of section 7 or that enable regulatory workarounds that could weaken species protections; the Services should instead adopt revisions that increase scientific transparency, preserve the best‑available‑science standard, and ensure that any changes do not narrow the statutory protections or reduce meaningful consultation for Federal discretionary actions.

First, the proposed reversion and edits to the environmental baseline and effects of the action definitions risk shifting focus away from biological outcomes toward administrative convenience; the environmental baseline must remain grounded in current best scientific information and the comparison of conditions with and without the proposed action. Second, removing offset language from the 2024 rule addresses statutory textual concerns but the Services must ensure that reasonable and prudent measures (RPMs) remain strictly limited to measures that avoid or minimize impacts rather than substitute offsite compensation that could permit net loss of habitat or population viability. Third, reinstating a reasonably certain to occur provision (50 CFR 402.17) is useful only if it is applied consistently with the best available science and does not create a higher evidentiary bar that excludes precautionary consideration of cumulative and climate threats. Fourth, the proposed changes interact with recent case law and Executive Orders, but legal alignment should not be used to erode biological protections or public participation in consultation processes.

Retain the best‑available‑science standard explicitly in regulatory text; clarify that RPMs cannot be used as offsets to justify otherwise harmful actions; define environmental baseline by biological function and time horizon; require cumulative and climate impact analysis in section 7 assessments; and preserve robust public and tribal consultation with accessible supporting analyses published in the docket.

Publish a redline of all regulatory changes, extend the comment period if substantive revisions are made, and commit to transparent reporting on how the final rule affects consultation timelines and conservation outcomes. The Services should finalize regulations that increase clarity and efficiency while strengthening, not weakening, statutory protections for listed species and their habitats.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.
By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.
The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.
The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
My family and I are active users of America’s public lands and waters. We have five children, and we regularly explore public lands in Utah together in our 1994 Toyota Land Cruiser. These trips are how our kids learn about conservation, responsibility, and respect for the outdoors. I’m writing in support of the Fish and Wildlife Service’s four proposed ESA regulatory updates because they move the ESA toward clearer, more practical, and more effective implementation.

For too long, ESA rules have been applied inconsistently in ways that restrict access and lawful use without actually recovering species. I support updates that focus on real, science-based results, respect multiple use and property rights, and provide more predictability for families, landowners, and local communities.

I support moving away from one-size-fits-all threatened species and 4(d) rules and toward species-specific approaches that target real threats on the ground. I also support revising ESA Section 7 consultation to be more practical and science-driven, including removing offset-style requirements that often don’t make sense for the species or habitat involved.

I support improving transparency and predictability in critical habitat designations and exclusions, as well as clearer standards for listing and delisting decisions. These changes can reduce uncertainty and litigation while keeping the focus on recovery rather than process.

These reforms matter to families like mine and to rural communities across Utah. ESA decisions affect access, local jobs, agriculture, energy, and recreation. Clearer rules reduce delays and uncertainty and make it easier for people to participate in conservation without fear of arbitrary restrictions.

They also matter for wildfire prevention. Responsible forest and rangeland management—like fuels reduction and post-fire recovery—can be slowed by overly broad ESA processes, even when projects reduce catastrophic fire risk. These reforms can help remove unnecessary barriers to work that protects habitat, watersheds, and communities.

Finally, these changes matter for recreation and access. Exploring public lands together, whether driving existing routes, camping, fishing, or just spending time outdoors, is a big part of our family life. ESA rules shouldn’t be used as a blanket justification for closures that aren’t tied to measurable recovery benefits. Conservation and access can coexist when rules are targeted, transparent, and grounded in science.

I urge the Services to finalize these reforms and refocus ESA implementation on common sense, transparency, and real recovery outcomes—using restrictions only when they are necessary, effective, and measurable.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. title: Comment from McNamara, Sarah

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

I am writing to strongly oppose any effort to weaken, dismantle, or repeal the Endangered Species Act.

The Endangered Species Act is one of the most effective conservation laws in U.S. history. It has prevented the extinction of hundreds of species, protected critical habitats, and preserved biodiversity that supports healthy ecosystems, clean water, agriculture, and local economies.

Weakening this law would have irreversible consequences. Once a species is extinct, it cannot be brought back. The ESA reflects our responsibility to future generations to protect wildlife and natural resources, not sacrifice them for short-term economic gain.

The Act is also widely supported by scientists, conservationists, Indigenous communities, and the public. It allows for science-based decision-making and balances environmental protection with responsible development.

I urge you to uphold and fully enforce the Endangered Species Act and reject any proposals that reduce its protections.

Thank you for considering my comment.

title: Comment from Burnet, Anna

text:
To Whom It May Concern,

The well-being of biodiversity in the United States is of deep interest to many citizens. The hundreds of thousands of comments submitted across all four of the proposed ESA rule changes are a testament to this. I urge you to listen.
This does not come from a place of outright objection, but out of concern that progress will be reversed for endangered species, such as the gray wolf and Florida manatee.
I want to highlight the importance of Section 7, which requires federal agencies to consult with USFWS/NMFS to avoid harming endangered species during federal projects. These agencies are experts in conservation, and allowing projects to proceed without their oversight could be detrimental to wildlife. The United States’ endangered species cannot afford such changes; their threatened populations are facing limited time and demand prioritization. I strongly implore the Service to uphold Section 7 protections and prioritize conservation science over expediency.
title: Comment from Velea, Stephanie

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Kaleyias, George

text: The Endangered Species Act is vital to protecting countless species from extinction. Wolves, for example, were wiped out of Yellowstone once. Thankfully, they were reintroduced and their numbers have increased, but they are still threatened, and therefore, need our protection. Wolves help balance the ecosystem. The prey wolves catch in the winter months help feed other species. There is a natural balance to the ecosystem when wolves are present. Allowing the hunting of wolves is a grave error and must be rectified. Threatened species, like wolves, rely on the blanket 4(d) rule for immediate protections. Another component of the current Endangered Species Act (ESA) is species-specific rules, which are necessary for long-term recovery of the species, require significant time and energy to be created so the blanket rule provides needed protections until species-specific rules are drafted. The broad baseline protections of the ESA ensure that species don’t fall prey to regulatory gaps or the influence of special-interest groups. Each of these components aids in the protection of all the species in North America. Another notable example is the Barred Owls on the west coast. The Barred Owls are being targeted due to the decline of the Spotted Owl. The Barred Owls are not a threat to the Spotted Owl. Barred and Spotted mate with one another naturally. The deforestation on the west coast is the cause of the Spotted Owl's decline. Greedy humans have used the Barred Owl as a scapegoat. Realistically, Spotted Owls are going to be collateral due to how similar in appearance they are to Barred Owls. The sharpshooters will not necessarily know the difference. The ESA should have protected the Spotted Owl from this situation. Unfortunately, Congress used a loophole to pass the plan which will cull about 450,000 Barred Owls. This plan will inevitably kill Spotted Owls and hundreds of owlets who are orphaned after their parents are shot. Section 7 of the ESA is crucial to ensuring that other agencies’ projects (oil drilling, mining, dams, timber sales) don’t further endanger wildlife. Furthermore, the Section 7 consultation process has been significant to the Act’s success in preventing the extinction of imperiled animals and plants; 99% of species listed under the Act survive today. The new proposed regulations would greatly limit the consultation process and impact both imperiled species and the critical habitat they rely on. This proposal would make it more challenging for the US Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) and the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) to prove that actions requested by other federal agencies would negatively impact listed species and critical habitat. This would exclude many indirect, cumulative, or climate-driven effects from being considered. The majority of Americans are in favor of the current rules surrounding the ESA and reject the proposed rules put forth by the Trump administration. North America is home to a variety of amazing species and we must safeguard them and their habitats. By rejecting the proposed rules, we can guarantee the species alive today will continue to live on and thrive for future generations to enjoy. If we accept the changes then there is no guarantee that species currently threatened or endangered will survive much longer. The survival of these species relies on the current ESA. We have an obligation to steward this planet in a way that allows all life to flourish. We only have one planet, which means we need to take extra care of the resources we have, including all life-forms. We have already lost too many to extinction. The current ESA is one of many laws which help us steward our planet properly. Please protect our beautiful planet by rejecting the proposals that would alter the Endangered Species Act.

title: Comment from Ingle, Tyler

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

title: Comment from Lewis, Diana

text:
As someone who lives on the Oregon coast I have the privilege of seeing the beautiful and magnificent Humpback Whales during their migration, one of our wildlife who have been successfully protected under the Endangered Species Act. As someone who cares very much about biodiversity and balanced ecosystems, the Endangered Species Act matters deeply to me.

For this reason, I am concerned about weakening protections for species who are already imperiled, on the brink of recovery or barely on their way to recovery.
I also care about science-informed stewardship of the wildlife in this country. Specific to this proposal, Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife. This is unacceptable. Federal oversight is often the only check on state wildlife systems that are already heavily shaped by industry interests. These rollbacks would also reduce public accountability at a time when most Americans support stronger environmental conservation protections. A democratic, science-based process requires transparency and meaningful review. The proposal also removes previous language that requires ESA listings to be made “without reference to economic or other impacts.” While science will still guide decisions, agencies could now include cost-benefit analyses for public review.

The Endangered Species Act works because it centers not only science but also public interest—not political pressure or economic influence. The ESA is an extremely popular policy, with Bipartisan support from 4 of 5 Americans. That is remarkable.

Because the ESA is non biased, science can tell us what species need to survive; values determine whether we choose to protect them. These proposed rules shift decision-making away from both. The proposed changes would allow industry considerations to outweigh both biological need and scientific reality, and we just cannot allow for this to occur.

I strongly urge the agency to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s strong, science-based protections. PLEASE strengthen, not weaken, federal safeguards so states and industry cannot sidestep responsibility to protect imperiled wildlife. I ask you to uphold the intent of the ESA: preventing extinction and ensuring future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems. Wildlife deserve so much more. Please do right by them.

12-22-25

I am submitting this comment as a concerned person for our environment. Biodiversity and healthy ecosystems matter very deeply to me and we cannot continue to attack our environment and expect it to be able to bounce back from our carelessness. The Endangered Species Act was put into effect in 1973 and has over the last 50 years helped both plants and animals recover from becoming extinct forever. The Center for Biological Diversity “has secured protections for more than 740 species and more than half a billion acres of wildlife habitat.” It is imperative that the ecological balance of our environment is more important than industry and profits.

Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4): Removing automatic protections from newly listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed.
Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)): Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide.
Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)): Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening ecosystem health. If economic interests weigh more than essential habitat, entire ecosystems are at risk, not just wildlife species.
Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7): Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife.
Federal oversight is often the only check on state wildlife systems that are already heavily shaped by industry profit interests. We must have laws to hold industry accountable to our fragile ecosystems, so we can preserve it for future generations before it is too late.

I urge you to uphold the intent of the Endangered Species Act to prevent destruction of lands and animals and preserve the ecosystem for our sons and daughters.

Ramona DeMarco

Big Bear City, CA 92314

I strongly oppose the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act Sect 7, interagency consultation regulations at 50 CFR part 402. These changes would significantly weaken species protections even though they are framed as clarifications.
Removing rules allowing for offset-based reasonable and prudent measures (RPMs) would reduce the impacts of incidental take. Section 7 authorizes RPMs to minimize impacts, so eliminating this flexibility would result in inadequate take that undermines biological benefit. The proposed rule removal would reduce the adaptation of science and evidence-based approaches to mitigate environmental impact.
The proposed reinstatement and expansion of section 402.17 will on the surface emphasize clear and substantial information, but in reality, it will systematically result in the exclusion of research that touches on complex scientific cause and effects that are critical to the ecosystem.
Furthermore, rule changes should be driven by ecologic needs or detrimental effects of existing rules instead of executive orders. The preamble of the rule change specifies that executive orders focused on energy development and de-regulation are driving the proposed rule change.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. The ESA should remain as it is written in its current form, and in its entirety, without redaction. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation. Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law, and importantly, it strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations. These protections have been proven to work to save cherished species from extinction such as the California Condor and our National Symbol, the Bald Eagle. These consultations have led to actions like fish passage improvements, spill operations, and habitat restoration. It is important for innumerable marine and aquatic species, such as salmon and Southern Resident orca in the Pacific Northwest, to require consultations. Without this requirement to consult, agency actions could disrupt their habitat and food resources and we could lose these species forever.

A nation's greatness is not measured by how much gold it can amass for a small number of billionaires, but by how effectively it protects and respects its most vulnerable who cannot speak for themselves.

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service,
I am writing to comment on the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) interagency cooperation regulations (Docket FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044-0001). The ESA’s section 7 consultation process plays a central role in safeguarding imperiled species and the ecosystems on which they depend by requiring federal agencies to ensure that their actions do not jeopardize the continued existence of listed species or destroy or adversely modify designated critical habitat.
The quality and integrity of the section 7 consultation process have direct biological consequences for species already on the brink. Habitat loss, degradation, and fragmentation remain the primary factors driving species toward extinction. Under section 7, federal agencies must consult with the Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA Fisheries when their actions may affect listed species or critical habitat. This consultation process is designed to identify and avoid or minimize harmful impacts before they occur. The proposed revisions would change key regulatory definitions and procedural elements of this framework. These changes risk narrowing the scope of what counts as an “effect of the action” and an “environmental baseline,” potentially excluding indirect, cumulative, or long-term impacts on species and habitat from federal review.
Scientific research shows that indirect and cumulative effects — such as habitat fragmentation, hydrological changes, or climate-driven ecosystem shifts — can be as detrimental to species survival as direct impacts. Excluding these from analysis could permit actions that incrementally erode population viability over time. Federal agencies must be required to examine all foreseeable effects of proposed actions, including indirect and cumulative impacts, so that conservation measures are meaningful and grounded in ecological reality.
The proposed revisions are described as efforts to “confirm the Services’ application of statutory requirements” and improve regulatory clarity. However, clarity should not come at the expense of ecological rigor. The consultation framework needs strong definitions that reflect how species respond to real-world stressors, not definitions that exclude relevant impacts merely because they are harder to quantify.
In addition, the ESA’s consultation process has been upheld repeatedly by federal courts as a key mechanism for preventing extinctions. Judicial precedent emphasizes that agencies must use the best available scientific data when analyzing impacts to listed species. Weakening the consultation threshold or narrowing what is considered an impact undermines that legal and scientific standard.
Strong, science-based interagency cooperation under section 7 benefits not only species but also federal agencies and project proponents by identifying conservation measures early and reducing costly delays from unforeseen environmental harm. Healthy ecosystems provide clean water, pollination, climate regulation, and other services that underpin economic and community wellbeing.
For these reasons, I respectfully urge you to revise the proposed rule so that the regulations governing section 7 fully reflect the biological needs of listed species and uphold the ESA’s statutory purpose. Protecting endangered and threatened species requires a consultation process that accounts for the full range of effects — direct, indirect, and cumulative — of federal actions. Clarity and predictability are important, but they must not come at the expense of meaningful conservation standards.
Thank you for considering my comments.

This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. The Section 7 consultation process is the cornerstone of the ESA, and the process impacts every listed species under the ESA.

ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation. Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law, and importantly, it strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.

Federal agencies such as NOAA Fisheries, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Bureau of Reclamation frequently consult under ESA Section 7 when operating dams, managing river flows, or authorizing water diversions. These consultations have led to actions like fish passage improvements, spill operations, and habitat restoration. It is important for innumerable marine and aquatic species, such as salmon and Southern Resident orca in the Pacific Northwest, to require consultations.

Without this requirement to consult, agency actions could disrupt their habitat and food resources and we could lose these species forever.

text:
Greetings,

As an American who cares deeply about protecting imperiled species and their habitats, I’m writing to express my opposition to the new regulations that would gut the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and I urge the Trump administration to withdraw these proposals. If they are finalized, the proposed regulations could harm imperiled species across the country, undercutting decades of conservation efforts.

The ESA is America’s single greatest tool to prevent species extinction and preserve this country’s biodiversity. Approximately 99% of the U.S. species listed under the Act are still with us—including some of America’s most iconic species, like the bald eagle—and hundreds of those species are on the road to recovery. I live near a rare urban old-growth forest, and it is a great joy to watch the bald eagles that nest in that park as they soar overhead. Sadly, we are in the middle of what is often called the Sixth Great Extinction as a result of human activity. At a time when one million species worldwide are threatened with extinction by 2050, we should be strengthening the laws and policies that protect imperiled species and their habitat, like the ESA. Unfortunately, the Trump administration is proposing the opposite.

If finalized, the proposed regulations would prioritize green-lighting destructive projects over protecting species at risk of extinction. These proposed rollbacks would make it easier for federal agencies to approve roads, pipelines, mines, and logging projects without fully assessing their impact on threatened and endangered species or their habitats. They would also make it more difficult to extend protections to threatened species, which would delay lifesaving action until a species' population is so small it may be challenging to save. Additionally, the proposed regulations would allow economic interests to influence decisions about which species and critical habitats warrant federal protection.

Decades of polling have shown strong bipartisan support for the ESA with approximately 84% of Americans supporting it, including me. That’s why I oppose these damaging rollbacks and urge the Trump administration to withdraw these proposals. We must prioritize our cherished wildlife and work to strengthen, not weaken, our nation’s best tool for helping to prevent extinction and putting species on the road to recovery.

Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,
June BlueSpruce

text:
I am concerned that the proposed revisions to the ESA Section 7 interagency consultation regulations weaken protections for listed species by narrowing what impacts must be considered and by increasing opportunities to exclude foreseeable harms from analysis.

Reinstating and expanding provisions related to “reasonably certain to occur,” combined with changes to the definition of environmental baseline, risks allowing agencies to discount indirect, cumulative, and climate-driven impacts that are foreseeable but complex. In practice, this shifts impacts out of the “effects of the action” and into the baseline, reducing the likelihood that jeopardy or adverse modification will be found even as conditions continue to degrade.

The ESA requires agencies to use the best available scientific information and to give the benefit of the doubt to species facing uncertainty. Standards such as “clear and substantial information,” additional causation filters, and expanded discretion-based exclusions risk elevating administrative convenience over precaution and conservation. This is particularly concerning given accelerating habitat loss and climate change, where future impacts are often probabilistic but well-supported by science.

While clarity in consultation procedures is important, Section 7 is a substantive safeguard, not merely a procedural exercise. Regulatory revisions should strengthen, not narrow, the scope of impacts considered when Federal actions may affect listed species or critical habitat.

I urge the Services to revise this proposal to ensure that foreseeable indirect and cumulative effects remain fully considered, that environmental baselines are not used to mask ongoing harm, and that Section 7 continues to function as a robust, science-driven conservation tool consistent with the ESA’s purpose of recovery.

title: Comment from Novak, Jeffrey

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Andrew, Karen

text:
I oppose the proposal to revise Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act to change the interagency consultation regulations.

It is essential that agencies communicate with each other and that any actions taken by a federal agency that could adversely affect a listed (endangered or threatened) species or critical habitat must be reviewed and only permitted if those actions are found to be benign. The language of 2024's Section 7 regulations must be retained and not the version that was written in 2019 by that administration, now back in office and hostile to our nation's treasures, our wildlife and plants.

The consideration of those potentially adverse effects would be narrowed if the proposed changes were to take place, including
- Eliminating the use of “offsets” in Reasonable and Prudent Measures (RPMs) under Section 7 consultations.
- Narrowing the definition of “environmental baseline,” limiting what background impacts can be considered during consultation.
- Tightening what counts as an impact “reasonably certain to occur,” raising the evidentiary threshold and excluding many indirect, cumulative, or climate-driven effects.
- Reinstating 2019 provisions that made it harder to evaluate cumulative and landscape-scale harms from federal actions.

The result would be that interagency communication would cease to operate effectively, thus allowing federal projects that would harm species at risk. If a permit to drill or mine or deforest or graze were submitted, under the revised language, the ability to prevent it from passing would be weakened or blocked entirely.

The core of protection of endangered and threatened species depends upon keeping Section 7 intact as currently written. It also curtails scientists' ability to advise the agencies involved based on risks we already see taking place: climate change (droughts, floods, intense rainfalls, fires), habitat fragmentation from forest loss, housing and industry development, pollution and roads, and landscape-scale stressors. Advisors would have great difficulty meeting the revised standard for "reasonably certain to occur' if the essential factors they need to present as legitimate scientific evidence are removed. It would also make it far more difficult to consult by requiring a constrained definition of an effect (especially long-term or geographical dispersed). Instead, those factors (climate change and instability, development, pollution, landscape stressors, long-term and geographically dispersed effects) must be considered. The language of a hostile administration that was written in 2019, and found inconsistent with the ESA's mandate, must be rejected, and the current language written and approved in 2024 must be retained.
title: Comment from Canepa, Judith

text: The Fish & Wildlife Service should NOT revise Endangered Species Act’s Section 7 interagency consultation regulations as proposed; it should restore the stronger 2024 Section 7 regulations and withdraw this revision. Weakening Section 7 consultation puts species survival at risk--climate impacts, cumulative habitat loss, and landscape-scale consequences must be included in consultations as they are essential to evaluating the cumulative and landscape-scale harms, and understanding the overall jeopardy posed, from federal actions. In addition, raising the threshold for “reasonably certain to occur” effects will erase legitimate scientific evidence and allow harmful actions to proceed without full review. The proposed rollback reinstates 2019 rules that courts and scientists criticized as inconsistent with the ESA’s conservation mandate. Section 7 consultation is the heart of the Endangered Species Act and should not be weakened.

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

For many species facing habitat fragmentation and climate stress, these effects are central to assessing risk. text:
Hello, my name is Sarah, I’m currently a Washington resident, and I am writing to voice my strong support for the Endangered Species Act. I strongly oppose the weakening of this critically important and successful program. We as a nation are destroying our great and beautiful lands and creatures. I hope we can all agree that we are interested in healthy ecosystems and the continued success with saving endangered and critical animals and habitats from the brink of extinction. These changes would undermine science and democratic decision-making. The Endangered Species Act works because it centers science and the public interest—not political pressure or economic influence. Science can tell us what species need to survive but the proposed changes would allow industry considerations to outweigh both biological need and scientific reality. We don’t need more corporations controlling such critical decision-making.

Removing automatic protections from newly listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed.
Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)): Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide.
Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)): Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening ecosystem health. If economic interests weigh more than essential habitat, entire ecosystems are at risk, not just wildlife species.
Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7): Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife.

Federal oversight is often the only check on state wildlife systems that are already heavily shaped by industry interests. These rollbacks reduce public accountability at a time when most Americans support stronger environmental conservation protections. A democratic, science-based process requires transparency and meaningful review.
I urge the agency to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s strong, science-based protections. Please strengthen, not weaken, federal safeguards so states and industry cannot sidestep responsibility to protect imperiled wildlife.I ask you to uphold the intent of the ESA: preventing extinction and ensuring future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems. Thank you.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

title: Comment from Yurok Tribe

text:
This proposal would revise the Endangered Species Act’s Section 7 interagency consultation regulations — the process that requires federal agencies to ensure their actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The rule would roll back the stronger 2024 Section 7 regulations and re-adopt the weaker 2019 Trump-era framework. It also narrows how effects on species and habitat can be analyzed. Key changes include:
•Eliminating the use of “offsets” in Reasonable and Prudent Measures (RPMs) under Section 7 consultations.
•Narrowing the definition of “environmental baseline,” limiting what background impacts can be considered during consultation.
•Tightening what counts as an impact “reasonably certain to occur,” raising the evidentiary threshold and excluding many indirect, cumulative, or climate-driven effects.
•Reinstating 2019 provisions that made it harder to evaluate cumulative and landscape-scale harms from federal actions.
•These changes directly weaken how Section 7 operates — the mechanism that prevents harmful federal projects (grazing permits, oil and gas drilling, dams, pipelines, timber sales) from further endangering wildlife.
Why this matters
Section 7 is the backbone of the ESA: it prevents federal agencies from approving projects that would jeopardize species or destroy critical habitat. These revisions would:
•Make it easier for federal agencies to overlook harmful impacts from pipelines, dams, mining approvals, grazing permits, and other federal actions.
•Reduce the ability of scientists to consider real-world risks such as climate impacts, cumulative habitat fragmentation, and landscape-scale stressors.
•Weaken the consultation process by limiting what counts as an effect, especially long-term or geographically dispersed ones.
Talking points for comments
•Section 7 consultation is the heart of the ESA; any weakening puts species survival at risk.
•Raising the threshold for “reasonably certain to occur” effects will erase legitimate scientific evidence and allow harmful actions to proceed without full review.
•The rollback reinstates 2019 rules that courts and scientists criticized as inconsistent with the ESA’s conservation mandate.
•Climate impacts, cumulative habitat loss, and landscape-scale consequences must be included in consultations as they are essential to understanding jeopardy.
•should be withdrawn; the Service should restore the stronger 2024 protections instead of narrowing them.
