title: Comment from Williamson County Conservation Foundation

text:
It is critical that you withdraw the proposed rule change to introduce an ambiguous definition of “recovery” and shorten the timespan for assessing threats to a species. This rule change will undermine the over five decades of progress in conservation made possible by the Endangered Species Act, which has saved 99% of listed species from extinction.

This change creates loopholes to circumvent the original intent of Congress in passing the ESA and of President Nixon in signing the act into law. As the Supreme Court ruled in Tennessee Valley Auth. v. Hill in 1978, “The plain intent of Congress in enacting [the ESA] was to halt and reverse the trend toward species extinction, whatever the cost.” For 50 years, the ESA and the coordination it enables between federal agencies have saved 291 species from extinction (Greenwald et al, 2019). It is the federal government’s responsibility, as delineated by Congress and the president, to ensure endangered species are protected from habitat harm caused by the actions of federal agencies. Species like the Canada lynx and the Mojave Desert tortoise are losing critical habitat to housing developments and road expansions, and cooperation by Housing and Urban Development with USFWS is key to limiting the environmental harm that these projects can cause.

The Endangered Species Coalition notes that coordination between government agencies, conservationists, and construction contractors is crucial to managing harm to ecosystems while still meeting construction needs and creating sustainable projects. Cooperation from the beginning empowers contractors with expert information on practical steps like renting equipment that cause less soil disturbance and pollution and using the latest in mapping and sensing technology. Wildlife corridors can be built into road infrastructure projects to give animals safe green spaces to inhabit and safe tunnels or bridges to cross roads. These strategies do not prevent infrastructure projects: research by Defenders of Wildlife found that no projects have been “halted or extensively changed” due to the ESA’s construction provisions. Wildlife protections can even boost property values, as a study by Resources.org found that homes within 2 km of critical habitats saw an appreciation in their value, supporting previous economic findings that people value open areas near their living spaces.

This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

In all, there is great potential for benefits to property value and sustainability of infrastructure projects if agencies coordinate with builders and conservationists. Congress and President Nixon made clear that this was the federal government’s responsibility, but the proposed rule change seeks to abdicate that responsibility. I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

text:
I am strongly opposed to proposed changes to ESA Section 7 regulations concerning Interagency Consultation. These changes would roll back 2024 regulations that protect listed species and critical habitats, and re-institute weaker 2019 rules that already have been rejected by scientists, and by the courts.

Do not raise threshold for harmful impacts to only consider harms that are “reasonably certain to occur”. This opens a loophole to ignore much important scientific evidence and allow irrevocable harms. By the time there is a “certainty” of harm, the damage from impacts often are irreversible. This dangerous change to the ESA would in itself be “reasonably certain” to result in species endangerment and extinction.

I also am deeply concerned that considering impacts on a piecemeal project-by-project basis ignores cumulative, landscape-scale, and longer term habitat deterioration, fragmentation, and destruction. Many native species have been extirpated or driven to the brink of extinction by exactly this failure of imagination and political will to see things whole. It is one of the biggest reasons why we needed to create and Endangered Species Act in the first place! It is essential that the ESA consider projects in the context of cumulative, landscape-scale, long-term impacts.

Earth’s biosphere is under tremendous stress, having lost over 70% of its biodiversity in the past 50 years. Coral reefs are dying and will not recover in our warming seas, this means fisheries will crash; rivers in Alaska are running orange from massive melting of permafrost, this means salmon cannot spawn. Forests are dying from too much logging that destroys habitat, worsens drought, lessens forests ability to store water and carbon, and increases wildfire risk. NOW IS THE WORST TIME TO WEAKEN THE ENDANGERED SPECIES ACT.

Human life is supported by the Earth’s biosphere. By seeking to weaken protections for threatened and endangered species, the Trump administration seeks to dig the graves of our children and grandchildren whose lives are tied to the fate of the biosphere. We stand at a fateful moment in human and planetary history, and it is imperative that we Americans choose the preservation of biodiversity on which all ecosystems and people depend.

By the time a species is endangered, it is often too late, too difficult, or too expensive to bring it back from the brink. The 2024 Section 7 regulations provide science-based protection that can keep many species from becoming endangered, and gives threatened species a far better chance to recover, and to be downlisted sooner. Weakening the Section 7 rules with looser standards and legal loopholes will allow habitat impacts that lead directly to species harms, endangerments, and extirpations.

I am appalled that the ESA is being altered based on executive orders instead of clear and concerning scientific realities. It is unacceptable to put short-term political and economic gains above long-term losses with unimaginable consequences. Wildlife is an essential public trust that cannot be placed at such risk at the whims of the current administration.

I beg you to reject proposed changes to Section 7 of the ESA.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed revisions to the Interagency Cooperation Regulations as applied to the U.S. Forest Service (USFS). The rule unlawfully weakens ESA Section 7 consultation requirements, disregards best available science, and conflicts with binding Supreme Court and Ninth Circuit precedent.

Section 7(a)(2) of the Endangered Species Act imposes a non-discretionary duty on the USFS to ensure that actions it authorizes, funds, or carries out are not likely to jeopardize listed species or destroy or adversely modify critical habitat (16 U.S.C. § 1536(a)(2)). The Supreme Court has held that Congress intended endangered species to receive the “highest of priorities, whatever the cost” (Tennessee Valley Authority v. Hill, 437 U.S. 153 (1978)). The proposed revisions improperly elevate administrative convenience and economic interests over this mandate.

Courts have consistently rejected regulatory efforts that weaken habitat protection. In Gifford Pinchot Task Force v. U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, 378 F.3d 1059 (9th Cir. 2004), the Ninth Circuit held that adverse-modification standards must protect habitat necessary for species recovery, not merely survival. In Cottonwood Environmental Law Center v. U.S. Forest Service, 789 F.3d 1075 (9th Cir. 2015), the court reaffirmed the USFS’s obligation to reinitiate consultation when new information—such as climate impacts—reveals previously unconsidered effects. The proposed rule attempts to evade these duties and is therefore unlawful.

The real-world consequences are evident on Forest Service-managed lands in the Eastern Sierra Nevada, including Bodie Hills and Conglomerate Mesa, which are threatened by mining proposals. These landscapes provide critical habitat for protected species including the Bi-State distinct population segment of greater sage-grouse (Centrocercus urophasianus) and the Owens Valley tui chub (Siphateles bicolor snyderi).

Mining causes foreseeable and cumulative harms—erosion, habitat fragmentation, cyanide and heavy-metal contamination, and long-term degradation of groundwater and spring systems—that must be analyzed under Section 7. These impacts are compounded by historic and ongoing water diversions associated with the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power, which continue to affect Mono Lake and connected ecosystems.

By minimizing indirect, cumulative, and climate-driven effects, the proposed revisions violate the ESA’s best-available-science requirement and are arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act (Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Ass’n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983)).

For these reasons, the USFS must withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety. Failure to do so will render the regulation legally indefensible and subject to judicial challenge.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
The ESA provides critical federal oversight to an assessment process that select industries would otherwise weaken, but this oversight is necessary to protect America's iconic wild species.

I grew up in Alaska, where having wild animals at your doorstep is a given. I've had the benefit of growing up witnessing major triumphs of the Endangered Species Act. Here, bald eagles seem as common as pigeons do in a city; they are a flagship success story of the Endangered Species Act helping an American icon recover to the point of no longer requiring the Act's protections. I grew up with a resident bald eagle pair that nested in our backyard, and every return to my childhood home is guaranteed several eagle sightings. In the summertime, my family alongside hordes of other of tourists would gasp over humpback whales in the Kenai Fjords and gray wolves in Denali National Park, two other iconic species that I might never have seen without the protections of the Endangered Species Act. Thus, first and foremost I speak as a concerned American about the negative cultural and economic impacts of weakening the Endangered Species Act.

Furthermore, as a professional ecologist, I know the scientific importance that the Endangered Species Act carries for protecting our country's beautiful plants and animals. As a scientist, I understand the data necessary for listing species for protection by the Endangered Species Act. We also know that the Endangered Species Act works—it has helped prevent the extinction of 99% of listed species. However, the proposed rules eschew science to the detriment of American values by allowing industrial desires to outweigh the biological realities that this country needs to ensure the cultural, economic, and innumerable ecological benefits of protecting endangered species.

I am concerned that the proposed changes to Section 7 will allow destructive projects to proceed without full review of the impacts of agency actions on endangered wildlife.

The proposed rule changes threaten democratic processes by reducing public accountability and transparent science. Thus, as a concerned American citizen and as a concerned scientist, I urge the agency to maintain the Endangered Species Act's science-based protections and current successes by withdrawing this proposed rule.

We oppose the proposed modification of the interagency cooperation rules because it:

•is prompted by political considerations rather than best available science
•is justified based on an opportunistic misreading of the Loper Bright decision
•does not meet Regulatory Planning and Review Standards

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

To Whom It May Concern,

This comment is in reference to Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044.

We are firmly and unequivocally opposed to this regulatory change regarding Section 7. We represent tens of thousands of supporters and donors who stand firmly against this regulatory change.

The NYC Plover Project is a non-profit organization founded in March 2021 to protect threatened and endangered species, preserve natural coastal ecosystems, and engage diverse New Yorkers to help safeguard these natural areas and the species that call them home. We are dedicated to the protection of the federally-threatened Atlantic Coast Piping Plover, the only federally-listed bird species under the Endangered Species Act of 1973 to be found nesting in New York City. The mission of the NYC Plover Project is to protect endangered Piping Plovers and other fragile beach-nesting birds on New York City’s beaches through education, community engagement, and volunteer stewardship.

We have implemented a volunteer program with 500+ volunteers who have worked more than 18,000 hours of service in our city’s public green spaces. In 2022, the National Park Service and the National Park Foundation bestowed the George and Helen Hartzog Award for Outstanding Volunteer Service, “Volunteer Group of the Year” for the entire nation, to the NYC Plover Project.

With regard to this regulatory change, the ESA’s Section 7 is one of the most important parts of the monumental law. As you know, this proposal would revise the Endangered Species Act’s Section 7 interagency consultation regulations, in an effort to jeopardize listed species and destroy their critical habitat. This opens further actions from large-scale damaging projects that will harm wildlife and their habitats.

What’s more is that this will make it easier for agencies to ignore the proven harmful impacts from mining, grazing, extraction and other intensive actions. And this does this while weakening the consultation process, essentially designed to rush things through.

By incorporating this Section 7 consultation change, the USFWS will be going against the very intention of the ESA. More species will be sent on a surefire path to extinction. Raising the threshold for “reasonably certain to occur” effects will erase legitimate scientific evidence and allow harmful actions to proceed without full review.

This is also legally without precedent as the rollback reinstates 2019 rules that courts and scientists criticized as inconsistent with the ESA’s conservation mandate. Climate impacts, cumulative habitat loss, and landscape-scale consequences must be included in consultations as they are essential to understanding jeopardy.

The rule must be withdrawn from consideration. The Fish and Wildlife Service must restore previous stronger protections, and not eliminate them.

Sincerely,

Chris Allieri
Executive Director
NYC Plover Project

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Re: Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; Interagency Cooperation Regulations

The Oregon Zoo respectfully submits these comments in opposition to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s (USFWS) proposed revisions to the interagency cooperation regulations implementing Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act (ESA). As a leader in wildlife conservation and a long-standing partner in species recovery and conservation with the USFWS, the Oregon Zoo is concerned that the proposed rule Section 7, which requires federal agencies to consult with the USFWS to ensure that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species.

The proposed rule would narrow the definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline,” limiting the scope of impacts that are considered during Section 7 consultation. The proposal also removes mitigation offset requirements that have long been used to avoid or minimize harm to listed species. These changes depart from decades of agency practice and judicial interpretation and would allow federal agencies to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects on listed species, leaving listed species more vulnerable to habitat loss and population decline.

For listed species like the Canada lynx or desert tortoise, robust interagency consultation under Section 7 has been essential to protect their dwindling habitat from new transportation, energy, or housing projects. Narrowing the scope of analysis involved in the consultation process creates risk that agency actions could harm species by promoting further habitat loss and population decline.

The ESA reflects a widely cherished commitment to protect not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them. This proposal undermines decades of legal precedent and Congressional intent, and for these reasons, the Oregon Zoo stands with the American conservation community and urges the USFWS to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety and retain the existing interagency cooperation framework. Instead, the Oregon Zoo urges the USFWS to affirm its commitment to the ESA’s core statutory purpose of protecting and restoring imperiled wildlife and the habitat that is crucial to their existence, an obligation that must not be weakened.

Thank you for your consideration of these comments.

Heidi Rahn
Director, Oregon Zoo

Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. These changes are designed to significantly weaken the ESA’s ability to prevent extinction, support species recovery, and protect ecosystems vital to wildlife and human communities.

The proposals would lead to a weakened scientific foundation for the ESA, fewer protections for vulnerable species, less habitat conservation amid climate change, an increased extinction risk for vulnerable species, less essential inter-agency cooperation, and higher recovery costs.

The ESA is one of the most successful conservation laws and has prevented 99% of listed species from extinction. At this vulnerable time in the world's history, there is no need to kneecap such a successful law. In a time of global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should strengthen its most effective wildlife protection law. I urge the agencies to withdraw the proposed changes. The USFWS should retain the existing framework rooted in science and legal precedent.
title: Comment from Herd, Dani

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed revisions to Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act of 1973. These changes would harm Gray Wolves by removing federal agency responsibility to consider whether actions jeopardize endangered or threatened species.
Such revisions create loopholes, reduce accountability, and allow inconsistent application of protections. They strip away precautionary measures that are vital to conserving species like the Gray Wolf, whose recovery remains fragile.
Gray Wolves are a keystone species, and weakening their protections risks destabilizing ecosystems and undoing decades of progress. Conservation decisions must be guided by science, not politics.
I urge the agency to reject these revisions and preserve Section 7 as a strong safeguard for endangered and threatened species.

title: Comment from Murphy, Stephen

text:
I write to strongly oppose the proposed revision to the regulations under the Endangered Species Act that would narrow interagency cooperation standards. By restoring a framework that reduces or removes protections designed to prevent harm to endangered and threatened species and their habitats, this rule undermines the ability to prevent habitat destruction, fragmentation, and other ecological damage before it happens.
This change does not just impact individual animals it puts entire ecosystems and future generations at risk. Habitats aren’t optional extras: they provide food, shelter, water filtration, climate resilience, and biodiversity. Without strong, enforceable habitat protections, species survival and the stability of our natural world becomes much less secure.
The proposed rule weakens the ability of federal agencies to meaningfully prevent harm, giving industries and developers leeway to degrade or destroy habitats without adequate oversight or consequences. Once natural habitats are lost, they are rarely restored fully and the loss accumulates over time, leading to species decline, increased vulnerability to climate impacts, and weakened ecosystem services that all people rely on.
This revision is harmful to everyone - humans, wildlife, plant life, current communities, and future generations because it erodes the foundational protections needed to preserve a livable, healthy planet. I urge the agency to reject this proposal and prioritize the long-term health and integrity of ecosystems over short-term economic or regulatory convenience.

title: Comment from Tarantino, Linda

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

title: Comment from Reeves, Leora

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Binette, Janet

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. The Section 7 consultation process is the cornerstone of the ESA, and the process impacts every listed species under the ESA.

ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation. Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law, and importantly, it strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.

Federal agencies such as NOAA Fisheries, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Bureau of Reclamation frequently consult under ESA Section 7 when operating dams, managing river flows, or authorizing water diversions. These consultations have led to actions like fish passage improvements, spill operations, and habitat restoration. It is important for innumerable marine and aquatic species, such as salmon and Southern Resident orca in the Pacific Northwest, to require consultations.

Federal water-management agencies, including the Bureau of Reclamation and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, consult to ensure water projects and river operations do not reduce habitat or food availability for the migrating whooping cranes and other listed species that rely on rivers and wetlands. Without this requirement to consult, agency actions could disrupt their habitat and food resources and we could lose these species forever.

text:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. Each of these changes would significantly weaken the ESA’s ability to prevent extinction, support species recovery, and protect ecosystems vital to wildlife and human communities.
Wildlife consultations are one of the ESA’s core safeguards that have forced federal agencies to stop and assess whether their actions will harm an endangered species. This safeguard has been the backbone of the ESA, the scientific gate that stopped dams, highways, pipelines, logging operations, and mining projects from forcing species toward extinction.
Under the new rule, key definitions are narrowed so agencies can ignore ongoing harms, dismiss indirect or cumulative impacts, and pretend slow-moving threats don’t count. They raise the evidentiary bar so high that unless damage is immediate and undeniable, it’s treated as speculative. It also strips the requirement to offset harm when federal projects kill wildlife, meaning agencies can destroy habitat and take endangered animals with no obligation to fix what they broke.

title: Comment from Herrmann, Terra

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to strongly oppose the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. Each proposal, separately and together, would severely weaken the ESA’s effectiveness in preventing extinction, aiding species recovery, and conserving vital ecosystems for both wildlife and human communities.

1. **Repealing the blanket 4(d) rule**: The ESA’s intent is to act before species are in crisis. The 4(d) rule has proven that precautionary measures reduce recovery costs and prevent further declines. Removing automatic protections would cause delays, require case-by-case decisions, and expose species to unnecessary risks, contradicting the ESA's preventive goals, and resulting in higher ecological and financial costs.

2. **Considering economic factors and weakening future-threat analysis**: The ESA mandates that decisions be based solely on scientific data, not economic impacts. Introducing economic considerations undermines scientific neutrality and risks delaying actions until species are nearly extinct. Ignoring climate-driven threats contradicts conservation science, making timely listings less likely and increasing preventable extinctions.

3. **Reducing critical habitat protections and redefining “harm”**: Habitat loss is the main driver of biodiversity decline. Cutting critical habitat designations weakens recovery plans. Narrowing “harm” to exclude habitat degradation overturns legal and scientific standards. This reduction would make consultations less effective, increase risks, and conflict with the ESA’s recovery goals.

4. **Creating loopholes for bypassing ESA protections**: Allowing agencies to override ESA protections, even when extinction is likely, undermines the ESA’s core purpose. These loopholes would decrease transparency and shift decisions away from science, disproportionately affecting imperiled species like Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves.

**Cumulative Impact**

Together, these proposals:

- Weaken the scientific foundation of the ESA,
- Delay protections for species in need,
- Reduce habitat conservation amid climate change,
- Heighten extinction risks domestically and internationally,
- Undermine inter-agency cooperation, and
- Increase recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has successfully prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct, grounded in science, precaution, and early action. These changes oppose those principles. At a time of severe biodiversity loss, the U.S. should strengthen—not weaken—its most effective conservation law.

**Request**

For the reasons outlined, I urge the agencies to withdraw these proposed changes and maintain the existing framework, rooted in science, legal precedent, and decades of success.

Thank you for considering this comment.

title: Comment from Myers, Jessica

text:
strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Gilliotte , Penny

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects may constitute the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal. If anything, Fish and Wildlife Services should be strengthening, not weakening, protections for federally listed species.

title: Comment from Schoenfeld, Melody

text:
I adamantly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

Endangered species need our help now more than ever. Do not roll back these life critical regulations that protect wildlife.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Protecting threatened species is not optional—it is a core promise built into the Endangered Species Act, and the blanket rule is essential to upholding Congress’s original intent. Weakening this safeguard would leave already-vulnerable species exposed to avoidable decline. Likewise, the proposed interagency cooperation rule would undermine the very heart of the ESA by shifting its focus from conservation to convenience, allowing commercial interests to overshadow the urgent needs of imperiled wildlife.
Critical habitat is the foundation of species recovery, especially as climate change accelerates habitat loss through drought, fires, shrinking snowpack, and vanishing rivers. Reducing habitat protections or narrowing the definition of “harm” ignores the reality that species cannot rebound without the space and resources to survive. With hundreds of species still waiting for protection—and many having already endured years of delay—now is the time to strengthen safeguards, not weaken them.
Excluding habitat to accommodate profit-driven development disregards both ecological science and public support. Americans overwhelmingly back strong wildlife protections because extinction is permanent; once a species disappears, it is gone forever. To hollow out the ESA is to unravel the biological foundations of a healthy planet. We must defend critical habitat, reject rollbacks, and honor our responsibility to protect the species that depend on us for their very survival.

title: Comment from Giovannini, Roberta

text:
Honorable officials,

The Endangered Species Act is the essential tool for stopping the extinction crisis in its tracks. We cannot guarantee species survival and recovery without the strong backstop of a fully protective ESA.  

I oppose any effort by this administration to weaken the Endangered Species Act. The proposed rules are yet another in a series of attacks on imperiled species and the places they live that ignore science and prioritize destruction over conservation. The proposed rules:

***Deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, greater sage grouse, and monarch butterfly could be left unprotected even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings.

***Narrow the definition of “critical habitat” to exclude currently unoccupied but historic habitat. Historic habitat is vital for recovery of imperiled species, especially as the areas where they currently live shrink due to the rapidly changing climate and the chain effects of ongoing biodiversity loss.

***Loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

***Violate the letter of the law by allowing “economic considerations” in decisions about whether to protect species that are scientifically shown to be at risk of extinction. With this rule, the federal government could decide against protecting an endangered species after considering lost revenue from prohibiting a golf course or hotel development to be built where the species lives.

***Alter the criteria for designating critical habitat to make it easier to exclude areas from protections by giving more weight to industry claims of economic impact.

With greater threats facing species than ever before, these attempts to weaken the ESA are dangerous.

More than a million of the Earth’s species face the possibility of extinction due to climate change, pollution, habitat loss, and exploitation. Even species that are not yet on the brink will face huge population declines. This extinction crisis is depleting fisheries, wiping out the pollinators that support our food supply, and making our rivers, wetlands, and forests disappear.

Humans are not isolated from the natural environment, and what happens to other creatures affects our existence, too.  

At a time when we must be redoubling our commitment to protect biodiversity and stop extinction, this administration’s proposals are dangerous and will delay the progress we must make to address the alarming rate of extinction our planet now faces.

Respectfully,
Caleb Merendino

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Schulkin, Karen

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Juracka, Kathleen

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

James Becker, United States Citizen, by the people, for the people, of the people

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Fountain, Nicole

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

I was 11 when the original act went into place. For years before that, our dad would tease us about seeing a bald eagle on the Connecticut River. Just about the time of the Bicentennial, he did actually see one. The Endangered Species Act in real time.
I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.
title: Comment from Underwood, M.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
