title: Comment from WOLFE, TERRY

text:
I disagree with the proposed changes to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is crucial to ensure federal actions don't harm listed species or destroy their critical habitats. These proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By altering key definitions, such as the “environmental baseline” and the criteria for effects "reasonably certain to occur," the rule risks allowing agencies to neglect cumulative, indirect, and climate-related impacts that are well-documented in ecological research. For many species, especially those facing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are major drivers of decline. Ignoring them contradicts both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

Eliminating offsetting measures, which have long been vital for mitigating harm when incidental take is unavoidable, further weakens conservation outcomes. While not replacements for avoidance, these requirements are crucial to ensure unavoidable impacts don’t cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA mandates a “conservation” approach that aims for recovery, not mere survival. These revisions shift consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and focus on strengthening, rather than weakening, protections for federally listed species.

This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Brachel, Tiana

text:
Endangered and Threatened Species: Interagency Cooperation
https://www.regulations.gov/document/FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044-0001

I am strongly against this proposed rule, which seeks to sacrifice the iconic lands and species we wish to preserve for future generations and that we help maintain as taxpayers. My understanding of this proposed rule is that it seeks to weaken protections of endangered habitats and species.

The new definition of environmental baseline as the “condition of the listed species or critical habitat in the action area without the consequences caused by the proposed action” does not take into consideration historical pristine habitat states that may have been degraded by past actions. It also does not take into consideration any anticipated impacts of all proposed Federal projects in the action area, and does not assess the consequences of other activities that are caused by the proposed action but that are not part of the action. This proposed definition is not an appropriate baseline for development of a plan to assist the species in question from a scientific or evolutionary perspective and in my view is inconsistent with the spirit and intent of the Endangered Species Act. It effectively lowers standards for appropriate habitat and normalizes suboptimal conditions (usually caused by human activity) as the baseline. This is unacceptable.

The proposed changes to “reasonable and prudent measures” weakens the ability of the participating agencies to fulfill the intent of the Endangered Species Act. Human activity has largely fragmented occupied habitats, and even an elementary school child understand tat habitats, far from being self contained, are impacted by other areas in varying degrees of proximity to the occupied habitat. Therefore, removing offsetting and mitigation references essentially hobble the Act by preventing the ability to implement broader mitigation activities. Not only would this decrease effectiveness of any measures taken within the occupied habitat, it would also block any ability to expand ranges and significantly improve population sized of the species in question.

The proposal to reinstate § 402.17 is at best unnecessary and in the worst case, weakens the Endangered Species Act. The text in 402.17(a) expounding on “reasonably likely to occur” requiring clear and substantial information, because it is not defined, adds no interpretive value. In addition, the list of factors in Section 402.17(a) regarding the definition of “effects of the action” are unnecessary interpretive additions that appear overly prescriptive relative to the statute. The following text expounding on consequences caused by the proposed action in Section 402.17(b) are particularly onerous because they provide little substantive metrics for decision making other than vague and potentially spurious rationales that an event is not reasonably likely to occur:
(1) The consequence is so remote in time from the action under consultation that it is not reasonably certain to occur; or

title: Comment from Prince, Tamara

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Dunurolgu, Haylei

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

title: Comment from Morin, Carla

text:
Recently, the Trump administration proposed revisions to 4 rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I STRONGLY oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would narrow the definition of “critical habitat” to exclude currently unoccupied but historic habitat. Historic habitat is vital for recovery of imperiled species, especially as the areas where they currently live shrink due to the rapidly changing climate and the chain effects of ongoing biodiversity loss.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations. Loosing species can have a negative impact on humans. For instance, the loss of mosquito-eating species can mean an increase in mosquito-borne diseases such as malaria, west nile, and zika. Keeping humans healthy requires that we keep our environment healthy as well.

Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Mead, Caroline

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Salland, Alicia

text:
I’m against the proposed changes to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is crucial to make sure federal actions don’t endanger listed species or destroy their critical habitats. The proposed changes would greatly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — such as the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the new rule risks allowing agencies to ignore cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that ecological research extensively documents. For many species, especially those facing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are leading causes of decline. Ignoring them contradicts both the purpose of the ESA and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been vital for reducing harm when incidental take is unavoidable, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements aren’t substitutions for avoidance, but they are crucial to make sure that unavoidable impacts don’t cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not just survival. These revisions shift consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead enhance, not diminish, protections for federally listed species.

text: Reinstating the 2019 consultation definitions of “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” will again narrow the impacts federal agencies must consider, excluding many cumulative and indirect threats that meaningfully affect species survival. Removing the 2024 offset provisions further weakens Section 7 outcomes. These revisions reduce accountability, impede recovery, and ultimately undermine the ESA’s protective purpose.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Ruby, Kenneth

text:
To the Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA Fisheries,

I’m commenting on this rule because weakening Section 7 consultation feels like taking the guardrails off at the exact moment the road is washing out. I’ve followed ESA consultations for years as an engaged citizen—they’re not perfect, but they’re one of the only reasons federal actions don’t steamroll species already struggling to survive.

This rule narrows definitions so much that entire categories of harm—like cumulative impacts and climate-driven effects—would get brushed aside. Anyone who spends time outdoors can tell you that climate stress is already harming species. Ignoring it in consultation isn’t just unscientific, it’s dangerous.

Eliminating offsetting measures is equally troubling. I know they’re not meant to replace avoidance, but they matter. I’ve watched projects in my region where offsetting was the difference between a population hanging on and disappearing.

The ESA’s mandate is recovery, not bare-minimum survival. This rule walks away from that responsibility and pretends that less information, less accountability, and fewer safeguards somehow amount to “efficiency.” What it really amounts to is risk—risk borne not by agencies or industries, but by species that can’t afford another wrong turn.

Please withdraw this rule. Our wildlife—and our future—deserve better.

Urgently,
A VERY Concerned Citizen of the United States of America

title: Comment from Simms, MaryJaye

text:
I urge you to maintain strong compliance measures for federal agencies. The proposed rule makes it easier to greenlight destructive activities, such as logging or drilling. These actions will put protected species in harm’s way.
ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation.
Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law and, importantly, strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.
title: Comment from CROOK, ELLEN

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Fay, Ann

text:
As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Moffett, Will

text:
To the Secretary of the Interior and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service:
My name is Brent Cheyne. I am the owner of Cheyne Farms and have served as the former President of the National Association of Wheat Growers, I have viewed agricultural policy from a national perspective. I am writing to express my strong support for the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations, specifically the renewed focus on "impacts" and the clarification of what is "reasonably certain to occur."
For years, operations in the Klamath Basin have been on the front lines of a regulatory environment that has felt more like a targeted dismantling of agriculture than conservation. We have seen our water cut off, our fields fallowed, and our regional economy threatened, all based on speculative science and a refusal to acknowledge the real-world costs of these decisions.
The Reality of "Impacts" on the Regional Tax Base
When the Service designates Critical Habitat or issues a Biological Opinion that restricts water, the "impact" isn't abstract. For Cheyne Farms and the broader community, it means:
•Ecological Collapses: The denial of water to farmers also denies water to the habitat for migrating birds on the Pacific Flyway, and the high-nutrient bird food needed from what the farmers leave in the fields for the migrating birds.
•Economic Devastation: We cannot plant crops without a reliable water schedule. The uncertainty alone destroys our ability to secure financing or invest in efficiency.
•Erosion of the Tax Base: The impact extends far beyond the farm gate. The Klamath Reclamation Project is the economic engine for Klamath, Modoc, and Siskiyou counties. When ESA restrictions force land to go fallow and farm incomes to plummet, the tax base across these three counties shrinks. This directly threatens funding for our schools, law enforcement, roads, and emergency services.
•Operational Chaos: We have faced years where the water we contracted for and paid for was withheld based on models that later proved to be flawed. This isn't just a loss of profit; it is a destabilizing force for the entire region.
I applaud the proposal to explicitly consider these economic and community impacts (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048). It is long past time for the federal government to weigh the cost of its actions against the benefits. If a Critical Habitat designation will hollow out the tax base of three counties for a negligible benefit to a species, the Secretary must have the discretion to say "no."
"Reasonably Certain to Occur": A Return to Common Sense
I also strongly support the reinstatement of the "reasonably certain to occur" standard in Section 7 consultations (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044).
•End the Speculation: We have been regulated based on "what if" scenarios and worst-case modeling that often contradict empirical observation. We have seen water sent downriver for fish that aren't there, or held in the lake for fish that don't need it at that level. The bias in federal funding of studies for pre-determined outcomes needs to stop.
•Causation Matters: The proposed rule requires a clear causal link between the Project's operation and the effect on the species. This is crucial. Our farms should not be penalized for ocean conditions, climate cycles, or the actions of others. If the Project isn't the cause of the decline, shutting down the Project shouldn't be the solution.
Conclusion
Cheyne Farms is committed to being a good steward of the land. We want healthy fish runs and a thriving ecosystem, including the Pacific Flyway. But we cannot survive in a system where the rules are rigged against us by biased models and unchecked administrative discretion.
These proposed rules represent a return to the rule of law and a fair application of the ESA. They acknowledge that agricultural communities have a right to exist and are essential to the nation's food security. I urge you to finalize them immediately.
Sincerely,

Brent Cheyne Owner, Cheyne Farms Former President, National Association of Wheat Growers Former Board Member, Klamath Irrigation District
title: Comment from Cheyne Farms

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

title: Comment from Garten, Michael

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

title: Comment from Overland, Tina

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Larson, Lanette

text:
I strongly oppose the suggested changes to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is crucial to ensure federal actions don't harm listed species or damage critical habitats. These proposed changes would weaken this process significantly.

By redefining key concepts such as the “environmental baseline” and the standard for impacts “reasonably certain to occur,” the rule risks letting agencies ignore cumulative, indirect, and climate-related effects that are well-documented in ecological studies. For many species, especially those affected by habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect impacts are major decline factors. Ignoring them contradicts the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

Furthermore, removing offsetting measures, crucial for minimizing harm when incidental take is unavoidable, undermines conservation results. While offsetting isn’t a replacement for avoidance, it's essential to ensure unavoidable impacts don't cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA mandates a focus on “conservation” for recovery, not just survival. These revisions stray from that legal requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead enhance, not diminish, protections for federally listed species.

Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.
title: Comment from Quintos, Diego

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to strongly voice my opposition to the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently under review. Each proposal, both individually and collectively, would substantially weaken the ESA’s capacity to prevent extinctions, promote species recovery, and conserve vital ecosystems essential to both wildlife and human communities.

1. **Removing default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)**

The ESA was crafted to act before species reach critical levels. The longstanding 4(d) rule is based on decades of scientific evidence that early, precautionary protections reduce recovery costs and prevent further declines. Ending automatic protections would cause unnecessary delays, lead to case-by-case rulemaking, and expose vulnerable species to avoidable harm. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive purpose and will increase ecological and financial costs over time.

2. **Making it harder to list species by allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis**

The ESA mandates that listing decisions be based solely on the best scientific data, not economic impacts. Introducing economic factors would contradict statutory language and undermine scientific objectivity, delaying protections until species face extinction. Ignoring threats like habitat loss and climate change disregards conservation science, making timely listing unlikely and increasing the risk of preventable extinctions.

3. **Reducing critical habitat protections and limiting the definition of “harm”**

Habitat loss is the primary driver of biodiversity decline. Reducing critical habitat designations, especially for areas essential for long-term recovery, undermines recovery planning. Narrowing “harm” definitions to exclude habitat degradation reverses decades of legal and scientific agreement. Weakening these definitions would make agency consultations less effective and increase biological risks, conflicting with the ESA’s recovery goals.

4. **Opening new loopholes that allow agencies or special committees to bypass ESA protections**

Creating loopholes for agencies to override ESA protections, even when extinction is foreseeable, conflicts with the ESA’s core purpose. These would incentivize exemptions, reduce transparency, and move decisions away from science-based analysis, disproportionately affecting species like the Florida panther, grizzly bear, and gray wolf, accelerating their declines.

**Cumulative Impact of These Proposals**

Taken together, these rules would weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation, delay or block necessary protections, reduce habitat conservation amid climate change, increase extinction risk, undermine inter-agency cooperation, and raise recovery costs for taxpayers. The ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct, succeeding due to its basis in science, precaution, and early action. At a time of global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should be strengthening—not weakening—its most effective wildlife protection law.

**Request**

For the reasons outlined, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed rule changes and maintain the existing regulatory framework, which is based on science, legal precedent, and decades of success.

Thank you for considering this comment.

This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Schaef, Dennis

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

text:

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. title: Comment from Hawver Scott, Timothy

text:
I am writing to urge you to not implement the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act's section 7 regulations, which would make changes around interagency cooperation.

Currently, to minimize harm to species and their habitats, federal agencies must consult with expert wildlife agencies before approving projects. This proposed rule would limit the scope of these consultations, allowing mining, logging, and other development projects to proceed before their impacts have been fully assessed.

Collaboration between agencies has been key to the Endangered Species Act’s 99% success rate. To weaken it and pave the way for projects that jeopardize the survival of endangered and threatened species alike would be a massive mistake. Please do not follow through with the implementation of this harmful rule.

text:

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

text:

The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.
title: Comment from Fritz, Elizabeth

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

title: Comment from Stimson, Christopher

text:
I am absolutely appalled at your illegal exports to dismantle the Endangered Species act! As a former Forest Service employee with a degree in resource management I know just how egregious your efforts are. Including this one where you’re trying to keep agencies from working together.

I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

Thank you for your attention to this matter!
