text:
Comment on FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044-0001, which makes it easier for federal agencies to greenlight destructive actions.

Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.

title: Comment from Balk, Garrick

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

title: Comment from Henderson, Madeleine

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA). These changes would significantly weaken protections for endangered and threatened species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA created strong, science-based safeguards, including the prohibition on “take,” the requirement that federal agencies ensure their actions do not jeopardize listed species, and the development of recovery plans for at-risk species.

Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum has stated that these revisions “restore the Endangered Species Act to its original intent” by providing “clear, consistent and lawful standards” that respect the livelihoods of Americans. However, the purposes of the ESA, as written in the statute, do not support weakening core protections. Congress explicitly stated that the Act exists to conserve ecosystems upon which species depend; to provide programs for the conservation of endangered and threatened species; and to implement relevant treaties for species protection.

Congress also made clear findings when passing the ESA:

Many species in the United States have already been rendered extinct due to economic growth and development carried out without adequate conservation;

Other species have been so depleted that they are now endangered or threatened; and

These species hold esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value for the nation.

The original legislative intent was not to lessen regulatory burdens on industries whose activities jeopardize biodiversity. Instead, it was to ensure that economic activity is tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” The proposed rules contradict this intent by undermining basic protections for threatened and endangered species and by narrowing the definition and use of critical habitat.

I oppose these rule changes, which would deprive newly listed threatened species of automatic protections against killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species currently being considered for listing—such as the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage-grouse, and Monarch butterfly—could remain unprotected for years even after federal listing decisions. The impacts extend to species not yet identified, including the roughly 80% of insect species still unnamed.

The Earth is experiencing an accelerating extinction crisis. Addressing this crisis requires strong, science-based ESA regulations, not weakened ones. I urge the agency to withdraw the proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s longstanding, effective protections.

title: Comment from Modoc Nation

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.
title: Comment from Janes, Kelly

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to firmly oppose the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently under review. Each proposal, both on its own and combined with the others, would significantly weaken the ESA’s power to prevent extinctions, support species recovery, and protect ecosystems vital to both wildlife and humans.

1. Removing automatic protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)

The ESA's design aims to act before species reach critical endangerment. The longstanding 4(d) rule is based on decades of scientific research, showing that early, precautionary measures reduce recovery costs and prevent further declines. Ending these automatic protections would lead to unnecessary delays, require individual rulemaking, and expose species to avoidable risks. This goes against the ESA’s preventive purpose and will lead to greater ecological and financial burdens in the future.

2. Introducing economic factors in the listing process and weakening future-threat analysis

The ESA mandates that listing decisions are based purely on the best scientific data, not economic factors. Introducing economic considerations would contradict statutory language, undermine objectivity, and delay protections until species are near extinction. Ignoring projected or climate-driven threats disregards current conservation science, which shows that gradual pressures like habitat loss and climate change risk species long before population declines are evident. Weakening future-threat criteria makes timely listing unlikely, increasing the chance of preventable extinctions.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and narrowing the definition of “harm”

Habitat loss is the primary driver of biodiversity decline both globally and nationally. Limiting critical habitat designations, especially for unoccupied or climate-refugia areas, undermines recovery efforts. Similarly, redefining “harm” so habitat degradation doesn't qualify would reverse long-standing legal and scientific precedent. Habitat destruction often indirectly kills wildlife, and the law recognizes this. Weakening these definitions reduces agency consultations' effectiveness, increases biological risk, and conflicts with the ESA’s recovery goals.

4. Creating loopholes that allow agencies to bypass ESA protections

Allowing agencies to override ESA protections, even when extinction is foreseeable, contradicts the ESA’s core mission. These loopholes would encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and move decision-making away from scientific analysis. This disproportionately affects species like Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves, accelerating their decline.

Cumulative impact of these proposals

Individually concerning, collectively these rules would:
• Weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation,
• Delay or obstruct necessary protections,
• Reduce habitat conservation amid climate change,
• Raise extinction risks for both domestic and global species,
• Undermine inter-agency cooperation, and
• Increase long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from extinction. It stands as a successful conservation law because it relies on science, precaution, and early action. These proposed changes starkly conflict with these principles. Amid unprecedented global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should strengthen, not weaken, its most effective wildlife protection law.

Request

For the reasons outlined, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed rule changes entirely and maintain the current regulatory framework, which is rooted in science, legal precedent, and decades of success.

Thank you for considering this comment.

text:
Subject: Protect Our Wildlife—Do Not Weaken the Endangered Species Act

To Secretary Doug Burgum and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service,

As a concerned citizen, urge you to maintain the Endangered Species Act (ESA) exactly as it is written and to reject the currently proposed amendments that threaten to dismantle America’s most effective wildlife protection law. For over 50 years, (and signed into law by a Republican) the ESA has prevented the extinction of 99% of the species under its care. We ask that you stand by science and conservation, rather than corporate interests, to ensure this legacy continues.

I staunchly oppose the following proposed changes to the ESA:

Removing the “Blanket Rule” for Threatened Species: I oppose ending the automatic protections for species listed as “threatened.” forcing them to wait for species-specific rules leaves them vulnerable to exploitation and hunting when they need help the most.
Prioritizing Profit Over Extinction: I reject the proposal to allow economic impacts to be weighed when deciding if a species should be listed. A species’ right to exist should be determined by biological science, not by the cost to industry.
Redefining “Harm” to Exclude Habitat Destruction: I oppose the proposal to rescind the definition of “harm” that includes habitat degradation. Destroying a wild animal’s home is the same as destroying the animal itself.
Limiting Critical Habitat Designations: I oppose rules that make it easier to exclude areas from “critical habitat” protection based on economic or national security claims, which will shrink the safe havens our wildlife desperately needs.
These changes will have devastating, real-world consequences for this country's iconic species.

I call on you to uphold your duty to steward our nation’s natural heritage. Please keep the Endangered Species Act strong, science-based, and free from economic loopholes.

Signed,
Brett Ochs, Boulder, CO
title: Comment from Ochs, Brett

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;

(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

title: Comment from st denis, pauline

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. These amendments, if enacted, would severely undermine the ESA’s effectiveness in preventing extinction, aiding species recovery, and conserving vital ecosystems.

1. Removing default protections for threatened species

The ESA is designed to act proactively, and the 4(d) rule exemplifies the importance of early protections. Eliminating these automatic safeguards would lead to unnecessary delays and expose at-risk species to harm, contradicting the ESA’s preventative intent and incurring greater ecological and economic costs.

2. Economic factors in listing species

ESA decisions should be based purely on scientific data, free from economic influences. Allowing economic considerations risks compromising objectivity and may delay vital protections, pushing species closer to extinction. Weakening future-threat analyses further undermines conservation efforts, ignoring science on slow-acting threats like habitat loss and climate change.

3. Diminishing critical habitat protections

Habitat loss is a key driver of species decline. Reducing critical habitat designations and altering the definition of “harm” would reverse years of legal precedent and undermine recovery efforts. These changes would decrease the efficacy of inter-agency consultations and increase biological risks.

4. New loopholes bypassing ESA protections

Introducing mechanisms that allow agencies to circumvent ESA protections conflicts with its core mission. Such loopholes would encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and affect species like Florida panthers and gray wolves.

Collectively, these proposals would erode the ESA’s scientific foundation, delay protections, diminish habitat conservation, and heighten extinction risks. The ESA has been successful because it is rooted in science and early intervention, preventing 99% of listed species from extinction.

In light of these concerns, I urge the agencies to withdraw these proposed changes and maintain the current regulatory framework, upholding its scientific and legal foundations.

Thank you for your consideration.

text:
I am writing to voice my strong opposition to the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. Each proposal, both individually and collectively, threatens to significantly undermine the ESA’s effectiveness in preventing extinction, aiding species recovery, and conserving ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. **Removing Default Protections for Threatened Species (Repeal of the Blanket 4(d) Rule)**

The ESA aims to act before species reach critical levels. The established 4(d) rule is supported by decades of scientific evidence demonstrating that early, precautionary measures lower overall recovery costs and prevent further declines. Abolishing default protections for threatened species would lead to unnecessary delays, necessitate case-by-case rulemaking for currently automatic protections, and expose vulnerable species to avoidable risk. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive intention and will result in increased ecological and financial costs over time.

2. **Making Listing Species Harder by Allowing Economic Considerations and Weakening Future-Threat Analysis**

According to the ESA, listing decisions must rely solely on the best available scientific data, excluding economic impacts. Introducing economic considerations—directly or indirectly—contradicts statutory language, undermines scientific objectivity, and risks delaying protections until species are nearly extinct. Additionally, limiting the use of projected or climate-driven threats overlooks current conservation science, which indicates that slow-burn pressures such as habitat loss, warming temperatures, and shifting ranges already pose significant risks long before declines are reflected in population statistics. Weakening future-threat criteria diminishes the likelihood of timely listings and increases the chance of avoidable extinctions.

3. **Reducing Critical Habitat Protections and Limiting the Definition of “Harm”**

Globally and in the United States, habitat loss remains the primary driver of biodiversity decline. Reducing critical habitat designations—especially unoccupied or climate-refuge areas crucial for long-term recovery—undermines recovery efforts. Similarly, narrowing the definition of “harm” so that habitat degradation no longer qualifies would undo decades of legal and scientific precedence. Habitat destruction often indirectly kills wildlife, a fact long recognized by law. Weakening these definitions would diminish the effectiveness of inter-agency consultations, heighten biological risks, and contradict the ESA’s recovery mandate.

4. **Opening New Loopholes for Agencies or Special Committees to Bypass ESA Protections**

Creating or broadening mechanisms allowing agencies to override ESA protections—even when extinction is foreseeable—conflicts with the ESA’s fundamental purpose. These loopholes would encourage project-by-project exemptions, reduce transparency, and divert decision-making away from science-based analysis. This would disproportionately impact wide-ranging and vulnerable species like the Florida panther, grizzly bear, and gray wolf, potentially accelerating declines in many already-stressed species.

The Cumulative Impact of These Proposals

While troubling individually, together these rules would:
- Undermine the scientific foundation of the ESA,
- Delay or block protections for at-risk species,
- Reduce habitat conservation amid accelerating climate change,
- Heighten extinction risks for both domestic and international threatened species,
- Undermine inter-agency cooperation, and
- Increase long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has prevented 99% of the species under its protection from extinction and remains one of the most successful conservation laws, thanks to its grounding in science, precaution, and proactive action. These proposed changes stand in stark contrast to these principles.

In a time of unprecedented global biodiversity loss, the United States should enhance—not weaken—its most effective wildlife protection law.

title: Comment from Sanghera, Kara

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I vehemently oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.

text:
I urge you to maintain strong compliance measures for federal agencies. The proposed rule makes it easier to greenlight destructive activities, such as logging or drilling. These actions will put protected species in harm’s way.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Wood, Peter

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes RECOVERY, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.
title: Comment from Wells, K.A.

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to voice my strong opposition to the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently under review. Each proposal—on its own and together—would drastically weaken the ESA’s capability to avert extinction, aid species recovery, and conserve ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. Removing default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)

The ESA intends to act before species reach crisis levels. The 4(d) rule, based on decades of scientific evidence, demonstrates that early, precautionary protections reduce recovery costs and prevent further decline. Eliminating default protections would cause unnecessary delays, require individualized rulemaking, and expose vulnerable species to preventable harm. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive purpose, leading to greater ecological and financial consequences over time.

2. Making it harder to list species by allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis

ESA mandates that listing decisions rely solely on the best scientific data, without economic influence. Allowing economic considerations undermines statutory language, threatens scientific objectivity, and risks delaying protections until species face extinction. Moreover, limiting future-threat analysis ignores conservation science, suggesting that threats such as habitat loss, climate change, and shifting ranges heighten risk before population declines are visible. Weakening these criteria diminishes timely listings and increases preventable extinctions.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and limiting the definition of “harm.”

Habitat loss is a leading driver of biodiversity decline globally and in the U.S. Cutting critical habitat designations, especially unoccupied or climate-refugia essential for recovery, undermines planning. Narrowing “harm” to exclude habitat degradation reverses longstanding legal and scientific precedents. Habitat destruction often indirectly kills wildlife, and this connection has long been recognized. Weakening these terms would make inter-agency consultations less effective and compromise ESA’s recovery mandate.

4. Opening new loopholes that allow agencies or special committees to bypass ESA protections

Creating mechanisms for agencies to override ESA protections—even when extinction is likely—conflicts with the ESA’s core mission. These loopholes encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decisions away from science-based analyses, affecting species like Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves, accelerating declines already under severe pressure.

The cumulative effect of these proposals

Individually concerning, these rules collectively:
- Weaken the scientific foundation of the ESA,
- Delay or block necessary protections,
- Reduce habitat conservation amid climate change,
- Raise extinction risks for domestic and international species,
- Undermine inter-agency collaboration,
- Increase taxpayer recovery costs.

The ESA has saved 99% of listed species from extinction, a success due to its grounding in science, precaution, and early intervention. These changes oppose those principles.

During unprecedented global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should reinforce, not weaken, this crucial wildlife protection law.

Request

For these reasons, I urge all four proposed rule changes to be withdrawn, keeping the current science-based regulatory framework grounded in legal precedent and decades of success.

Thank you for considering this comment.

title: Comment from Brooks, Dr John

text:
I oppose the proposed changes to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is vital to ensure federal actions do not endanger listed species or destroy critical habitats. These changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing essential definitions—such as the "environmental baseline" and the standard for effects "reasonably certain to occur"—the rule risks allowing agencies to ignore cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are extensively documented in ecological literature. For many species, especially those facing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are major factors in their decline. Leaving them out of consideration contradicts both the ESA's purpose and the "best available science" standard.

Additionally, removing offsetting measures, which have been crucial in reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. While not replacements for avoidance, these requirements are essential to ensure unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA mandates a "conservation" focus that promotes recovery, not just survival. These revisions shift consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

title: Comment from Abashian, Tamara

text:
I am submitting this comment because our environment is extremely important. Health ecosystems and biodiversity matter deeply to me. It is our duty to protect all living creatures. The Endangered Species Act works because it is science based and it centers around those scientific findings and public interest. The proposed changes would be detrimental and it would allow considerations to outweigh biological need and scientific reality.
Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4): Removing automatic protections from newly listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed.
Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)): Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide.
Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)): Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening ecosystem health. If economic interests weigh more than essential habitat, entire ecosystems are at risk, not just wildlife species.
Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7): Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife.
I urge to to please withdraw these proposed rules. We need to maintain the ESA's strong, science-based protections. Those protections need to be strengthen so federal safeguards will not allow states and industries to sidestep responsibility to protect imperiled wildlife.
Science must guide the decisions that are made about our wildlife. Corporations have to abide to those regulations and should not be allowed to influence.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Fox, Lynda

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text: I oppose these changes. They would cause irreparable harm to at-risk species and essential habitat and worsen the biodiversity and extinction crisis. Uphold the ESA’s mission by rejecting these changes.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text: In the entire universe, we - and every species we know of - have only one planet to live on. As the Earth’s most intelligent and destructive species, it falls to humanity to help preserve habitat and biodiversity for every other being on this planet, including this area we love and call home: the United States. The consequences of carelessness, of selfishness, of greed for land are unknown, but will almost certainly be grave for all. The web of nature is interconnected in ways we do not fully understand, and each time we lose a species, we lose a piece of the strength and resilience of our ecosystem. Please, preserve the Endangered Species Act. To weaken it weakens us all.

title: Comment from Simmons, Patricia

text:
I am submitting these comments because healthy and well-balanced biodiversity and ecosystems matter deeply to me. I live in the beautiful state of Montana and regularly see the effects of habitat loss, and I am extremely concerned about weakening protections for imperiled species. This is the time to incorporate science-informed stewardship of the wildlife in this country and not allow your politics to drive the decisions.
The Endangered Species Act (ESA) works because it centers both science and the public interest, as it should, and NOT political pressure or economic influence. The science tells us what species need to survive, and values determine whether we choose to protect them. These rules shift decision-making away from both. The proposed changes would allow industry considerations to outweigh both biological need and scientific reality.
Proposals:
1)Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4): Removing automatic protections from newly-listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin; newly-listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed;
2)Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)): Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide;
3)Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)): Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening ecosystem health. If economic interests weigh more than essential habitat, entire ecosystems are at risk, not just wildlife species; and
4)Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7): Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife.

The only check on state wildlife systems is, oftentimes, on the federal level, which is already heavily shaped by industry interests. At a time when most Americans support stronger environmental conservation protections, which is evident in my state of Montana, these rollbacks reduce public accountability. Transparency is required for a science-backed and democratic science-based process, on which the ESA is founded.

In closing, I fervently encourage you to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s strong, science-based protections, post haste. It is my strong hope you will strengthen and not weaken the federal safeguards so states and the industry cannot sidestep responsibility to protect endangered wildlife. Please uphold the intent of the ESA, which is to prevent extinction and ensure future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems.

title: Comment from Thompson, Sandra

text:
The Endangered Species Act (ESA) was created 51 years ago and since then has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a passionate admirer and fierce supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the ESA, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The ESA reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them (ecosystems that are there very core of our country and fuel billions of tourism dollars every year if you want a financial reason), an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully and strongly urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.

More than 99% of species under the ESA's care have been saved or are on the path to recovery. The ESA has protected millions of acres of natural habitat, including forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans. To achieve this success, ESA listings must be guided by science and be free of economic considerations, and projects must be held accountable for taxpayer-funded actions that would harm listed species.

I am also concerned that the administration's proposal is opposed by the majority of Americans. A recent peer-reviewed paper, "Support for the US Endangered Species Act Is High and Steady Over the Past Three Decades," authored by Professor Vucetich, shows that 84% of Americans support the Endangered Species Act. This support for the ESA is consistent among people living in urban, suburban, and rural environments.

We should strengthen the ESA to protect manatees, monarch butterflies, red knots, wolverines, and other species that need to be recovered. This proposal puts our wildlife at even greater risk of extinction.

title: Comment from Snellgrove, Dade

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Neste, Lisa

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. The Section 7 consultation process is the cornerstone of the ESA, and the process impacts every listed species under the ESA.

ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation. Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law, and importantly, it strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.

Federal agencies such as NOAA Fisheries, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Bureau of Reclamation frequently consult under ESA Section 7 when operating dams, managing river flows, or authorizing water diversions. These consultations have led to actions like fish passage improvements, spill operations, and habitat restoration. It is important for innumerable marine and aquatic species, such as salmon and Southern Resident orca in the Pacific Northwest, to require consultations.

Federal water-management agencies, including the Bureau of Reclamation and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, consult to ensure water projects and river operations do not reduce habitat or food availability for the migrating whooping cranes and other listed species that rely on rivers and wetlands. Without this requirement to consult, agency actions could disrupt their habitat and food resources and we could lose these species forever.

title: Comment from Wilson, Gloria

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.

More than 99% of species under the ESA's care have been saved or are on the path to recovery. The ESA has protected millions of acres of natural habitat, including forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans. To achieve this success, ESA listings must be guided by science and be free of economic considerations, and projects must be held accountable for taxpayer-funded actions that would harm listed species.

I am also concerned that the administration's proposal is opposed by the majority of Americans. A recent peer-reviewed paper, "Support for the US Endangered Species Act Is High and Steady Over the Past Three Decades," authored by Professor Vucetich, shows that 84% of Americans support the Endangered Species Act. This support for the ESA is consistent among people living in urban, suburban, and rural environments.

We should strengthen the ESA to protect manatees, monarch butterflies, red knots, wolverines, and other species that need to be recovered. This proposal puts our wildlife at even greater risk of extinction.

This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Kerzner, Allison

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. The Section 7 consultation process is the cornerstone of the ESA, and the process impacts every listed species under the ESA.

ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation. Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law, and importantly, it strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.

Federal agencies such as NOAA Fisheries, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Bureau of Reclamation frequently consult under ESA Section 7 when operating dams, managing river flows, or authorizing water diversions. These consultations have led to actions like fish passage improvements, spill operations, and habitat restoration. It is important for innumerable marine and aquatic species, such as salmon and Southern Resident orca in the Pacific Northwest, to require consultations.

Federal water-management agencies, including the Bureau of Reclamation and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, consult to ensure water projects and river operations do not reduce habitat or food availability for the migrating whooping cranes and other listed species that rely on rivers and wetlands. Without this requirement to consult, agency actions could disrupt their habitat and food resources and we could lose these species forever.
title: Comment from Smith, Carol

text:

title: Comment from Smith, Carol

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

title: Comment from Jenkins, Noah

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.
title: Comment from Nyssen, Amber

text:
I am submitting this comment in firm opposition to the proposed revisions to Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Section 7 is one of the most critical components of the ESA, requiring federal agencies to ensure that any actions they authorize, fund, or carry out do not jeopardize the continued existence of listed species or destroy or adversely modify their critical habitat. This consultation process is the backbone of effective, science-driven conservation.

The proposed revisions threaten to weaken this process by reducing the scope, clarity, and rigor of agency consultation. By limiting when consultations are triggered, narrowing definitions, or reducing the consideration of indirect or cumulative effects, these changes would make it far more likely that harmful activities proceed without adequate scientific review. Such weakening could lead to more habitat loss, greater fragmentation of ecosystems, and increased risk to already imperiled species.

Section 7 has been instrumental in preventing extinction and in promoting recovery by ensuring that federal actions account for long-term ecological impacts. Diluting these safeguards would shift the burden away from science-based evaluations and toward decisions that may prioritize short-term convenience or economic interests over the protection of irreplaceable species and ecosystems.

For these reasons, I strongly oppose the proposed revisions to ESA Section 7. Maintaining a robust, transparent, and science-centered consultation process is essential to the success of the ESA and to our national commitment to conserving biodiversity. Any attempt to weaken this process threatens not only individual species but the ecological integrity that supports healthy environments and human well-being.

I urge the agency to uphold the full strength of Section 7 and protect the consultation framework that has proven vital to preventing extinctions and promoting recovery for nearly fifty years.

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.

I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.
