title: Comment from Emanuel, Karen

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

title: Comment from Vancouver Audubon Society

text:
I am an Environmental Scientist and I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

Do the right thing! Do better! The world laughs as we weaken our regulations, destroy our biodiversity, and pave our wildlands.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Thank you.
title: Comment from Breda, Bo

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.

text:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to voice my firm opposition to the four proposed amendments to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently under review. Each of these changes—both individually and collectively—would severely undermine the ESA’s crucial role in preventing extinction, promoting species recovery, and preserving the ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. Repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule removing default protections for threatened species

The ESA aims to take action before species reach critical threat levels. The 4(d) rule, long-established, is based on scientific evidence showing that early, precautionary measures lower recovery costs and prevent further population declines. Eliminating default protections would cause unnecessary delays, necessitate case-by-case rulemaking for protections that are now automatic, and expose vulnerable species to preventable harm. This approach contradicts the ESA’s preventive nature and would lead to higher ecological and financial costs in the future.

2. Allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis in species listing

The ESA mandates that listing decisions be based solely on the best available scientific data, not economic impacts. Including economic factors would contradict statutory language, compromise scientific integrity, and risk delaying protections until species face imminent extinction. Moreover, limiting projections or climate-driven threat assessments ignores conservation science, which shows that long-term pressures like habitat loss, warming temperatures, ocean acidification, and shifting ranges already endanger species before population declines are measurable. Weakening future-threat criteria makes timely listings less probable, increasing the risk of preventable extinctions.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and narrowing the definition of “harm”

Habitat loss is the leading cause of biodiversity decline globally and nationally. Reducing critical habitat designations, especially unoccupied or climate-refuge areas crucial for recovery, undermines recovery plans. Similarly, narrowing “harm” definitions to exclude habitat degradation reverses decades of legal and scientific precedent. Habitat destruction indirectly kills wildlife, and this has long been recognized by law. Weakening these definitions would make inter-agency consultations less effective, increase biological risks, and conflict with the ESA’s recovery objectives.

4. Creating new loopholes for bypassing ESA protections

Expanding mechanisms by which agencies can bypass ESA protections, even when extinction is likely, conflicts with the ESA’s primary goals. These loopholes would encourage project-specific exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decision-making away from scientific analysis. This would disproportionately affect species such as Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves, potentially accelerating declines of already vulnerable species.

Cumulative impact of these proposals

While each proposal is concerning on its own, together, these rules would:
- weaken the scientific basis of the ESA,
- delay or block protections for species in need,
- reduce habitat conservation amid accelerating climate change,
- increase extinction risk for both domestic and international species,
- undermine inter-agency cooperation, and
- raise long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct. It stands as one of the most successful conservation laws because it is rooted in science, caution, and proactive measures. These proposed changes directly contradict those principles. During a time of unprecedented global biodiversity loss, the United States should bolster its most effective wildlife protection law, not weaken it.

Request

For the reasons outlined above, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed rule changes and retain the existing regulatory framework, which is grounded in science, legal precedent, and decades of successful application.

Thank you for considering my comments.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

title: Comment from Anderson-Gips, Rose

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I request that you reject the proposed rules, which would:

**Deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse, and Monarch butterfly could be left unprotected for years even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings.

**Narrow the definition of “critical habitat” to exclude currently unoccupied but historic habitat. Historic habitat is vital for recovery of imperiled species, especially as the areas where they currently live shrink due to the rapidly changing climate and the chain effects of ongoing biodiversity loss.

**Loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

**Violate the letter of the law by allowing “economic considerations” in decisions about whether to protect species that are scientifically shown to be at risk of extinction. With this rule, the federal government could decide against protecting an endangered species after considering lost revenue from prohibiting a golf course or hotel development to be built where the species lives.

Thank you.

text:
PUBLIC COMMENTS FOR THE FEDERAL REGISTER

Re: Proposed Rollback of the Endangered Species Act
To Whom It May Concern: REMOVE THE REGIME INSTEAD
I submit these comments in strongest possible opposition to the proposed rollback of protections under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). As an independent 2028 presidential candidate, I consider it my duty to document for the public record that this attempt to gut the ESA is illegitimate, reckless, and contrary to the interests of the American people, the environment, and future generations.
This nation is facing a profound governance crisis. The current federal leadership has lost public trust through sustained disregard for constitutional norms, democratic processes, and environmental stewardship. The ESA is one of the most successful conservation laws in the world, responsible for preventing the extinction of bald eagles, condors, wolves, and thousands of irreplaceable species. Any administration acting without moral authority and without a functioning democratic mandate has no legitimacy in dismantling such foundational protections.
The attempt to weaken the ESA must be viewed in the broader context:
• a rapidly destabilizing climate,
• collapsing biodiversity,
• unprecedented corporate capture of environmental policy, and
• increasing hostility toward renewable energy, sustainability, and scientific consensus.
These proposed changes would accelerate species loss, degrade habitat, jeopardize tribal and rural communities, and further damage the United States’ standing in international environmental law and global cooperation. Nations such as Bolivia, under Evo Morales, have affirmed the rights of nature, recognizing that the environment is not a commodity but a living system worthy of respect and legal protection. The United States should be advancing, not regressing from, this global movement.
Any rulemaking carried out under conditions of democratic instability, constitutional crisis, or compromised public institutions must be considered suspect and subject to future challenge. This proposed policy represents a breach of the public trust doctrine, violates long-standing environmental obligations, and is contrary to both national and international expectations for responsible ecological stewardship.
For the record, I urge the reviewing agency and all future courts to treat this proposal as unlawful, illegitimate, and contrary to the public interest, and to restore, uphold, and strengthen the Endangered Species Act as Congress originally intended.
Respectfully submitted,
Trista Tramposch DI GENOVA
Independent Candidate for President, 2028
Tucson, Arizona

I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.
More than 99% of species under the ESA's care have been saved or are on the path to recovery. The ESA has protected millions of acres of natural habitat, including forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans. To achieve this success, ESA listings must be guided by science and be free of economic considerations, and projects must be held accountable for taxpayer-funded actions that would harm listed species.

A recent peer-reviewed paper, "Support for the US Endangered Species Act Is High and Steady Over the Past Three Decades," authored by Professor Vucetich, shows that 84% of Americans support the Endangered Species Act. This support for the ESA is consistent among people living in urban, suburban, and rural environments.

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you for your time.
title: Comment from Nicolai, Nicola

I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.
title: Comment from Cherry, Amy

text:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA). For more than five decades, the ESA has been one of our nation’s most effective conservation tools—protecting 99% of the species listed under its care from extinction. This remarkable success rate is not just a statistic; it represents the survival of irreplaceable species and the preservation of ecosystems that ultimately sustain human life.

Many whale species—key engineers of ocean health—owe their survival to the protections afforded by the ESA. Whales play a crucial role in maintaining marine ecosystems, supporting healthy fish populations, and even helping regulate our climate. Weakening the ESA would put these species, and the ecological services they provide, at greater risk.

I urge you to maintain strong compliance measures for federal agencies. The proposed rule makes it easier to greenlight destructive activities, such as logging or drilling. These actions will put protected species in harm’s way.

ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation.
When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation.

Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law and, importantly, strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.

Protecting endangered species is not only a moral responsibility; it is a practical investment in our own future. Biodiverse ecosystems support cleaner air, cleaner water, stronger food systems, and greater climate resilience. The long-term benefits to human health, economic stability, and environmental security far outweigh any short-term administrative or industrial convenience.

I urge you to reject the proposed changes and preserve the ESA’s full strength. Our shared future—and the future of countless species—depends on it.

Sincerely,
Christine Goldfuss

title: Comment from Donovan, Mark

text: I am submitting this comment because healthy ecosystems and the protection of imperiled species matter deeply to me, and the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has long stood as our nation’s strongest science-based framework for preventing extinction and promoting recovery. The proposed revisions to the Section 7 interagency cooperation regulations in Docket FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044 would weaken crucial safeguards by narrowing the scope and application of federal consultations that ensure agency actions do not jeopardize endangered or threatened species or adversely modify their habitats. Under the ESA, all federal agencies are required to consult with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service before taking any action that may affect listed species or critical habitat. This process exists precisely because federal actions without proper scientific review have historically contributed to species decline. The proposed revisions seek to revert to an earlier regulatory framework that reduces the breadth of what must be considered during consultation, including how “effects of the action,” “environmental baseline,” and indirect impacts are defined and assessed. The Administration’s stated intent, as described in the Federal Register, is to align the regulations with statutory language while making procedures more “straightforward,” but in practice these changes weaken the very protections that help identify and mitigate harms before they occur. Strong, science-based consultation is vital for identifying risks to species from federal projects as varied as infrastructure build-outs, land management decisions, water diversions, and energy development. Without comprehensive, forward-looking review, agencies may approve actions that cumulatively degrade habitat, disrupt critical ecological processes, or push already vulnerable species closer to extinction. Weakening consultation requirements reduces transparency and limits meaningful public scrutiny of decisions that affect biodiversity and ecosystem health. Interagency cooperation under Section 7 is often the only mechanism for ensuring that federal actions account for cumulative and indirect impacts on wildlife, especially in contexts where state environmental review processes are under-resourced or inconsistent. Rolling back these safeguards in the name of regulatory “clarity” risks substituting efficiency for effectiveness, prioritizing ease of federal permitting over the ESA’s statutory purpose of conserving species and the ecosystems upon which they depend. The ESA was designed to function as science-driven law, not a tool to be reshaped based on short-term administrative priorities. As the scale of biological threats grows — from climate change to habitat loss to invasive species — the need for robust, thorough consultation protocols increases, not decreases. Consultation requirements help ensure that federal actions are informed by the best available science and that mitigation measures are identified and implemented when impacts are unavoidable. Weakening these requirements undermines both species protection and public trust in federal decision-making. Federal oversight serves as a vital check when multiple agencies’ actions intersect with wildlife conservation, supporting democratic accountability and allowing stakeholders and the public to participate meaningfully in environmental stewardship. Narrowing definitions of what must be considered during consultation reduces opportunities to address cumulative impacts and ignores how ecological interactions operate in real worlds, not neatly compartmentalized regulatory categories. For these reasons, I urge the agencies to retain robust Section 7 consultation standards that fully consider indirect, cumulative, and long-term effects on listed species and their habitats. Please ensure that interagency cooperation regulations remain grounded in the best available science and preserve the transparency and accountability essential to the ESA’s conservation mission. The ESA’s strength has always derived from its rigorous, predictable, and science-based application. Weakening consultation in pursuit of administrative convenience would place at greater risk the very species the law was enacted to protect. I urge you to reject revisions that reduce the scope or effectiveness of federal consultation and instead strengthen Section 7 processes to reflect ecological complexity, scientific evidence, and the public interest.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. The Section 7 consultation process is the cornerstone of the ESA, and the process impacts every listed species under the ESA.

ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation. Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law, and importantly, it strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.

Federal agencies such as NOAA Fisheries, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Bureau of Reclamation frequently consult under ESA Section 7 when operating dams, managing river flows, or authorizing water diversions. These consultations have led to actions like fish passage improvements, spill operations, and habitat restoration. It is important for innumerable marine and aquatic species, such as salmon and Southern Resident orca in the Pacific Northwest, to require consultations.

Federal water-management agencies, including the Bureau of Reclamation and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, consult to ensure water projects and river operations do not reduce habitat or food availability for the migrating whooping cranes and other listed species that rely on rivers and wetlands. Without this requirement to consult, agency actions could disrupt their habitat and food resources and we could lose these species forever.

I urge you to preserve the ESA’s current protections and continue to rely on science-driven decision-making.

As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

title: Comment from Walthinsen, Laura

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,

Pamela Phillips

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

title: Comment from Stuckart, Hannah

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.
The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.
The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.
title: Comment from Miles, Carole

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service,

I am deeply concerned and strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Section 7 interagency consultation regulations published on November 21, 2025. These revisions would dramatically weaken one of the most effective tools in the Endangered Species Act by excluding indirect, cumulative, and climate-related effects from review and eliminating the requirement for compensatory mitigation.
Section 7 is crucial to ensuring that other agencies’ projects (oil drilling, mining, dams, timber sales) don’t further endanger wildlife. For fifty years it has forced federal agencies to look before they leap, requiring meaningful consultation whenever their actions might harm listed species or critical habitat. Narrowing the definition of “effects of the action” and raising the bar for proving harm will allow destructive projects to move forward with little or no scrutiny — exactly what industry lobbyists have wanted for decades.
The Section 7 consultation process has been instrumental to the Act’s remarkable success in preventing the extinction of imperiled animals and plants; 99% of species listed under the Act survive today. That extraordinary record did not happen by accident — it happened because the current rules require agencies to consider the full scope of impacts and to offset unavoidable harm. Rolling back those safeguards, as was attempted in 2019 and rightly reversed in 2024, puts hundreds of already-struggling species at immediate risk.
I am tired of seeing sound science and long-term public interest sacrificed to short-term private profit. Please withdraw this proposal and retain the strong, science-based Section 7 regulations that have made the Endangered Species Act the gold standard for wildlife protection worldwide.
Thank you for considering my comments.
title: Comment from Douglass, Vanessa

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service,

I’m beyond frustrated that we are doing this all over again.
Every few years, the same thing happens: a new administration comes in, decides its real job is to hand out favors to campaign donors and industry buddies, and the Endangered Species Act gets dragged out as the punching bag. This proposal to resurrect the restrictive 2019 Trump rules and throw out the science-driven 2024 improvements is just the latest chapter in that tired, shameful story.
The 2024 rules finally let biologists use real climate science to define the “foreseeable future” and protect species before they’re down to the last handful. This proposal deliberately guts that so we have to wait until extinction is basically guaranteed before we’re allowed to act. That is a choice, not an accident.
It also makes it nearly impossible to protect unoccupied habitat that recovering species desperately need. Gray wolves, for example, are hanging on in roughly 10–12% of their historic range. True recovery means giving them room to come back, not locking the door forever because a mining company or developer wants the land today.
I’m sick of watching money and political payback trump biology. The American people own this wildlife and these public lands, not the lobbyists who write the checks. We deserve an Endangered Species Act that puts stewardship first, not one that’s constantly watered down to pad the bottom line of a few connected industries.
Please reject this proposal in its entirety and keep the stronger, forward-looking 2024 regulations in place.
title: Comment from Douglass, Vanessa

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

title: Comment from Botticelli, Jessica

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,

Melinda Adkins

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. The Section 7 consultation process is the cornerstone of the ESA, and the process impacts every listed species under the ESA. We need the ESA -- we need to protect wildlife for the health of the planet and future generations.

ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation. Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law, and importantly, it strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.

Federal agencies such as NOAA Fisheries, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Bureau of Reclamation frequently consult under ESA Section 7 when operating dams, managing river flows, or authorizing water diversions. These consultations have led to actions like fish passage improvements, spill operations, and habitat restoration. It is important for innumerable marine and aquatic species, such as salmon and Southern Resident orca in the Pacific Northwest, to require consultations.

Federal water-management agencies, including the Bureau of Reclamation and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, consult to ensure water projects and river operations do not reduce habitat or food availability for the migrating whooping cranes and other listed species that rely on rivers and wetlands. Without this requirement to consult, agency actions could disrupt their habitat and food resources and we could lose these species forever.

text:
To Whom It May Concern:
I am writing to urge the strongest possible protections for wildlife and the habitats essential to their survival. Recent regulatory changes issued under the Trump administration-four federal rules that weakened core components of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) -significantly undermined the nation's ability to safeguard imperiled species. These changes reduced the role of science in listing decisions, limited the consideration of climate change impacts, altered the treatment of threatened species, and introduced economic factors into processes that have historically been science-driven.
The ESA has been one of the most successful conservation laws in existence, preventing the extinction of countless species and contributing to the recovery of many others. Weakening its provisions at a time when biodiversity is declining globally runs counter to both scientific evidence and the public interest. Restoring and strengthening these protections is essential.
I therefore urge the agency to:
1. Reverse rules that weakened the ESA and reinstate science-based decision-making
free from non-biological considerations.
2. Ensure full protection for threatened species, maintaining the precautionary measures that have been critical to preventing further decline.
3. Account for climate change and cumulative environmental stressors in all habitat and species assessments.
4. Prioritize habitat conservation and connectivity, including migration routes and breeding areas vital to long-term species survival.
5. Promote transparent, inclusive, and science-forward rulemaking, with meaningful opportunities for public and tribal
input.
Protecting biodiversity is not only an ecological imperative but a practical one. Healthy ecosystems provide clean air and water, support resilient landscapes, and sustain cultural, recreational, and economic benefits for communities across the country. Strong ESA protections remain one of the most effective tools we have to preserve these shared national
resources.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment. I encourage the agency to adopt forward-looking, science-based policies that restore the full strength and intention of the Endangered Species Act.

title: Comment from Barbieri, Kristine

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

text:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. Each of these changes would significantly weaken the ESA’s ability to prevent extinction, support species recovery, and protect ecosystems vital to wildlife and human communities.

Specifically, I oppose:

4. **Creating Loopholes to Bypass ESA Protections**

Allowing agencies to override protections conflicts with the ESA’s core purpose. These loopholes incentivize exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decisions away from science, disproportionately affecting species like Florida panthers and gray wolves.

Collectively, these four proposals would:

- Weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation
- Delay protections for vulnerable species
- Reduce habitat conservation amid climate change
- Increase extinction risk
- Undermine inter-agency cooperation
- Raise recovery costs

The ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from extinction, making it one of the most successful conservation laws. These proposals conflict with its foundational principles.

In a time of global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should strengthen its most effective wildlife protection law.

For these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw the proposed changes and retain the existing framework rooted in science and legal precedent.

text:
To whomever it may concern,



I am writing to express my strong support for the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and to urge you to maintain its protections for endangered and threatened species.



The ESA is important to me because I care deeply about the species Mystic Aquarium works with, including marine mammals, sea turtles, and other coastal and marine wildlife. These animals play vital roles in their ecosystems, inspire people through education and outreach, and are central to our research, rescue, and conservation programs. Protecting them helps preserve the biodiversity and health of our oceans and coasts, and ensures that future generations can experience and learn from these remarkable species.



As a lifelong resident of the shoreline community in Connecticut, I have a fundamental understanding that we are cohabitating in our environment with the animals all around us. If species are removed from protections under the ESA, research and conservation efforts would dwindle and cause a lapse of knowledge about the species; which could ultimately lead them back to being placed under protection once more. Habitat conservation is equally as important as animals under the ESA; weakening protections would only allow for the continuation of habitat loss thanks to climate change and other factors. As someone who knows just how important our daily lives, miles from the beach or thousands away, are affected by the crucial protections under the ESA.



I am concerned that the proposed changes—such as removing recovery as a basis for delisting, allowing agencies to limit critical habitat protections, reducing mitigation requirements, and eliminating default protections for threatened species—could weaken safeguards for vulnerable wildlife. These changes could slow recovery efforts, increase stress on wild populations, and place additional pressure on the programs Mystic Aquarium supports.



Maintaining strong, science-based protections under the ESA is essential for giving these species a chance to recover and thrive, for supporting healthy ecosystems, and for ensuring that our shared natural heritage is preserved. I urge you to preserve the ESA’s current protections and continue to rely on science-driven decision-making.



Thank you for your attention to this important issue and for considering my comments.



Sincerely,

Adrien Winterholer





Affiliation: Mystic Aquarium

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.
title: Comment from Milonas, Nikolaos

text:
I am writing to formally oppose the proposed rule (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044) regarding "Interagency Cooperation" under Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act (ESA). This proposal threatens to dismantle the core mechanism of the ESA—the consultation process—by narrowing what impacts federal agencies must consider and limiting their accountability for environmental harm.
I strongly urge you to withdraw this proposal for the following reasons:
1. "Effects of the Action" Definition Ignores Climate Reality
The proposed revisions to the definition of "effects of the action" would artificially limit what federal agencies are required to consider during consultation. By restoring 2019-era limitations, the rule effectively allows agencies to ignore "remote" or "speculative" consequences. In the context of the climate crisis, this is a disastrous loophole. It allows agencies to approve massive fossil fuel or infrastructure projects while disregarding their downstream contribution to climate change—the very threat driving many species toward extinction.
2. Manipulating the "Environmental Baseline" Masks Harm
The proposal alters how the "environmental baseline" is calculated, potentially allowing agencies to ignore the degraded state of a species' habitat. By treating ongoing harmful activities as part of the status quo rather than as active threats that need to be addressed, the Services are essentially "grandfathering in" destruction. This makes it mathematically impossible to determine when a tipping point has been reached, ensuring that "death by a thousand cuts" continues unchecked.
3. Removing "Offset" Provisions Discourages Restoration
By removing the 2024 provisions regarding "offsets" (mitigation measures), the rule reduces the incentive for agencies to proactively restore habitat to balance out the harm their projects cause. Effective consultation should not just limit damage; it should ensure that development contributes to, or at least does not undermine, recovery goals. Removing these tools turns the consultation process into a rubber stamp for destruction rather than a tool for conservation.
4. Limiting Programmatic Consultation Increases Bureaucracy and Risk
The proposed changes to programmatic consultation frameworks appear designed to reduce oversight rather than improve efficiency. By weakening the requirements for re-initiation of consultation when new information becomes available, the rule ensures that agencies will continue to rely on outdated science even when we know a species is in steeper decline than previously thought.
The Section 7 consultation process is the "look before you leap" provision of the ESA. Weakening it blinds federal agencies to the true cost of their actions and guarantees that the U.S. government will be complicit in the extinction of the very species it is legally mandated to protect.
I urge you to reject these dangerous rollbacks and maintain a strong, science-based consultation process.

text:
I am against the proposed changes to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is crucial to ensure that federal actions don't endanger listed species or damage critical habitats. These changes would greatly weaken the process.

By narrowing essential definitions, such as the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur,” the rule risks allowing agencies to ignore cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts, which are well documented in ecological studies. For many species, particularly those facing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are major causes of decline. Ignoring them contradicts both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. While not a substitute for avoidance, offsetting is essential to ensure that unavoidable impacts don’t cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate aimed at promoting recovery, not merely survival. These revisions move consultation away from that legal requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead enhance protections for federally listed species.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
