title: Comment from Hollub, Judyth

text:
I urge you to maintain strong compliance measures for federal agencies. The proposed rule makes it easier to greenlight destructive activities, such as logging or drilling. These actions will put protected species in harm’s way.
ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation.
Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law and, importantly, strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.
Please don't make it easier for industry to destroy what's left of our natural world. It's important for more than just a few animals. Recreational opportunities, tourism, and general health and safety, rely on a healthy environment, and maintaining that requires cooperation.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
Without federaly mandated cooperation, endangered species like the canadian lynx will be wiped out due to expansion of roads and housing developments.

This is not a problem only one rule such as the ESA’s Threatened Species Blanket Rule (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029) can fix. But leaving the blanket rule in place will help us create a better and brighter world for future generations.

Please don't allow endangered species to become extinct. I am begging that you reconsider and allow rules and acts such as the blanket rule to remain intact and in place.
title: Comment from Strickland, Caitlen

text:
I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.
title: Comment from Sharp, Cori

text: Please protect wildlife, they deserve to stay in their homes and be conserved

Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Carr, Laurie

text:
I oppose changes to the current legislation.

We need inter-agency cooperation in the protection of endangered and threatened species, wildlife, and their habitats.

title: Comment from Bernardi, Robert

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

title: Comment from Kuhns, Sandy

text:
I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

title: Comment from Johnson, Amanda

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

title: Comment from Dunson, Adam

text:
We are a wildlife scientist and a wildlife attorney based in Charlottesville, Virginia. We write to oppose implementation of 90 FR 52600-01, titled Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation Regulations. We ask that USFWS and NMFS decline finalization of 90 FR 52600-01. In any further proceedings for this rulemaking, we ask that USFWS and NMFS address the following concerns.
Factors like habitat loss, disease, pesticides, and climate change drove the rusty-patched bumble bee (Bombus affinis) to be listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act (ESA) in 2017. If finalized, 90 FR 52600-01 would severely limit the efficacy of the ESA as applied to listed species like B. affinis. The proposed rule narrows and raises evidentiary thresholds when determining whether federal actions will impact listed species by excluding scientifically relevant information from impacts assessments. This is especially true for B. affinis and other species whose natural history and behavior are not fully understood. For, example, the rule:
1.Introduces a “but-for” standard of causation for determining which effects of a federal action are considered to impact listed species. This addition would allow the Service to permit federal actions that would negatively impact listed species if the species was already declining from other causes. Many listed species, such as B. affinis, and their critical habitats are threatened by multiple, interrelated causes (e.g., habitat loss, climate change, pesticides), but this rule abdicates the Service’s responsibility to “insure that any action…is not likely to jeopardize the continued existence of listed species or result in the destruction or adverse modification of critical habitat.” 15 U.S.C. § 1536(a)(2).
2.Adds more qualifications to the definition of an “environmental baseline” for the purposes of determining the effects of a proposed federal action (e.g., “evaluated at the time of the proposed action,” “current condition…as would be reasonably expected to occur”). These modifications invite the dismissal of ecologically relevant data from consideration if a) it was collected prior to the action proposal or b) it fails to meet the ‘reasonably expected’ standard, even if it represents best available science. As a result, the Service’s assessment of the environmental baseline will be more limited in scope, and fewer federal actions will be considered to “jeopardize the continued existence of listed species or result in the destruction or adverse modification of critical habitat.” Id.
3.Prohibits USFWS and NMFS from suggesting “offsetting” as a reasonable and prudent measure. As a result, USFWS would propose fewer measures to lessen the impacts of proposed agency actions. For example, USFWS would not be able to propose cleaning up a nearby Superfund site affecting bumblebee habitat. Instead, offsetting would only be allowed as “mitigation and enhancement measures” pursuant to exemptions from ESA protections. Id. § 1536(h)(1)(B), for cases when the Service found the agency action would necessarily violate the ESA regardless of any reasonable and prudent measures. As noted above, rule changes would make this finding of adverse effect increasingly rare. Thus, deletion of the “offset” clause unjustifiably limits the USFWS in its duty to propose all measures “necessary or appropriate to minimize such impact.” Id. § 1536(b)(4)(ii).
4.Defines when an effect is “reasonably certain to occur” for purposes of evaluating the (cumulative) effects of a proposed action, stating that an effect is not reasonably certain to occur “[i]f the consequence would occur regardless of whether the proposed action goes forward.” If finalized, this rule permits USFWS to allow actions that harm listed species, if the species already face other threats. For example, if B. affinis populations are harmed by impaired habitat quality due to pesticide use in adjacent private land, USFWS could find that the populations would perish regardless of any federal action and allow such action to continue despite any real damages they would cause.
5.The proposed rule makes no mention of how the Services will consider pending rules if they implement the proposed regulations.
We request USFWS and NMFS refrain from finalizing 90 FR 52600-01, Interagency Cooperation Regulations. Furthermore, we request USFWS and NMFS to address the above concerns. We request USFWS and NMFS clearly articulate the standard for methods of scientific analysis to be used during section 7 consultations and explain how scientifically relevant information will be weighed in determining the effects of federal actions. We also request the Service clarify how it will address actions pending at the time these proposed rules may be finalized and request the Service consider pending actions under the rules applicable at the time of publication.

title: Comment from Arneson, Cynthia

text:
It should absolutely not be easy for the government agencies to permanently destroy and pollute land necessary for threatened and endangered species to survive and thrive. The amount of protected land that has been set aside for wildlife which is inclusive of parks, sanctuaries, refuges and private land owned by concerned individuals has decreased monumentally over the last few decades. This land is irreplaceable as is the wildlife that depends on it.

I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. The Section 7 consultation process is the cornerstone of the ESA, and the process impacts every listed species under the ESA.

ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation. Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law, and importantly, it strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.

Federal agencies such as NOAA Fisheries, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Bureau of Reclamation frequently consult under ESA Section 7 when operating dams, managing river flows, or authorizing water diversions. These consultations have led to actions like fish passage improvements, spill operations, and habitat restoration. It is important for innumerable marine and aquatic species, such as salmon and Southern Resident orca in the Pacific Northwest, to require consultations.

Federal water-management agencies, including the Bureau of Reclamation and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, consult to ensure water projects and river operations do not reduce habitat or food availability for the migrating whooping cranes and other listed species that rely on rivers and wetlands. Without this requirement to consult, agency actions could disrupt their habitat and food resources and we could lose these species forever.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
Dear Director Nesvik and Acting Director Menashes,
I am writing in opposition to the four proposed rules regarding the Endangered Species Act found in the following dockets:

FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048
FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029
FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044
FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039

As someone concerned with the protection of birds across the United States, and someone who believes in the power and importance of the Endangered Species Act as a tool to boost recovery and prevent extinction, I request that these proposed rules be withdrawn and the current statutory language stay in place.

Species like the Hawaiian Coot, Nene, Marbled Murrelet, and Eastern Black Rail are facing high pressure from invasive species, habitat loss, and climate change. Threatened species such as the Florida Scrub-Jay have long escaped being designated as “endangered” because of crucial protections in the blanket 4(d) rule. Additionally, birds such as the Whooping Crane and Streaked Horned Lark could be harmed by federal projects from other agencies, making clear inter-agency communication important.

I believe that the proposed rules would weaken the Endangered Species Act for birds, making important tools such as critical habitat designations, inclusion of historical baselines in listing decisions, and blanket protections for threatened species inaccessible.

Please withdraw the proposed rules in dockets FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044, and FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039. Given the ongoing declines of birds confirmed by scientific studies, now is not the time to weaken ESA protections. As a scientist who directly works to inform effective conservation and management strategies for animals protected by the Endangered Species Act, I must emphasize how important it is that the ESA remains unaltered. Thank you for your consideration.
Sincerely,
Rebecca Eiseman

title: Comment from Herzstein, Sandra

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

title: Comment from Kvalevog, Alice

text:
I’m writing to oppose the Trump administration’s proposed changes to Endangered Species Act (Act) rules, which will reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I completely support the Endangered Species Act, which has been critical in preserving many rare and declining wildlife species in the U.S.

I strongly oppose efforts to reduce protections for “threatened” species under the Act. Removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed is a highly inefficient way to manage the Act and will place a large burden on overworked agency staff, further delaying important protections for species.

Listing decisions should be based only on biology and the extent of threats, not economics, to ensure that species most need care and attention receive protection under the Act. I am also opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

I am opposed to any weakening of the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

We need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever because of the expanding pressure on wildlife caused by human population growth and development. Wildlife recovery efforts in our nation need to be strengthened, not weakened. Thank you.

title: Comment from Bouilland, Stacy

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

title: Comment from Pilant, Kate

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

title: Comment from Koenker, Eugenia

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:

title: Comment from Dey, Kavi

text:
Regulatory rules should not be altered to follow Executive Orders. Executive Orders do not supersede U.S. Codes. These proposed rules would erode safeguards essential to preventing extinctions, recovering imperiled species, and conserving the habitats on which endangered plants and wildlife depend.

Section 7 consultation is a crucial ESA check and balance on federal agency actions, ensuring those actions do not jeopardize species’ survival and recovery or destroy or degrade critical habitat. The proposed changes would undermine the conservation of endangered and threatened species nationwide, weaken protections for their critical habitat, delay their recovery, and ultimately make recovery of endangered or threatened animals and plants far more costly and complex.

Raising the effects threshold dismisses valid science and permits harmful actions without full review. The rollback reverts to the 2019 rules, which faced heavy criticism for conflicting with the ESA’s conservation goals. Climate impacts, habitat loss, and landscape effects must be included in consultations to assess jeopardy properly. The proposed rule change should be withdrawn, and stronger 2024 protections should be restored or expanded.

Changing the definition of environmental baseline to ignore “…consequences to listed species or designated critical habitat from ongoing agency activities or existing agency facilities that are not within the agency's discretion…” conflicts with the goal of species recovery. Section 7 is intended to involve outside agencies’ expertise to share knowledge and align missions, ensuring that actions do not jeopardize species’ survival and recovery or harm critical habitat.

Consultation is the heart of the Endangered Species Act. It has been instrumental to the ESA’s remarkable success in preventing the extinction of imperiled animals and plants; 99% of species listed under the Endangered Species Act survive today. The Supreme Court supported the Act, explaining that the Act represents “the institutionalization of caution,” and Congress clearly intended the consultation process to give “the benefit of the doubt” to species based on the best available scientific information.

The Trump administration’s proposed rollbacks to the Section 7 regulations also ignore the basic fact that the single most significant driver of extinction here and around the world is habitat loss. If we do not protect the last few places that endangered wildlife and plants call home, then those highly imperiled species simply have no future.

Limiting Section 7 consultation to actions within the jurisdiction of the regulatory
agency – leaving out actual, concrete harms caused by a proposed action if those harms happened to fall outside that agency’s sphere, would put blinders on the expert wildlife
agencies during the consultation process – the harm to species and habitat would still occur, but it would no longer be assessed as required by the Act. All actions must be considered.

The rule changes proposed here would undermine the Section 7 consultation process by ignoring the impact of past federal agency actions. In the new definition, past actions would not be considered, overlooking possible cumulative effects on species. For example, grizzly bears in the Northern Rocky Mountain ecosystem might not receive full consideration of past and current impacts of logging on their habitat. Instead, only impacts from future logging projects or other forest-altering activities would be weighed against their status.

Additionally, the proposed rule would no longer allow the creation of habitat offsets as reasonable and prudent measures for species conservation or recovery. This change would significantly impact grizzly bear recovery in the Northern Rocky Mountain ecosystem. Offsets that designate additional suitable habitat to mitigate habitat loss elsewhere are essential for creating connected and recovering populations.

Collectively, these proposed changes would shift the ESA away from science-based, precautionary conservation and toward increasingly discretionary, economically driven decision-making.

The ESA’s successful recovery of endangered species depends on strong, consistent implementation grounded in biological need rather than political or economic pressure.

I urge the Services to withdraw these proposals. Thank you for considering these comments.
title: Comment from Bachman, Chris

text:

Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law and, importantly, strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.

title: Comment from Austin, James

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. The Section 7 consultation process is the cornerstone of the ESA, and the process impacts every listed species under the ESA.

ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation. Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law, and importantly, it strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.

Federal agencies such as NOAA Fisheries, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Bureau of Reclamation frequently consult under ESA Section 7 when operating dams, managing river flows, or authorizing water diversions. These consultations have led to actions like fish passage improvements, spill operations, and habitat restoration. It is important for innumerable marine and aquatic species, such as salmon and Southern Resident orca in the Pacific Northwest, to require consultations.

Federal water-management agencies, including the Bureau of Reclamation and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, consult to ensure water projects and river operations do not reduce habitat or food availability for the migrating whooping cranes and other listed species that rely on rivers and wetlands. Without this requirement to consult, agency actions could disrupt their habitat and food resources and we could lose these species forever.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Rudolph, John

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

title: Comment from Markuson, James

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

text:
Federal agencies must review their projects to ensure they don’t jeopardize any listed species. The proposed rules mostly exclude the consideration of long-term threats to the recovery of listed species. Instead, the focus would shift to direct, immediate effects.

Ideally, we’d identify at-risk species before their populations drop to critically low levels. That’s the best time to intervene, when conservation options are likely to be more ecologically, socially, and economically viable.
I urge you to withdraw this rule change.
A Concerned Citizen

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
The Endangered Species Act (ESA) has prevented nearly 99% of listed species from becoming extinct. This track record is built on the regulations established or amended 30 to 50 years ago and not on those established or amended in the last ten or twenty.
I do not consider the ESA as it stands an "undue burden" on the use of domestic energy resources, and I encourage the Administration to look elsewhere to solve energy deficiencies.
America's wildlife is part of our nation's history, and the proposed changes, such as the removal of the ESA's Blanket 4(d) Rule, are an un-American motion that will erase said history. I was taught in American schools to never forget history, and that requires protecting it.
I encourage the Administration to withdraw all proposed changes to the ESA in order to ensure our country’s wildlife, and our nation's identity, will continue to be protected for generations to come.
title: Comment from Pezick, Julia

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

title: Comment from Miller, Christopher

text:
Docket No. FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044
Submitted from the perspective of the Fair Start Movement (Zero-Baseline Framework)

This is where baseline shifting quietly converts the Endangered Species Act from a preventative statute into a damage-acceptance regime.

From the perspective of the Fair Start Movement’s zero-baseline framework, the proposed revisions to the definition of environmental baseline represent not a neutral clarification, but a structural failure. By redefining the baseline as the “current condition” of listed species or habitat as would reasonably be expected to occur, while expressly incorporating accumulated and ongoing degradation, the rule normalizes historic harm and evaluates new federal actions against an already-violated condition rather than against the Act’s conservation mandate.

Under a zero-baseline approach, the baseline is not a moving snapshot of damage but the point at which legal protection is supposed to begin. When past and present degradation are embedded into the baseline itself, prevention collapses into comparison. The ESA’s duty to insure against jeopardy is effectively replaced with permission to manage decline, so long as each new action does not significantly exceed the already-normalized level of harm.

This approach transforms cumulative loss into regulatory context and then treats that context as justification. Over time, harm becomes the reference point, compliance becomes relative, and statutory protection erodes without any single action appearing to cross a clear legal threshold. That is the mechanics of baseline shifting.

The Endangered Species Act was enacted to prevent extinction and halt decline—not to ratify prior losses or accept continued degradation as inevitable. A regulatory framework that measures impacts against a depleted baseline undermines the Act’s preventative purpose and conflicts with Congress’s intent that federal actions affirmatively safeguard listed species and critical habitat.

For these reasons, the Services should reject any definition of environmental baseline that embeds historic or ongoing harm as the lawful reference point for future action and should reaffirm a genuinely preventative standard consistent with the ESA’s conservation mandate.

text:
I'm outraged to learn that the Trump administration is trying to dismantle our most successful conservation law: the Endangered Species Act.

Since its passage in 1973, this landmark act has prevented the extinction of roughly 300 species — and more than 99% of the species under its care have been saved or are on their way to recovery. This incredible law has also protected millions of acres of forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans.

The proposed rollbacks will be devastating if finalized. They'll strip vital protections from our nation's most vulnerable species and pave the way for widespread habitat destruction — all in the name of profiteers, polluters, and special interests.

The Endangered Species Act works, and it has for decades. It’s the reason bald eagles, alligators, gray whales, and other iconic species are still around today. We should work to *strengthen* the Act — not weaken it.

I stand with most Americans in supporting the Endangered Species Act and the strong protections it provides to the United States’ most endangered animals and plants. I strongly oppose rollbacks to the Act and urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA Fisheries to stop this attempt to dismantle it by withdrawing the administration's destructive proposals immediately.

I urge you to maintain strong compliance measures for federal agencies. The proposed rule makes it easier to greenlight destructive activities, such as logging or drilling. These actions will put protected species in harm’s way.
ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation.
When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation.
Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law and, importantly, strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.

text:
Oceana submits these comments on both proposed joint rules by the Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service (collectively “the Services”).

Oceana opposes the proposed joint rules because they would undermine the language and purpose of the Endangered Species Act (ESA), rolling back decades of success in protecting and recovering imperiled species.

Oceana is an ocean conservation organization solely focused on protecting the world’s oceans, with over a million members and supporters in the United States. Oceana advocates for science-based policies that rebuild abundant and biodiverse oceans. In the United States, Oceana campaigns to stop overfishing, reduce bycatch, protect habitat, protect the North Atlantic right whales, stop illegal fishing, stop the expansion of offshore drilling, and stop plastic pollution at the source.

The ESA has been immensely successful at protecting and recovering at-risk species in the ocean. The law has led to population growth for many, like the Florida manatee whose status was changed from endangered to threatened in 2017. And that success can in large part be attributed to the discretion that the ESA explicitly affords the Services in their mission to conserve endangered and threatened species. By using the law to its full extent, the Services could do even more to help recover species, like better protecting the critically endangered North Atlantic right whale from the threats of vessel strikes and fishing gear entanglement.

The proposed rules move the Services in the wrong direction. Oceana recommends the Services withdraw the unnecessary proposed rules and instead return to the pre-2019 regulations that have a proven record of success. The Services should focus on fully implementing and effectively enforcing the requirements of the ESA.

title: Comment from Canright, Rebecca

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. The Section 7 consultation process is the cornerstone of the ESA, and the process impacts every listed species under the ESA.

ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation. Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law, and importantly, it strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.

Federal agencies such as NOAA Fisheries, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Bureau of Reclamation frequently consult under ESA Section 7 when operating dams, managing river flows, or authorizing water diversions. These consultations have led to actions like fish passage improvements, spill operations, and habitat restoration. It is important for innumerable marine and aquatic species, such as salmon and Southern Resident orca in the Pacific Northwest, to require consultations.

Federal water-management agencies, including the Bureau of Reclamation and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, consult to ensure water projects and river operations do not reduce habitat or food availability for the migrating whooping cranes and other listed species that rely on rivers and wetlands. Without this requirement to consult, agency actions could disrupt their habitat and food resources and we could lose these species forever.

title: Comment from Ashley, Kris

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Houser, Brian

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

title: Comment from Willis, Sean

text: I feel the proposed changes to the coordination between federal agencies regarding development and usage of critical habitats will be nothing but harmful to threatened and endangered wildlife. I feel that coordination between departments is critical to making sure that all relevant parties have the needed information to make ethical decisions. Oversight from the department of fishing and wildlife, as well as other environmental protection agencies also helps to make sure no corners are being cut at the cost of endangered or threatened wildlife. I live in New Jersey, near the Pine Barrens, and I know that if given the choice, land developers would replace habitats critical for unique and endangered wildlife with condos and Walmarts. New Jersey has so much history and culture linked to he Pine Barrens, and much of that is linked to the specific flora and fauna of the area. However, if a federal agency, or some other national entity came along and didn't coordinate with the local agencies and authorities, there's a very good chance they would make harmful decisions without being aware of what they would be destroying. We can't expect every person to know of the intricacies of every area they want to develop, so coordination with local entities is vital to making sure that pertinent information and regulations are communicated. I also feel that the narrowing of definitions that qualify a species or habitat as endangered or threatened is harmful, and will only allow for corners to be cut and loopholes to be created. It feels like the goal of these changes are to make a species even more at risk before protections will be extended to them, which will ultimately do nothing but hurt their chances of recovery.

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent and undermines the original intent of Congress to advance science-based conservation.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. Introducing ambiguity in the definition of “recovery” raises serious concerns about the premature removal of protections for threatened and endangered species. If applied loosely, at risk species could lose ESA protection before populations are truly stable and resilient. The proposed rule also shortens the time horizon for assessing threats, limiting USFWS’ ability to account for long-term or emerging risks like habitat loss or climate change. Together, these changes could lead to delisting decisions that ignore cumulative and dynamic threats, undermining decades of recovery efforts and accelerating species decline, contrary to the ESA’s purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Curtis, Jonie

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.
