text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Ruthe Heimel
title: Comment from Heimel, Ruthe

text:
Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text: I oppose the proposed changes to Endangered Species Act implementation. These rollbacks prioritize economic considerations over science-based conservation. The ESA has prevented extinction for 99% of listed species. Allowing economic factors in listing decisions overrides peer-reviewed scientific evidence. Weakening critical habitat designations removes essential safeguards. Excluding climate change considerations ignores the leading driver of species decline. title: Comment from Nesbit, Jackson

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. The Section 7 consultation process is the cornerstone of the ESA, and the process impacts every listed species under the ESA. This rule change makes corruption just as easy as writing a big check to the right person in the government. This is a mechanism for the lawless to get their way, without regard to long standing laws and rules.

ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation. Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law, and importantly, it strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.

Federal agencies such as NOAA Fisheries, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Bureau of Reclamation frequently consult under ESA Section 7 when operating dams, managing river flows, or authorizing water diversions. These consultations have led to actions like fish passage improvements, spill operations, and habitat restoration. It is important for innumerable marine and aquatic species, such as salmon and Southern Resident orca in the Pacific Northwest, to require consultations.

Federal water-management agencies, including the Bureau of Reclamation and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, consult to ensure water projects and river operations do not reduce habitat or food availability for the migrating whooping cranes and other listed species that rely on rivers and wetlands. Without this requirement to consult, agency actions could disrupt their habitat and food resources and we could lose these species forever.
title: Comment from Adams, Joseph

text:
Do not revise Section 7.
Section 7 consultation is the heart of the ESA; any weakening puts species survival at risk. Raising the threshold for “reasonably certain to occur” effects will erase legitimate scientific evidence and allow harmful actions to proceed without full review. Climate impacts, cumulative habitat loss, and landscape-scale consequences must be included in consultations as they are essential to understanding jeopardy. The rollback reinstates 2019 rules that courts and scientists criticized as inconsistent with the ESA’s conservation mandate. The rule should be withdrawn; the Service should restore the stronger 2024 protections instead of narrowing them.

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

title: Comment from Villalobos, Parker

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Cassandra

text:
Public Comment on ESA Section 7 Interagency Consultation Regulations
Docket: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044

I am writing as a Hawaiʻi resident to strongly oppose the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) Section 7 interagency consultation regulations. These changes would weaken one of the ESA’s important safeguards by limiting how federal agencies evaluate the impacts of their actions on listed species and critical habitat.

Hawaiʻi has the highest proportion of endangered species in the United States, and Haleakalā National Park protects more endangered species than any other U.S. national park. Many of these species persist in small, isolated populations and depend on careful, comprehensive consultation to prevent additional harm from federal actions. The Section 7 process is essential to ensuring that agency decisions do not incrementally degrade the habitats and ecological conditions these species require.

The proposed rule narrows what effects may be considered during consultation by restricting the environmental baseline, raising the threshold for what impacts are deemed reasonably certain to occur, and limiting the evaluation of cumulative and landscape-scale effects. For island ecosystems like those in Hawaiʻi, these limitations substantially increase the risk that significant harm will be overlooked or underestimated.

The ESA requires federal agencies to use the best available scientific and commercial data and to ensure their actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy or adversely modify critical habitat. Weakening the consultation framework undermines this mandate and reduces the effectiveness of interagency review.

I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to withdraw this proposed rule and retain the stronger 2024 Section 7 regulations. A robust consultation process is essential to the continued protection of Hawaiʻi’s imperiled species and the integrity of places like Haleakalā.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.

More than 99% of species under the ESA's care have been saved or are on the path to recovery. The ESA has protected millions of acres of natural habitat, including forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans. To achieve this success, ESA listings must be guided by science and be free of economic considerations, and projects must be held accountable for taxpayer-funded actions that would harm listed species.

I am also concerned that the administration's proposal is opposed by the majority of Americans. A recent peer-reviewed paper, "Support for the US Endangered Species Act Is High and Steady Over the Past Three Decades," authored by Professor Vucetich, shows that 84% of Americans support the Endangered Species Act. This support for the ESA is consistent among people living in urban, suburban, and rural environments.

We should strengthen the ESA to protect manatees, monarch butterflies, red knots, wolverines, and other species that need to be recovered. This proposal puts our wildlife at even greater risk of extinction.

text:
Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text:
I am against the proposed changes to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is crucial for ensuring federal actions do not threaten listed species or damage critical habitats. These changes would greatly weaken this process.

By narrowing essential definitions, such as the “environmental baseline” and the standard for “reasonably certain to occur” effects, the rule might allow agencies to ignore cumulative, indirect, and climate-related impacts that are well-supported by ecological research. For many species, especially those facing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are main factors in their decline. Ignoring them contradicts both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

Additionally, removing offsetting measures, which have historically been vital for minimizing harm when incidental take can't be avoided, further compromises conservation efforts. Offsetting requirements do not replace avoidance, but they are crucial to ensuring that unavoidable impacts don’t weaken populations over time.

The ESA mandates a “conservation” focus that promotes recovery, not just survival. These revisions shift consultation away from that legal requirement. I strongly encourage the Services to withdraw this proposal and enhance, rather than reduce, protections for federally listed species.

text: The Endangered Species Act (ESA) has for over five decades protected America’s wildlife, saving numerous species from extinction. Such a vast undertaking cannot be adequately managed without interagency cooperation. The proposed rule changes (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044) undermine this cooperation and put our wildlife at risk. text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. The Section 7 consultation process is the cornerstone of the ESA, and the process impacts every listed species under the ESA.

ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation. Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law, and importantly, it strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.

Federal agencies such as NOAA Fisheries, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Bureau of Reclamation frequently consult under ESA Section 7 when operating dams, managing river flows, or authorizing water diversions. These consultations have led to actions like fish passage improvements, spill operations, and habitat restoration. It is important for innumerable marine and aquatic species, such as salmon and Southern Resident orca in the Pacific Northwest, to require consultations.

Federal water-management agencies, including the Bureau of Reclamation and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, consult to ensure water projects and river operations do not reduce habitat or food availability for the migrating whooping cranes and other listed species that rely on rivers and wetlands. Without this requirement to consult, agency actions could disrupt their habitat and food resources and we could lose these species forever.

text:
Although the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service (collectively, "the Services") present these revisions as a clarification of "statutory requirements." I oppose these changes because they fundamentally weaken the Section 7 consultation process, which serves as the "heart" of the ESA’s protective measures.
I oppose this proposal based on the following critical concerns:
1. Dilution of the "Jeopardy" Standard
Section 7 requires federal agencies to ensure that their actions are not likely to "jeopardize the continued existence" of listed species. Any revision that narrows the definition of "jeopardy" or "adverse modification" of habitat would allow federal projects—such as dam construction, mining, or highway expansion—to proceed despite clear ecological risks. These revisions appear to create a higher threshold for intervention, making it harder for the Services to halt destructive federal actions.
2. Reduction of Federal Accountability
The strength of Section 7 lies in its mandate for federal agencies to consult with the Services. By "revising" these regulations, the Services risk creating loopholes that allow agencies to self-determine that their actions have "no effect" on listed species. Reducing the rigor of these consultations removes the necessary checks and balances that prevent federal taxpayer dollars from funding the extinction of domestic wildlife.
3. Ignoring Cumulative Impacts and Climate Change
Under the guise of "streamlining," these proposed revisions often ignore the cumulative effects of multiple federal actions. In 2025, any regulation that fails to explicitly account for the compounding pressure of climate change and habitat fragmentation is scientifically inadequate. The Services should be strengthening the consultation process to address long-term environmental shifts, rather than making it easier for agencies to bypass comprehensive ecological reviews.
4. Prioritizing Efficiency over Conservation
The Services state the intent is to "confirm the application of statutory requirements," but the practical effect is a shift toward administrative convenience. The ESA was not designed for efficiency; it was intended to protect species. These revisions prioritize the speed of project approvals over the biological integrity of the ecosystems the Services are legally sworn to protect.
I believe the proposed revisions to the Section 7 interagency cooperation regulations represent a retreat from the Services' conservation mandate. By lowering consultation standards and weakening harm definitions, the Services are abdicating their responsibility to ensure that federal actions do not drive species toward extinction. I urge the Services to maintain the strongest possible protections and reject these weakening amendments.

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Jamie Michelle Thomas

text:
Reducing required cooperation between and amongst agencies when complying with the ESA’s requirements to safeguard imperiled species and their habitats.
I oppose any and all efforts to weaken the Endangered Species Act and urge you to withdraw the proposed rule changes. The proposed rules:

Deprive species newly listed as “threatened” with extinction of protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take,” even when that take is amongst the greatest drivers of the species' decline. This makes no sense. We must address each of the threats that are causing imperilment.

Fail to protect important habitat that was historically occupied but is currently unoccupied by narrowing the definition of critical habitat. Protecting historical habitat is often vital to the recovery of imperiled species. The goal of the ESA is to get species out of the proverbial emergency room, which inherently necessitates increasing populations and restoring species to historic range. Failing to protect historically occupied habitat fundamentally undermines the effectiveness of the law. Holistic approaches to species recovery is essential in the face of climate change impacts to habitat.

Reduce cooperation between and amongst agencies tasked with implementing the ESA. This change would make it easier for agencies to green light destructive extractive proposals even when doing so will clearly further imperil listed species. Again, this proposed change undermines the letter and intent of the ESA.

Allow consideration of economics in decisions of whether to protect species the science clearly shows are at risk of extinction, in direct violation of the ESA. The ESA clearly states that preventing extinction is the priority, and the Supreme Court has agreed. This regulatory change flips that on its head and allows short term potential lost profits to trump species safeguards.

Each of these proposed changes undermines the letter and intent of the ESA, a law passed with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed by a Republican President who stated upon doing so: “[T]his legislation provides the Federal Government with needed authority to protect an irreplaceable part of our national heritage—threatened wildlife. Nothing is more priceless and more worthy of preservation than the rich array of animal life with which our country has been blessed. This important measure grants the Government both the authority to make early identification of endangered species and the means to act quickly and thoroughly to save them from extinction.” - President Nixon.

It is a betrayal of this legacy to undermine the efficacy of the law by making these ill advised regulatory changes. We all should be proud of the effectiveness of the ESA. Take for example, the bald eagle, our national bird and symbol of the USA - without the ESA's protections, we likely would have lost this iconic species. Now, Americans across the country are able to see bald eagles flying free.

As we confront the dual biodiversity-loss and climate crises, weakening the ESA is not only short sighted, it is dangerous. Protecting species and their habitats benefits humans as well - the law safeguards forest habitats that clean the air, watersheds and wetlands that filter drinking water for millions of Americans, pollinators that support our food supply, and estuaries that mitigate flooding. Humans are not isolated from the impacts of increasingly severe weather events and damaged ecosystems that are the symptoms of a rapidly changing climate.

Please rescind the four proposed rules (docket numbers: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048-0001, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029-0001, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044-0001, and FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039-0001) undermining the Endangered Species Act for the benefit of wildlife, fish, plants and humans alike.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.
By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.
The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.
The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

text:
My name is Dylan Harrell. I was born and raised in Eastern North Carolina. Growing up, I bore witness to the ecological wonder that was the Pocosin Lakes National Wildlife Refuge, and within this, the establishment of the Red Wolf Center. Set up as a site that would provide health check ups and rehabilitation for injured wolves, this and other sites like it have proved crucial in mitigating the catastrophic past that this species has endured, from habitat loss, to encroachment and over-hunting by humanity. Though the countless efforts of those that have manned this center have been nothing short of heroic, still the red wolf remains as the most endangered wolf species in the United States and still teeters dangerously close to extinction in the wild. The reason I provide this is to better convey why wildlife conservation is so important to me. This is how I grew up, knowing my home was once home to an amazing species of wolf, unlike any that any other legion could lay claim to. The red wolf was our pride, our symbol of hope and identity in a town that is well below the poverty line in which industry does not exist, and has not existed for decades. Though the red wolf is so symbolic to us, we are still to blame for its low population, for the over-hunting, for the massacring of countless individuals. Now we must face the consequences and support every call to action that aids in establishing legislation that protects other species of wildlife.

I call upon you now to support scientific based evidence when voting in any matter regarding wildlife. The proper research based opinions of wildlife experts are the only true information we should base any legislation regarding wildlife on. The individuals who have dedicated their entire professional careers to better understanding the daily experiences of our natural wildlife, and the impact these experiences have on the natural order of the land around them, are who should be consulted when creating legislation. This goes hand in hand with the Endangered Species Act (ESA). The ESA incorporates and pushes scientific research to the forefront of protections and legislation meant to shield wildlife from harm. The ESA is not based on personal or political gain, as no legislation regarding wildlife should ever be. It serves no ulterior motives, and therefore, must be upheld and protected within our democratic society. We are still a democracy, one in which the voices and beliefs of the people are carried and conveyed by those they elect to represent them. The people have spoken, and continue to voice their discontent with anti-wildlife and more recently anti-wolf and anti-predator legislation such as HR-845. The people want natural species protected on the federal level. Canceling acts such as the ESA will only cause turmoil and the fallout will be catastrophic for wildlife who have no political party affiliation, who have no voice in our human society, who cannot defend themselves in the Senate or in the woods against a hunter armed with an assault rifle.

I urge you to uphold the Endangered Species Act. Continue to fight misinformation with scientific based research. Protect species through proper educated analysis. Do not let wildlife fall victim to political greed. Vote against proposed anti-wolf and anti-predator legislation. Vote for the protection and conservation of natural habitats. Vote for the protection of newly-listed endangered species, so that recovery efforts may successfully take place. Vote for us, for the people, who only wish to see our wildlife prosper, free and wild, as they have always been and should continue to be. Thank you for your commitment to seeing these points upheld, and for your continued efforts to help protect wildlife in this country, The United States of America.
-Dylan Harrell

text:
Testimony on the Proposed Changes to Interagency Cooperation Regulations (Docket: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044)

Aloha,

I am submitting this testimony to express strong opposition to the proposed rollback of Section 7 consultation regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

Section 7 consultation is the backbone of the ESA, ensuring that federal projects—such as pipelines, dams, mining, and logging—do not jeopardize the survival of threatened and endangered species. Weakening these standards raises the threshold for “reasonably certain to occur” effects, which risks erasing legitimate scientific evidence and allows harmful actions to proceed without full review. Wildlife cannot survive what amounts to “death by a thousand projects,” and any rollback threatens species already under pressure from climate change, habitat loss, and cumulative impacts.

The proposed rule reinstates elements of the 2019 regulations, which were widely criticized by courts and scientists as inconsistent with the ESA’s conservation mandate. Climate-driven, cumulative, and landscape-scale consequences must be included in consultations to accurately assess jeopardy, and narrowing these requirements undermines the law’s purpose.

For these reasons, I urge the Fish & Wildlife Service to withdraw this proposed rule and restore the stronger 2024 consultation protections, which provide the comprehensive safeguards necessary to protect our nation’s wildlife.

Mahalo for your attention and consideration.
Jessica dos Santos

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service,

I am submitting comments regarding proposed changes to interagency cooperation regulations under section 7 of the Endangered Species Act.

As a first-year college student who has recently studied wildlife management and conservation history, I have learned that collaboration—not fragmentation—is what allowed the ESA to succeed. Interagency consultation ensures that infrastructure, development, and conservation coexist rather than conflict.

Reasonable and Prudent Measures are not punishments; they are safeguards. They help agencies minimize unintended harm to species while allowing projects to proceed. Any changes that narrow their scope risk shifting ecological costs onto wildlife that cannot adapt quickly enough.

I also learned that wildlife disease monitoring is a critical public service. Federal and state wildlife laboratories track diseases like avian influenza that affect wildlife, agriculture, and people. Weakening interagency coordination undermines early detection and response capacity.

The history of conservation shows that when we invest in cooperation—such as the Migratory Bird Treaty or wildlife restoration funding—species recover. When coordination weakens, decline accelerates.

Aldo Leopold, known as the father of wildlife management, warned that political and economic systems alone are insufficient to conserve land; conservation succeeds only when people truly want it and support it through their collective will, not merely through laws or economic incentives, ultimately resting on the ethical will of society. The public response to this and other ESA proposals suggests that such will is not lacking. What is often scarce is not concern, but the time allowed for it to be expressed. Conservation ultimately rests on collective ethical responsibility, and interagency cooperation is how that ethic becomes action.

I urge U.S. Fish and Wildlife to ensure that any regulatory revisions strengthen—not dilute—the protective intent of section 7 and the collaborative spirit that has long defined effective wildlife conservation.

Respectfully,
Jennifer Puccio

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Jenn Koski
title: Comment from Koski, Jenn

text:
I oppose this action.

" Strengthen Certainty, Reduce Burdens and Uphold the Law" are not legitimate reasons for changing America's bedrock environmental laws in this way. These proposed revisions strengthen certainty for commercial interests rather than wildlife, reduce burdens that are hypothetical, and uphold the law by applying the Supreme Court’s decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo to situations that are not analogous.

There is no justification for these revisions of the Endangered Species Act. They act against recovery of species by reducing protection of critical habitat and promote commercial and economic considerations over science.

Changes to the fundamental building block of environmental regulation should come from agency scientists and public comment, not unqualified administrators.

These proposed regulation revisions are motivated by partisan, political considerations rather than sound scientific research and analysis. They lose sight of the purpose of ESA by emphasizing energy, agricultural and infrastructure priorities. Actions based on Executive Orders 14154, “Unleashing American Energy,” and 14219, “Department of Government Efficiency,” along with Secretary’s Order 3418, are inherently flawed.

There is no energy emergency. The United States produced more crude oil than any nation at any time for the past six years in a row. The reason the US imports oil is because many refineries are old and configured for specific grades of oil not produced in the US. Increasing production will not make the US oil and gas independent or significantly lower the cost of gasoline. Demand for oil fluctuates and influences prices. Renewable solar and wind energy are cheaper to produce than fossil fuels and cause much less environmental damage. Recently, renewable energy supplied more than half of the United States’ electricity generation for an entire month.

Do not implement these proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act.

Though many are trying, you cannot reverse extinction. Regarding trophic levels, bears and gray wolves are top consumers. Recently the bill, H.R. 845, passed, stripping and blocking restoration protections for gray wolves nationwide, ahead of these four rule makings against the Endangered Species Act. Gray wolves were vanished from Yellowstone for decades because of colonization, farming, and human-wildlife conflicts. In other words, humans forgetting that we’re visitors to these natural spaces. During 1926-1995, elk populations grew over the park’s carrying capacity. As a result, overgrazing along streams where willows weep brought about erosion. Without the willow’s shade and additional vegetation for nesting, aquatic species and birds suffered. Coyote populations took advantage of the gray wolf’s absence by hunting small mammals, initial prey for foxes and raptors. Another unfavored outcome was that the park’s primary consumers experienced a logistic growth due to limited prey until gray wolves’ reintroduction in 1995. This reintroduction reduced elk populations, bringing Yellowstone’s carrying capacity back in balance as a whole. The last three decades of American bison restoration shows, too, how substantial these animals are for the continent’s prairies ecologically. Prairies are also home to the native and critically endangered Black-footed ferret. Similar to gray wolves and the American bison, the Sea otter is a keystone species for marine habitats along the west coast. We’ve already seen the devastating, ecological collapse of Sea otter populations because of the 19th-century global fur trade, mining, and oil spills (1969 Union Oil and 1989 Exxon Valdez). With all that said as informative reminders, the Endangered Species Act has done so much to make sure that the air we breathe; the water we drink; the food we eat; the majestic awe of the bear, big cat, bison, condor, elk and wolf; the cleverness of the Black-footed ferret and Sea otter; the elegance of the monarch butterfly; of native flowers blooming in spring; the hum of a bee; the wind’s whisper through a willow; the bird song we hear continues. As a studying naturalist, I encourage you to honor and protect the Endangered Species Act. With it and backed by scientists, we can continue to help in restoration and sustainability nationwide for generations to come. When we protect the Endangered Species Act, we’re saving what’s left of the continent’s natural spaces. Endangered Species Act protections give ecosystems, plants, and wildlife a supportive chance for survival.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

text:
Dear Sirs,
As someone residing in California and frequently witnessing the repercussions of habitat loss, I am deeply concerned about the potential weakening of protections for endangered species. I firmly believe in the importance of science-informed stewardship of the wildlife in our country.
The Endangered Species Act stands as a testament to the effectiveness of a system that prioritizes science and the public interest over political pressure or economic influence. It empowers science to guide us in understanding the needs of species for survival, while values play a crucial role in determining whether we choose to protect them. However, the proposed changes to the rule would shift decision-making away from both science and values, potentially jeopardizing the survival of imperiled species.
One significant concern is the proposed classification rule (Section 4), which aims to remove automatic protections from newly listed species. This move places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even commence. Newly listed species could be left unprotected while recovery efforts are delayed, exacerbating their vulnerability.
Another concern lies in the proposed 4(d) rule (Section 4(d)), which seeks to eliminate the blanket rule for threatened species. This change would result in inconsistent protections and delays in recovery for imperiled wildlife, especially at a time when they require the fullest protection possible.
Furthermore, the proposed exclusion rule (Section 4(b)(2)) narrows the criteria for critical habitat exclusions. This could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, posing a threat to ecosystem health. If economic interests are given precedence over essential habitat, entire ecosystems, not just individual species, are at risk.
Lastly, the proposed consultation rule (Section 7) limits federal review of agency actions. This limitation would facilitate the progress of destructive projects without fully assessing their impacts on endangered wildlife.

In light of these concerns, it is crucial to emphasize the importance of the democratic process and accountability in environmental conservation. Federal oversight serves as a vital check on state wildlife systems that are already heavily influenced by industry interests. These rollbacks reduce public accountability, especially at a time when a significant portion of the American population supports stronger environmental conservation protections.
A democratic, science-based process requires transparency and meaningful review to ensure that the best interests of endangered species are prioritized.
I strongly urge the agency to rescind these proposed rules and uphold the ESA’s robust, science-based protections.
Please prioritize strengthening, rather than weakening, federal safeguards to ensure that states and industry are held accountable for protecting endangered wildlife.
I respectfully request that you adhere to the ESA’s original intent: to prevent extinction and guarantee that future generations will inherit thriving and resilient ecosystems.

PLEASE STOP THIS BILL FROM PASSING!!
Stephanie Holzner, Ph.D.
title: Comment from Holzner, Stephanie

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
Public Comment (Oppose weakening; strengthen the ESA)

To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service:

I’m submitting this comment regarding FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, and FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039 to strongly oppose any weakening of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and to urge the Service to maintain and strengthen its full protections.

The ESA remains one of our nation’s most effective, science-based conservation laws. It protects wildlife before extinction becomes inevitable, and it protects the habitat and ecological processes species need to survive and recover. Weakening the ESA shifts costs onto the public, future landowners, and future taxpayers—while increasing the risk of irreversible biodiversity loss.

I urge the Service to reject changes that reduce protections, including anything that would:
•Narrow or weaken the definition of “harm” or “take,” or make enforcement harder in practice
•Undercut critical habitat designations or make them optional, delayed, or overly restricted
•Create broad exemptions that weaken Section 7 consultation (the federal duty to avoid jeopardy and adverse modification)
•Allow political or economic pressure to override best available science in listing, delisting, or recovery decisions
•Reduce consideration of cumulative impacts (habitat fragmentation, development pressure, water withdrawals, pollution, invasive species, and climate-driven stressors)

Instead, the Service should strengthen implementation by:
1.Keeping decisions grounded in best available science and transparent, peer-informed analysis
2.Protecting habitat up front (because preventing habitat loss is cheaper and more effective than trying to rebuild populations later)
3.Ensuring consistent, enforceable standards across regions so protections do not depend on where a species lives
4.Improving recovery planning with measurable benchmarks, clear timelines, and robust monitoring
5.Investing in proactive conservation and partnerships (landowner incentives, habitat connectivity, watershed restoration), while maintaining strong backstop protections when voluntary measures aren’t enough
6.Strengthening capacity for timely consultation and permitting by adequately staffing field offices—so projects can move forward without sacrificing species survival

The ESA is not just about protecting individual species—it’s about protecting the natural systems that support clean water, healthy soils, flood protection, fisheries, outdoor recreation, and local economies. Once species and habitats are gone, we don’t get them back.

Please maintain the ESA’s full intent and authority and reject any proposal that weakens protections for listed species or their habitat. I respectfully urge the Service to move in the opposite direction: strengthen habitat safeguards, improve recovery outcomes, and ensure the Act remains durable, enforceable, and science-driven.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Sincerely,
Christopher McCarty
Alexandria, VA

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act. The ESA is an important piece of legislation with bipartisan support. It has served as a model for conservation and has saved hundreds of species from extinction. The most recent revisions to the ESA, which took place in 2024, provided additional beneficial protections to more than 1300 species of plants and animals currently listed under the Act. The current proposed revisions would roll back these important protections and ultimately hinder the recovery of many species and their habitats.

The Orca Network staff and Board of Directors urge you to withdraw the proposed revisions to 50 CFR Part 402, which will weaken the requirements regarding interagency cooperation. One of the hallmarks of the Endangered Species Act is the interagency consultation under Section 7 to avoid or minimize incidental take from federal actions. Requiring this cooperation improves transparency and adherence to existing protections, ultimately upholding the law, and we strongly support the current language.
title: Comment from Orca Network

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.
By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.
The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.
The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.
title: Comment from Mosley, Grace

text:
I oppose this action.

" Strengthen Certainty, Reduce Burdens and Uphold the Law" are not legitimate reasons for changing America's bedrock environmental laws in this way. These proposed revisions strengthen certainty for commercial interests rather than wildlife, reduce burdens that are hypothetical, and uphold the law by applying the Supreme Court’s decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo to situations that are not analogous.

There is no justification for these revisions of the Endangered Species Act. They act against recovery of species by reducing protection of critical habitat and promote commercial and economic considerations over science.

Changes to the fundamental building block of environmental regulation should come from agency scientists and public comment, not unqualified administrators.

These proposed regulation revisions are motivated by partisan, political considerations rather than sound scientific research and analysis. They lose sight of the purpose of ESA by emphasizing energy, agricultural and infrastructure priorities. Actions based on Executive Orders 14154, “Unleashing American Energy,” and 14219, “Department of Government Efficiency,” along with Secretary’s Order 3418, are inherently flawed.

There is no energy emergency. The United States produced more crude oil than any nation at any time for the past six years in a row. The reason the US imports oil is because many refineries are old and configured for specific grades of oil not produced in the US. Increasing production will not make the US oil and gas independent or significantly lower the cost of gasoline. Demand for oil fluctuates and influences prices. Renewable solar and wind energy are cheaper to produce than fossil fuels and cause much less environmental damage. Recently, renewable energy supplied more than half of the United States’ electricity generation for an entire month.

Do not implement these proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act.
title: Comment from Breeding, Noreen

text:
Federal agencies must work together to ensure infrastructure projects do not jeopardize endangered wildlife. But this new rule change would weaken that cooperation, posing a big problem for species like the Canada lynx, whose habitat is threatened by the expansion of roads and housing developments.

Use this sample message or write your own.
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.
