title: Comment from Dollar, Chelsea

text:
December 21, 2025

Brian Nesvik
Director U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
1849 C Street, NW
Washington, DC 20240
United States

RE: Docket Number: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044
Dear Director Nesvik,

I am writing on behalf of Sea and Sage Audubon Society to urge you to reconsider weakening the Endangered Species Act (ESA) through proposed rules changes, Docket Number: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; and FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; and FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029: and FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048. Sea and Sage Audubon Society is an Orange County, California chapter of the National Audubon Society with nearly 7,000 local members and supporters dedicated to the protection of birds and their habitats.

The proposed changes to the ESA would replace science-based, economically balanced measures for listing, protecting, and recovering endangered species with heavily weighted economic considerations that will put many species at risk. The ESA has been very successful in stabilizing and saving most of the species listed since 1973. Many factors contribute to species becoming endangered, but habitat loss, poisoning, and pollution are among the top, and they are difficult to reverse quickly. And while few species have reached the point of delisting and removal from the list, many species, such as the California Condor, Peregrine Falcon, Bald Eagle, California Pelican, and California Least Tern, are considered stable or have been delisted due to science-based, economically balanced ESA efforts.

The ESA already takes economic considerations into account during all phases, including during the critical habitat designation process. The new proposed changes would undermine the ability to keep endangered populations stable or in recovery. Newly threatened species may not receive adequate protection to keep them from being added to the list, further harming the species that the original 1973 law aims to protect, and potentially creating many financial impacts in the future.

FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044 Limiting and reducing the importance of species recovery during Section 7 Consultations will alter the FWS's ability to adequately protect species in peril from further harm.

And, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039 redefining Section 4 listing criteria to increase economic considerations will weaken the intent of the I973 law to protect species and balance economic considerations,

FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048 This proposed rule change would give too much emphasis to economic considerations, replacing the protection of threatened and endangered species secondary to factors not considered in the 1973 law,

FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029 Removing the blanket 4(d) rule will weaken Section 7 consultations that would delay or reduce critical habitat safeguards, putting species at further risk, and will substantially increase the costs of recovery in the future.

Cumulatively, the proposed rules changes would severely impact the effectiveness of the ESA and contradict the intent of the landmark 1973 law. We urge you to decline these proposed rules changes and to work within the existing ESA framework, which has been very effective and balances science-based protections with adequate economic considerations.

Thank you for your consideration.

Scott Thomas
Vice Chair of Conservation
Sea and Sage Audubon Society
title: Comment from Sea and Sage Audubon Society

text:
I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

The mandate of the Fish & Wildlife Service is to work with others to conserve, protect, and enhance fish, wildlife, plants, and their habitats for the continuing benefit of the American people. Its purpose is to protect the natural world so current and future generations can live with, live from, and find awe in lands, waters, and wildlife.
I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.
title: Comment from GUBELMAN, ERIN

text:
I write to oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize the survival of listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process and thereby undermine the effectiveness of the ESA.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in scientific literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of species decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation and species recovery outcomes, in violation of the intent and purpose of the ESA. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time, potentially leading to extinction.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement and undermine the intent and efficacy of the law. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

title: Comment from Severson, Katy

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Hosseini, Danny

text:
Section 7 covers consultation among federal agencies to ensure agency actions don’t undermine endangered or threatened species or hurt critical habitat. It requires agencies to consult with USFWS and National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) before carrying out any action that could (1) jeopardize species’ survival and recovery and (2) destroy or degrade critical habitat.

The new regulations change rules that implement Section 7 of the Act, and thus greatly limit the consultation process and impact both imperiled species and the critical habitat they rely on.

This proposal would make it more challenging for USFWS and NMFS to prove that actions requested by other federal agencies would negatively impact listed species and critical habitat. This would exclude many indirect, cumulative, or climate-driven effects from being considered.

REASONS AGAINST: Proposed Rule: Section 7: Interagency consultation
- Section 7 is crucial to ensuring that other agencies’ projects (oil drilling, mining, dams, timber sales) don’t further endanger wildlife.
- The Section 7 consultation process has been instrumental to the Act’s remarkable success in preventing the extinction of imperiled animals and plants; 99% of species listed under the Act survive today.

title: Comment from Biller, Dakotah

text:
Science has historically led the rules in defining listing requirements and conditions for protecting critical habitats.

This rule would reinstate the 2019 Trump listing and critical habitat regulations and would narrow the interpretation of listing requirements, making it harder to list species as endangered or threatened and easier to delist a species. These changes would make it more challenging to grant Endangered Species Act protections for species that are impacted by climate change, drought, disease, and other effects. The US Fish and Wildlife Service would also be limited in their ability to designate currently unoccupied wolf habitat as critical, even if those areas are essential for future wolf expansion and recovery.

REASONS AGAINST: Proposed Rule: 50 CFR Part 424: Listing and Critical habitat rules
- True endangered species conservation requires forward-thinking and future projections. Removing the ability to list species by narrowing the scope of “foreseeable future” hinders our ability to proactively save species before they hover on the brink of extinction.
- True recovery looks at all areas a species did roam, and could roam in the future – not just where they’re currently found. Gray wolves only occupy 10-12% of their historical range but will rely on unoccupied areas if the species is going to truly recover.
- FWS and NMFS should reject this proposed rule and rely on the improvements made in 2024.

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

title: Comment from Poppe, Patty

text:
(1)I support the assertion in the proposed rule that any changes in regulations would not apply retroactively to consultations finalized prior to the effective date of the final rule. I suggest taking this one step further and stating that consultations initiated prior to the effective date of the final rule be allowed to be completed under the regulations in effect at initiation if the parties to the consultation agree to do so.

(2)The issues and litigation on ESA Section 7 are complex and I request that the public comment period be extended an additional 90 days, especially given that the proposed rule was published on the Friday before Thanksgiving with only the minimum 30-day public comment period provided.

(3)The proposed rule mischaracterizes the impact of Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (603 U.S. 369, 2024) on this matter. In the Supreme Court’s decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, the court found, “The Administrative Procedure Act requires courts to exercise their independent judgment in deciding whether an agency has acted within its statutory authority, and courts may not defer to an agency interpretation of the law simply because a statute is ambiguous.” Of course, agencies must adhere to the law as written, and regulations are promulgated by agencies to clarify how those laws are to be followed. This ruling does not imply changes to the ESA or its implementing regulations are necessary, simply that the courts must use their independent judgement in interpreting the law. Therefore, the Services must not rely on this argument to propose changes to standing laws and regulations. Those proposed changes in the implementing regulations that use this argument for the stated purpose of the proposed changes should be abandoned. Likewise, simply reverting back to a previous set of regulations/rules simply because a new administration believes it “reflects the single best reading of the statute” is inadequate. Instead, this change should be justified as to why the proposed change is necessary and why the “current” best reading of the statute is valid given a history of the “best reading” by other qualified experts.
title: Comment from Williams, Lisa

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rule because it will significantly weaken the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Preservation of biodiversity is not only ethical - it is critical for human health and prosperity as well.

Human Health: The "One Health" framework, which is acknowledged by the World Health Organization (WHO) and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), recognizes that the health of people is closely connected to the health of animals and our shared environment. For example, ticks and tickborne diseases that afflict many Americans every year are closely correlated with deer population numbers; therefore, it is important that we protect animals that control deer populations. Some of these predator populations are critically threatened.

Human Prosperity: Ecosystem services are the 100% FREE benefits that nature provides to us, like clean air, fresh water, food, and climate regulation. Many species literally clean up the world FOR us. However, we only get to keep these free services if we preserve biodiversity.

Therefore, I oppose removing automatic protections for threatened species and limiting "critical habitat." These are disastrous measures that will immediately undermine biodiversity, and by proxy human health and prosperity. Habitat depletion is a leading harm to endangered species and also leads to a rise in issues like zoonotic diseases, which hurt humans too.

I oppose letting economic factors influence wildlife protection decisions. This is very short-sighted and again, neglects all the free services we get from wildlife.

Finally, I oppose reducing collaboration with state wildlife experts and weakening scientific standards used to evaluate habitat protections. All policy decisions should be made by conferring scientists and scientific data.
title: Comment from Selechnik, Ph.D., Dan

text:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed changes outlined in the document FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044-0001, which threaten to negatively impact the critical protections currently in place for endangered species. As a concerned citizen and advocate for wildlife, I believe these changes could have irreversible consequences for the delicate ecosystems and the species that rely on them for survival.

Threats to Endangered Species will face a vital impact. The changes being proposed in this document represent a dangerous shift in the approach to wildlife conservation. Here are a few examples, it weakens habitat protections, reducing funding for conservation programs, relaxing enforcement of the Endangered Species Act. These proposed adjustments fail to recognize the gravity of the current biodiversity crisis we face. We are already witnessing alarming rates of species extinction due to habitat destruction, climate change, and illegal poaching. To weaken protections at this point would only exacerbate these challenges.

Endangered species and their habitats need more protection, not less. As we see with species impacted, habitat destruction, pollution, and climate change continue to put their survival at risk. Reducing or removing legal safeguards that protect these species would be a grave mistake and could accelerate their decline.

Recommendations for Action. Rather than dismantling protections, I strongly urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to focus on the following actions to strengthen efforts to protect endangered species. For example, maintain or Strengthen Habitat Protections. Strong and enforceable habitat protections are critical for the survival of endangered species. We must ensure that ecosystems are preserved, and that development or industrial activities do not disrupt the balance of these habitats. In addition, increase Investment in Conservation Programs. We need more resources, not fewer, to support wildlife monitoring, research, and conservation initiatives. These programs are essential for tracking the health of endangered species and ensuring their long-term survival. Enforce existing laws and regulations. Instead of rolling back protections, it’s imperative to focus on more rigorous enforcement of the Endangered Species Act and other key wildlife laws. This includes combating illegal poaching, reducing habitat fragmentation, and addressing climate change. Finally, work with communities and local governments. Collaboration with local communities is vital for effective conservation. By providing education, resources, and support to local stakeholders, we can ensure that wildlife protection efforts are sustainable and supported by those most affected.

This is a time for a call for immediate action. I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to reconsider these proposed changes and to maintain the strong protections that are crucial to preserving our planet’s biodiversity. The continued survival of endangered species depends on the decisive actions we take today, and weakening these protections will only make it harder for future generations to experience the rich diversity of wildlife that we still have left.

Thank you for your time and attention to this critical issue. I look forward to hearing about your commitment to safeguarding the future of endangered species.

Sincerely,

Kathleen Pease
title: Comment from Pease, Kathleen

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. title: Comment from Elwell, Theresa

text:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to express strong concern regarding the proposed changes to Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) in docket FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044, particularly provisions affecting federal consultation and interagency cooperation. Section 7 is the backbone of the ESA’s preventative framework, ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy or adversely modify critical habitat.

The proposal threatens to weaken this framework in ways that will have serious and lasting consequences for endangered and threatened species.

First, narrowing or expediting consultation requirements undermines the preventative intent of Section 7. Consultation exists to identify and address impacts before harm occurs. Reducing the scope, depth, or timing of consultation shifts ESA enforcement from prevention to damage control, often after habitat loss or species decline has already occurred.

Second, increased reliance on informal consultation, programmatic approaches, or agency self-determination risks sidelining the expert scientific review provided by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA Fisheries. Section 7 was designed to ensure independent biological expertise is applied consistently across federal actions. Weakening this role increases the likelihood of flawed analyses, cumulative impacts being overlooked, and species being placed at unnecessary risk.

Third, the proposed changes create greater inconsistency and legal uncertainty. Allowing agencies broader discretion to bypass or abbreviate consultation will result in uneven application across projects, regions, and species. This not only harms conservation outcomes but also increases litigation risk, delays projects, and undermines regulatory predictability for all stakeholders.

Fourth, weakening interagency consultation disproportionately impacts habitat protection, particularly in cases involving incremental or landscape-level impacts. Many federal actions individually appear minimal but collectively contribute to habitat fragmentation, reduced connectivity, and long-term decline. Robust consultation is essential to evaluate these cumulative effects, especially in the face of climate change.

Fifth, diminishing Section 7 safeguards undermines interagency accountability. The ESA requires federal agencies to share responsibility for species conservation. Reducing mandatory consultation or oversight shifts conservation from a shared legal duty to a discretionary consideration, contrary to the plain language and intent of the statute.

Finally, the proposal risks prioritizing administrative efficiency over biological integrity. While efficiency is important, it should not come at the expense of species survival. The ESA’s success rests on its precautionary approach—ensuring that federal actions err on the side of conservation when scientific uncertainty exists.

For these reasons, I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to maintain strong, mandatory consultation requirements for federal actions. Preserve the central role of expert biological review by FWS and NOAA Fisheries. In addition, ensure cumulative and climate-related impacts are fully evaluated. Also, reject changes that allow agencies to bypass or dilute consultation obligations.

Section 7 has proven effective precisely because it prevents harm before it occurs. Weakening federal consultation requirements threatens the integrity of the Endangered Species Act and places vulnerable species at unnecessary risk.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit comments on this important proposal.

Respectfully,

Kathleen Pease
title: Comment from Pease, Kathleen

text: The economic impact of designating Critical Habitat should not carry the same weight as scientific research. I encourage USFWS and NMFS to keep the methods of designating Critical Habitat under the ESA as they read now. Sea turtles need continued protection if they are downlisted under the ESA in the future. The “blanket rule” ensures that species are protected when they are at their most vulnerable – before they are considered “endangered” of becoming extinct. I encourage USFWS and NMFS to keep the “blanket rule” under the ESA as it stands now. One of the most pressing threats to all sea turtle species is impacts from climate change on land and at sea. This rule change will make listing species and habitat more difficult and make delisting easier, which will result in fewer protections. I encourage USFWS and NMFS to keep listing criteria under the ESA as it stands now. Agencies must continue to coordinate and share information to reduce potential harm to wildlife. I encourage USFWS and NOAA to keep interagency cooperation requirements under the ESA as they stand now.
title: Comment from Sivulich, Lenore

text:
As a third-generation Oregonian who has spent a lifetime learning from and enjoying the outdoors, I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. The United States is exceptional not only because of its people, but because of its extraordinary diversity of landscapes, ecosystems, flora, and fauna. Protecting that natural heritage is a responsibility we owe to future generations.

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Hartigan, Hugh

text:
To Whom It May Concern,

I submit this comment to express concern regarding proposed changes to Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) under docket FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044, which governs federal consultation and interagency cooperation. Section 7 is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not contribute to the decline or extinction of listed species and that conservation responsibility is shared across federal agencies.

The proposed revisions risk weakening Section 7 in ways that fundamentally alter its protective function.

Section 7 consultation serves as an early-warning system, identifying potential impacts before federal actions cause irreversible harm. Provisions that reduce consultation requirements, expand exemptions, or allow agencies greater discretion to determine when consultation is necessary undermine this preventative purpose. Once damage to species or habitat occurs, mitigation is often ineffective or impossible.

In addition, changes that streamline or curtail consultation diminish the role of expert biological analysis by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA Fisheries. These agencies provide independent scientific review that is critical to evaluating species status, habitat needs, and cumulative effects. Allowing action agencies to limit or bypass this expertise increases the risk of incomplete or biased analyses.

The proposal also threatens to weaken consideration of cumulative and indirect impacts. Many federal projects appear minimal in isolation but collectively contribute to habitat fragmentation, altered hydrology, increased disturbance, and long-term population decline. Robust interagency consultation is one of the few mechanisms capable of addressing these landscape-scale impacts, particularly as climate change intensifies existing threats.

Furthermore, weakening Section 7 undermines interagency accountability. The ESA explicitly requires all federal agencies to carry out their missions in a manner that conserves listed species. Reducing consultation obligations shifts this responsibility from a legal duty to a discretionary practice, contrary to the statute’s plain intent.

Finally, the proposed approach prioritizes administrative efficiency over ecological integrity. While efficiency is a valid goal, it should not override the ESA’s mandate to prevent jeopardy to species and adverse modification of critical habitat. Weakening Section 7 protections may lead to short-term project approvals but will result in long-term ecological, legal, and economic costs.

For these reasons, I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to:

Maintain strong, mandatory Section 7 consultation requirements;

Preserve the independent scientific role of FWS and NOAA Fisheries;

Ensure cumulative, indirect, and climate-related impacts are fully analyzed;

Reject changes that allow federal actions to proceed without meaningful consultation.

Section 7 has been one of the ESA’s most effective tools because it prevents harm before it occurs and ensures federal agencies share responsibility for conservation. Weakening this provision threatens species recovery and undermines the integrity of the Act.

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comment on this proposal.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Borchers, Kris

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text: I am strongly opposed to the proposal to revise the Endangered Species Act’s Section 7 interagency consultation regulations.   It is arbitrary and backward to limit what factors are considered as relevant when considering species impacted by the ESA.   It is purposely limiting to set thresholds such as “reasonably certain to occur”.  Factors such as climate change and habitat fragmentation are relevant and mustn’t be ignored, simply because they are longer term, and harder to quantify and predict.   The ESA requires that decisions be based on the best available science.    Limiting what factors are included and excluded nullifies a key component of the ESA.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I am a biologist and concerned US citizen and voter, writing to strongly oppose the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s proposed 2025 revisions to the interagency cooperation regulations implementing Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act (ESA). As a photographer and outdoorswoman, I deeply value the wild species that the ESA protects. As an ecologist, I know that species from hellbenders to whales are key members of ecosystems that keep our nation’s environment healthy.

Section 7 consultation is the backbone of the ESA’s preventative framework. It ensures that federal agencies identify, avoid, and minimize harm to listed species and their critical habitat before irreversible damage occurs. The proposed rule would significantly weaken this framework by eroding scientific rigor, narrowing the scope of consultation, and expanding agency discretion in ways that undermine the ESA’s clear conservation mandate.
In particular, the proposed changes appear designed to streamline consultations at the expense of substance. This is short-sighted in the extreme. By limiting when consultation is required, constraining the analysis of indirect and cumulative effects, and increasing reliance on informal or expedited processes, the rule reduces meaningful review of federal actions that may jeopardize species survival. Efficiency cannot lawfully or responsibly come at the cost of biological reality.

The proposal also diminishes the role of the best available science in consultation decisions. Section 7 was intended to ensure that expert wildlife agencies provide independent, science-based analysis of agency actions. Weakening consultation standards or allowing action agencies greater latitude to define impacts risks politicizing decisions and sidelining scientific expertise—precisely what Congress sought to avoid when it enacted the ESA.
Equally concerning, the proposed rule reduces transparency and accountability. Section 7 consultations create an administrative record that allows the public, courts, and decision-makers to understand how impacts to species were evaluated and addressed. Diluting consultation requirements and documentation will make it harder to detect errors, challenge unlawful actions, or ensure compliance with the ESA.

The ESA is one of the world’s most effective conservation laws, and it has protected 99% of the species listed under it. Our nation’s species are part of our national heritage and should be protected for future generations. This rule, plus the gutting of staff and budget at US Fish and Wildlife Service and other conservation agencies, is an attempt to allow our nation’s valuable natural resources to be plundered by already-wealthy corporations. In essence, it is selling off our future to the wealthy few.

At a time when climate change, habitat loss, and infrastructure expansion are accelerating threats to biodiversity, weakening interagency cooperation is both short-sighted and dangerous. Federal actions—from permitting to land management to infrastructure development—play a decisive role in species recovery or decline. Strong, enforceable consultation requirements are essential to preventing extinction and fulfilling the ESA’s preventative purpose.

For these reasons, I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to withdraw the proposed 2025 revisions to the interagency cooperation regulations and instead uphold robust, science-based Section 7 consultation that fully protects endangered and threatened species and their critical habitat.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Sincerely,
Carol Blaney, MA Botany, MS Resource Interpretation
United States

title: Comment from Chittum, Samme

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. The Section 7 consultation process is the cornerstone of the ESA, and the process impacts every listed species under the ESA. Rewriting this rule is inefficient and foolhardy at best; malicious and greedy at its worst.

ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation. Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law, and importantly, it strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.

Federal agencies such as NOAA Fisheries, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Bureau of Reclamation frequently consult under ESA Section 7 when operating dams, managing river flows, or authorizing water diversions. These consultations have led to actions like fish passage improvements, spill operations, and habitat restoration. It is important for innumerable marine and aquatic species, such as salmon and Southern Resident orca in the Pacific Northwest, to require consultations.

Federal water-management agencies, including the Bureau of Reclamation and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, consult to ensure water projects and river operations do not reduce habitat or food availability for the migrating whooping cranes and other listed species that rely on rivers and wetlands. Without this requirement to consult, agency actions could disrupt their habitat and food resources and we could lose these species forever.

title: Comment from Sanchez, Mary

text:

title: Comment from Lutz, Natalie

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

text:
To Whom It May Concern,

Although I am not familiar with every legal term in the proposed rule, the core issue is clear: weakening or “deregulating” the Endangered Species Act (ESA) undermines the very purpose for which it was enacted. The ESA was designed to prevent the irreversible loss of species and to ensure that federal actions do not push vulnerable wildlife closer to extinction. That purpose has not changed, and the need for strong protections remains as urgent as ever.

Decades of research demonstrate that the ESA’s existing consultation and critical habitat requirements are effective. A quantitative analysis published in Bioscience found that species with designated critical habitat for at least two years were more than twice as likely to show improving population trends compared to species without such protections. Additional reviews of ESA implementation show that many listed species experience measurable recovery when the law’s safeguards are fully applied, underscoring the importance of maintaining strong regulatory standards.

Weakening consultation requirements would reduce accountability, increase the risk of harm to already‑vulnerable species, and contradict the statute’s intent as established by Congress. The evidence consistently shows that strong, science‑based oversight is essential for species recovery.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw the proposed rule and maintain the current consultation standards to ensure continued compliance with the ESA and to uphold the expectations of the American public.

Sincerely,

Tina L. Turner
title: Comment from Turner, Tina

text:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to firmly oppose the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently being considered. These proposals, both individually and collectively, would substantially weaken the ESA’s capacity to prevent extinction, assist in species recovery, and protect the ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. Removing default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)

The ESA’s goal is to act before species reach critical levels. The 4(d) rule is based on extensive scientific evidence indicating that early protections lower recovery costs and prevent further declines. Eliminating default protections would cause unnecessary delays, require case-by-case rulemaking, and expose vulnerable species to harm. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive intent and will result in higher ecological and financial costs in the long term.

2. Making it harder to list species by allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis

ESA decisions should rely solely on the best scientific data, not economic impacts. Allowing economic factors would undermine scientific objectivity and delay protections. Additionally, ignoring climate-driven threats overlooks current conservation science, which shows that factors like habitat loss and warming temperatures threaten species long before declines are visible. Weakening future-threat criteria increases the risk of preventable extinctions.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and limiting the definition of “harm”

Habitat loss is a leading cause of biodiversity decline. Reducing critical habitat designations, particularly in vital recovery areas, undermines recovery efforts. Narrowing the definition of “harm” to exclude habitat degradation reverses longstanding legal and scientific precedent. These changes would weaken inter-agency consultations, heighten biological risk, and conflict with the ESA’s recovery goals.

4. Opening new loopholes that allow agencies or special committees to bypass ESA protections

Creating loopholes that allow agencies to override ESA protections conflicts with the ESA’s core purpose. These would encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decision-making away from science-based analysis. This would disproportionately impact species like the Florida panther, grizzly bears, and gray wolves, accelerating declines in already pressured species.

Cumulative Impact

Collectively, these proposals would weaken the scientific foundation of the ESA, delay or block protections, reduce habitat conservation, increase extinction risk, undermine inter-agency cooperation, and elevate long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from extinction due to its grounding in science, precaution, and early action. These proposed changes contradict these principles. In a time of significant global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should strengthen—not weaken—its most effective wildlife protection law.

Request

For the reasons outlined, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed rule changes and retain the current regulatory framework, grounded in science, legal precedent, and successful implementation.

Thank you for considering this comment.

FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text:
Please do not weaken protections for for threatened species.

The Endangered Species Act is designed to be preventative, not reactive. Delaying protections until species are already in severe decline undermines recovery and increases extinction risk.

ESA listing and habitat decisions must remain based on the best available science, as required by law.

Habitat protection is central to species recovery. Habitat loss is the leading cause of extinction, and critical habitat protections are among the ESA’s most effective tools.

Cumulative and indirect impacts matter. Many species are harmed by multiple stressors over time, not a single action in isolation.

Weakening protections for threatened species increases the likelihood that they will become endangered.

Southern Resident killer whales are critically endangered and depend on healthy Chinook salmon populations for survival and recovery.

Weakening protections for threatened and endangered salmon stocks directly impacts Southern Resident killer whales by reducing prey availability.

Broad, forward-looking habitat protections are essential as climate change alters prey distribution, ocean conditions, and ecosystem function.

Federal actions that degrade salmon habitat, increase vessel disturbance, or fragment ecosystems can collectively undermine recovery even when individual impacts appear small.

The Endangered Species Act is one of the most effective wildlife conservation laws in the world, credited with preventing extinction for the vast majority of species listed under it.

These proposed changes would affect protections for many of the most iconic and beloved endangered species in the United States, including bald eagles, Florida manatees, sea turtles, gray wolves, grizzly bears, Pacific Right Whale, Hawaiian monk seals, whooping cranes, and numerous pollinators, freshwater fish, and native plants. Weakening ESA implementation will affect wildlife across terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems nationwide.

The loss or decline of these species directly impacts the American people. Healthy wildlife populations support clean water, fisheries, agriculture, pollination, flood control, cultural heritage, recreation, and local economies. When species disappear, ecosystems become less stable and communities lose the natural services they rely on for health, livelihoods, and resilience in the face of climate change.

text:
Section 7 consultation is a critical safeguard ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or adversely modify critical habitat. This process protects not only biodiversity but also economic certainty, by identifying risks early and reducing litigation and project delays.

The ESA’s strong performance—preventing extinction for roughly 99% of listed species (USFWS)—demonstrates that rigorous, science-based consultation works. Weakening consultation standards would align U.S. policy with global patterns of wildlife decline, where lack of cumulative impact analysis has resulted in costly environmental degradation (WWF, Living Planet Report, 2024).

title: Comment from Come, Amanda

text:
I strongly oppose proposals to weaken the Endangered Species Act by excluding habitat damage from the definition of “take” and by incorporating financial considerations into listing and protection decisions.

Habitat loss and degradation are the primary drivers of species decline and extinction worldwide. In the United States, the vast majority of species listed under the Endangered Species Act are threatened not primarily by direct killing, but by the destruction, fragmentation, or degradation of the habitats they require to survive and reproduce. Treating habitat damage as separate from harm to species ignores decades of ecological science and undermines the biological reality that species cannot persist without suitable habitat.

Redefining “take” to exclude habitat destruction would significantly weaken the Act’s core protective mechanism. It would allow activities that eliminate breeding grounds, migration corridors, food sources, and shelter to proceed unchecked, even when the foreseeable outcome is population decline or local extinction. This approach creates a loophole that permits indirect but inevitable harm while claiming compliance with the law’s intent.

I am also deeply concerned about proposals to factor financial or economic analysis into decisions about whether a species warrants protection. The Endangered Species Act was intentionally designed to be science-based. Its purpose is to prevent extinction, not to weigh the short-term economic convenience of human activities against a species’ right to exist. Introducing financial considerations at this stage shifts the Act away from objective biological assessment and toward subjective, politically influenced decision-making.

Short-term economic calculations consistently underestimate long-term costs. Healthy ecosystems provide essential services including clean water, pollination, flood mitigation, soil stability, and climate resilience. The loss of species and habitats ultimately imposes far greater economic and social costs than proactive conservation ever does. Once species are gone and ecosystems are degraded, restoration is often impossible.

Weakening habitat protections and prioritizing near-term financial interests represents poor stewardship of our shared natural heritage. It transfers irreversible environmental damage to future generations, who will bear the consequences without having had a voice in these decisions. Conservation laws exist precisely because markets and short-term incentives fail to account for long-term ecological stability.

The Endangered Species Act has been one of the most effective conservation tools in the world, preventing the extinction of the vast majority of species listed under it. Its success is rooted in its clear, science-driven mandate. Diluting that mandate by ignoring habitat loss and prioritizing economic considerations will erode its effectiveness and accelerate biodiversity loss at a time when ecosystems are already under unprecedented stress.

I urge decision-makers to uphold the original intent of the Endangered Species Act by maintaining strong habitat protections, preserving a science-based decision framework, and rejecting changes that would lead to short-sighted outcomes with irreversible environmental consequences.

title: Comment from Bane, Rachael

text:
I am submitting comments on proposed rule "FWS-HQ-2025-0044 ESA Proposals Regarding Interagency Consultation". My comments are based upon my formal training at the University of Montana and my undergraduate and graduate degrees in Wildlife Biology, and my 41 years of professional positions in wildlife research and management, with 37 of those years spent as a professional Wildlife Biologist and Tribal Wildlife Program Manager on the 1.33 million-acre Flathead Indian Reservation in Montana. In that capacity, I worked closely with many agency staff to conserve, manage and recover species listed as Endangered or Threatened under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). I strongly oppose this revision to the current required process of interagency consultation. The proposal directly contradicts the original intent of the ESA by discarding proven realistic avenues of interagency review and consultation when an agency proposes an activity that might adversely impact a species listed under the ESA and relying on careful and competent review based upon sound and credible scientific data.
Under ESA prior to 2019, actions by Federal agencies on Federal land and lands affected by federal actions were required to comply with the ESA’s requirement to analyze the affected environment and impacts to listed species and critical habitat to reduce the potential of “take” or chances of jeopardy to those species. The amendments proposed reduce or complicate consultation and counter scientifically-based analysis by introducing the terms to provide exemptions for “economic, commercial and national security”, but it does not clearly identify details of those. Many species and habitats have been adversely impacted by such actions, and that is why such activities were addressed in the ESA.
The proposal revision would significantly restrict impact analysis of the “affected environment” and to ignore any activity not under the direct discretion of the Federal agency, including ongoing agency activities and existing agency facilities. However, these types of activities are important in considering impacts of proposed projects on species and habitats. In my experience, through reasonable consultation, most proposed activities with appropriate and realistic mitigation measures, including forest and range management, dam reconstruction, highway reconstruction and many other smaller projects were approved. In short, the consultation process worked very well.

The proposal re-defines how “harm” is evaluated and defines it as only direct killing or injury, and it drops scientifically-valid evaluation of harm which includes “significant habitat modification or degradation” that injures or kills species by disrupting essential behaviors such feeding, breeding and shelter. Most species listings relate to habitat loss and modification as leading causes of extinction and harm. Using the proposed definition of harm would seriously reduce careful analysis of impacts and make those important factors inconsistent with ESA.

The proposed revision would restrict complete analysis of a project’s impacts to listed species and habitats. Use of commercial and economic data to determine impacts as “reasonably certain to occur” obscures and counters the best scientific analysis. The proposal aims to avoid “reasonably certain to occur” finding by dropping and/or side-stepping many activities If these exemptions are added to proposed economic, administrative and legal requirements, the combination of these exempted factors creates a very inaccurate and skewed analysis. Additionally, it fails to consider cumulative effects that might lead to a tipping point of adverse effects to a species or habitat. Why is no justification to drop analysis of these factors provided? These flaws could have very significant impacts on listed species or habitats.

Although the reason for the revisions proposed is to reduce confusion by reducing burdens and maintaining flexibility of choice, they would instead further confuse the environmental baseline analysis, which should be driven by the needs of the species, instead of by a set of irrelevant exemptions. The proposed regulations would thus serve to exempt most potential consequences to listed species or habitats if “the agency has no ability to prevent the consequences due to it limited statutory authority or the consequences would occur regardless of whether the proposed action goes forward.” These exemptions mean if an action is so dire, it does not require analysis and therefore “take” would not be quantified nor jeopardy applied. This completely deviates from the purpose of the ESA and the rational and reasonable consultation process that currently exists and has worked well in both managing and recovering listed species.

I strongly oppose adoption of this proposed revision, and I respectfully request that it be dropped from further consideration.
