title: Comment from Carim, Kellie

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to an even higher risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular. Logistically, there is no valid reason for these proposals to suggested or created in the first place.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery. This will have strong negative effects on not only the many essential species, but to human life as well, as we have seen the effects of air pollution and constant environmental imbalance with the escalation of land development.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based. By now, we should have more than enough evidence that we, as a species, cannot afford to have the greedy higher-ups in this country to continue destroying our environment, much less the animals that we are meant to share it with.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species. If the threat of mass extinction was not enough, this blatant attempt to silence the U. S. Fish and Wildlife Services, National Marine Fisheries Services, and their genuine input to try and help care for those around them is nothing short of insulting and careless.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same disgusting attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased in the slightest over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever. If we unnecessarily stripped of the rights we have as citizens to care for the beautiful animals that help define our land, including wolves and bears, then all of the bloodshed that follows will be on the government's hands, especially the Senate's.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Bauhof , Katie

text:
I am submitting this comment in strong support of maintaining and strengthening interagency cooperation regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

The ESA is one of our nation’s most effective and science-based environmental laws, and its success depends heavily on robust coordination between federal agencies, including the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Section 7 interagency consultation is a cornerstone of the Act, ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize the continued existence of endangered or threatened species or destroy or adversely modify their critical habitats.

Any regulatory changes that weaken interagency cooperation, reduce consultation requirements, limit the use of the best available science, or prioritize short-term economic or administrative convenience over long-term ecological integrity would undermine the intent and effectiveness of the ESA. Such changes risk accelerating biodiversity loss, destabilizing ecosystems, and eroding public trust in federal environmental stewardship.

Healthy ecosystems support clean water, food security, climate resilience, and economic stability for communities across the United States. Protecting endangered and threatened species is not only a legal obligation but also a moral responsibility to future generations.

I urge the Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA to:
•Preserve strong, enforceable interagency consultation requirements
•Ensure decisions are guided by the best available science
•Maintain transparency and public accountability
•Reject any provisions that would weaken protections for endangered and threatened species or their habitats

The ESA has prevented the extinction of hundreds of species and remains a vital safeguard for our nation’s natural heritage. Please uphold the full intent of the law and ensure that interagency cooperation continues to serve as a meaningful and effective conservation tool.

Thank you for considering my comment and for your commitment to protecting wildlife, ecosystems, and the public interest.

text:
Saturday, December 20, 2025
  
I oppose all current efforts to alter the U.A. Endangered species Act (ESA).
 
I oppose the proposed changes to the ESA.
 
The ESA should be strengthened to prevent extinction and to promote legal recovery of more listed species. The best available science provision of the ESA needs strengthening to keep up with current consensus and progress in science. The significant portion of range provision of the ESA and recent court decisions affirming its interpretation of historic range should be added to FWS and NMFS regulations. Recent interpretations of adequacy of regulatory mechanisms should be added to FWS and NMFS regulations to strengthen the protective power of the ESA.Illegal take of listed species should be more effectively enforced again. Respect the original intent of the Congress of 1973 that prioritized preventing extinction over economic or development activities. Amend regulations to implement the ESA that add more public trust principles (fortify the citizen suit provision, strengthen the best available science provision, reaffirm the priority of preventing extinction and restoring listed species over current profiteering interest groups, and break the link between ESA implementation and special interests in state, tribal, and local jurisdictions).
Please include the literature in Appendix 1 in the public administrative record.

He and his lab http://faculty.nelson.wisc.edu/treves/ have authored >160 scientific articles which are free on the latter website. The Carnivore Coexistence Lab is best known for gold-standard experiments on non-lethal prevention of predation on domestic animals, estimates of illegal wolf-killing and cryptic poaching, and our work on risk maps to predict human-carnivore conflict sites. In 2025, Adrian earned the Chancellor’s Distinguished Teaching Award, UW-Madison’s highest honor for teaching. He earned his PhD at Harvard University in 1997 and has worked in non-profit and academic organizations ever since.

text:
The Miccosukee Tribe of Indians of Florida (the “Tribe”) submits this comment in response to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service (collectively, the “Services”) proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act (“ESA”) implementing regulations published in the Federal Register on November 21, 2025, Docket Nos. FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039; FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044; FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029; FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.

The Tribe has been at home in the Everglades since time immemorial. It maintains deep cultural and spiritual connections to the land, water, and wildlife of the region. Numerous species protected under the ESA—including the Florida panther (Puma concolor coryi), the wood stork (Mycteria americana), and the Everglade snail kite (Rostrhamus sociabilis plumbeus)—are culturally significant to the Tribe and play an important role in the ecosystems that encompass the Tribe’s lands and waters. The proposed regulatory changes would significantly weaken protections for these species and their habitats, contrary to the ESA’s statutory purpose and the federal government’s trust responsibilities to Tribal Nations. The Tribe therefore opposes their implementation for numerous reasons, detailed below.

First, the proposal to eliminate the longstanding “blanket rule” protections for threatened species under ESA Section 4(d) would delay or deny essential safeguards for species listed as threatened under the ESA. Requiring species-specific rules before ESA protections may apply to species listed as threatened creates regulatory gaps, during which development or other federal actions may proceed without precautionary, science-based safeguards. For Tribal communities, such delays risk harming culturally important species and the ecosystems they rely on.

Second, several of the proposed revisions introduce new limitations that discourage or preclude critical habitat designation. For example, the proposed addition to 50 C.F.R. § 424.12(1)(ii), allowing the Secretary to forgo designation where threats to habitat “stem solely from causes that cannot be addressed through management actions resulting from consultations under section 7(a)(2),” risks creating a broad exemption to critical habitat designation for actions that do not trigger section 7 consultation. If an action does not require section 7 consultation (because it is not solely tied to a federal agency, require federal authorization, or receive federal funds), important critical habitat designations will not be made, increasing the risk that listed species’ habitat, and therefore the species themselves, will be negatively impacted, in areas prone to development like south Florida. It is the Tribe’s opinion that this phrase be entirely omitted from the provision.

Third, the proposed revisions to 50 C.F.R. § 424.12(b)(2) governing designation of unoccupied critical habitat constrain the Secretary’s ability to protect listed species in ways inconsistent with the ESA’s Congressional mandate. The requirement that the Secretary determine with “reasonable certainty” that an unoccupied area will contribute to species conservation introduces a level of confidence that is unachievable in prospective conservation decisions. Species recovery often depends on protecting habitat before it is occupied, particularly in dynamic ecosystems such as the Everglades. Replacing a precautionary, science-informed approach with a de facto requirement for near certainty risks excluding areas that are essential for long-term species survival and adaptation. It is the Tribe’s opinion that “reasonable certainty” be exchanged with “likelihood.”

Fourth, these proposed regulatory changes collectively shift ESA implementation away from its preventative and recovery-oriented purpose and toward a framework that prioritizes economic and development interests. As written, the proposed regulations increase the likelihood that large-scale land use and energy development will proceed at the expense of imperiled species and Tribal interests. At a time of accelerating biodiversity loss, they weaken science-based species protections and increase the risk of irreversible harm to species and ecosystems that are culturally and spiritually significant to the Tribe, rather than strengthen them.

The Tribe respectfully requests that the Services withdraw or substantially revise its proposed regulation revisions, remove provisions that unduly restrict critical habitat designation, elevate conservation considerations rather than economic interests, and preserve science-based decision-making in ESA implementation.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA), including Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, Endangered and Threatened Species: Critical Habitat, and Endangered and Threatened Species: Interagency Cooperation. Collectively, these proposals undermine the ESA’s core purpose and place threatened and endangered species at heightened risk of extinction. Taken together with related proposed rules (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, and FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048), they dismantle longstanding conservation regulations that have proven both effective and widely supported.

First, the proposed changes to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, including the elimination of the blanket 4(d) rule, would significantly weaken protections for threatened species. The blanket 4(d) rule provides a clear, effective, and legally defensible conservation framework while still allowing the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to tailor species-specific rules where appropriate. Removing this baseline protection increases the risk of population declines and places unnecessary administrative burdens on the agency by requiring individual 4(d) rules for every newly listed threatened species—delaying protections when they are most urgently needed.

Second, the proposed rule titled Endangered and Threatened Species: Critical Habitat would substantially erode the designation and protection of habitat essential to species recovery. Allowing federally managed public lands to be excluded from critical habitat designation based on economic considerations prioritizes short-term development over long-term conservation. This approach would enable energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial activities in areas that threatened and endangered species rely upon for survival. Given that most imperiled species now occupy only small fractions of their historical range, weakening critical habitat protections represents a serious setback to recovery efforts and a clear concession to industry interests.

Third, the proposed changes introduce economic considerations into decisions about whether to list a species as threatened or endangered. This shift contradicts a foundational principle of the ESA: that listing decisions must be based solely on the best available scientific and commercial data. Injecting economic analyses at this stage risks politicizing a science-driven process and delaying or denying protections to species facing imminent threats.

Fourth, the proposed rule Endangered and Threatened Species: Interagency Cooperation would weaken the interagency consultation process with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service. Framed as an effort to “streamline” consultations, this proposal would instead reduce expert oversight and allow federal agencies to move forward with projects without fully accounting for their impacts on imperiled species. Such changes threaten the effectiveness of one of the ESA’s most important safeguards against federal actions that jeopardize listed species and their habitat.

Together, these proposals revive regulatory rollbacks similar to those advanced during the first Trump administration—measures that are inconsistent with both the ESA’s proven record of success and public support. Since its enactment, the ESA has prevented extinction for 99 percent of the species it protects, and recent polling shows that more than four out of five Americans support the law across political and geographic boundaries.

The need for strong species protections has only grown. Accelerating habitat loss, expanding development, and climate change demand robust implementation and enforcement of the ESA—not its erosion.

For these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw the proposed rules on Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, Critical Habitat, and Interagency Cooperation, and to uphold the full protections of the Endangered Species Act for the benefit of America’s wildlife and the ecosystems on which they depend.
title: Comment from Carrell, Quinlan

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposal to remove the requirement that project proponents offset habitat losses for endangered and threatened species under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

The ability of the Fish and Wildlife Service to require full habitat offsets—rather than minimal or partial mitigation—is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not result in a net loss of habitat for imperiled species. Allowing developers to merely mitigate impacts without fully replacing lost habitat undermines the purpose of the ESA and places endangered and threatened species at greater risk of decline.

Habitat loss is the primary driver of species extinction. When mitigation fails to fully offset habitat destruction, the cumulative impacts of development steadily erode the ecosystems species depend on to survive and recover. Removing offset requirements institutionalizes incremental habitat loss and contradicts the ESA’s mandate to avoid jeopardy and promote conservation.

Habitat offsets also provide clarity, accountability, and fairness by ensuring that those who benefit from development bear responsibility for addressing its ecological impacts. Eliminating this requirement shifts the burden of environmental harm onto wildlife, ecosystems, and future generations, while weakening incentives for responsible project design and planning.

The Biden-era rule appropriately recognized that meaningful mitigation must account for the full scope of ecological loss, including fragmentation, functional degradation, and long-term recovery needs. Rolling back these protections sacrifices ecological integrity for short-term convenience and undermines decades of conservation progress.

I urge the Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA to retain strong habitat mitigation and offset requirements and to reject any proposal that allows irreversible habitat loss for endangered and threatened species.

Please uphold the full intent of the Endangered Species Act and ensure that development does not come at the expense of species survival and recovery.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

text:
Under the ESA, the government designates critical habitat to protect threatened and endangered wildlife. But this rule change would allow the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to prioritize economic interests over habitat conservation needs for newly listed species. That’s a major setback for wildlife like wolverines, which depend on large, connected landscapes that are easily fragmented by development, drilling and mining.

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

The Endangered Species Act’s long-standing “blanket rule” automatically gives newly listed threatened species the same baseline protections as endangered species while the USFWS identifies species-specific safeguards. This proposed change will eliminate the “blanket rule,” which means species that could be listed in the future—like the northwestern pond turtle—may lose the standard protections vital to their recovery.

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

The government must consider future threats when deciding whether to list a species. Under this rule change, however, agencies will not be required to look as far down the road. That spells trouble for species that could be listed, like Crater Lake’s Mazama newt. The newt faces worsening problems like invasive species and climate change.

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent and undermines the original intent of Congress to advance science-based conservation.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. Introducing ambiguity in the definition of “recovery” raises serious concerns about the premature removal of protections for threatened and endangered species. If applied loosely, at risk species could lose ESA protection before populations are truly stable and resilient. The proposed rule also shortens the time horizon for assessing threats, limiting USFWS’ ability to account for long-term or emerging risks like habitat loss or climate change. Together, these changes could lead to delisting decisions that ignore cumulative and dynamic threats, undermining decades of recovery efforts and accelerating species decline, contrary to the ESA’s purpose.

I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. The Section 7 consultation process is the cornerstone of the ESA, and the process impacts every listed species under the ESA.

ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation. Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law, and importantly, it strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.

Federal agencies such as NOAA Fisheries, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Bureau of Reclamation frequently consult under ESA Section 7 when operating dams, managing river flows, or authorizing water diversions. These consultations have led to actions like fish passage improvements, spill operations, and habitat restoration. It is important for innumerable marine and aquatic species, such as salmon and Southern Resident orca in the Pacific Northwest, to require consultations.

Federal water-management agencies, including the Bureau of Reclamation and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, consult to ensure water projects and river operations do not reduce habitat or food availability for the migrating whooping cranes and other listed species that rely on rivers and wetlands. Without this requirement to consult, agency actions could disrupt their habitat and food resources and we could lose these species forever.

Federal agencies such as NOAA Fisheries, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Bureau of Reclamation frequently consult under ESA Section 7 when operating dams, managing river flows, or authorizing water diversions. These consultations have led to actions like fish passage improvements, spill operations, and habitat restoration. It is important for innumerable marine and aquatic species, such as salmon and Southern Resident orca in the Pacific Northwest, to require consultations.

Federal water-management agencies, including the Bureau of Reclamation and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, consult to ensure water projects and river operations do not reduce habitat or food availability for the migrating whooping cranes and other listed species that rely on rivers and wetlands. Without this requirement to consult, agency actions could disrupt their habitat and food resources and we could lose these species forever.

text: Do not weaken the Endangered Species Act!!  The Endangered Species Act is one of the most successful conservation laws in U.S. history, preventing extinction for more than 99 percent of listed species. Reinstating the 2019 regulatory framework would weaken its science-based, precautionary protections by reopening loopholes that allow agencies to discount real-world threats such as climate change, habitat loss, and water degradation. Framing consultation as a bureaucratic burden prioritizes short-term industrial interests over long-term ecological health, while limiting mitigation tools removes flexible, practical ways to reduce harm and allow responsible projects to proceed. These changes are not supported by new scientific evidence, have already led to costly litigation and uncertainty, and disregard strong public support for robust endangered species protections—particularly from coastal and Tribal communities that depend on healthy ecosystems. At a time of accelerating biodiversity and climate crises, federal policy should strengthen, not undermine, our obligation to recover at-risk species and safeguard the ecosystems that sustain us all.

title: Comment from Fanchon, Magali

text:
There are about 70,000 public comments on this specific proposal. About 300,000 comments on all four proposals combined. The people care deeply about habitat conservation. Americans care deeply about the ESA. This large number of comments have been left despite the legalese that the proposed rules are written in. Sometimes it feels like I'm getting a new degree just to understand what is being proposed. And I have a bachelors in speech, language and hearing sciences.

And the summaries are written as though the proposals are a good thing. Even when they really aren’t. This rule summary is: "The proposed revisions to the interagency cooperation regulations confirm the Services' application of statutory requirements for interagency cooperation, while continuing to provide for the conservation of listed species."

If you read (and decode) that paragraph it sounds like the endangered species are still going to have conservation efforts as the top priority. But if you dig deeper you learn more about the offset requirement, and learn that that is not true.

The offset rule means that developers would have to fully replace any habitat that they destroy. This proposal removes that requirement. So developers can "mitigate" habitat loss.

Mitigate means “try to avoid” it means to “minimize” it means to prevent a “total loss”. What it is is a loophole. Developers won’t actually have to conserve the listed species regardless of what the summary says. They will be able to “mitigate” habitat loss. That is such a broad term. And it’s broad on purpose to protect the developers. This puts endangered and threatened species at a substantially greater risk.

If developers are going to damage natural habitats they should absolutely fully replace it.

I urge you to 1) stop hiding behind legalese but more importantly 2) to reject this proposal and keep the offset requirement.

Thank you.
title: Comment from Brooks, Susannah

text:
RE: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048 Endangered Species Act/Consideration of Economic Costs

The Board of the Panhandle Chapter of Trout Unlimited (PCTU) has reviewed the proposed rule to narrow the interpretation of “Critical Habitat” under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). PCTU is based in northern Idaho with over 275 members. Our mission and values align with those of the national organization Trout Unlimited; namely the conservation of trout and salmon and the habitats they reside in, to ensure their enjoyment by current and future generations.

According to the information provided, changes in ESA rules are necessary to ensure other federal actions, and in particular mineral and energy extraction projects, can be permitted in an expedient fashion. The information also states that the changes are necessary to more thoroughly consider the economic impacts of ESA implementation for a given species.

PCTU members, and thousands of other anglers, have benefitted enormously from protections provided to bull trout, a “threatened” species which is widely distributed in our geographic area. Recovery efforts in our area have not only produced a state record (catch and release) bull trout, but have facilitated benefits for westslope cutthroat trout, kokanee, and other fisheries. In our part of Idaho, collaborative efforts to restore bull trout have engaged anglers, businesses, industries, Tribes and others to implement conservation measures made available through the nexus of listed bull trout. Bull trout are recovering, and petitions for ESA listing of westslope cutthroat trout early this century were obviated, in part because bull trout conservation helped bolster cutthroat trout populations. The thriving and economically important Lake Pend Oreille fishery is a result of efforts to recover bull trout.

We are concerned that placing more emphasis on the economic aspects of implementing ESA will focus on consequences as opposed to beneficial outcomes. In particular we are concerned that short term economic benefits focused on activities such as development and extraction have the potential to outweigh long term sustained economic benefits associated with species recovery in an analysis. In the case of potential listings for native trout and salmon, that would eventually result in not only the loss of species, but the loss of fishing (both recreational and in some cases commercial) and other valuable (to include economically valuable) aspects of healthy native salmonid populations. Unless an economic analysis is thorough enough to look at the effects broadly (long term v short term, impositions on infrastructure and other tax supported aspects of development, are examples) this proposed change has the potential to severely compromise the ability to effectively implement the letter and intent of the ESA. Thus, we oppose the rule as proposed.

In Idaho and elsewhere, there are numerous examples of collaborative efforts to effectively implement ESA , to include working in designated Critical Habitat, while finding paths forward for other land and water uses to occur in ways that are economically viable for those stakeholders looking to extract, develop, or otherwise modify natural resources. We strongly encourage any modifications to rules be focused on facilitating effective collaboration amongst stakeholders.

Thank you for considering these comments.
Charles E. Corsi, President
Panhandle Chapter Trout Unlimited

text:
Please accept our attached comments. Below is a back-up copy of our attached comment.

22 December 2025

Director Brian Nesvik
U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
1849 C Street NW
Washington, DC 20240

Re: Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation Regulations

Dear Director Nesvik:

The Endangered Species Act (ESA) is the United States’ strongest and most effective law for preventing extinction and restoring imperiled wildlife and ecosystems. Since its passage in 1973, the ESA has prevented the loss of more than 99 percent of the species it protects, including the bald eagle, gray whale, and American alligator. These successes demonstrate that when science guides policy, recovery is possible.

Healthy wildlife populations and intact ecosystems provide irreplaceable services: clean water, fertile soils, pollination of crops, climate regulation, and natural pest control. The ESA’s requirement that listing decisions, habitat protections, and recovery plans be based on the “best available scientific and commercial data” is essential in an era of accelerating habitat loss, climate change, and biodiversity decline. Weakening that standard in favor of short‑term profit risks permanent ecological damage and cascading species loss.

Corporate profit is inherently focused on short time horizons, not long‑term ecological stability. Industries that benefit from lax regulation—such as fossil fuels, industrial agriculture, and real estate development—can degrade habitats faster than species can adapt. Once a species is gone, no amount of money can bring it back. Using rigorous, independent science to set limits and guide conservation ensures that economic activity takes place within ecological boundaries. The ESA embodies a moral and practical commitment: we do not knowingly drive species to extinction, and we recognize that our own survival is tied to the health and diversity of the natural world.

For these reasons, I oppose efforts to weaken the ESA through changes to the interagency cooperation regulations and urge the Service to reject any rollback of science‑based protections. In particular:

The ESA is one of the most successful conservation laws in history, preventing extinction for over 99 percent of listed species; weakening its implementation directly threatens that success.
Restoring the 2019 framework reopens loopholes that allow agencies to discount real‑world risks to imperiled plants and animals, contrary to the Act’s precautionary purpose.
The proposed changes recast science‑based consultation as a bureaucratic “burden,” subordinating wildlife protection to short‑term industrial and energy interests.
Narrowing what counts as “effects of the action” makes it easier to dismiss climate, water, and habitat impacts that scientists know are driving extinction.
Removing or limiting offsetting tools undercuts flexible, practical ways to reduce harm to species while still allowing many projects to proceed responsibly.
Courts have already seen extensive litigation over the 2019 rules; reviving them invites further lawsuits, wasting public resources and creating uncertainty for agencies and businesses.
Americans across urban, rural, and suburban communities overwhelmingly support strong endangered species protections; this rule disregards that long‑standing public consensus.
By making consultation weaker and more convoluted, the rule shifts risks and costs onto coastal, Indigenous, and rural communities that depend on healthy ecosystems and species.
The proposal is driven by deregulatory and energy‑expansion directives, not by new science showing species are safer or habitats more secure.
At a time of accelerating biodiversity and climate crises, federal rules should reinforce—not erode—our obligation to recover at‑risk species and safeguard the ecosystems that sustain us all.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this important rulemaking. I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to uphold the ESA’s science‑based protections and to reject any changes that would weaken interagency consultation or diminish safeguards for threatened and endangered species.

Sincerely,

Marc Cooke
President, Wolves of the Rockies
Stevensville, Montana

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.
By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.
The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.
The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

title: Comment from Gianni, Nicole

text:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to submit a public comment expressing serious concern regarding the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations governing interagency cooperation.

As a physician, I view environmental protection not as a separate issue from human well-being, but as a foundational public health responsibility. Healthy ecosystems buffer disease, protect water and air quality, and sustain the biological systems upon which human life depends. The ESA’s interagency consultation process has long served as a critical safeguard to ensure that federal actions do not unintentionally undermine these systems.

The proposed restoration of the 2019 definitions of “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline,” coupled with the removal of compensatory mitigation considerations, significantly weakens this safeguard. By excluding offsets that address cumulative and long-term impacts, the rule risks obscuring the true ecological consequences of federal actions. In medicine, ignoring cumulative risk factors leads to preventable harm; the same principle applies to environmental decision-making.

Further, narrowing consultation requirements to only those harms deemed “reasonably certain” and directly caused by an action fails to reflect ecological reality. Environmental systems are interconnected, and impacts are often indirect, synergistic, and delayed. Restricting analysis to only the most immediate and isolated effects prioritizes administrative convenience over biological accuracy and species survival.

While alignment with legal precedent is important, the ESA was intentionally designed to be precautionary. It recognizes that uncertainty is inherent in complex biological systems and that federal agencies have a responsibility to avoid actions that could contribute to irreversible harm. Limiting consultation to only those effects agencies can easily foresee or directly control risks turning the ESA from a preventative law into a reactive one.

The strength of the ESA lies in its comprehensive, science-based approach to conservation. Weakening interagency consultation undermines the law’s ability to prevent extinction before it occurs—when intervention is most effective and least costly, both ecologically and economically.

I respectfully urge the agency to reconsider these proposed changes and to preserve a robust interagency consultation framework that fully accounts for cumulative, indirect, and long-term impacts. Protecting endangered species ultimately protects ecosystem stability, public health, and future generations.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment and for your consideration of the enduring connection between environmental integrity and human health.

Sincerely,
A concerned physician and conservation advocate

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text:
I am writing as a wildlife biologist who has monitored populations over decades, and who often considers what is meant by baseline conditions. I am concerned that the proposed rule will weaken protections for threatened and endangered species and their habitats. The proposed changes would not only modify definitions so that threats to species and their habitats could be harder to identify, but also eliminate the requirement to mitigate those harms. The proposed definition of “environmental baseline” is contrary to any standard use of this term, as it would potentially include substantial harmful changes that happen to not be caused by the agency. As ecologists, when we consider baseline conditions we typically consider past conditions, with a focus on conditions under a scenario of natural disturbance regimes, not regimes caused by industrial activities or development. As our environment undergoes more rapid changes, we do have to consider how to ensure species persistence in new locations where conditions to which they are adapted may now be more likely to occur. I request that the administration withdraw the current rule, conduct a thorough literature review of what is meant by environmental baseline, and reconsider their decision based on a better understanding of this complex issue. I suggest two citations that may be useful starting points.

Jachowski, D.S., Kesler, D.C., Steen, D.A. and Walters, J.R., 2015. Redefining baselines in endangered species recovery. The Journal of Wildlife Management, 79: 3-9.

Soga, M. and Gaston, K.J., 2018. Shifting baseline syndrome: causes, consequences, and implications. Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment, 16: 222-230.

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.

More than 99% of species under the ESA's care have been saved or are on the path to recovery. As a lifelong taxpaying citizen of these united states, I am vehemently opposed to the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

Defend the Endangered Species Act
Dec. 10, 2025, 9:50 a.m.
A montage of species impacted by changes to the Endangered Species Act.
The federal government is considering four changes to the Endangered Species Act that would severely weaken our most powerful tool for saving wildlife. Speak up for America’s wildlife and defend the Endangered Species Act by submitting a comment to the Federal Registry opposing these changes.

Submit your comments to defend the ESA
If you have one minute for wildlife: Submit one comment.
If you have a few minutes for wildlife: Submit all four comments.

The deadline to submit public comments is Monday, Dec. 22. Submit your comments below:

Expand all
1. Protect habitats over profits
2. Safeguard threatened species
3. Save wildlife from future threats
4. Guarantee federal agencies cooperate for wildlife
Federal agencies must work together to ensure infrastructure projects do not jeopardize endangered wildlife. But this new rule change would weaken that cooperation, posing a big problem for species like the Canada lynx, whose habitat is threatened by the expansion of roads and housing developments.

Use this sample message or write your own.
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

Thank you,

Heather M Leach

Kentucky
title: Comment from Leach, Heather

text:
I very strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would both undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both highly effective and extremely popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on the small amount of land left that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy very small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, and critically pertaining to this proposal - undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species. This is dangerous and unacceptable.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, none of these actions are either aligned with the law's record of success or with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. The ESA was enacted just in the nick of time. Increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I most strongly urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival. Intact ecosystems are themselves becoming endangered and humans depend on this vital web of life for our own survival as well.
title: Comment from Pakradooni, Jennie

text:
I oppose the proposed changes to these ESA implementing regulations. These substantive changes will harm many species in the United States.

The proposed change would substantially revise Section 7.
Specific Comments:
•Section 7 consultation is the heart of the ESA for regulation of federal agency actions; any weakening puts species survival at risk.
•Raising the threshold for “reasonably certain to occur” effects will erase legitimate scientific evidence and allow harmful actions to proceed without full review.
•It reinstates previous 2019 rules that courts and scientists criticized as inconsistent with the ESA’s conservation mandate.
•Climate impacts, cumulative habitat loss, and landscape-scale consequences should be included in consultations as they are essential to understanding jeopardy.
•These changes directly weaken how Section 7 operates, the mechanism that prevents harmful federal projects (grazing permits, oil and gas drilling, dams, pipelines, timber sales) from further endangering wildlife.
title: Comment from Metzler, Glenn

text:
I am appalled by the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, and I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Section 7 wildlife consultations are a core piece of the ESA’s safeguards that for decades have forced federal agencies to stop and assess whether their actions will harm an endangered species. This safeguard has stopped dams, highways, pipelines, logging operations, and mining projects from quietly driving species toward extinction. But under this proposed rule, key definitions will be changed, so that agencies can ignore ongoing harms, dismiss indirect or cumulative impacts, and pretend slow-moving threats don’t count. It also removes the requirement to offset harm when federal activities kill wildlife and destroy habitat, so they can do that without having to set anything right again.

The ESA requires a conservation mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move interagency consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

The threat to wildlife and habitat has not decreased since the introduction of the ESA; rather, it has increased due to habitat loss, destruction, and climate change. Weakening the ESA will only drive species further toward extinction. Not only that, but weakening the Act is counter to what most Americans want. Recent polls, such as the one conducted by Atomik Research before the 2024 election on behalf of the Indianapolis Zoological Society, showed that 87% of Americans, both Democrats and Republicans, believe that the federal government should do more to strengthen the Endangered Species Act.

I strongly oppose the proposed changes in Docket FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029 that would eliminate or weaken the automatic protections historically provided to threatened species under Section 4(d) of the Endangered Species Act.

Removing these default safeguards and replacing them with species-by-species rules creates unnecessary delays and regulatory gaps at a critical stage when species are already in decline.

I respectfully urge the Services to retain the existing Section 4(d) framework and ensure that all threatened species receive timely, consistent protections based on the best available science.

text:
To whom it may concern,

I’m writing to strongly oppose the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. These changes would severely weaken the ESA's ability to prevent extinctions, aid in species recovery, and protect critical ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. Removing default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)

The ESA aims to act before species reach critical levels. The 4(d) rule is based on decades of scientific evidence showing that early protections lower recovery costs and prevent declines. Removing these protections would lead to unnecessary delays, needing individual rulemaking, and would expose vulnerable species to avoidable harm. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive goals and will incur greater ecological and financial costs over time.

2. Making it harder to list species by allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis

The ESA mandates that listing decisions rely solely on the best scientific data, not economic impacts. Introducing economic factors would undermine scientific objectivity and delay necessary protections. Limiting the consideration of future threats disregards current conservation science, which acknowledges that issues like habitat loss and climate change threaten species long before population declines become evident. Weakening these criteria makes timely protection less probable and increases the risk of preventable extinctions.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and limiting the definition of “harm”

Habitat loss is the leading driver of biodiversity decline. Reducing critical habitat designations undermines recovery efforts, while narrowing the definition of “harm” would undo years of legal and scientific precedent. Habitat destruction often indirectly harms wildlife, a fact long recognized by the law. Weakening these definitions would reduce the effectiveness of inter-agency consultations and increase biological risks.

4. Opening new loopholes that allow agencies or special committees to bypass ESA protections

Creating loopholes for agencies to bypass ESA protections contradicts the ESA’s purpose. These would encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and move decision-making away from science-based analysis, disproportionately impacting species like the Florida panther and gray wolves.

The cumulative impact of these proposals

Collectively, these changes would:
• weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation,
• delay or block necessary protections,
• reduce habitat conservation,
• increase extinction risk,
• undermine inter-agency cooperation,
• and raise long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has historically prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct, proving its effectiveness through science, precaution, and early action. These proposals conflict with those principles.

In a time of global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should strengthen—not weaken—its most effective wildlife protection law.

Request

For these reasons, I urge the withdrawal of all four proposed rule changes and retaining the current regulatory framework, grounded in science and successful implementation.

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.
title: Comment from Searles, Bob

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
These revisions to the Endangered Species Act would prohibit the use of historic population levels in setting environmental baselines and would require the use of current population levels. This makes no sense as it would lock in decisions based on current, low population levels. There is an old saying that those who ignore history, are doomed to repeat it.

The prohibition offsets would mean that additional habitat could not be set aside for insurance against the existing habitat becoming inhospitable to the species. But offsets are needed as a tool for species recovery. Offsets should certainly be allowed where and when they are needed.

Incredibly 'incidental take' (i.e. accidental killing) would not be regarded as detrimental. This is straight out of George Orwell's 1984. 'Incidental take ' most definitely is detrimental and needs to be minimized.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Eaton, Kathleen

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

title: Comment from Lynch, Rachel

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.

I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Angel Valkolilja

text:
Hello.

I am writing as I am extremely concerned about the protentional changes to the Endangered Species Act if Revision FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044 is adopted. This proposal is very alarming. It would set the current population levels of endangered species as the "baseline", rather than using historic species levels. This makes no sense; if a species is already endangered its population levels are dramatically below historical levels and in many cases not sufficient to maintain the population, or the species in general.

This measure would also not allow "offsets", alternative habitats to be set aside to aid in species recovery when existing areas have become inhospitable. The use of offsets, has been an important conservation tool for some highly endangered species, for instance the Guam rail. The rail's habitat on Guam became uninhabitable due to the accidental introduction of Brown snakes. So the species has been introduced to the nearby islands of Rota and Cocos (which are free of Brown snakes) to increase the population numbers until the time it can be reintroduced to Guam.

This revision would also eliminate "incidental take" as detrimental to an endangered species. This would allow many entities to take precedence over protection of endangered species. Not acceptable!

This revision should not be allowed to pass, it would great reduce the ability of the FWS to protect endangered species.

Sincerely,

Ellen M. Lawler
