Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival

title: Comment from Myers, Sarah

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I submit this comment to oppose the proposed revisions to section 7 consultation regulations, which would significantly weaken protections for listed species and critical habitat.

Section 7 consultation serves as the primary means by which the ESA's protections are implemented across federal activities. Through consultation, agencies must ensure their actions are "not likely to jeopardize the continued existence of any endangered species or threatened species or result in the destruction or adverse modification of [critical] habitat" (16 U.S.C. § 1536(a)(2)). This applies to thousands of federal actions annually, making consultation the ESA's most widely applied provision. Weakening consultation standards directly determines whether listed species survive and recover.

The proposed restrictions on the "environmental baseline" and on effects "reasonably certain to occur" are inconsistent with ecological reality and with the "best available science" standard. Species exist in complex environments shaped by multiple stressors operating across temporal and spatial scales. An action's effects cannot be meaningfully assessed in isolation.

Climate change provides the clearest example. Rising temperatures, altered precipitation, ocean acidification, and shifting phenology already affect listed species. These effects interact with proposed federal actions in predictable ways. A water diversion sustainable under historical hydrology can push a species toward extinction when combined with reduced snowpack. Coastal development manageable under stable sea levels becomes catastrophic when combined with storm surge intensification.

Excluding these interactions from analysis does not make them disappear—it makes them invisible to decision-makers, leading to approval of actions whose impacts are systematically underestimated.

For numerous listed species, particularly those affected by habitat fragmentation, indirect and cumulative effects are primary drivers of population decline. Road construction fragments habitat, increasing edge effects. Upstream development degrades downstream water quality. Noise and light pollution disrupt breeding and foraging. These effects are well-documented and entirely foreseeable, yet the proposed rule would effectively exclude many from consultation analysis.

Aquatic species are especially vulnerable. Salmon and steelhead depend on water temperature, flow timing, sediment load, and passage barriers. Consultation on any single water project must account for how it interacts with other diversions and dams in the watershed. Constraining analysis to direct effects only guarantees cumulative impacts will push species toward extinction while each individual action is deemed insignificant.

The proposed elimination of offsetting requirements removes an important mechanism for ensuring unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively degrade populations. Habitat restoration, captive breeding support, and threat reduction elsewhere have contributed meaningfully to recovery efforts. Their removal reflects a shift from recovery orientation to mere survival, contrary to the ESA's express conservation mandate.

Ecosystem services depend on functional consultation. Many listed species provide ecosystem services extending beyond the species themselves. Riparian vegetation stabilizes stream banks and filters pollutants. Predator species regulate herbivore populations, preventing overgrazing. Soil organisms maintain nutrient cycling and carbon sequestration. Pollinator species support agricultural productivity.

When consultation analysis is narrowed, we undermine these ecosystem functions. Costs manifest as degraded water quality, increased flooding, reduced agricultural yields, and diminished carbon storage—costs falling on communities and taxpayers.

The proposed revisions would weaken the ESA's primary implementation mechanism in ways inconsistent with statutory text, purpose, and scientific understanding. I urge the Services to withdraw this proposal and instead strengthen consultation requirements.

Section 7 consultation represents a commitment that the federal government will not, through its own actions, drive species to extinction. This commitment is not merely legal or administrative—it is moral. We have the knowledge to understand how our actions affect other species and the capacity to act in ways allowing both human activities and species conservation.

Our children will judge us by what we chose to save and what we allowed to disappear. Strong consultation requirements ensure that when federal actions affect listed species, those effects are identified, assessed, and minimized. Weakening these requirements is a choice to look away, to accept decline, to prioritize short-term convenience over long-term responsibility. That is not worthy of a nation that committed itself to preventing extinction. I urge you to maintain consultation standards that give meaning to that commitment.

text:
Rule 0044-0001, regarding: Environmental Baseline & inter-agency cooperation

I strongly urge you to withdraw the proposed rule, as it runs directly counter to Congress’s original intention for the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Should this proposed rule be implemented, it would further weaken the ESA, with the likely result being many more species being unnecessarily pushed into extinction, which in turn will lead to a further unraveling of the already-frazzled web of life.

The proposed rule will increase the potential for federal agencies to ignore or disregard negative environmental impacts resulting from governmental or corporate actions, which will further jeopardize threatened and endangered species. It will reduce sharing of information between agencies, and reduce transparency. The American public already is distrustful of government, and rightly so. There is very good reason for this.what is needed is more transparency, not less.

Regarding the proposed rule changes for the definition of “environmental baseline” limiting impacts that can be counted to a species and their habitat is just a way to avoid accounting for what is. Avoiding looking at the full scope of threats species face, including indirect and cumulative impacts, will inevitably result in increased biodiversity loss. Closing ones eyes to reality is not a good place to make decisions from, especially ones that can push species into extinction.

The failure of the Trump Administration to see that in prioritizing corporate profits over a healthy and sustainable environment, it actually reduces America’s national security. Without a healthy and sustainable environment, which is inseparable from a healthy biodiversity, this country can never be secure, as we, and future generations, are all absolutely dependent upon this environment for our survival. Any further destruction of our environment ultimately threatens our national security. Beyond that, it is simply immoral to allow other species to be pushed by humans into extinction. Other species have as much right to exist as do humans.

For these reasons, I very strongly urge you to withdraw this proposed rule. Thank you for considering my comments.

Sincerely,
Russell Wray

text:
I submit this comment in opposition to the proposed rule that would reinstate the 2019 regulations governing interagency cooperation under Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act. I have professional experience implementing the ESA, including service with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service working on Endangered Species Act and CITES matters. I currently lead a nature technology company focused on nature-based risk analytics.

The proposed rule would revise regulations for interagency consultations by reinstating 2019 definitions and removing the 2024 provisions allowing offsets as reasonable and prudent measures. These changes would narrow the scope of consultations and reduce federal agency obligations to avoid jeopardizing listed species or destroying critical habitat. ESA Section 7 mandates that federal agencies ensure their actions are not likely to jeopardize endangered or threatened species, based on the best scientific data available. TVA v. Hill, 437 U.S. 153 (1978), held that the ESA requires halting extinction "whatever the cost." The proposed rule's approach to interagency cooperation undermines this mandate by facilitating actions that could harm species without adequate review.

Under FCC v. Fox Television Stations, 556 U.S. 502 (2009), and DHS v. Regents, 140 S. Ct. 1891 (2020), agencies must provide good reasons and address reliance interests when changing positions. The 2024 rulemaking determined the 2019 regulations were inadequate. This rule reverses those findings without new evidence, ignoring consultation processes relied upon by conservation programs developed under the 2024 framework.

Robust interagency cooperation is vital for species recovery and climate adaptation. Narrowing consultation requirements would limit consideration of cumulative impacts and long-term threats affecting listed species.

Executive Order 14154's premise of reducing undue burdens lacks support. A 2015 analysis of data from January 2008 through April 2015 examined 88,290 Section 7 consultations and found that no projects were stopped or underwent major changes as a result of U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service findings, indicating an even lower impact on development than previously estimated. The 2022 National Survey of Fishing, Hunting, and Wildlife-Associated Recreation estimates wildlife-related activities contribute approximately $395 billion annually to the U.S. economy.

I urge the Service to withdraw this proposed rule.

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

For more than 50 years, the Endangered Species Act has represented a promise I believe in deeplythat we would not stand by while wildlife quietly disappears from our landscapes and our lives. Because of this law, 99% of listed species have been saved from extinction. That success matters to me personally because once a species is gone, it is gone forever, and with it a piece of the world we are responsible for protecting. I am urging the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which weakens a core safeguard of the Endangered Species Act, erodes long-standing legal requirements, and turns away from Congress’s clear intent that federal agencies work together to ensure their actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or destroy the habitats they depend on to survive.

The Endangered Species Act reflects values that guide how I believe we should care for the world around us—stewardship, humility, and responsibility to future generations. It recognizes that protecting imperiled species also means protecting the ecosystems that sustain all life. Narrowing the definitions of “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline,” and removing mitigation offset requirements, risks allowing harm to occur without fully reckoning with its consequences. When cumulative and indirect impacts are minimized or ignored, it is wildlife that pays the price.

Weakening these consultation standards feels like turning our backs on species already struggling to survive. It increases the likelihood of extinction, accelerates habitat loss, and unravels decades of careful conservation work. These are not abstract losses—they are permanent, irreversible, and deeply felt.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain the existing consultation standards that uphold the heart of the Endangered Species Act. The choices made now will shape the world we leave behind. I ask that you act with care and compassion, so that future generations inherit a country where wildlife still exists not just in stories, but in the living landscapes we share.

title: Comment from Roller, Henry

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA §7 interagency consultation regulations.

Section 7 consultation exists to ensure that federal actions, taken together and over time, do not undermine the survival and recovery of listed species. The proposed rule weakens that safeguard by narrowing what impacts must be considered.

By constricting the environmental baseline and tightening the standard for effects deemed “reasonably certain to occur,” the rule shifts consultation from a cumulative, forward-looking analysis to a narrow, project-by-project review. In practical terms, this changes the question from “does this action contribute to long-term decline?” to “can this action be justified in isolation?”

Many of the most serious threats to species — habitat fragmentation, incremental development, climate-driven change — arise from accumulation, not single actions. Excluding those effects from consideration is inconsistent with ecological reality and the ESA’s best-available-science requirement.

The removal of offsetting measures further weakens consultation by eliminating a tool that has helped prevent unavoidable impacts from compounding over time. The ESA’s mandate is conservation, meaning recovery and resilience. I urge the Services to withdraw this proposal and retain a consultation framework that reflects cumulative impacts and long-term species viability.

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

title: Comment from Mulligan, William

text:
I am deeply concerned about proposals to roll back lifesaving Endangered Species Act (ESA) protections for endangered wildlife and their habitats and oppose any effort to weaken the ESA.

The proposed rules/ changes to the ESA ignore science and prioritize destruction over conservation. They attack imperiled species and the places they live by:
(1) Depriving newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, greater sage grouse, and monarch butterfly could be left unprotected even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings.
(2) Narrowing the definition of “critical habitat” to exclude currently unoccupied but historic habitat. Historic habitat is vital for recovery of imperiled species, especially as the areas where they currently live shrink due to the rapidly changing climate and the chain effects of ongoing biodiversity loss.
(3) Loosening compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.
(4) Violating the letter of the law by allowing “economic considerations” in decisions about whether to protect species that are scientifically shown to be at risk of extinction. With this rule, the federal government could decide against protecting an endangered species after considering lost revenue from prohibiting a golf course or hotel development to be built where the species lives.
(5) Altering the criteria for designating critical habitat to make it easier to exclude areas from protections by giving more weight to industry claims of economic impact.

With greater threats facing species than ever before, these attempts to weaken the ESA are dangerous, absolutely unacceptable, and must not be allowed.

Protections under the ESA are our most effective tool for combating the appalling decline of wildlife across the nation. Hundreds of species were on a path to extinction until they were saved by this law’s protections, including bald eagles and gray wolves. And a million species are at risk of extinction in the coming decades, including grizzly bears, Florida panthers, and manatees. Right now, we have a choice between bringing endangered wildlife back from the brink, or losing them forever. We must act while we still can.

More than four out of five Americans support the ESA. Please uphold this essential law and protect imperiled wildlife.

Thank you for your consideration.

title: Comment from Cantrell, Jami

text:
I am writing to formally express my opposition to any proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA), particularly those outlined in docket FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039 concerning Section 4.
The Endangered Species Act has been one of the most effective environmental protection laws in the United States. Section 4, which governs the listing, delisting, and classification of species, must remain grounded in the best available scientific data and insulated from political or economic pressure. Any weakening of these standards risks delaying protections for vulnerable species and accelerating biodiversity loss at a time when ecosystems are already under significant stress.
Proposed changes that reduce scientific rigor, limit consideration of long-term threats, or make it more difficult to list species in need of protection would undermine the core purpose of the ESA. The Act was designed to be precautionary, recognizing that waiting until species are near extinction often makes recovery far more difficult or impossible.
Protecting endangered and threatened species also protects ecosystems, public lands, and the long-term environmental health that communities depend on. I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to uphold the integrity of the Endangered Species Act and to reject any revisions to Section 4 that would weaken its effectiveness or enforcement.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment and for considering public input on this critically important issue.

title: Comment from Terada, Justin

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.
Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.
The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.
For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

title: Comment from Pfister, Sarah

text:
I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever.
Thank you.

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. The Section 7 consultation process is the cornerstone of the ESA, and the process impacts every listed species under the ESA.

ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation. Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law, and importantly, it strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.

Federal agencies such as NOAA Fisheries, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Bureau of Reclamation frequently consult under ESA Section 7 when operating dams, managing river flows, or authorizing water diversions. These consultations have led to actions like fish passage improvements, spill operations, and habitat restoration. It is important for innumerable marine and aquatic species, such as salmon and Southern Resident orca in the Pacific Northwest, to require consultations.

Federal water-management agencies, including the Bureau of Reclamation and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, consult to ensure water projects and river operations do not reduce habitat or food availability for the migrating whooping cranes and other listed species that rely on rivers and wetlands. Without this requirement to consult, agency actions could disrupt their habitat and food resources and we could lose these species forever. We should be strengthening the work of these agencies, not undermining it!

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.

I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted, Lisa Sanchez

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. Each of these changes would significantly weaken the ESA’s ability to prevent extinction, support species recovery, and protect ecosystems vital to wildlife and human communities.

4. **Creating Loopholes to Bypass ESA Protections**

Allowing agencies to override protections conflicts with the ESA’s core purpose. These loopholes incentivize exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decisions away from science, disproportionately affecting species like Florida panthers and gray wolves.

Collectively, these four proposals would:

- Weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation
- Delay protections for vulnerable species
- Reduce habitat conservation amid climate change
- Increase extinction risk
- Undermine inter-agency cooperation
- Raise recovery costs

In a time of global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should strengthen its most effective wildlife protection law.

For these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw the proposed changes and retain the existing framework rooted in science and legal precedent.

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

RE: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

title: Comment from Spencer, Michelle

text:
I am writing to oppose the proposed revisions to the Section 7 consultation regulations. These changes significantly weaken the only mechanism that ensures the federal government "does no harm" to the nation's most vulnerable wildlife.

1. The Loss of Compensatory Offsets By removing "offsets" from the definition of reasonable and prudent measures, the Services are stripping away a vital tool for species recovery. If a federal project—such as a bridge or energy facility—unavoidably destroys critical habitat, the only way to ensure the species' survival is to require the restoration of habitat elsewhere. Eliminating offsets means that federal projects will result in a "net loss" for species, leading to a "death by a thousand cuts" as small portions of habitat are destroyed project by project with no requirement for replacement.

2. "Grandfathering" Environmental Damage via the Baseline The proposed definition of "environmental baseline" is scientifically flawed. Treating the ongoing harm from existing federal facilities as a fixed, unchangeable reality ignores the reality of ecosystem health. If an existing dam is currently killing endangered fish, that impact should be addressed during consultation for new operations, not excused as a permanent feature of the landscape. This "baseline" approach prevents the Services from ever fully addressing the cumulative impacts of federal infrastructure.

3. The Narrow "But For" Causation Test The return to a strict "but for" and "reasonably certain to occur" test for the effects of an action ignores the complexities of modern ecology. Many threats to species are the result of multiple, intersecting factors. By narrowing the scope of what counts as an "effect," the Services are choosing to ignore indirect impacts—such as increased traffic, pollution, or secondary development—that are well-documented consequences of federal actions.

4. Prioritizing Project Scope over Species Survival The insistence that protective measures must only be "minor changes" that do not alter the scope or timing of a project places a higher value on administrative timelines than on the prevention of extinction. Section 7 was intended to be a "stop and think" provision. If a project in its current "design or location" will jeopardize a species, the law should require significant changes, not just "minor" tweaks that fail to address the underlying biological threat.

Conclusion These changes represent a retreat from the federal government’s responsibility to lead in conservation. I urge the Services to keep the 2024 protections in place and ensure that federal agencies are held fully accountable for the environmental costs of their actions.

text:
Dear Sir or Madam,
I submit this comment in strong support of retaining the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations finalized in 2024. These regulations restore scientific integrity to ESA implementation and are essential for the long-term survival and recovery of species such as grizzly bears (Ursus arctos horribilis) and gray wolves (Canis lupus).

The ESA was designed to operate on the precautionary principle: when the best available science demonstrates a significant risk of extinction, protection must come first. The 2024 regulations appropriately reaffirm this mandate by ensuring that listing, delisting, and recovery decisions are based on biological status, population viability, and habitat conditions—not short-term political or economic considerations.

Grizzly bears and wolves provide clear, well-documented examples of why these safeguards are necessary. While some subpopulations show localized increases, neither species has achieved secure, rangewide recovery. Grizzly bears remain fragmented into small, isolated populations that are highly vulnerable to genetic bottlenecks, habitat loss, increased human conflict, and climate-driven changes in food availability. Wolves, similarly, continue to face intense pressure from habitat fragmentation, human-caused mortality, and management actions that can rapidly reverse population gains.

Ecological science consistently demonstrates that premature removal of protections places recovering species at high risk of population decline. Both grizzlies and wolves are slow-reproducing, long-lived species whose recovery depends on landscape connectivity, stable mortality rates, and long-term management continuity. Once protections are weakened, population losses can occur faster than recovery efforts can respond.

Beyond their conservation status, these species play critical ecological roles. Wolves are a keystone predator, influencing prey behavior and abundance in ways that shape vegetation, river systems, and overall biodiversity. Grizzly bears act as ecosystem engineers and nutrient distributors across large landscapes. The loss—or functional disappearance—of these species would degrade ecosystem resilience at a time when climate change is already placing unprecedented stress on natural systems.

The 2024 ESA regulations reflect decades of peer-reviewed science and conservation experience showing that strong, consistent federal protections are essential until recovery is biologically secure and durable. Weakening these rules would not represent progress—it would represent a return to the conditions that caused these species to decline in the first place.

Science tells us what is at stake. But there is also a deeper responsibility here. Allowing species like grizzly bears and wolves to slip back toward extinction would be a failure not just of policy, but of stewardship. Future generations deserve ecosystems that are whole, functioning, and wild.

I respectfully urge you to retain the 2024 Endangered Species Act regulations in full and to continue implementing the ESA in a manner that is guided by science, precaution, and long-term ecological responsibility.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.
title: Comment from Earls, Brian

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. These changes, both individually and collectively, would weaken the ESA's effectiveness in preventing extinction, aiding species recovery, and conserving vital ecosystems for both wildlife and human communities.

1. Removing default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)

The ESA is intended to act before species reach critical levels. The 4(d) rule has proven through decades of scientific evidence that early, precautionary protections reduce recovery costs and prevent further declines. Removing default protections would cause unnecessary delays and expose vulnerable species to avoidable threats, contradicting the ESA's preventive goals and increasing ecological and financial costs over time.

2. Making it harder to list species by allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis

The ESA mandates that listing decisions rely solely on scientific data, not economic impacts. Allowing economic considerations would undermine scientific objectivity and risk delaying protections until species face extinction. Moreover, neglecting projected or climate-driven threats disregards current conservation science, which shows that slow-burn pressures are risks long before population declines are visible. Weakening these criteria reduces the likelihood of timely listing and increases preventable extinction risks.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and limiting the definition of “harm”

Habitat loss is a primary driver of biodiversity decline. Reducing critical habitat designations undermines recovery planning, while narrowing the definition of “harm” reverses long-standing legal and scientific precedent. Weakening these definitions undermines inter-agency consultations and increases biological risk, opposing the ESA’s recovery mandate.

4. Opening new loopholes allowing agencies or special committees to bypass ESA protections

Creating loopholes for agencies to bypass ESA protections, even when extinction is foreseeable, contradicts the ESA’s purpose. This would encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decision-making away from science-based analysis. It would disproportionately affect species like Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves, accelerating declines in already pressured species.

The cumulative impact of these proposals

Together, these rules would weaken the scientific foundation of the ESA, delay protections, reduce habitat conservation, increase extinction risks, undermine cooperation, and escalate recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has successfully prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct. These proposed changes conflict with the principles of science, precaution, and early action. In the face of global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should enhance—not weaken—its most effective wildlife protection law.

Request

Therefore, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed changes and retain the current framework, which is supported by science, legal precedent, and decades of success.

Thank you for considering this comment.

While avoidance of harm should always be the priority, offsets have been key to ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not accumulate and push populations closer to jeopardy.

I strongly urge the Services to reject these changes and instead reinforce the protections that enable listed species to recover and thrive.

Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044

To:
The Honorable Doug Burgum, Secretary of the Interior U.S. Department of the Interior 1849 C Street, N.W. Washington, D.C. 20240
The Honorable Howard Lutnick, Secretary of Commerce, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, D.C. 20230

RE: USFWS Docket Nos. FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029 and FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048
Joint NMFS-USFWS Nos. FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044 and FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039

Dear Burgum and Lutnick,

I oppose these proposed rules that reduce the ability of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) to support the recovery of species in the United States of America.
To recover species, we must use the best scientific data available. Anything less will decrease the ability to recover species and worst-case scenario cause irreparable loss to threatened and endangered species. Giving economic considerations equal or more important billing than the best science available is a grievous mistake and will cause species to go extinct. First, economic considerations do not undergo the same rigors of the scientific process. People can make unsubstantiated claims about economic considerations. Second the recovery of the species and the ability for to sustain itself and the other key ecological factors that are related to that species is valuable now and in the future. Economic considerations are short sighted and will ultimately cause worse economic situations with biodiversity and ecosystem collapse.

To recover species preserving critical habitat and preventing it from getting developed into impermeable surfaces is essential. There are endangered species such as San Bernardino Kangaroo Rats that have population cycles that naturally have large fluctuations. The proposed rules would lead to extinctions because they do not include unoccupied habitat. However, if you are looking the species at a time in their cycle when they are rare habitat will appear unoccupied but they will need that habitat when they are at the large part of the cycle. If the habitat is taken away during the small part of the cycle then they will never be able to recover and be a species that can sustain themselves in the future. Extreme weather events are more and more common. The next extreme weather event such as unprecedented flooding or heat may cause unoccupied habitat to be important in recovery in the future.

Thank you,
Thea Wang, PhD
Glendale, CA

text:
The Endangered Species Act is the essential tool for stopping the extinction crisis in its tracks. We cannot guarantee species survival and recovery without the strong backstop of a fully protective ESA.

I oppose any effort by this administration to weaken the Endangered Species Act. The proposed rules are yet another in a series of attacks on imperiled species and the places they live that ignore science and prioritize destruction over conservation. The proposed rules:

***Deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, greater sage grouse, and monarch butterfly could be left unprotected even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings.

***Narrow the definition of “critical habitat” to exclude currently unoccupied but historic habitat. Historic habitat is vital for recovery of imperiled species, especially as the areas where they currently live shrink due to the rapidly changing climate and the chain effects of ongoing biodiversity loss.

***Loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

***Violate the letter of the law by allowing “economic considerations” in decisions about whether to protect species that are scientifically shown to be at risk of extinction. With this rule, the federal government could decide against protecting an endangered species after considering lost revenue from prohibiting a golf course or hotel development to be built where the species lives.

***Alter the criteria for designating critical habitat to make it easier to exclude areas from protections by giving more weight to industry claims of economic impact.

With greater threats facing species than ever before, these attempts to weaken the ESA are dangerous.

More than a million of the Earth’s species face the possibility of extinction due to climate change, pollution, habitat loss, and exploitation. Even species that are not yet on the brink will face huge population declines. This extinction crisis is depleting fisheries, wiping out the pollinators that support our food supply, and making our rivers, wetlands, and forests disappear.

Humans are not isolated from the natural environment, and what happens to other creatures affects our existence, too.

At a time when we must be redoubling our commitment to protect biodiversity and stop extinction, this administration’s proposals are dangerous and will delay the progress we must make to address the alarming rate of extinction our planet now faces.

Sincerely,
Sarah F.

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

text:
Public Comment Opposing Proposed Revisions to ESA Section 7 Interagency Consultation Regulations

My name is Ron Goodwin, and I am submitting this comment to oppose the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act Section 7 interagency consultation regulations. This comment should be considered alongside my prior submissions opposing the rollback of the threatened species blanket 4(d) rule, the proposed changes to the Listing and Critical Habitat Rules (50 CFR part 424), and the revisions to the Critical Habitat Exclusion Rule under Section 4(b)(2). Taken together, these rulemakings would weaken every major stage of ESA implementation—listing, habitat protection, and federal action review.

Section 7 consultation is the heart of the Endangered Species Act. It is the mechanism that ensures federal actions do not jeopardize the continued existence of listed species or destroy or adversely modify critical habitat. Any weakening of this process places species survival at direct risk by allowing harmful projects to proceed without adequate scrutiny.

Raising the threshold for what constitutes effects that are “reasonably certain to occur” would erase legitimate scientific evidence from consultations. This change would allow agencies to ignore foreseeable harms supported by climate models, land-use trends, and ecological data, even when those harms are well documented. As with narrowing the “foreseeable future” in listing decisions or delaying protections for threatened species, this proposal artificially limits science in ways that favor development over conservation.

The proposed rollback would reinstate elements of the 2019 Section 7 rules that courts and scientists criticized as inconsistent with the ESA’s conservation mandate. Returning to these flawed standards moves ESA implementation backward, not forward, and undermines decades of progress in interagency accountability.

Effective consultation must consider climate impacts, cumulative habitat loss, and landscape-scale consequences. Species do not experience threats in isolation, and consultations that ignore cumulative and climate-driven effects fail to meaningfully assess jeopardy. When combined with weakened critical habitat protections and expanded exclusions, narrowing Section 7 analysis further compounds the risks to wildlife and ecosystems.

For these reasons, the proposed rule should be withdrawn. The Services should restore and retain the stronger 2024 Section 7 protections rather than narrowing them to accommodate short-term project approvals at the expense of long-term species survival.

Consistent with my prior public comments, I urge the Services to uphold the Endangered Species Act’s science-based framework and reject regulatory changes that weaken its most essential safeguards.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Respectfully,
Ron Goodwin

text:
My name is Dr. Reilly Jackson and I am a wildlife research biologist that has trained in worked in the US for nearly 15 years. I have worked on many scientific research projects that provide the best available science to inform activities related to the listing, habitat designation, and recovery of Threatened and Endangered species under the Endangered Species Act. Today, I am writing to express my opposition to the federal government's proposal to revise the Endangered Species Act’s Section 7 interagency consultation regulations. These changes will directly weaken how Section 7 operates and will likely challenge how the best available science is incorporated when assessing species.

The federal government previously instituted similar language in the ESA in 2019, after which several court cases occurred challenging the federal government’s implementation of the ESA (Ctr. for Biological Diversity v. Haaland,No. 19-cv-5206 (N.D. Cal.) (related to California v. Haaland, 19-cv-6013, and ALDF v. Haaland, No. 19-cv-6812). This proposed language and implementation change will again open the federal government to numerous lawsuits and will largely act inconsistently with the ESA’s conservation mandate. Specifically, this language revision will allow for major threats to listed species, such as climate impacts, cumulative habitat loss, and landscape-scale changes, to be ignored during the consultation process, despite the fact that the best available science demonstrates the important effects these threats have on species (Kerr and Deguise 2004, LeDee et al. 2021, Abrahams et al 2023). It is the role of the Services to follow the best available science without economic interests clouding judgement and this proposed rule revision will reduce the efficacy of the ESA.

Thanks,
Reilly Jackson

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to voice my firm opposition to the four proposed amendments to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations under review. Each proposal would, individually and collectively, undermine the ESA’s capacity to avert extinctions, facilitate species recovery, and conserve essential ecosystems for both wildlife and human communities.

1. Removing default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)

The ESA is designed to take preventive action before species crises occur. The 4(d) rule, backed by decades of scientific research, proves that early, precautionary protections reduce recovery costs and prevent further declines. Eliminating these automatic protections would cause unnecessary delays, requiring individual rulemaking and exposing vulnerable species to avoidable harm. This contradicts the preventive intent of the ESA and will result in higher ecological and financial costs long-term.

2. Making it harder to list species by allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis

The ESA mandates that listing decisions rely solely on the best available scientific data, not economic impacts. Factoring in economic considerations would undermine the law’s intent, delay protections, and place species on the brink of extinction. Ignoring projected threats, like habitat loss and climate change, disregards conservation science, threatening species before declines become evident. Weakening these criteria will likely result in preventable extinctions.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and limiting the definition of “harm”

Habitat loss is a primary cause of biodiversity decline. Reducing critical habitat designations undermines recovery efforts. Narrowing the definition of “harm” excludes habitat degradation, reversing legal and scientific precedents. This weakens inter-agency consultations, increases biological risks, and conflicts with the ESA’s recovery goals.

4. Opening new loopholes that allow agencies or special committees to bypass ESA protections

Creating mechanisms for agencies to override ESA protections, even with foreseeable extinction outcomes, conflicts with the ESA’s purpose. These loopholes encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decisions away from science-based analysis, disproportionately impacting imperiled species like Florida panthers and gray wolves.

The collective impact of these proposals:

These rules, if enacted, would weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation, delay protections, reduce habitat conservation, increase extinction risks, undermine cooperation, and raise recovery costs. The ESA, preventing 99% of listed species from extinction, is effective due to its grounding in science and early action. These proposals contradict those principles.

In a time of significant global biodiversity loss, the United States should reinforce, not weaken, its most effective wildlife protection law.

Request

For these reasons, I urge the agencies to rescind all four proposed rule changes and maintain the existing, scientifically grounded regulatory framework.

Thank you for considering this comment.

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. The Section 7 consultation process is a cornerstone of the ESA, and the process impacts every listed species under the ESA; thus weakening section 7 puts species survival at risk in contradiction to the purpose of the ESA. Raising threshold for impacts and/or ignoring cumulative or climatic effects is dangerous to the survivals of species, and not supported by Science. Climatic impacts and landscape scale consequences need to be included in consultations in order to be consistent with the law.

ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation. Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law, and importantly, it strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.

Federal agencies such as NOAA Fisheries, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Bureau of Reclamation frequently consult under ESA Section 7 when operating dams, managing river flows, or authorizing water diversions, as each agency has differing areas of expertise. These consultations have led to actions like fish passage improvements, spill operations, and habitat restoration. It is important for innumerable marine and aquatic species, such as salmon and Southern Resident orca in the Pacific Northwest, to require consultations.

Federal water-management agencies, including the Bureau of Reclamation and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, consult to ensure water projects and river operations do not reduce habitat or food availability for the migrating whooping cranes and other listed species that rely on rivers and wetlands. Without this requirement to consult, agency actions could disrupt their habitat and food resources and we could lose these species forever.

Maintaining or improving of ecosystems that can result from section 7 consultations, is not just important to individual threatened or endangered species, but all species that use an ecosystem, including people (e.g. the health of fisheries, the maintenance of areas where people live or vacation, etc.). The 2019 rules to which the present rule change is equivalent, were criticized by the courts and by scientist as inconsistent with ESA’s conservation mandate; hence are in contradiction to the stated purpose of the Endangered Species Act and not supported by science; so the stronger 2024 protections should be maintained.
title: Comment from Padgett, Marianne

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

text: Allowing economic interest to be the priority goes directly against the ESA’s essential purpose of making decisions based on the best scientific data available, not on cost or political pressure. Uphold the integrity of the ESA by keeping decisions rooted in science, maintaining strong habitat protections, and saying no to these rollbacks.  Our future depends on keeping these protections secure.
title: Comment from Hoover, Karen

text:
Strong interagency cooperation is necessary to ensure consistent enforcement, science-based decisions, and accountability. Weakening coordination increases loopholes, conflicting standards, and preventable harm to protected species.
I oppose any rollback or weakening of the Endangered Species Act. Reducing
protections will result in fewer safe places for wildlife, increased habitat loss, and long-term harm to ecosystems that also support clean water, food security, and fire resilience for human communities.
The ESA has been
overwhelmingly successful, preventing extinction in approximately 99% of listed species. Weakening these protections prioritizes short-term profit over the long-term survival of species and ecosystems we all depend on. Once species are prematurely delisted, we repeatedly see a cycle of overharvest, inadequate population data, and increased mortality from hunting, poaching, vehicle strikes, and habitat encroachment. This "yo-yo"
cycle puts species like wolves and grizzly bears at continued risk.
True conservation requires precaution, accurate science, and strong habitat protections, not regulatory leniency that favors exploitation over ecological integrity.

title: Comment from Kurtz, Rebecca

text:
To whom it may concern,

I respectfully submit this public comment in opposition to the proposed changes to Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations, as outlined in the Department’s press release dated November 19th 2025. I urge the reconsidering changes to the following rules, which, if finalized, would undermine longstanding protections for wildlife and habitats that have successfully prevented extinction for hundreds of species.

Reinstating outdated definitions of “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” will severely limit federal agencies' responsibilities to protect listed species during project reviews. Section 7 consultations have prevented many destructive projects or led to mitigations that preserved habitat, protected breeding grounds, or safeguarded water flows for fish. One such success story is of the Florida Panther in which Section 7 was utilized to help steer development of wildlife crossing protecting the species. The changes proposed would allow damaging projects to move forward without full review. Conservationists and legal experts warn that agencies could now “greenlight actions without fully assessing the impact on threatened and endangered species”. Without robust consultation, road projects may lack wildlife crossings, dams may disrupt salmon runs, or development may fragment panther corridors in Florida.
