title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
Federal agencies must work together to ensure infrastructure projects do not jeopardize endangered wildlife. But this new rule change would weaken that cooperation, posing a big problem for species like the Canada lynx, whose habitat is threatened by the expansion of roads and housing developments.

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

title: Comment from Winne , Deborah

text:
I live in Oregon, right along the Columbia River. I see the river everyday. I know that in that river are thousands of trout, salmon, and sturgeon which are so important to the ecosystems of the PNW. Salmon are central to so many other species here, especially the Orca, or Killer Whale. Salmon are overfished by humans and have a hard time replenishing the population because of the multiple dams in the rivers Oregon, Washington, and Idaho. Those dams prevent adult fish from returning to their native waters to breed and hatch eggs. Many of the large dams in the Columbia prevent salmon from returning to the smaller rivers that feed into the Columbia, such as the Willamette, the Sandy, and most important, the Snake River. Furthermore, dams cause river temps to rise, so when the young salmon are
venturing to the ocean from the tributaries, they are at risk of dying in warming river temps. Climate change also has a large play in this, but saving salmon can be helped by tearing down the man useless dams along the Columbia. We are endowed by God to be stewards of the land, rivers, forests, and mountains. We are endowed by God to be stewards of the thousands of beautiful animals that live in the United States. So many of our lawmakers and stewards from generations before us understood this and made laws to protect our beautiful lands and animals from the dangers that stood to overtake them, especially when capital is in play. We are not meant to tear up this country and destroy it, we are meant to keep it beautiful and safe, especially when it comes to the balance of nature created by God.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

I am writing to oppose the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act’s Section 7 interagency consultation regulations. Section 7 is the backbone of the ESA because it ensures that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. Weakening this process undermines the Act’s most important preventive safeguard.
The proposed changes would limit the consideration of cumulative, long-term, and climate-related impacts by narrowing what qualifies as an effect that is “reasonably certain to occur.” This risks excluding well-supported scientific evidence and allows harmful federal projects to proceed without full and informed review. title: Comment from Lovice, Leanne

text:
My name is Nathaniel Hawley. I am a citizen with a B.S. in Wildlife Conservation and Management, and I am submitting this comment because section 7 consultation rules shape whether projects actually avoid jeopardy and avoid destroying or adversely modifying critical habitat in the real world.

I oppose this proposed rule revising the interagency cooperation regulations at 50 CFR part 402. The proposal is explicitly framed as rolling back the 2024 section 7 regulations and replacing them with the 2019 framework, with only limited exceptions, plus additional edits on concepts like the environmental baseline and what is “reasonably certain to occur.”

First, the proposal rescinds the 2024 changes that allowed “offsetting” reasonable and prudent measures in incidental take statements and reverts to the pre-2024 approach. I understand the legal argument being made, but the practical effect is obvious: it reduces the Service’s ability to ensure that authorized take is paired with measures that actually compensate for harm to listed species. In a world where projects are moving faster than recovery, this reads like lowering the bar at exactly the wrong time.

Second, the proposal reinstates and expands a framework that can narrow what effects even get analyzed by leaning hard on proximate-causation style concepts through “reasonably certain to occur” factors. The text emphasizes screening out consequences that are remote in time, geographically remote, or reachable only through a lengthy causal chain, and it adds considerations like remaining state or local administrative discretion and whether the action agency lacks the ability to prevent the consequence due to limited statutory authority. That combination creates a predictable incentive to argue that foreseeable harms “don’t count” because they are indirect, complicated, or partly outside the action agency’s control. The outcome is fewer impacts analyzed, fewer impacts addressed, and more risk pushed onto species already hanging on.

Third, the proposed edits to “environmental baseline” matter because baseline framing can decide the whole consultation. The proposal clarifies baseline as the current condition “as would reasonably be expected to occur” without the consequences caused by the proposed action. If this is implemented in a way that treats degraded conditions as the accepted starting point, it will normalize decline and make it easier to conclude actions are acceptable so long as they do not look dramatically worse than an already broken status quo. This is managed loss.

I am frustrated because section 7 is supposed to be the safety net that prevents federal actions from pushing species closer to extinction, not a process that gets engineered to be easier for agencies and applicants. I am asking you to withdraw this proposed rule and retain, at minimum, the 2024 improvements rather than reverting broadly to the 2019 framework. If you move forward anyway, you should keep a clear, enforceable ability to require measures that meaningfully address incidental take, and you should ensure the “reasonably certain to occur” approach is applied in a way that captures foreseeable indirect effects using the best available science instead of providing a checklist for excluding them.

Respectfully,
Nathaniel Hawley

text: I am a nature lover and actively care for wildlife in my profession. I am from Arizona. I have spent my life loving, learning about, and protecting all wildlife, but especially endangered species. I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the definitions of  “effects of the action”, “environmental baseline”, and  “reasonable and prudent measures” under the Endangered Species Act. “Effects of the action” makes terminology more vague and, therefore more difficult for those trying to enforce the utmost penalty of the ESA of 1973 if someone breaks the rules. The “environmental baseline” terminology undermines the severity of the original language. The change of “consequences” to “impacts” does not accurately describe the situation. “Consequences” inherently has a connotation with weight to it to further the importance of the “environmental baseline,” and “impacts” does not accurately describe the trajectory, as it can be positive or negative leaning (no urgency behind the word). Lastly, the terminology “reasonable and prudent measures” describes the potentiality of “incidental takes”. One of the strongest points of the ESA (1973) is that “incidental takes” are prevented altogether. Adding this term would weaken the argument that the ESA (1973) prevents “incidental takes” of species from the environment. I urge you to maintain a strong science-based interpretation of “effects of the action”, “environmental baseline”, and “reasonable and prudent measures” by withdrawing these damaging proposed changes.
title: Comment from Brown, Jennifer

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

changes would make it easier to delist and harder to relist Americas gray wolves, opening the door for increased vulnerability, more fragile populations, and inadequate recovery that is driven by political decisions rather than best available science.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. This set of regulatory rollbacks would dismantle the Endangered Species Act and drive hundreds of imperiled animals and plants closer to extinction. Taken together, these proposals would significantly weaken protections for climate-impacted species and species newly listed as threatened, while making it easier to sideline science in favor of short-term industrial interests.

Critical to the success of the ESA was the assurance that federal agency actions do not undermine endangered or threatened species or harm critical habitat. Through consultation and cooperation among federal agencies, actions that could (1) jeopardize species’ survival and recovery and (2) destroy or degrade critical habitat could be avoided. The new regulations greatly limit the consultation process and impact both imperiled species and the critical habitat they rely on. This would make it more challenging for USFWS and NMFS to prove that actions requested by other federal agencies would negatively impact listed species and critical habitat. This would exclude many indirect, cumulative, or climate-driven effects from being considered.

Section 7 is crucial to ensuring that other agencies’ projects such as oil drilling, mining, dams, and timber sales, don’t further endanger wildlife. The Section 7 consultation process has been instrumental to the Act’s remarkable success in preventing the extinction of imperiled animals and plants.

These revisions are a direct attack on the ESA specifically and on wildlife in general. They are neither aligned with the law’s record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it’s enaction, the Endangered Species Act has been extraordinarily successful, sparing 99 percent protected species from extinction. In addition, the ESA has garnered widespread and overwhelming support among the U.S. public, regardless of political affiliation, socioeconomic status, or geographic location.

The need for species protection is ongoing, despite the success of the ESA in it’s current form, increased threats from development and climate change are ever present. Full implementation and enforcement of the Endangered Species Act in it’s current form is imperative.

These regulatory changes must be retracted, imperiled wildlife and their natural habitats depend on the ESA for survival.

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

text:
RE: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044 - Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation Regulations

I strongly oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7.

CONSULTATION AMONG AGENCIES IS ESSENTIAL. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken that process.

RISKS OVERLOOKING CUMULATIVE, INDIRECT, AND CLIMATE-DRIVEN IMPACTS. The rule narrows key definitions, including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur.” Narrowing those definitions risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, those indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

OFFSETTING MEASURES ARE ESSENTIAL. The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

CONCLUSION. The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. The revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the agency to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

COMMENTS ON THE 4 PROPOSED RULES

ENORMOUS SUCCESS OF THE ESA. The ESA is one of the most impactful and successful environmental laws in American history and is a global model. Since its passage in 1973, more than 99% of the species under its care have been saved or are on their way to recovery. To achieve that success, ESA listings have been guided by science, not by politics.

84% OF AMERICANS SUPPORT THE ESA. Professor Vucetich’s research, “Support for the U.S. Endangered Species Act Is High and Steady Over the Past Three Decades,” confirms that public backing for the ESA has remained consistently high (around 84% support) and stable from 1996 to 2025. Opposition to the ESA has remained low (about 12%). Support for the ESA is strong and consistent among Americans in urban, suburban, and rural areas. The research underscores that public support relies on the ESA being guided by science to protect species.

CORPORATE PROFITS AT THE EXPENSE OF WILDLIFE/ECOSYSTEMS. Looking at all 4 proposed rules, it’s clear their purpose is to significantly weaken the ESA for the benefit of developers. The proposed rollbacks are similar to those of the first Trump administration: their aim is to make it easier for industries to get away with harming endangered species and their habitat in pursuit of corporate profits.

Most Americans are, however, unwilling to sacrifice our natural world for the sake of corporate profits. Most Americans think we can do it all: we are a great nation because we can innovate to protect endangered species AND to promote economic prosperity.

IMPACT OF WILDLIFE EXTINCTIONS ON HUMAN LIFE. More than a million of the Earth’s species face the possibility of extinction caused by climate change, pollution, habitat loss, and exploitation. Even species that are not yet on the brink will face huge population declines. The extinction crisis is depleting fisheries, wiping out the pollinators that support our food supply, and making our rivers, wetlands, and forests disappear. Mass extinctions put not only species but also whole ecosystems at risk.

Humans are not isolated from the natural environment. What happens to other creatures and to ecosystems also affects our existence. We have no idea how catastrophic the mass extinctions of wildlife will be for humanity.

As Chief Justice Warren Burger pointed out, it’s vital to protect diverse species because “they are keys to puzzles which we cannot solve, and may provide answers to questions which we have not yet learned to ask.”

THANK YOU for the opportunity to express my opinion on the proposed ESA rule changes.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.
Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.
The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.
For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

text:
RE: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044 Endangered Species Act/Restrictions on Consultation

The Board of the Idaho Panhandle Chapter of Trout Unlimited (PCTU) has reviewed the proposed rule change regarding restrictions on consultation for species listed as “Threatened” or “Endangered” under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). PCTU has over 275 members, and our mission and values align with those of the national organization Trout Unlimited; namely the conservation of trout and salmon and the habitats they reside in, to ensure their enjoyment by current and future generations.

According to the information provided by USFWS, a change in the rule is necessary to ensure other federal actions, and in particular mineral and energy extraction projects, can be permitted in an expedient fashion. The information also suggests the proposed rule changes will provide higher degree of clarity in determining whether actions that will occur in the presence of listed species are under Federal purview, and a process for determining if those actions will negatively affect conservation and recovery of the species being considered.

PCTU members, and thousands of other anglers, have benefitted enormously from protections provided to bull trout, a “threatened” species which is widely distributed in our geographic area. Recovery efforts in our area have not only produced a state record (catch and release) bull trout, but have facilitated benefits for westslope cutthroat trout, kokanee, and other fisheries. In our part of Idaho, collaborative efforts to recover bull trout have engaged anglers, businesses, industries, Tribes and others to implement conservation measures made available through the nexus of listed bull trout. Bull trout are recovering, and petitions for ESA listing of westslope cutthroat trout early this century were obviated, in part because bull trout conservation helped bolster cutthroat trout populations.

We are concerned that modifying definitions and descriptions of how potential impacts will be assessed, and /or whether they fall under a federal nexus will not only create confusion but lower the bar for permitting or implementing actions that may be harmful to listed species. For example, replacing “best available scientific information” with “clear and substantial information” leaves the door open to ignoring the best scientific information. It is not evident what constitutes either “clear” or “substantial”, whereas the term “best available scientific information” can be assessed by virtue of literature searches , review of reports, and/or testimony from recognized experts. This proposed change has the potential to severely compromise the ability to effectively implement the letter and intent of the ESA.

The proposed rule also cites the fact that the “Handbook” for consultation, that was supposed to be developed to reduce confusion, has not been finished, thus it is time to move away from that. Why not prioritize finishing it? Overall we find the rationale for changing the rules at best non-compelling and confusing, and worse, likely to weaken the effectiveness of the Act. We are opposed to the rule change as proposed.

In Idaho and elsewhere, there are numerous examples of collaborative efforts to effectively implement ESA while finding paths forward for other land and water uses to occur in ways that are economically viable for those stakeholders looking to extract, develop, or otherwise modify natural resources. We strongly encourage any modifications to rules be focused on facilitating effective collaboration amongst stakeholders. We find no compelling evidence that is a centerpiece of the proposed changes. Please drop the rule as proposed, complete the handbook so all have the same "sheet of music", and revise to retain "best available science".

Thank you for considering these comments.
Charles E. Corsi, President
Panhandle Chapter Trout Unlimited

I oppose the new proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. It is offensive that this popular and necessary piece of legislation has faced continued attack this year. These changes go against the law's original intent and leaves threatened and endangered wildlife at risk of extinction. The American people have been adamant, time and time again, in expressing that native flora and fauna are worth protecting.The four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) diminish the regulation required to continue valuable conservation work and will undo decades of conservation, leaving vulnerable species without protection.

Eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Removing the phrase “without reference to possible economic or other impacts of such determination” from the end of 50 CFR 424.11(b) goes against the intent of the Endangered Species Act as a whole. Putting our native species above profit is the fundamental point of the ESA. Development and destruction of habitat, whether outright or caused by secondary means, for private or commercial gain is the primary reason, aside from culling en masse, for species decline. The ESA intentionally includes the phrase “without reference to possible economic or other impacts of such determination” to make the intent of protection without exception for industry explicit. It is not possible to make the proposed revision without compromising the integrity of the ESA both in purpose and in function. Further, corporate profits have and continue to climb to record highs year after year. Sacrificing what the majority of Americans want protected for short term gains of industry is an insult to the American people and to the spirit of our country.

Changing the verbiage “The foreseeable future extends as far into the future as the Services can make reasonably reliable predictions about the threats to the species and the species' responses to those threats.” to “The term foreseeable future extends only so far into the future as the Services can reasonably determine that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are likely.” creates a loophole emanating from proving ability to ‘reasonably determine’ rather than allowing ‘reasonably reliable predictions’ which is the limit of scientific projection. I trust the designation of a species’ safety status can be considered a scientific process. Reasonably reliable predictions are what scientists use and as such is appropriate wording in this situation, changes would diminish clarity and invite contestation. Predictions cannot determine, but they are nonetheless the best decision making tool we have in the realm of scientific inquiry and application.

The proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Reducing the requirements of a species habitat to be considered critical is a mistake considering the already minimal range endangered and threatened species typically inhabit or can inhabit compared to their historical range. It is clearly another attempt to ignore the purpose of the ESA in an effort to allow profit seeking entities to take advantage for themselves that which belongs to all Americans.

We have undeniable evidence of the success of the Endangered Species Act - 99 percent of the species protected are extant. Climate change, pollution, and habitat loss continue to reduce viable habitat for all species. Because of this, we should be strengthening the ESA, but these proposed changes do the opposite. Curtailing interagency collaboration with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore the negative impact of development on imperiled species. Please stop making unpopular and damaging policy changes that destroy the fabric of our nation. I sincerely urge you to rescind the proposed changes completely and immediately.
title: Comment from Wunder, Megan

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular. There is no good reason to change these rules, only bad ones.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species. Reverting to flawed 2019 language undermines the enforcement of this popular and effective law in order to benefit a few corporations and individuals at the expense of our environment, endangered and threatened species, the critical habitat on which they depend, and every single American alive now and born in the future. The proposed changes to language seem minor, but would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Barbeau, Nicole

text:
I unequivocally oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump administration. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife, the habitat they depend upon for their survival, and the American people who enjoy the diversity of our nation's land and animals.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
Please do not move forward with this rule, we share our country with animals that can't defend themselves from human habitat destruction. The implementation of this rule will have ecological and cultural effects that will make future America unrecognizable.

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text: I object to the changes proposed by U.S. Fish and Wildlife to the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Greed is the underlying driving force for the proposed changes. I urge you to allow the ESA to remain in its current form to help ensure the survival of the species it protects, as it has done for 50 years. Rule changes that provide for prioritizing economic interests over science and biodiversity must be rejected. The proposed revisions aim to reduce regulatory burdens on industries like logging, mining, and energy. In essence, these proposed rule changes seek to streamline ESA Section 7 consultations by limiting the scope of federal agency review, which will have a very negative impact on the evaluation of projects for the harm they cause endangered species.

title: Comment from Adams, Luke

text:
Endangered and Threatened Species: Interagency Cooperation

Docket ID: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044

I am a native of the Greater Houston area in Texas. I graduated from Texas A&M University with a B.S. in Wildlife and Fisheries Sciences. I have over 9 years of experience working with, caring for, educating the public about, and participating in research on endangered and threatened species of wildlife. I currently work as an endangered species observer on dredging projects in U.S. waters. My job as an observer is mandated under Section 7 of the ESA, allowing the consulting agency that contracts me to work with the U.S. Army Corp of Engineers as well as dredging companies. My personal experience working on these projects and seeing the impacts on our local wildlife and ecosystems first-hand are the reasons I oppose any changes that would weaken Section 7 of the ESA. A single dredging project will impact thousands of bottom dwelling creatures such as flounder, skates, rays, crustaceans, mollusks, as well as bottom-dwelling fish like catfish. Dredging can also impact endangered and threatened species such as migratory birds living along shorelines, sea turtles and marine mammals foraging in coastal areas, and sturgeon. These projects also impact tourism as areas of beach will be restricted from the public and can deter folks from visiting and contributing to the local economy due to the unappealing scenery. Texans and non-residents spend billions of dollars annually birding, hunting, fishing, and wildlife watching along with other recreational activities. Texas also ranks 4th nationwide in seafood production, with commercial fishing bringing in over $200 billion annually. I strongly oppose the proposed changes to Section 7 as it will harm the seafood industry which millions of Americans depend on to feed their families. The Fish & Wildlife Service must maintain the stronger 2024 protections to safeguard wildlife and their habitats, or federal projects will proceed without full scientific review and cost coastal communities in the U.S. economic harm.

title: Comment from Christensen, Grace

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

title: Comment from Schles, Ken

text:
Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. As with most things, success is much more difficult when acting in a vacuum, and it would only create opportunities for one federal entity subverts the work of the other. The proposed changes would significantly weaken the interagency consultation process.

By narrowing key definitions, including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur," the rule creates risk where none previously existed. These risks would allow agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature and have significant negative outcomes for species. For many of these species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. While it isn't as obvious as "cutting down a tree = decline of species" type impacts, it is in many ways more important to address because of being less obvious. Fewer people who think about could lead to increased damage. Excluding these cumulative, indirect, or climate-driven impacts from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

Another dramatic negative of this proposal is the removal of offsetting measures. These have long been a vital tool for reducing harm when incidental damage cannot be avoided. In an ideal world, prevention is what should be striven for above all else. However, reality ensures this is impossible. Mitigating this through offsetting measures is therefore essential, and removing those measures further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are necessary for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. The goal should be that the species recovers to the point where our intervention is no longer needed, not through extinction, as these and other proposed rule changes clearly would prefer, but through revitalization. These revisions move consultation away from the statutory requirement that the ESA conserves. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species. These species are not only ecologically important but also important for their inherent value as living beings and should be protected.

text:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to comment specifically on the proposed revisions in docket FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044 concerning environmental baselines, habitat offsets, and the treatment of incidental take under the Endangered Species Act.
First, the proposal to prohibit the use of historic population levels when establishing environmental baselines is deeply concerning. Relying solely on current population levels implicitly treats today’s often-depleted populations as “normal,” while disregarding well-documented historical declines caused by habitat loss, overexploitation, and other human-driven pressures. This approach ignores essential ecological context and risks institutionalizing a “shifting baseline,” where each generation accepts diminished conditions as the standard. Effective species recovery requires understanding where populations were historically and why they declined, not just where they happen to be today.

Second, the proposed restriction on the use of habitat offsets undermines a critical conservation tool. Offsets allow for the protection or restoration of alternative habitats when existing habitat becomes degraded or unsuitable due to climate change, development, or other factors. Prohibiting offsets reduces flexibility in conservation planning and may limit opportunities for proactive recovery, particularly for species whose habitats are already fragmented or changing rapidly. Rather than strengthening species protection, this change would narrow the options available to support long-term resilience and recovery.

Finally, the proposal’s treatment of “incidental take” is especially troubling. Allowing incidental take to be excluded from consideration as detrimental to species recovery contradicts both common sense and conservation science. Any authorized level of harm or mortality must be evaluated in the context of a species’ overall status and recovery goals. Treating incidental take as inherently non-detrimental risks normalizing ongoing losses that, when accumulated over time, can significantly impair recovery efforts—particularly for species with small or declining populations.

Taken together, these changes would weaken the scientific foundation of the Endangered Species Act and reduce its effectiveness as a recovery-focused law. They prioritize administrative convenience over ecological reality and risk enabling further declines in already vulnerable species. I strongly urge the agency to reconsider these revisions and retain protections that reflect historical context, scientific evidence, and the long-term goal of species recovery.
Thank you for the opportunity to provide comment on this important matter.

text:
I respectfully submit this comment to oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency cooperation regulations under Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act (ESA). These changes risk weakening one of the most critical mechanisms of the ESA by reducing the effectiveness, scope, and rigor of federal consultation intended to prevent harm to listed species and their designated critical habitats.

Section 7 is a foundational component of the ESA. It requires federal agencies to ensure that their actions are not likely to jeopardize the continued existence of endangered or threatened species or result in the destruction or adverse modification of critical habitat. This consultation process is preventative by design and has been repeatedly recognized as essential for identifying, avoiding, and minimizing impacts before irreversible harm occurs. Weakening consultation standards undermines the statute’s core purpose of conserving imperiled species and the ecosystems upon which they depend .

The proposed rule would revise definitions and procedural requirements in ways that could narrow the scope of actions subject to consultation, reduce the use of best available scientific information, or expedite reviews at the expense of biological rigor. Such changes increase the likelihood that cumulative and indirect impacts to species and habitats will be overlooked. Scientific evidence consistently shows that habitat loss and degradation are the primary drivers of species endangerment, and Section 7 consultation is one of the few tools that directly addresses these threats across federal actions .

Strong, consistent consultation requirements also provide clarity and predictability for federal agencies, project proponents, and conservation partners. Maintaining robust Section 7 regulations helps avoid litigation, supports informed decision-making, and improves outcomes for both conservation and development by identifying conflicts early in the planning process. Diluting consultation requirements may create short-term administrative efficiencies but will ultimately increase ecological risk and long-term costs.

The ESA has an established record of success, with the vast majority of listed species persisting due to its protections, including the consultation framework under Section 7. At a time of accelerating climate change, biodiversity loss, and increasing pressure on natural systems, it is especially important to strengthen, not weaken, interagency cooperation and science-based review .

For these reasons, I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to reject any revisions that weaken Section 7 consultation standards and to retain strong, precautionary interagency cooperation regulations that fully uphold the intent and effectiveness of the Endangered Species Act.

text:
Dear Members of Congress,

I am writing to express serious concerns regarding the proposed rule FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, which revises Interagency Cooperation under Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act of 1973 (ESA). These changes would weaken the consultation process that requires federal agencies to evaluate and avoid actions that may jeopardize endangered or threatened species or degrade their critical habitat.

Revising key portions of Section 7 in this manner would be detrimental to the continued existence and recovery of Gray Wolves. The interagency consultation process is one of the ESA’s most important safeguards, ensuring that federal actions—such as infrastructure projects, land management decisions, energy development, and permitting—are reviewed for their potential impacts on imperiled species. Making consultation less protective increases the likelihood that harmful actions will be approved without sufficient analysis or mitigation.

The proposed changes risk removing essential federal agency considerations regarding whether an action may harm endangered or threatened species, including the Gray Wolf. By creating loopholes, reducing accountability, and allowing inconsistent application of protections, this rule undermines the precautionary approach that has been fundamental to species conservation under the ESA. Without strong consultation requirements, federal actions may proceed even when scientific evidence indicates significant risk to species survival or habitat integrity.

For Gray Wolves, weakened consultation increases the likelihood of habitat fragmentation, reduced prey availability, increased human-wildlife conflict, and population instability. Wolves depend on large, connected landscapes and coordinated management across jurisdictions. Federal actions that degrade habitat or disrupt recovery efforts can have lasting impacts on pack structure and long-term viability.

The implications of this rule extend well beyond Gray Wolves. Numerous endangered and threatened species rely on Section 7 consultations to prevent irreversible harm from federal activities. Species such as the Florida panther, Mexican gray wolf, red wolf, grizzly bear, sage grouse, Pacific salmon, sea turtles, and the North Atlantic right whale all depend on rigorous interagency review to address threats from development, transportation projects, water management, and energy infrastructure. Weakening consultation requirements increases the risk of cumulative impacts that drive continued decline, even when species are formally protected.

The Endangered Species Act has been effective because it emphasizes science-based decision-making, interagency accountability, and proactive harm avoidance. Diluting these principles under Section 7 undermines the law’s intent and reduces its ability to prevent extinction before it occurs.

I respectfully urge Congress to oppose regulatory changes that weaken interagency cooperation and consultation under the Endangered Species Act. Maintaining strong, enforceable consultation requirements is essential to protecting Gray Wolves, conserving other imperiled species, and ensuring that federal actions are consistent with the nation’s longstanding commitment to biodiversity conservation.

Thank you for your time, attention, and consideration of these concerns.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposal to remove the requirement that project proponents offset habitat losses under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

Allowing mitigation without requiring full offsets ignores the reality that partial or temporary measures often fail to replace the ecological value of lost habitat. For endangered and threatened species already under severe pressure, incremental habitat losses—even when “mitigated”—can accumulate and result in long-term population declines. Offsetting habitat loss is one of the most effective tools available to ensure that development does not come at the expense of species survival and recovery.

The Biden-era rule appropriately recognized that avoiding, minimizing, and offsetting impacts are all necessary components of effective mitigation. Removing the offset requirement weakens this framework and creates a net loss of habitat over time, directly contradicting the ESA’s conservation and recovery goals.

This proposal prioritizes short-term development convenience over long-term ecological stability and increases extinction risk for imperiled species. Habitat loss is the leading driver of biodiversity decline, and policies that allow permanent losses without full replacement undermine the purpose of the ESA.

I urge the agency to retain strong mitigation requirements, including habitat offsets, to ensure that permitted activities do not result in net harm to endangered and threatened species.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

As someone who values wildlife, ecosystem health, and science-informed public policy, I am deeply concerned about proposed changes that would weaken federal oversight and interagency cooperation under the Endangered Species Act.

Section 7 consultation is a cornerstone of the ESA. It ensures that federal agencies do not authorize, fund, or carry out actions that jeopardize imperiled species or destroy critical habitat. To whomever it may concern,

I am writing to express my strong support for the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and to urge you to maintain its protections for endangered and threatened species.

The ESA is important to me because I care deeply about the species Mystic Aquarium works with, including marine mammals, sea turtles, and other coastal and marine wildlife. These animals play vital roles in their ecosystems, inspire people through education and outreach, and are central to our research, rescue, and conservation programs. Protecting them helps preserve the biodiversity and health of our oceans and coasts, and ensures that future generations can experience and learn from these remarkable species.

I have worked as a volunteer for 17 years in Mystic Aquarium’s Animal Rescue Program, which has been rescuing, rehabilitating and releasing sick, injured and stranded marine animals along the Northeastern coastline since 1975. Every year, our team responds to animals harmed by threats that the ESA was designed to mitigate: entanglement in fishing gear, vessel strikes, habitat degradation, pollution, and climate driven events such as cold stunning. These incidents are not rare anomalies, but are daily realities. Many of the animals we treat are members of populations that remain extremely vulnerable, with slow reproductive rates and long recovery timelines. Even small regulatory shifts can have outsized impacts on their survival.

I am concerned that the proposed changes—such as removing recovery as a basis for delisting, allowing agencies to limit critical habitat protections, reducing mitigation requirements, and eliminating default protections for threatened species—could weaken safeguards for vulnerable wildlife. These changes could slow recovery efforts, increase stress on wild populations, and place additional pressure on the programs Mystic Aquarium supports.

Maintaining strong, science-based protections under the ESA is essential for giving these species a chance to recover and thrive, for supporting healthy ecosystems, and for ensuring that our shared natural heritage is preserved. I urge you to preserve the ESA’s current protections and continue to rely on science-driven decision-making.

Thank you for your attention to this important issue and for considering my comments.

Sincerely,
Laura Wyeth
Mystic Aquarium Animal Rescue Program Volunteer

However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Upon signing the Endangered Species Act, President Nixon was quoted as saying, "Nothing is more priceless and more worthy of preservation than the rich array of animal life with which our country has been blessed." Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

Extinction is forever. Nothing is more precious than our one planet that we share. In all decision-making, we must consider the legacy we leave behind for our children, nature, and the Earth.

In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed regulatory changes to the Endangered Species Act referenced in this docket.

The Endangered Species Act is one of the most successful and scientifically grounded conservation laws in U.S. history. Its core strength lies in decisions based on the best available science, precautionary protections for threatened species, and enforceable safeguards for critical habitat and interagency consultation. The proposed changes would undermine these foundations.

Specifically, I am concerned that these revisions would:
•Weaken protections for threatened species by limiting or delaying application of Section 4(d) safeguards;
•Narrow or complicate the designation and protection of critical habitat, even when habitat loss is a primary driver of extinction;
•Reduce the effectiveness and accountability of interagency consultation under Section 7;
•Introduce unnecessary ambiguity that benefits short-term development interests over long-term species recovery.

As a Florida resident, I have seen firsthand how strong ESA protections are essential for species such as the Florida panther, manatee, sea turtles, and other imperiled wildlife already facing intense pressure from habitat loss, climate impacts, and expanding development. Weakening ESA regulations will increase extinction risk, shift costs to states and taxpayers, and invite further litigation rather than providing regulatory certainty.

Congress designed the ESA to err on the side of preventing irreversible harm. These proposed changes move in the opposite direction and are inconsistent with the statute’s purpose, scientific consensus, and public interest.

Weakening ESA protections is particularly dangerous in fast-growing states like Florida, where development pressure already outpaces conservation and recovery efforts.

I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to withdraw these proposals in full and maintain robust, science-driven ESA regulations that prioritize species recovery and habitat protection.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.
title: Comment from Kanter , Eustacia

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed legislation and any related actions that would weaken the Endangered Species Act.
The Endangered Species Act has functioned for more than fifty years as a science-based safeguard against extinction. Altering its core processes, particularly the scientific consultation framework, undermines the integrity of decisions meant to protect species already facing severe ecological pressure. Replacing evidence-driven evaluation with political or economic considerations puts both wildlife and ecosystems at unnecessary risk.

Slowing the listing of imperiled species while accelerating the removal of protections contradicts the purpose of the Act. Recovery from endangerment is not linear, and premature delisting increases the likelihood of population collapse rather than long-term stability. These changes favor speed over accuracy and weaken accountability.

Transferring management authority to states while species remain federally listed is also deeply concerning. Wildlife does not conform to state boundaries, and inconsistent protections create gaps that exploitation can easily exploit. Federal oversight exists precisely because national coordination is essential for effective conservation.

These proposals come at a time when federal agencies responsible for implementing the Endangered Species Act are already experiencing significant staffing and resource reductions. Weakening the law while simultaneously reducing enforcement capacity compounds the threat and increases the likelihood of irreversible harm.

The Endangered Species Act has prevented extinction for the vast majority of species under its protection and has helped preserve ecosystems that provide clean water, agricultural stability, and climate resilience. It is one of the most effective and publicly supported environmental laws in the United States, with broad bipartisan approval.

I urge the government to reject any legislation or regulatory changes that erode the scientific foundation, enforcement strength, or national scope of the Endangered Species Act. Protecting imperiled species and their habitats is not optional, it is a responsibility to current and future generations.

It is difficult to view these changes as anything other than an intentional weakening of a law that has worked. The Endangered Species Act is not failing; it is being deliberately undermined to accommodate short-term interests that benefit from fewer limits and less oversight. Calling this process “reform” does not change the reality that it reduces protections, sidelines science, and shifts risk onto species that already have no margin left.
