text:
As a born and raised Texan, I feel very protective of our country's natural spaces and the creatures that live in them. We have a shared fondness for our deer, fowl, and fish, certainly, but also the creatures big and small that have lived here as long as we have, if not longer. Part of good environmental stewardship is understanding that ecosystems are complex and intricately woven. To that end we should take the preservation of each of its component parts very seriously. Experience has shown us, both in our own country and across the world, that loss of even just a few keystone species can cause a cascade of environmental damage that is much harder to fix than it is to prevent. We must be proactive, we must be cautious, we must be zealous in maintaining our natural spaces.
The Endangered Species Act, environmental protection policies broadly, are expressly premised on the notion that our natural resources are an innate good and of an innate value that is worth preserving so that future generations may all have a chance to experience the unique grandeur and bounty of America's wilderness. This premise is directly undercut by such proposals among these 4 bills like allowing for the consideration of economic costs or benefits when determining listing status or protections for potentially Endangered or Threatened species. If such considerations are to be allowed we then resign ourselves to the inevitability of losing our natural spaces as the projected cost of leaving land undeveloped, resources unextracted, becomes greater and greater.
Other sections claim changes for clarity, or to put more specific bounds on terms like "foreseeable future." Others seemingly seek to allow greater autonomy among states in presiding over the protection of their own ecosystems and species. In principle I don't disagree, but in my estimation these are not arguments made in good faith, but rather nicely painted words that intend to obfuscate a desire to side-step federal protections and, again, undermine the efficacy of the Endangered Species Act.
To my eyes, all 4 of these bills disagree with the foundational premise of Environmental Protection as a legal concept, as stated before: the natural bounty of America is inherently valuable to the degree that it should be preserved indefinitely for each subsequent generation. To loosen and "clarify" sections of the relevant rules as in these proposals, to me, shows a willingness to instead consume more than our fair share of our country as it becomes convenient to do so, leaving less to use and less to experience for those who come after us. I personally find this unacceptable and contemptible.
I strongly urge all 4 proposals be rejected.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I'm outraged to learn that the Trump administration is trying to dismantle our most successful conservation law: the Endangered Species Act.

Since its passage in 1973, this landmark act has prevented the extinction of roughly 300 species — and more than 99% of the species under its care have been saved or are on their way to recovery. This incredible law has also protected millions of acres of forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans.

The proposed rollbacks will be devastating if finalized. They'll strip vital protections from our nation's most vulnerable species and pave the way for widespread habitat destruction — all in the name of profiteers, polluters, and special interests.

The Endangered Species Act works, and it has for decades. It’s the reason bald eagles, alligators, gray whales, and other iconic species are still around today. We should work to *strengthen* the Act — not weaken it.

I stand with most Americans in supporting the Endangered Species Act and the strong protections it provides to the United States’ most endangered animals and plants. I strongly oppose rollbacks to the Act and urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA Fisheries to stop this attempt to dismantle it by withdrawing the administration's destructive proposals immediately.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

text:
I am submitting this comment because biodiversity, healthy ecosystems and conservation of species matter deeply to me.
As a scientist who lives in Australia and regularly sees the effects of habitat loss, I am concerned about weakening protections for imperiled species. I see the effects of ecosystem restoration and how policy can positively impact biodiversity and endangered species in my country, such as increasing protection for the Australian night parrot, once thought to be extinct.
Conservation is known to protect and restore populations of endangered species in the States, such as with the California Condor, and I care about science-informed stewardship of the wildlife in the USA. The accelerating loss of species is one of the greatest environmental challenges of our time. Losing biodiversity threatens cultural values, economic stability and society’s wellbeing.

The Endangered Species Act works because it centers science and the public interest—not political pressure or economic and industry influence.
Science tells us what species need to survive; values determine whether we choose to protect them. These rules shift decision - making away from both. Science also tells us the impacts of loss of species - trophic shifts and a run-on effect that causes harm to even more species, and eventually us.

The proposed changes would allow industry considerations to outweigh both biological need and scientific reality - both of which are proven to support conservation.

Specifically, my concerns with the new proposed changes are:
- Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4): Removing automatic protections from newly listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed.

- Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)): Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide.

- Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)): Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening ecosystem health. If economic interests weigh more than essential habitat, entire ecosystems are at risk, not just wildlife species.

- Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7): Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife. 

Federal oversight is often the only check on state wildlife systems that are already heavily shaped by industry interests. These rollbacks reduce public accountability at a time when most Americans - and members of the public around the world - support stronger environmental conservation protections. The public wants these species to remain protected, why doesn't industry and government? A democratic, science-based process requires transparency and meaningful review.

I urge the agency to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s strong, science-based protections. Strengthen, not weaken, federal safeguards so states and industry cannot sidestep responsibility to protect imperiled wildlife. I ask you to uphold the intent of the ESA: preventing extinction and ensuring future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems. Endangered species deserve more than a political process designed to let them fade away.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

title: Comment from Frischie, Stephanie

text:
I’m deeply concerned by the proposed rollbacks to the Endangered Species Act—these changes threaten the very foundation of wildlife recovery in my home state of Washington. Rather than weakening protections, we should strengthen the ESA, which has already proven critical to our region’s ecological and economic well-being.

Recovery of Salmon, Steelhead, and Bull Trout
Federal ESA protections, in partnership with state grants, have funded habitat restoration projects across Washington—like the $50 million+ in grants awarded in 2024 to restore riparian zones, reduce sedimentation, and improve fish habitat for salmon, steelhead, and bull trout. In August 2024, a court ordered removal of the century-old Electron Dam on the Puyallup River, citing ESA violations. This win will reopen critical spawning habitat for Chinook salmon, steelhead, and bull trout. [rco.wa.gov] [earthjustice.org]

Forest Protection Plans & Riparian Conservation
Through an innovative 50-year Habitat Conservation Plan—endorsed by USFWS and NOAA Fisheries—roughly 2.6 million acres of working forest in Washington have implemented streamside buffers, protecting ESA-listed species while allowing sustainable forestry. This plan exemplifies how federal-state-private cooperation can succeed. [wfpa.org]

Protection of Iconic Wildlife
ESA safeguards have enabled recovery efforts for gray wolves, southern resident orcas, western pond turtles, Canada lynx, and Pacific martens across Washington. Weakening the Act’s habitat or “blanket” protections risks undoing decades of progress. [cascadepbs.org], [seattlemag.com]

Efficiency and Outcomes
Contrary to criticism of bureaucratic slowdowns, the ESA’s Section 7 consultations in Washington typically conclude within two weeks, and formal consultations within about 60 days—far briefer than critics suggest.

The proposed regulatory changes—reducing “blanket” protection for threatened species, narrowing critical habitat designation, and injecting economic considerations into listings—would significantly erode these proven recovery outcomes and complicate coordinated federal-state efforts. [cascadepbs.org], [wildlife.org]

Washington has already witnessed the tangible benefits of a robust ESA. Weakening it now risks reversing restoration of salmon runs, rebuilding wildlife corridors, and strengthening forest conservation. We cannot afford to degrade the science-based framework that has kept species from extinction, revitalized ecosystems, and supported our communities.

Preserving and reinforcing—not dismantling—ESA protections is essential to safeguarding Washington’s natural heritage and ensuring continued recovery for the species that define our region.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
1.The ESA is one of the most successful conservation laws in history, preventing extinction for over 99% of listed species; weakening its implementation directly threatens that success.

3. The proposed changes reframe science-based consultation as a bureaucratic “burden,” subordinating wildlife protection to short‑term industrial and energy interests.

4. Narrowing what counts as “effects of the action” makes it easier to dismiss climate, water, and habitat impacts that scientists know are driving extinction.

5. Removing offsetting tools undercuts flexible, practical ways to reduce harm to species while still allowing many projects to proceed responsibly.

6. Courts have already seen extensive litigation over the 2019 rules; reviving them invites more lawsuits, wasting public resources and creating uncertainty for agencies and businesses.

7. Americans across urban, rural, and suburban communities overwhelmingly support strong endangered species protections; this rule ignores that long‑standing public consensus.

8.By making consultation weaker and more convoluted, the rule shifts risks and costs onto coastal and tribal communities that depend on healthy ecosystems and species.

9. The proposal is driven by executive orders focused on deregulation and energy expansion, not by new science showing species are safer or habitats more secure.

10. At a time of accelerating biodiversity and climate crises, federal rules should reinforce, not erode, our obligation to recover at‑risk species and safeguard the ecosystems that sustain us all.

text:
I am submitting this public comment to express my opposition to any revisions within the proposed rule titled Endangered and Threatened Species: Interagency Cooperation that would weaken, narrow, or reduce the effectiveness of interagency consultation and cooperation under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

Interagency cooperation is a foundational pillar of the ESA. Section 7 consultation exists to ensure that federal actions do not jeopardize the continued existence of endangered or threatened species or result in the destruction or adverse modification of critical habitat. Any changes that reduce the rigor, scope, or enforceability of this process undermine the very purpose of the Act.

I am particularly concerned about provisions that:
•Limit when or how federal agencies must engage in consultation
•Allow agencies to self-determine impacts without adequate oversight
•Shorten timelines in ways that compromise scientific review
•Reduce transparency, accountability, or public participation
•Weaken protections for designated or proposed critical habitat

Effective interagency cooperation ensures that decisions are informed by the best available science and that environmental considerations are meaningfully integrated into federal planning. Weakening consultation requirements increases the likelihood of irreversible harm to species and ecosystems, often shifting costs to future generations, local communities, and taxpayers.

The ESA’s consultation framework is not a bureaucratic burden—it is a preventative mechanism. It helps agencies identify alternatives, avoid conflicts, and reduce litigation by ensuring that federal actions proceed responsibly and lawfully. Rolling back these safeguards may create short-term efficiencies, but it does so at the expense of long-term ecological stability and legal certainty.

In an era of accelerating biodiversity loss and climate disruption, the need for strong interagency coordination is greater than ever. Federal agencies must work together—not in silos—to uphold conservation responsibilities and protect the natural systems that sustain human life and economic resilience.

I urge you to reject any revisions that weaken interagency cooperation under the Endangered Species Act and instead maintain robust, science-based consultation processes that protect endangered and threatened species and their habitats.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit this comment and for your consideration of the long-term public interest.

Respectfully,
Michaela Purvines
Evergreen Colorado

text:
Re: Public Comment on Proposed Revisions to 50 CFR Part 402 (Interagency Cooperation Under Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act)
Docket No.: FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044

Dear Administrative Record:

I submit this comment in my personal capacity as a concerned citizen regarding the proposed revisions to 50 CFR Part 402, which governs interagency cooperation and consultation under section 7 of the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

Section 7 is the ESA’s primary accountability mechanism for federal agencies. It ensures that federal actions do not jeopardize the continued existence of listed species or destroy or adversely modify designated critical habitat. Because federal activities shape land use, infrastructure, water management, and energy development nationwide, the consultation framework established in Part 402 is indispensable to the Act’s effectiveness.

While I understand the desire to improve administrative efficiency and clarity, several aspects of the proposed revisions risk narrowing the scope and substance of consultation in ways that are inconsistent with the ESA’s preventive and science-based purpose.

My comments focus on three interrelated concerns.

1. Consultation Must Fully Account for Indirect and Cumulative Effects

The proposed revisions would reinstate regulatory language that narrows how the “effects of the action” are evaluated, particularly with respect to indirect and cumulative effects.

In contemporary ecological contexts, species decline rarely results from a single action in isolation. Habitat fragmentation, altered flow regimes, climate-driven stressors, and incremental development interact over time. Section 7 consultation exists precisely to ensure that federal agencies confront those realities rather than segment them into artificial silos.

A consultation framework that discounts reasonably foreseeable indirect or cumulative effects risks transforming Section 7 into a procedural formality rather than a substantive conservation safeguard.

2. The “Environmental Baseline” Should Not Be Used to Normalize Ongoing Degradation

The concept of the environmental baseline plays an important role in consultation, but it must be applied with care. Treating existing degradation as a neutral starting point can unintentionally institutionalize decline.

If consultation evaluates new federal actions against an already impaired baseline without accounting for the trajectory of decline, the result is a regulatory ratchet that allows incremental harm to accumulate without meaningful review.

Section 7 should function as a brake on continued degradation, not as a mechanism that accommodates it.

3. Consultation Should Remain a Substantive Conservation Tool, Not a Streamlined Checkpoint

The ESA requires federal agencies to “insure” that their actions avoid jeopardy and adverse modification. That language reflects a substantive duty, not merely a procedural one.

To the extent the proposed revisions emphasize speed, predictability, or reduced scope at the expense of biological rigor, they risk weakening this duty. Efficiency has value, but not when it undermines the careful analysis needed to prevent irreversible harm.

In an era of accelerating environmental change, consultation must remain adaptive, precautionary, and grounded in the best available science.

Conclusion

50 CFR Part 402 determines whether Section 7 operates as Congress intended: as a meaningful safeguard ensuring that federal actions do not push imperiled species closer to extinction. I urge the Services to retain a robust consultation framework that fully accounts for indirect and cumulative effects, resists normalization of ecological decline, and preserves the ESA’s substantive conservation mandate.

Regulatory certainty should flow from clear scientific standards and transparent analysis—not from narrowing the lens through which federal impacts are evaluated.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit this comment.

text:
Founded in 1936, The Wildlife Society is an international network of over 11,000 leaders in wildlife science, management and conservation who are dedicated to excellence in wildlife stewardship. The mission of The Wildlife Society is to empower wildlife professionals to advance conservation through science, community, and professional excellence. As a professional scientific and educational organization, The Wildlife Society refrains from advocacy where it cannot ground its views on science. 

The Arizona Chapter of The Wildlife Society (AZTWS) was established in 1968 and is dedicated to promoting sound management and conservation of Arizona’s wildlife resources. Membership is open to all professionals, students and laypersons interested in wildlife research, management, education, and administration. Our chapter works to maintain communication among wildlife professionals, encourage communication between those professionals and the public, support continuing education through grants, hold workshops and regional meetings, encourage student involvement in the wildlife profession, and actively participate in shaping management and conservation policy through letters, public statements and resolutions.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) have announced four proposed rule changes that will narrow the definitions of critical habitat, alter criteria for listing or delisting a species, and change regulations with regard to Section 7 under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). We, the AZTWS, are committed to ensuring that decisions under the Act remain transparent, grounded in rigorous scientific analysis—including data from states, tribes, and peer-reviewed climate research—and free from economic or political influence. We further advocate for adequate federal funding and staffing to support efficient listing and recovery processes, collaborative conservation actions, and transparent rulemaking that strengthens the protection, restoration, and management of critical habitats essential to the recovery of endangered and threatened species.

As stated above, E.O. 14154, “Unleashing American Energy,” issued January 20, 2025, directed all departments and agencies to review agency actions that impose an undue burden on the identification, development, or use of domestic energy resources, and, as appropriate and consistent with applicable law, consider suspending, revising, or rescinding agency actions that conflict with this national objective. Section 7 of the ESA (titled Interagency Cooperation) mandates cooperation between federal agencies and USFWS to ensure federal actions don't harm listed species or their critical habitats, primarily through a consultation process where agencies assess potential "jeopardy" or "adverse modification" and implement conservation measures, making it central to federal project planning and environmental compliance. When federal agencies propose actions that include development of energy resources, and that project may affect listed species, they need to simply conduct a consultation with the USFWS and develop a Biological Opinion. Under these proposed regulatory revisions, offsets would no longer be available to the Services for incorporation into reasonable and prudent measures, and the USFWS would only incorporate avoidance and minimization measures within the action area as part of the reasonable and prudent measures. Consultations under Section 7 of the ESA can be an extremely creative process incorporating conservation measures listed in a Recovery Plan. Wildlife biologists with the USFWS, in cooperation with the Federal action agency, have the best expertise to develop reasonable and prudent measures within Biological Opinions.

AZTWS requests reinstatement of broader, scientifically supported definitions of “effects” that include indirect and cumulative impacts. We ask the USFWS and NOAA to allow inclusion of mitigation or offsets when supported by clear, reliable evidence, and we recommend requiring climate-driven effects, landscape-scale habitat trends, and cumulative threats be incorporated in all baselines and effects analyses.

Thank you for your considerations to our comments on the USFWS four proposed rule changes.

Regards,

Holly Hicks, President

Arizona Chapter of The Wildlife Society

text:
I am writing this to express my strong opposition to the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. The changes would be detrimental to the health of our environment and nation as a whole. As someone who has enjoyed the outdoors--whether it be fishing, camping, hikinng, or participating in ecotourism trips--it pains me to think that the decades we have spent in reviving keystone species and restoring some of the most beautiful landscapes in our country should now be threatened and all that work undone.

Since its introduction 51 years ago, the Endangered Species Act has been instrumental and fundamental in our efforts at environmental conservation and the preservation of our wildlands that have been the true great inheritance for all Americans. We cannot weaken it now. We should not be question or introduce ambiguity in terms like "recovery" or what constitutes "critical habitats."

By eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule", this increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

I strongly urge our representatives to oppose these changes as polls have shown that the majority of the public supports wildlife conservation, even amongst hunters, fishermen, ranchers, etc. We all recognize that our future and well-being, as well as those of our posterity, depends on our ability to defend and preserve our wildlands.

I am writing this to express my strong opposition to the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. The changes would be detrimental to the health of our environment and nation as a whole. As someone who has enjoyed the outdoors--whether it be fishing, camping, hikinng, or participating in ecotourism trips--it pains me to think that the decades we have spent in reviving keystone species and restoring some of the most beautiful landscapes in our country should now be threatened and all that work undone.

Since its introduction 51 years ago, the Endangered Species Act has been instrumental and fundamental in our efforts at environmental conservation and the preservation of our wildlands that have been the true great inheritance for all Americans. We cannot weaken it now. We should not be question or introduce ambiguity in terms like "recovery" or what constitutes "critical habitats."

By eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule", this increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

I strongly urge our representatives to oppose these changes as polls have shown that the majority of the public supports wildlife conservation, even amongst hunters, fishermen, ranchers, etc. We all recognize that our future and well-being, as well as those of our posterity, depends on our ability to defend and preserve our wildlands.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed revisions to the Section 7 consultation regulations at 50 CFR Part 402. This proposal would weaken critical protections for endangered and threatened species by rolling back important improvements made in 2024 and reinstating problematic provisions from the 2019 regulations. The changes would undermine the effectiveness of interagency consultation, reduce transparency, and make it harder to protect species from harmful federal actions.

The proposal to eliminate offsetting reasonable and prudent measures represents a significant step backward for species conservation. The 2024 rule appropriately recognized that minimizing the impacts of incidental take sometimes requires compensatory mitigation to ensure species survival. While the Services claim that terms like offset and mitigation lack statutory basis, the Endangered Species Act explicitly authorizes regulations necessary and appropriate to minimize take impacts. Compensation for unavoidable harm is a well-established conservation tool that helps ensure federal actions do not drive species toward extinction. Eliminating this option will leave some species inadequately protected when direct avoidance measures prove insufficient.
The proposed reinstatement of Section 402.17 and its reasonably certain to occur standard creates confusion and tension with the statutory requirement to use best available science. The phrase clear and substantial information suggests a heightened evidentiary burden beyond what the Act requires. This could lead federal agencies to exclude important indirect and cumulative effects from consultation simply because causal chains involve multiple steps or uncertainty exists. Climate change impacts, habitat fragmentation effects, and other complex consequences affecting species often involve some uncertainty but are nonetheless real and significant. The proposed standard could provide agencies cover to ignore these effects.

The modifications to the environmental baseline definition are unnecessary and risk introducing inconsistency into consultation practice. The 2024 definition clarified that federal agencies must consider impacts from their ongoing activities and existing facilities when those remain within agency discretion to modify. This common-sense principle ensures agencies account for their continuing role in species threats. The proposed reversion to emphasizing ongoing activities while downplaying discretion could allow agencies to avoid responsibility for modifiable impacts simply by characterizing them as pre-existing baseline conditions.

The proposal lacks adequate justification for its sweeping changes. The Services cite executive orders directing agencies to reduce regulatory burdens and ensure consistency with statutory text, but provide insufficient analysis of how the 2024 rule departed from the Act or imposed undue burdens. The consultation process existed for decades under various regulatory frameworks, and the 2024 improvements reflected lessons learned and best practices developed through experience. Discarding recent improvements without thorough evaluation risks returning to approaches that proved inadequate.

The timing and process for this rulemaking raise concerns about adequate consideration of impacts. The Services provide only a brief comment period during the holiday season and offer limited analysis of how the changes would affect ongoing consultations and species conservation. Federal agencies, project applicants, and conservation practitioners need clear, stable regulatory frameworks to plan their work. Constant regulatory changes create confusion and uncertainty that ultimately harm both protected species and those seeking to comply with the law.

These proposed changes would particularly harm species already facing severe threats from climate change, habitat loss, and other stressors. The stricter causation standards and elimination of offsetting measures could leave species vulnerable to death and injury from federal actions that consultation is meant to prevent. This contradicts the fundamental purpose of Section 7, which requires federal agencies to ensure their actions do not jeopardize species survival or destroy critical habitat.

I urge the Services to withdraw this proposed rule and maintain the 2024 consultation regulations that better serve species conservation while providing workable processes for federal agencies. If the Services proceed despite these concerns, they should at minimum retain the offsetting measures provisions, maintain the 2024 environmental baseline definition, and remove the problematic clear and substantial information language from Section 402.17.

It also removes requirements for mitigation or offsets when federal agencies cause unavoidable harm to species or habitat. Both of these proposed regulations weaken the Endangered Species Act.

FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048 expands the circumstances under which areas may be excluded from critical habitat for economic or national security reasons.

Instead, USFWS would create species-specific 4(d) rules for each threatened listing - a slower and more resource-intensive process that will significantly increase species listing times and delay protections for many species.  The proposed rule increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. Trying to compare economic benefits to the threat of species extinction is of dubious value. Who derives these economic benefits? How sustainable are these economic benefits? Since the onset of the industrial revolution in the late 1700s extinction rates are at least 50 times (perhaps 1000 times) greater than the background extinction rate through geologic time. Humans are driving species to extinction without understanding what it is we are destroying.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled plants and wildlife.

text:
Personal Public Comment Opposing the Proposed Changes to the Endangered Species Act

A letter to the government and public servants elected to represent the health and safety of its constituents, including the biodiversity upon which we all depend.

For more than five decades, the Endangered Species Act has stood as one of America’s most effective tools for preventing extinctions. Its strength lies in a commitment to clear, science-based decision-making and an understanding that safeguarding at-risk species is a matter of national importance. The proposed revisions would erode the Act’s foundational principles. By introducing uncertainty, weakening longstanding protections, and narrowing the pathways through which vulnerable species receive attention and support, these changes would make it harder for species to persist and recover.

I oppose the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act (ESA), published on November 21, 2025. I am are deeply concerned about the cumulative impacts the proposed changes would have on the conservation of imperiled species and their habitats.

The proposed revisions mirror changes introduced in 2019 that were ultimately withdrawn because they undermined the ESA’s purpose. Then, and now, the proposed measures run afoul of scientific expertise and legal precedent – and go against strong public, bipartisan support for a robust, science-driven ESA that preserves our shared natural heritage.

Revised interagency consultation provisions under Section 7 would reduce the rigor and transparency of federal decision-making. Several proposed revisions narrow what qualifies as an “adverse modification” of habitat or restrict when federal agencies must consult with the Services. These changes are likely to result in fewer consultations, weaker analyses, and diminished habitat protections. Given that habitat loss is a leading driver of insect decline, it is essential that Section 7 processes remain robust.
The ESA is an essential safeguard at a time when biodiversity loss is accelerating. Weakening the Act’s regulatory foundation would have long-lasting consequences for wildlife, ecosystems, and the human communities that depend on them. For the reasons summarized in this letter, I respectfully request that the relevant U.S. agencies (FWS, DOI, NOAA, DOC) withdraw all proposed revisions. title: Comment from Murphy, Emily

text:
I object to the proposed rule changes.
These changes are not minor technical adjustments or routine administrative cleanups. They represent a fundamental shift in how the federal government interprets and applies the law that has, for more than fifty years, stood between countless species and extinction.Since its passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act has operated on a simple but powerful premise: when a species is at risk of disappearing forever, decisions about its fate should be guided by the best available science, not political convenience or short-term economic pressure.The law has prevented the extinction of roughly 99 percent of the species placed under its protection and has driven some of the most celebrated conservation recoveries in American history.One of the most consequential changes would dismantle the long-standing “blanket 4(d) rule,” which automatically extends key protections to species listed as threatened. Under the current system, newly listed threatened species receive safeguards similar to endangered species unless the Fish and Wildlife Service deliberately crafts a tailored rule.Removing that default flips the logic of protection, forcing conservationists to argue for safeguards species by species, often while populations continue to decline. In a time when climate change and habitat loss are accelerating, delay can be fatal.Other proposed revisions would narrow how critical habitat is designated and considered, making it easier for federal agencies to approve projects that degrade or fragment the very places species need to survive and recover.Habitat loss is already the single greatest driver of extinction, yet these rules would make it more difficult to protect unoccupied but ecologically essential areas—precisely the landscapes species may need as climate conditions shift. This approach treats conservation as a static exercise, ignoring the reality that wildlife must move, adapt, and expand to survive in a rapidly changing world.Equally troubling are changes to the interagency consultation process, the mechanism that requires federal agencies to ensure their actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed revisions would weaken consultation standards, reduce accountability, and make it easier for agencies to conclude that harmful projects pose no meaningful risk.This is not an abstract concern. From roads and pipelines to dams, mines, and timber sales, countless federal actions hinge on these consultations. Weakening them increases the likelihood that irreversible harm will be approved with minimal scrutiny. Again, I object to this proposed rule revision and others that would irrevocably endanger the process by which biodiversity is supported and ensured.
title: Comment from Donnelley, Myra

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from McCloe, Lynn

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act because they weaken the law’s foundational purpose and place already vulnerable species at even greater risk of extinction. Collectively, the four proposed rules (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, and FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) dismantle long-standing conservation measures that have demonstrated both effectiveness and broad public support.

First, removing the blanket 4(d) rule for threatened species would substantially increase the likelihood of further population declines. This rule has long served as a clear, efficient, and legally sound mechanism for extending baseline protections while still allowing the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to tailor species-specific exceptions when appropriate. Eliminating it would not only reduce protections but would also create additional administrative burdens by requiring the agency to draft individual 4(d) rules for every newly listed threatened species.

Second, the proposed changes to critical habitat regulations would significantly weaken both the listing process and habitat designation. Allowing federal lands to be excluded from critical habitat protections based on economic considerations would prioritize short-term development interests—such as energy projects, grazing, and logging—over the ecological needs of imperiled species. At a time when many listed species occupy only small remnants of their historical range, narrowing the scope of critical habitat designation would further compromise their ability to survive and recover in the face of ongoing habitat loss, pollution, and climate change.

Third, introducing economic factors into decisions about whether to list a species undermines a core principle of the ESA: that listing determinations must be based solely on the best available scientific and commercial data. This shift invites political and economic pressure into what has historically been a science-driven process, weakening the credibility and effectiveness of species protections.

Fourth, weakening interagency consultation requirements threatens to erode meaningful oversight of federal actions that may affect listed species. Efforts framed as “streamlining” consultation risk sidelining the expertise of wildlife agencies and reducing their role in evaluating and minimizing project-related impacts on threatened and endangered species.

Taken together, these proposals revive approaches that previously sought to limit the scope and effectiveness of the ESA. Such changes are inconsistent with the law’s proven success and with public support for wildlife conservation. Since its passage, the ESA has prevented the extinction of the vast majority of species under its protection, and public polling continues to show strong bipartisan support for the law.

The challenges facing imperiled species have not diminished over time. On the contrary, increasing development pressures and accelerating climate impacts make strong, science-based implementation of the ESA more critical than ever. For these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw these proposed regulatory changes and uphold the Endangered Species Act’s essential role in conserving America’s wildlife and the habitats upon which they depend.
title: Comment from Manjarrez, Bridget

text:
I strongly oppose any effort to weaken the Endangered Species Act. The ESA is one of the most effective conservation laws in the world and remains a critical safeguard against the ongoing extinction crisis. Diluting its protections is not a minor regulatory change. It is a decision to allow preventable extinctions to occur.

The proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, including FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044 and FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048, represent a disturbing pattern of attacks on imperiled species and the habitats they depend on. They ignore well-established science, undermine decades of conservation progress, and prioritize short-term economic interests over the survival of plants and animals that cannot advocate for themselves.

The proposed rules would:

***Deny newly listed threatened species automatic protection from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take,” leaving species such as the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, greater sage grouse, and monarch butterfly exposed even after they are officially recognized as at risk of extinction.

***Narrow the definition of “critical habitat” by excluding unoccupied but historic habitat. These areas are often essential for recovery, especially as climate change and habitat loss make current ranges increasingly unviable.

***Weaken federal agency accountability, making it easier to approve destructive activities like logging, mining, and drilling even when those actions place protected species in direct harm’s way.

***Most troubling, the proposed rules would inject “economic considerations” into decisions about whether species and their habitats deserve protection. This approach fundamentally distorts the purpose of the ESA. The Act was intentionally designed to be science-based and precautionary, not a cost-benefit analysis where extinction can be justified because protecting wildlife might interfere with development or reduce profits. Allowing economics to override biological reality is not pragmatic. It is morally and legally indefensible.

***Alter critical habitat designation standards to make it easier to exclude areas from protection based on industry claims of economic impact, further stacking the deck against species already struggling to survive.

At a time when more than one million species face the risk of extinction globally, weakening the ESA is reckless and dangerous. Biodiversity loss threatens food security, clean water, ecosystem stability, and the health of human communities. We are not separate from the natural world, and sacrificing species and ecosystems for short-term economic gain ultimately harms us all.

This is a moment that demands stronger protections, not rollbacks. I urge the administration to withdraw these proposed rule changes and uphold the Endangered Species Act as Congress intended, guided by science, focused on recovery, and committed to preventing extinction rather than negotiating its price.
title: Comment from van der Lee, Aniko

If you care about the economy, level of habitable land, general human wellbeing, etc, you will not pass this.

I appeal to you in this way: this is not about saving species for the sake of saving species. This is about saving species because they benefit us. Their benefit to their ecosystems is, in turn, benefit to us as humans.

Let's look at the wolves in Yellowstone. Wolves were once eradicated from Yellowstone. In their absence, their main prey source, elk, became overpopulated and overgrazed. The overgrazing caused soil to become unstable and fall into/change the course of/pollute rivers. Overgrazing took away habitat for other animals like insects, which pollinate crops, for one. With no grass for grasshoppers to eat, there are no grasshoppers for mice to eat, and no mice for coyotes to eat, and so on. With no coyotes to keep the mouse population in check and no habitat for mice, they invade our homes. When wolves were reintroduced, the ecosystem rebalanced itself. Also, Yellowstone draws in millions as a tourist attraction every year, including just for the wolves themselves.

Saving the wolves of Yellowstone, in turn, not only improved the ecosystem, but also fixed habitats and made them more beautiful and thus more appealing to come to from far away. Wolves and bison both live there, both endangered, and draw in tourists to see these rare animals. Books, games, documentaries, and more all have been born from Yellowstone, generating more money.

This is just one example using charismatic fauna. Endangered plants can be keeping soil in place to combat eroding shorelines. Even insects are important. Every single organism is important and every single organism benefits its ecosystem in some way (including mosquitos). We are at the mercy of the ecosystem; if we allow it to be destroyed, it will destroy us as a consequence. Hunting wolves to extinction led to pollution and unstable soil, both of which directly impact humans.
Repealing the ESA shows that you know nothing about the world we share and you act brashly with no thought for future generations or that you care about what you propose. To propose such a change, you should be deeply informed about the topic in question which it is clear that you aren't because, if you were, you would not have proposed it in the first place.

So, I implore you, even if you have no value for biodiversity, consider the socioeconomic impact, environmental damage, and how endangered animals benefit us as humans.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.
By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.
The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.
The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.
As a retired federal natural resource specialist and now researcher, I know that in natural resource management we absolutely need to look at the big picture and how all the components of the ecosystem interact. This requires temporal context, including looking for cumulative impacts over time. We absolutely also need to address the impacts of climate change, which are real. Do not make these proposed changes; future generations will suffer!

text:
I am opposed to these proposed changes, and any changes that would weaken or limit the enactment of the Endangered Species Act. A vast majority of Americans want a strong Endangered Species Act, and want it strongly enacted, and fully funded. I am concerned the proposed changes would weaken key provisions requiring interagency consultations whenever a federal activity could harm threatened and endangered species.

The Section 7 regulations of the ESA currently require the designation of critical habitat for threatened and endangered species in nearly all cases through interagency consultations. Federal agencies are therefore prohibited from funding, permitting, or taking actions that destroy or adversely modify critical habitat. Through consultation with the National Marine Fisheries Service for marine and anadromous species, or the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service for all other species, federal agencies avoid causing serious harm to the recovery of threatened and endangered species by not destroying or degrading critical habitat.

The proposed changes to key provisions including the changes to the definition of “destruction or adverse modification” of critical habitat, will significantly weaken the interagency function of the Act. Also, the narrow definition of "effects of the action" and "environmental baseline" of critical habitat essential for the imperiled species’ recovery will eliminate provisions allowing consideration of important threats, particularly from long-term cumulative climate-driven impacts. Habitat loss and degradation due to climate shifts and other human activities remain the primary cause of species loss and endangerment, so effective protection of adequate critical habitat (including unoccupied habitat) is therefore essential for successful for the recovery of endangered and threatened species.

I feel that this revised definition of adverse modification is fundamentally inconsistent with the intent of the ESA and the will of the majority of Americans for its enactment. The definition should absolutely include cumulative climate-driven impacts to ensure the survival and recovery of imperiled species. I would like this proposed revision to be withdrawn in favor of a definition of adverse modification that incorporates cumulative threats of climate at a biologically meaningful landscape scale in all baseline effect analyses.

I also believe the inclusions of offsets into RPMs should be retained in these sections as appropriate measures for consideration.

text:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to any efforts to weaken or alter the Endangered Species Act (ESA). For more than fifty years, the ESA has served as one of the most effective conservation laws in the United States, protecting vulnerable species and preserving the ecosystems upon which both wildlife and people depend.
The ESA is grounded in sound science and long-term stewardship. It recognizes that once a species is lost, it cannot be recovered. Altering the Act to prioritize short-term economic or political interests over ecological integrity risks irreversible damage to biodiversity, natural resources, and environmental stability. Healthy ecosystems provide essential services—clean air and water, pollination, flood control, and climate resilience—that benefit communities and economies nationwide.
Weakening protections for endangered and threatened species also undermines the precautionary principle that has guided responsible environmental policy. The current framework ensures decisions are based on the best available science rather than shifting political or commercial pressures. Any dilution of these standards increases the likelihood of extinction, ecosystem collapse, and costly remediation efforts in the future.
Additionally, the Endangered Species Act has demonstrated that conservation and economic development are not mutually exclusive. Many recovery efforts have succeeded while allowing responsible land use and innovation. Rather than altering the Act to reduce protections, resources should be directed toward improving implementation, funding recovery programs, and fostering collaboration among stakeholders.
For these reasons, I urge you to oppose any changes that would weaken the Endangered Species Act. Protecting our nation’s wildlife heritage is not only an environmental responsibility, but a moral obligation to future generations.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely, Michelle

text:
I am writing to oppose the proposed revisions to how the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service evaluates federal actions under section 7 of the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Section 7 is one of the ESA’s most powerful and effective safeguards, ensuring that federal agencies consult with the Service to prevent their actions from harming listed species or destroying critical habitat. Weakening this process would have serious consequences for species already facing mounting threats.

The proposed rule would significantly narrow the scope of impacts considered during a section 7 consultation. By directing the Service to disregard many indirect, cumulative, and climate‑driven effects, the rule would prevent the agency from fully evaluating the real‑world consequences of federal actions. Indirect and cumulative impacts—such as increased pollution, altered hydrology, or long‑term habitat degradation—are often the very factors that push species toward extinction. Excluding them from analysis undermines the scientific integrity of the consultation process and ignores the interconnected nature of ecosystems.

Climate‑driven impacts are especially critical to consider. As temperatures rise, precipitation patterns shift, and extreme weather events become more frequent, species are experiencing rapid changes to their habitats and life cycles. A consultation process that cannot account for these realities will fail to protect species from the threats they are actually facing.

These proposed changes would directly affect conservation efforts in Central Texas. For species like the Barton Springs and Austin Blind salamanders, which depend on stable groundwater conditions and are highly sensitive to changes in water quality and flow, indirect and cumulative impacts are often the most significant. Highway expansion projects by agencies such as TXDOT and CTRMA can alter recharge zones, increase runoff, and degrade spring habitats—even when the impacts are not immediate or direct. If the Service is no longer required to consider these effects during section 7 consultations, it will be far more difficult to secure meaningful protections for these salamanders and the fragile aquifer systems they rely on.

For these reasons, I urge the Fish and Wildlife Service to reject the proposed changes and maintain a comprehensive, science‑based approach to section 7 consultations. Protecting endangered and threatened species requires evaluating the full range of impacts—direct, indirect, cumulative, and climate‑driven—and the ESA’s implementation must continue to reflect that reality.

These landscapes have shaped my understanding of how fragile and interconnected our natural systems are, and I am deeply troubled by the proposed weakening of Endangered Species Act protections.
In coastal California, I've witnessed the delicate balance that supports species like the snowy plover and California least tern. At Lake Tahoe, I've seen firsthand how even small changes in habitat can ripple through an ecosystem. The clarity of that alpine lake depends on intact watersheds and healthy forests that provide refuge for species like the Sierra Nevada yellow-legged frog and countless others.
The current proposal to remove automatic protections for newly listed species is particularly concerning. When a species reaches the point of requiring ESA listing, immediate action is critical—not bureaucratic delays that could allow further decline during the most vulnerable period.
Similarly, eliminating consistent baseline protections for threatened species invites a patchwork approach that could leave wildlife unprotected in precisely the places where they're struggling most. The coastal and alpine environments I care about don't recognize administrative boundaries, and our protections shouldn't either.
I'm also concerned about changes that would expand the ability to exclude critical habitat based on economic considerations. Both the California coast and the Tahoe Basin face intense development pressure. Allowing economic interests to override habitat science would undermine the ecosystems that sustain not only endangered species but also the recreational opportunities and natural heritage that define these regions.
Weakening federal consultation requirements would further reduce accountability for projects that could harm imperiled wildlife. In California, where we've seen the consequences of habitat fragmentation and water management conflicts, strong federal oversight provides essential safeguards that complement state efforts.
I urge you to withdraw these proposed rule changes and maintain the ESA's foundation in biological science and comprehensive protection. The Act has succeeded because it prioritizes recovery over convenience. These proposed changes would reverse that priority at exactly the wrong moment in our biodiversity crisis.
