text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

I am writing to oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. I am an underwater photographer who works in both marine and freshwater environments, and I derive part of my income as well as a deep sense of purpose from healthy, functioning ecosystems. Through my work, I have spent years observing California’s kelp forests, headwater streams, and remote coastal and freshwater habitats. These are places whose survival often depends on strong federal protections when other pressures would otherwise push them toward collapse.
I have seen firsthand how fragile these systems already are. Kelp forests are declining under the combined stress of warming waters, altered food webs, and cumulative human impacts. Headwater freshwater ecosystems are especially vulnerable. Though often out of sight, they are critical to downstream rivers, fisheries, and communities. These are exactly the kinds of places the Endangered Species Act was designed to protect when short term economic interests threaten long term ecological health.
The proposed rule changes would undermine that purpose. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule for threatened species weakens protections at the stage when they matter most. Recovery depends on early and consistent safeguards. Forcing case by case determinations opens the door to delay, inconsistency, and political influence that the ESA was intended to prevent.
Similarly, narrowing the criteria for critical habitat exclusions under Section 4(b)(2) risks allowing economic considerations to outweigh the protection of essential habitat. A species cannot be protected without protecting the environment it depends on. When habitat is compromised, recovery becomes impossible, and the damage extends beyond individual species to entire ecosystems.
Limiting federal consultation under Section 7 further erodes accountability. Federal oversight is often the only effective check on state wildlife governance systems that are already heavily shaped by industry interests. Reducing the scope of review makes it easier for harmful projects to proceed without fully assessing their impacts on imperiled wildlife and the ecosystems that support them.
Taken together, these changes would hollow out the Endangered Species Act and leave it unable to meet its core mission. At a time of accelerating biodiversity loss and climate driven ecosystem stress, weakening one of our most effective conservation laws is a serious mistake.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Please accept the attached submission of 427 public comments in response to several proposed regulatory changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA), including proposed revisions to ESA Sections 4(b), 4(d), 4, and 7.

While many of these comments share similar language and concerns, each represents an individual comment submitted by a distinct member of the public. Several comments are further customized and personalized. Although these comments are transmitted together for administrative convenience, they should be reviewed, counted, and considered as individual public comments and not as a single consolidated submission.

Collectively, these comments express strong opposition to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s and National Marine Fisheries Service’s proposed revisions to the ESA. For more than fifty years, the ESA has been one of our nation’s most effective conservation laws, preventing the extinction of 99 percent of listed species. It is not broken. The proposed rules would undermine this success by elevating speculative or industry-driven economic considerations over the best available science and the survival and recovery of imperiled species.

Across the attached comments, individuals raise serious concerns that the proposed changes would:

Encourage the exclusion of critical habitat based on speculative or industry-provided economic information, contrary to the ESA’s science-based mandate and longstanding legal precedent;
Weaken listing decisions by improperly treating economic impacts as “commercial data,” despite decades of agency practice and court rulings to the contrary;
Delay or deny essential protections for newly listed threatened species by eliminating automatic take prohibitions under Section 4(d);
Narrow the scope of Section 7 consultations by restricting consideration of cumulative, foreseeable, and baseline impacts that are often decisive for species survival;
Limit recognition of climate-driven risks by unduly constraining the concept of the “foreseeable future”;
Undermine protections for distinct populations and recovery efforts by narrowing interpretations of “species” and restricting critical habitat to currently occupied areas.

As reflected in these comments, such changes would place already vulnerable species at heightened risk, including northern spotted owls, northwestern pond turtles, salmon and steelhead populations, wolverines, and wolves. In states like Oregon, where species face compounding pressures from habitat loss, climate change, and drought, the consequences of these revisions would be immediate and lasting.

The ESA’s strength lies in its consistent, science-based application and its clear focus on preventing extinction and promoting recovery. The attached commenters urge the Services to withdraw these proposals and to uphold the ESA’s longstanding, legally sound protections for wildlife and the ecosystems upon which they depend.

As a citizen of the United States, I take tremendous pride in our unique, awe-inspiring native wildlife species. These species are an integral part of my state and national identity, both for me and many others. The Endangered Species Act is a critical piece of legislation that has a proven track record of success for ensuring the protection of these species both for current citizens of the U.S. and for posterity, having prevented an estimated 291 species’ extinction and saved an estimated 99% of listed species (Greenwald et al. 2019 “Extinction and the U.S. Endangered Species Act”). In summary, the proposed changes would hinder the Endangered Species Act’s proven effectiveness and ultimately, lead to population declines of our beloved native species. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.
The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.
The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

Sincerely,
Dr. Danielle Tarbert, Diplomate American College of Zoological Medicine
title: Comment from Tarbert, Danielle

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text: The Endangered Species Act is one of the most effective, accountability‑driven conservation tools we have. title: Comment from Ziemba, Amy

text:
Species richness and healthy ecosystems are deeply and profoundly connected to human well-being in both a physical and emotional capacity, which is why I adamantly and vehemently OPPOSE all four proposed rules changes designed to weaken the Endangered Species Act. The ESA has helped to protect habitat that is enjoyed by all from hunters and nature enthusiasts to tourism industry and more.
Healthy, biodiverse ecosystems provide essential services such as clean air, clean water, pollination of crops, and natural disease regulation. For example, diverse ecosystems can reduce the spread of infectious diseases by limiting the dominance of disease-carrying species (often called the “dilution effect”), which directly benefits human health. Studies also show that people exposed to greener, more biologically diverse environments experience lower stress, improved mood, and reduced risks of anxiety and depression. Biodiversity-rich green spaces are linked to better psychological restoration than less diverse or degraded environments. This is why every species habitat we threaten with human development or industrial activity without the strictest protections in place impacts our own state of wellbeing. Protecting species also personally goes far beyond my own benefit as a human-being because I view the natural world as inherently valuable, independent of what benefits it brings to me, and I am certainly not alone. Most Americans are in support of stronger environmental protection and wildlife conservation measures.

All of this combined and more is why it is incredibly crucial to protect and uphold, even strengthen the ESA, especially in the era in which we now find ourselves. The scales have always been tipped well-against the natural world’s favor as species and their natural habitats don’t have the power of human industrial lobbyists, corporate money and extraction interests on their side, in fact those entities tend to all to often be in exact opposition and constant conflict with our environmental and ecological world. Look at any map showing the scale of habitat fragmentation and loss in our country over time. It’s only getting worse.
These proposed rules should be withdrawn to prevent weakening the Endangered Species Act and to keep its protections firmly based on science.
•Please withdrawal Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4): Removing automatic protections from newly listed species puts vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery can begin. These species may remain unprotected while recovery plans are delayed.
•Please withdrawal Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)): Removing the standard protections for threatened species would lead to uneven safeguards and slow recovery, even though these species need strong protection now.
•Please withdrawal Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)): Narrowing the rules for excluding critical habitat could let economic concerns outweigh habitat protection, putting ecosystems at risk—not just individual species.
•Please withdrawal Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7): Reducing federal review would allow harmful projects to move forward without fully considering their impact on endangered wildlife.
These proposed rule changes are not grounded in sound science, ecology, or a fair democratic process. Limiting public comment to just 30 days—timed right before the holidays—undermines meaningful public participation on changes of enormous consequence. After more than 30 years witnessing the devastation caused by habitat loss in my home region, I know how difficult it already is to protect wildlife. Weakening transparency and review only pushes us further in the wrong direction. I strongly oppose all four proposals, which together would dismantle the most effective law we have to protect wild species and wild places. Attacking the Endangered Species Act runs directly counter to the public interest. What is at stake is irreversible: once species and ecosystems are lost, they are gone forever. The ESA works. It should be upheld and strengthened—not weakened. Thank you.

Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Public Comment on Federal Register Docket FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation Regulations

I strongly oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency cooperation regulations under Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that would eliminate the ability of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service to require offsets for unavoidable impacts to habitat as part of reasonable and prudent measures in incidental take statements. Under the stronger 2024 rules, agencies could require project proponents to not only mitigate impacts but to offset habitat losses in a way that fully replaces the ecological functions lost to federal actions. Removing this requirement weakens a critical tool for ensuring that unavoidable impacts to listed species and their habitats do not further imperil already vulnerable populations.

Habitat loss remains the leading cause of species imperilment and extinction, and meaningful conservation depends on a mitigation hierarchy that first avoids, then minimizes, and finally offsets impacts if necessary. Allowing mitigation alone — without ensuring that lost habitat is replaced with ecologically equivalent habitat — undermines that hierarchy and shifts the balance in favor of development rather than conservation. This change risks accelerating declines of species that are already struggling to survive federal actions that alter or destroy critical habitat.

Further, weakening Section 7 protections runs counter to the ESA’s statutory purpose of conserving threatened and endangered species and the ecosystems upon which they depend. Robust interagency cooperation is essential to ensure that federal actions do not jeopardize the continued existence of listed species or result in the destruction or adverse modification of habitat. The proposed rollback of offset requirements would diminish regulatory certainty for species conservation and provide less incentive for project proponents to design actions that truly avoid and minimize harm to imperiled wildlife and plants.

For these reasons, I urge the Services to retain and strengthen the ability to require habitat offsets in incidental take statements, ensuring that unavoidable habitat losses are fully compensated, and that the ESA’s conservation mandate remains robust and effective.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Respectfully, Robin Jaffin
title: Comment from Jaffin, Robin

text:
I have significant concerns about the proposed changes to ESA consultation regulations. Removing “but that are not part of the action” from the definition of Effects of the Action diminishes clarity and limits consideration of indirect, cumulative, and interrelated impacts. I urge FWS to retain this phrase alongside the reference to §402.17.

I also oppose removing language in §402.14(i)(2) and §402.14(i)(3) that allows mitigation measures outside the project area. Offsite measures—such as noise barriers or habitat restoration—are often the most effective for minimizing take and supporting recovery. Eliminating this flexibility will harm conservation outcomes.

Regarding reinstatement of §402.17, I am concerned that proposed parameters for “reasonably certain to occur” are too narrow and will lead to harm. Sections 402.17(a)(4) and (b)(4) should be rescinded; limiting analysis only to activities the Services can prevent ignores cumulative impacts and undermines ESA’s mandate. Additionally, §402.17(b)(5) needs clarification to ensure consequences are analyzed at a scale and magnitude commensurate with the proposed action, including cases where the action exacerbates existing impacts.

Thank you for considering these comments. I urge FWS to maintain flexibility and clarity to ensure scientifically sound decisions that advance species recovery.

I am writing to oppose the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act Section 7 interagency consultation regulations. My perspective comes from hands-on experience with an animal science degree upcoming in spring of 2026, work experience in wildlife rehabilitation, field research, and rescue work, where I have directly interacted with species affected by habitat loss, fragmentation, and other environmental stressors.

In both research and rehabilitation settings, I have seen firsthand that species decline is rarely caused by a single, isolated action. Instead, it results from the accumulation of indirect, long-term, and often climate-driven impacts over time. text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Hills For Everyone (HFE) writes to oppose the proposed section 7 rule because it would materially weaken the consultation framework that safeguards listed species and their habitats. By reverting most interagency cooperation regulations to the 2019 baseline and narrowing concepts such as the “environmental baseline,” “effects of the action,” and “reasonably certain to occur,” the rule shifts emphasis away from precautionary, science‑based conservation and toward limiting federal responsibility, especially where other legal or administrative constraints exist.

First, redefining “environmental baseline” and re‑framing which activities and facilities are treated as outside a federal agency’s discretion risks undercounting the true cumulative impact of federal actions on already‑stressed ecosystems. By placing more impacts into the baseline and outside the “action,” the rule invites incremental degradation to be normalized rather than addressed through robust avoidance and minimization measures. In a highly fragmented, urban‑interface landscape like the Puente–Chino Hills, where listed species depend on fine‑scale habitat quality and connectivity, this underestimation of cumulative harm will accelerate biodiversity loss and undermine long‑term recovery prospects.

Second, reinstating and expanding the “reasonably certain to occur” framework, while simultaneously rescinding 2024 provisions that allowed for offsetting reasonable and prudent measures, narrows the range of foreseeable effects and available conservation tools during consultation. By emphasizing the limits of agency authority and treating many consequences as too remote or indirect to count, the rule will allow more federal projects, including energy, water, transportation, and other infrastructure actions, to proceed without fully accounting for foreseeable harms to listed species and critical habitat.
For our organization, which depends on strong, enforceable section 7 consultations to maintain viable populations of state and federally listed species and to restore ecological processes across the Puente–Chino Hills landscape, these changes would significantly weaken one of the most important statutory backstops for biodiversity conservation and conflict directly with Congress’s directive that all federal agencies “insure” their actions are not likely to jeopardize listed species or destroy or adversely modify their critical habitat.

We urge reconsideration of the proposed amendments and do not support the modifications as they will harm a scientific consultation process aimed at protecting listed species.

I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.
By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.
The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.
The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

title: Comment from Roeper, Nancy

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule.
The proposed rule is significantly flawed procedurally. The comment period for this proposed rule violates the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) and Executive Order (EO) 12866 on regulatory planning and review. The APA requires federal agencies to "give interested persons an opportunity to participate in the rule making through submission of written data, views, or arguments with or without opportunity for oral presentation." 5 U.S.C. § 553(c).
Section 6(a)(1) of EO 12866, which implements the rulemaking provisions in the APA, states that federal agencies "should afford the public a meaningful opportunity to comment on any proposed regulation, which in most cases should include a comment period of not less than 60 days."
The comment period for this proposed rule is only 31 days, from November 21 through December 22, 2025. A proposed rule of this importance should have a comment period of at least 60 days. The comment period for the proposed rule should be extended at least 29 days to comply with the rulemaking requirements in the APA and EO 12866. If the comment period is not extended, the proposed rule will be in violation of the APA, which prohibits federal agency actions that are arbitrary and capricious and otherwise not in accordance with legal requirements.
I strongly oppose the substance of this proposed rule, which would significantly weaken protection of threatened and endangered species and their habitat. The proposed rule would include a new definition for the term “environmental baseline” as the “condition of the listed species or critical habitat in the action area without the consequences caused by the proposed action.” The new definition would not account for pristine habitats that may have been degraded by past actions. The new definition also would not account for any impacts of proposed actions or the consequences of other activities that are caused by the proposed action. The new definition would thus unacceptably lower standards for appropriate habitat and normalize as the baseline suboptimal conditions usually caused by human activity. Accordingly, the proposed definition would not establish an appropriate baseline for protection of threatened and endangered species and would be inconsistent with the Endangered Species Act.

The proposed changes to the term “reasonable and prudent measures” would weaken the ability of participating agencies to fulfill the intent of the Endangered Species Act. Human activity has largely fragmented occupied habitats, and occupied habitats, far from being self-contained, are impacted by other areas in varying degrees of proximity. The proposed changes would preclude implementation of broader mitigation measures, which would decrease the effectiveness of any measures taken in occupied habitat and would preclude expansion of ranges to improve population size.

The proposal to reinstate § 402.17 is at best unnecessary and at worst would weaken the Endangered Species Act. The text in § 402.17(a) requiring “clear and substantial information” for a finding of “reasonably likely to occur” adds no value because “clear and substantial information” is not defined. In addition, the list of factors in § 402.17(a) regarding the definition of “effects of the action” are unnecessary and overly prescriptive. The following text on the consequences of the proposed action in  § 402.17(b) is not implementable because it contains no substantive metrics for decision-making other than the following vague and potentially spurious rationales that a consequence is not reasonably likely to occur: (1) The consequence is so remote in time from the proposed action under consultation that it is not reasonably certain to occur; (2) the consequence is so geographically remote from the immediate area involved in the proposed action that it is not reasonably certain to occur; or (3) the consequence is reached only through a lengthy causal chain that involves so many steps as to make the consequence not reasonably certain to occur.

No value is added by proposed § 402.17 because it contains no specific metrics and no guidelines for the level of evidence to be considered. As a result, this proposed revision would provide additional opportunities to challenge agency decisions, resulting in confusion, delay, wasted taxpayer dollars, and potential irreversible impacts on threatened and endangered species.

The proposed changes should not be adopted because they would weaken existing protections for threatened and endangered species, increase inefficiencies, and engender more legal challenges.

text:
strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

I oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation Regulations. title: Comment from Clemmens, Grace

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

title: Comment from Frantz, CJ

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

It is necessary that this proposed rule is NOT approved.

title: Comment from Clark, Cindi

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) Section 7 interagency consultation regulations. These changes would weaken one of the most critical safeguards preventing federal actions from causing irreversible harm to imperiled species and the ecosystems on which they depend.

Section 7 consultation is grounded in the best available science and is essential for ensuring that federal agencies do not jeopardize the continued existence of listed species or destroy or adversely modify designated critical habitat. The proposed revisions would narrow the scope of analysis, limit consideration of indirect and cumulative effects, and allow agencies greater discretion to avoid or minimize consultation. This undermines the precautionary, science-based framework that Congress intentionally built into the ESA.

These changes are particularly concerning given the accelerating biodiversity crisis and the increasing pressures of climate change, habitat fragmentation, and development. Weakening consultation requirements ignores the reality that species decline is often driven by the accumulation of multiple stressors over time. Failing to fully analyze these impacts increases the risk of extinction and places short-term administrative convenience above long-term ecological and economic stability.

The ESA has a proven record of preventing extinction while allowing responsible development to proceed. Section 7 consultations routinely result in project modifications—not prohibitions—that reduce harm, avoid litigation, and provide regulatory certainty. Rolling back these protections is likely to increase legal challenges, create confusion among agencies, and ultimately delay projects rather than streamline them.

I urge the agency to withdraw the proposed revisions and instead strengthen interagency consultation to reflect current science, uphold the intent of the ESA, and ensure that federal actions do not contribute to the permanent loss of our nation’s wildlife and natural heritage.

The question isn’t whether we can afford to protect endangered species. It’s whether we can afford not to.

text:
Proposed Revisions to Endangered Species Act Regulations — Habitat Migration and Climate Change
Submitted to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service / Department of the Interior

My name is Joanne Gold and I oppose the failure of the proposed revisions to adequately address habitat migration driven by climate change.

Climate change is already altering ecosystems through rising temperatures, shifting precipitation patterns, sea-level rise, and increased extreme weather events. As conditions change, species must be able to move to remain viable.

Limiting habitat protections to historically occupied areas ignores current scientific understanding of climate-driven ecological change. Static, backward-looking habitat protections prevent species from adapting to new conditions and effectively trap them in environments that may no longer support survival or recovery.

A modern implementation of the Endangered Species Act must incorporate forward-looking habitat protections that reflect ecological reality and climate-driven habitat shifts.

I urge the agency to explicitly account for habitat migration and climate change in ESA regulations.

Thank you for considering this comment

The criteria for delisting a species would be lowered, possibly removing protections before it would be warranted

To be clear, I strongly OPPOSE the Proposed Rule set forth in FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044. Great harm will result if this Proposed Rule is enacted. I do not believe that the benefits of this Proposed Rule outweigh the risks of degrading our environment.

Please take these comments into consideration when reviewing this Proposed Rule.

I hike, birdwatch, and generally enjoy the biological diversity of our environment here, which is represented by many threatened and endangered species.
I was very much in favor of the existing rules, and DO NOT want them to change.
Biological opinions should not include cost-benefit analyses. A species recovery is dependent on biological, regulatory, and environmental factors, and MUST NOT be swayed by economic factors. Habitat for threatened and endangered species is being lost at an alarming rate, and when destroyed for a project, it must be offset elsewhere or we will eventually end up with little or no habitat, and we WILL lose species. Please RETAIN the old rule and continue to offset habitat losses in addition to mitigating them.
Thank you for considering my comments.

I support the 2024 rule. Leave it in place

This attitude is dangerous and shortsighted, and is threatening and endangering not only individual species, but entire ecosystems (habitats) as well.

text: I strongly oppose the proposed changes to this CFR section to reduce the habitat mitigation requirements of the Endangered Species Act. title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.
title: Comment from Karasik, Marisa

text:
I appreciate the opportunity to submit comments on several proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act. Section 7 of the ESA currently mandates interagency cooperation with the intention of maintaining transparency and adhering to existing protections for species as outlined. Continuing to require interagency collaboration assists in upholding the law as well as imparting equal and shared responsibility to continue to provide struggling species with the laws, protections, habitats, and resources they need to recover and survive.

title: Comment from Voight, Carly

text:
I am submitting this comment today because I believe that we, as a country, have a duty to our wild lands and all the creatures living in them. Biodiversity and healthy ecosystems are important for our planet's future, and if we are to ensure that future we need to stick to science-based stewardship of our lands and animals. The Endangered Species Act works because it focuses on science, rather than political or economic influences. However, the proposed changes would allow industry considerations to outweigh what science says, and what our endangered species need. Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife. These proposed changes will undermine the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat. By narrowing the definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removing mitigation offset requirements, these changes will allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

President Theodore Roosevelt was a great pioneer of conservation, and through conservation hoped to preserve the natural wealth of the United States for the public, and not leaving it for the economic benefit of entrepreneurs and corporations. Our natural resources are not infinite; our forests and the creatures living within them are finite. We have already driven hundreds, if not thousands, of species to extinction across the world. The Endangered Species Act is one of the greatest pieces of legislation we have made in striving towards that goal of conservation, as it has helped safeguard and bring back from the brink iconic species such as the bald eagle, the American bison, the Florida panther, and the sea otter. In order to continue protecting these species, I ask you to continue to uphold the intent of the ESA: preventing extinction and ensure future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems. Most Americans support stronger environmental conservation protections; please strengthen, not weaken, federal safeguards for our most vulnerable species so that industries and states cannot sidestep responsibility to protect our wildlife.

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.
title: Comment from Mohler , Erykah

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Dugan, Katrina

text:
I spend much of my life outdoors, teaching, studying, and working within California’s ecosystems. I see firsthand how fragile many of these systems already are and how quickly damage compounds when protections are weakened. Because of this lived experience, I strongly oppose any effort to dilute the Endangered Species Act. The ESA is not abstract policy to me. It is one of the few tools that has consistently slowed biodiversity loss in real places, with real consequences.

The strength of the Endangered Species Act lies in its refusal to treat extinction as negotiable. It places biological reality ahead of convenience and recognizes that once species and habitats are lost, they cannot be recovered through economic compromise. Proposals that insert industry flexibility or political discretion into decisions meant to be guided by ecological science fundamentally misunderstand how ecosystems function. Nature does not respond to timelines, markets, or lobbying pressure.

Removing automatic protections for newly listed species creates an unnecessary and dangerous gap at the very moment when intervention matters most. Species are often listed only after years of decline. Any delay in protection increases the likelihood that recovery becomes impossible. Similarly, weakening protections for threatened species ignores decades of conservation science showing that early, consistent safeguards are far more effective than reactive measures taken after populations collapse.

Critical habitat protections are equally nonnegotiable. Habitat is the foundation of survival. Allowing economic considerations to outweigh the preservation of essential habitat does not merely threaten individual species but destabilizes entire ecological networks. These losses ripple outward, affecting pollination, water quality, soil stability, and climate resilience. As an educator, I teach that ecosystems are interconnected systems, not isolated assets that can be selectively compromised.

Limiting federal consultation and oversight further erodes accountability. In many cases, federal review is the only mechanism ensuring that wildlife protection is not subordinated to local or industrial interests. Reducing this oversight increases the likelihood that environmentally destructive projects proceed without fully acknowledging their long term consequences.

The Endangered Species Act reflects a societal commitment to responsibility, restraint, and stewardship. Weakening it sends the opposite message, that extinction is acceptable if it is economically convenient. I urge your agencies to abandon these proposed changes and reaffirm the ESA’s original purpose. Protecting imperiled species is not an obstacle to progress. It is a measure of whether progress is worth pursuing at all.

text: I am submitting this comment because I am an ethicist (PhD, 2019) and the lives of living beings, the preservation of their and our human ecosystems, and the wellbeing of the planet matters to me as a matter of values and personal morality. title: Comment from Ambrose, Elyse

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term.
