title: Comment from Mayne, Nicole

text:
1. Threatened Species Protections – Elimination of the Blanket 4(d) Rule

The blanket 4(d) rule is a long-standing, science-based policy that ensures newly listed threatened species receive immediate protections when they are most vulnerable. Eliminating this rule would create dangerous regulatory gaps, leaving species exposed to harm while species-specific rules are developed. These individualized rules are slow, resource-intensive, and highly susceptible to political pressure from industries seeking exemptions.

Species-specific 4(d) rules cannot replace broad baseline protections. The ESA requires decisions to be based on the best available science, not executive actions aimed at weakening environmental safeguards. The Fish and Wildlife Service should retain the blanket 4(d) rule to prevent unnecessary delays and further species decline.

2. ESA Section 7 Interagency Consultation Regulations

Section 7 consultation is the heart of the ESA. It ensures that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. Rolling back the stronger 2024 regulations and reinstating the weaker 2019 framework significantly undermines this essential safeguard.

The proposal raises the threshold for impacts considered “reasonably certain to occur,” excluding indirect, cumulative, and climate-driven effects that are well-supported by science. It also narrows the definition of the environmental baseline and limits the evaluation of cumulative and landscape-scale harms. These changes would allow harmful federal projects—such as oil and gas development, pipelines, dams, grazing permits, and timber sales—to proceed without a full and honest assessment of their impacts.

Climate change, habitat fragmentation, and cumulative loss are primary drivers of extinction risk and must be considered in Section 7 consultations. The proposed rollback reinstates provisions widely criticized by courts and scientists as inconsistent with the ESA’s conservation mandate. The Service should withdraw this rule and restore the stronger 2024 protections.

3. Critical Habitat Exclusion Rule – ESA Section 4(b)(2)

Reinstating the 2020 Critical Habitat Exclusion Rule improperly elevates economic and political considerations over the biological needs of imperiled species. The framework is biased toward excluding habitat, particularly for industry, energy development, ranching, and private landowners, even when scientific benefits of designation are substantial.

Habitat loss is the primary driver of extinction. Weakening critical habitat protections directly harms recovery prospects and contradicts the ESA’s purpose to conserve ecosystems upon which listed species depend. Exclusions must be based on clear scientific evidence, not speculative or inflated economic concerns. The Service should reject this proposal and ensure critical habitat decisions prioritize long-term conservation outcomes.

4. Listing and Critical Habitat Rules – 50 CFR Part 424

The proposed rollback of the 2024 Listing and Critical Habitat rules would narrow how the “foreseeable future” is interpreted for threatened species, make it harder to designate unoccupied critical habitat, and complicate listing, delisting, and climate impact considerations.

The ESA requires use of the best scientific and commercial data available. Many species threatened by climate change depend on future-oriented science. Artificially narrowing the foreseeable future restricts the ability to act before populations collapse, undermining the preventative intent of the ESA. Recovery often requires habitat beyond the small areas species currently occupy; restricting unoccupied critical habitat contradicts the Act’s recovery mandate.

Reinstating the 2019 regulations moves ESA implementation backward, not forward. The Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA Fisheries should retain the 2024 improvements and uphold science-based, forward-looking protections.

title: Comment from Albert, Brynn

text:
I am appalled and horrified that this proposal would essentially gut and totally rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it, for the sake of our children and grandchildren and the world as we know it. The ESA is one of the most successful wildlife laws in the world, with more than 99% of species under the ESA's care getting either saved or are on the path to recovery. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.

The ESA has protected millions of acres of natural habitat, including forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans. To achieve this success, ESA listings must be guided by science and be free of economic considerations, and projects must be held accountable for taxpayer-funded actions that would harm listed species.

When we harm wildlife to the point of extinction, the ecosystems they tend and live in change, and that impacts whole communities and biomes in ways we can't predict even when we are just thinking on a selfish, immediate, economic basis. We should strengthen the ESA to protect manatees, monarch butterflies, red knots, wolverines, and other species that need to be recovered. This proposal puts our wildlife at even greater risk of extinction.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
Good Evening,

I respectfully submit this comment in opposition to the proposed revisions to Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act of 1973 (ESA).

Section 7 is a practical and preventative provision of the ESA. It ensures that federal agency actions—such as energy development, mining, dam construction, and timber sales—are reviewed to avoid unintentionally pushing already-imperiled species closer to extinction. This process does not prohibit development; it provides a check to ensure projects proceed responsibly and with awareness of risk.

The Section 7 consultation framework has played a central role in the Act’s effectiveness. As a result, approximately 99 percent of species listed under the ESA remain extant today. This record reflects a system that works as intended: preventing irreversible loss while allowing economic activity to continue.
The proposed revisions would weaken this safeguard by limiting how impacts are assessed.

Excluding consideration of past federal actions would prevent agencies from accounting for cumulative effects—often the most significant factor affecting species already under stress. Additionally, removing habitat offsets as reasonable and prudent measures would reduce flexibility and eliminate a tool that has allowed conservation and development to coexist.

Human activity has reshaped nearly every working landscape through agriculture, infrastructure, and development. These changes have brought real economic benefits, but they have also reduced the margin for error for certain species. When declines occur in species such as the Whooping Crane, they reflect long-term landscape alteration rather than natural failure.

At the same time, the recovery of species such as Sandhill and Whooping Cranes demonstrates that consistent, well-applied conservation policy can succeed. These recoveries have also supported local economies through wildlife-related tourism in Nebraska and other regions, showing that conservation outcomes and economic interests are not mutually exclusive.

From a broader stewardship perspective, extinction represents a permanent consequence of human action. Once a species is lost, it cannot be restored by future growth, innovation, or mitigation. Section 7 functions as a prudent safeguard against such irreversible outcomes.

For these reasons, I urge the agency to retain strong Section 7 protections and reject revisions that weaken cumulative impact analysis or remove proven conservation tools. Doing so reflects responsibility, foresight, and respect for the land and resources entrusted to future generations.

Thank you for all of your efforts, your time, and your service to our great nation.

Sincerely,

Kylee Warren
Lewellen, NE

title: Comment from Arnold, Travis

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. The Section 7 consultation process is the cornerstone of the ESA, and the process impacts every listed species under the ESA.

ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation. Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law, and importantly, it strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations.

Federal agencies such as NOAA Fisheries, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Bureau of Reclamation frequently consult under ESA Section 7 when operating dams, managing river flows, or authorizing water diversions. These consultations have led to actions like fish passage improvements, spill operations, and habitat restoration. It is important for innumerable marine and aquatic species, such as salmon and Southern Resident orca in the Pacific Northwest, to require consultations.

Federal water-management agencies, including the Bureau of Reclamation and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, consult to ensure water projects and river operations do not reduce habitat or food availability for the migrating whooping cranes and other listed species that rely on rivers and wetlands. Without this requirement to consult, agency actions could disrupt their habitat and food resources and we could lose these species forever.
title: Comment from Walters, Shawn

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.
title: Comment from Techanchuk, Eleanor

text:
Docket No. FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044

I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service (“the Services”) to withdraw the proposed rule changes regarding interagency cooperation under Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

Interagency Consultation Is Essential to ESA Compliance

Interagency consultation is the cornerstone of effective species protection under the ESA. Section 7 requires federal agencies to ensure that actions they authorize, fund, or carry out are not likely to jeopardize the continued existence of listed species or destroy or adversely modify designated critical habitat, and to do so in consultation with the appropriate Service.

The proposed rule would weaken this statutory mandate by removing or narrowing long-standing compliance measures, reducing transparency, and limiting the Services’ ability to fully evaluate the consequences of federal actions. Consultation is inherently collaborative and ensures that wildlife experts assess project impacts, minimize incidental take, and uphold the law’s core purpose: species survival and recovery.

The Proposed Rule Undermines Section 7 by Narrowing Key Definitions

The proposed revisions would affect projects requiring federal authorization, funding, or occurring on federal lands and would, among other things:
(a) Narrow the definition of “effects of the action” and limit what consequences are considered “reasonably certain to occur,” excluding many foreseeable adverse impacts from analysis;
(b) Reclassify many action-related impacts as part of the “environmental baseline,” thereby shielding them from scrutiny during consultation;
(c) Remove the Services’ authority to require reasonable and prudent measures that include mitigation, offsets, or habitat replacement for incidental take;
(d) Presume mitigation will occur even without enforceable commitments;
(e) Disregard adverse impacts to critical habitat unless they appreciably diminish the habitat “as a whole”;
(f) Relieve the Services of their duty to reinitiate consultation when unanticipated harmful effects arise;
(g) Allow action agencies’ self-assessments to replace independent biological opinions;
(h) Exempt certain land management plans from reinitiation of consultation when new species are listed or new critical habitat is designated; and
(i) Impose arbitrary and ambiguous deadlines that undermine meaningful consultation.

Taken together, these changes would allow significant adverse effects to listed species and their habitats—particularly rare plants and climate-vulnerable ecosystems—to occur without adequate analysis or accountability.

Consultation Is Efficient and Economically Beneficial

Section 7 consultation does not impede progress or economic development. Healthy ecosystems support tourism, fisheries, agriculture, water quality, and climate resilience. Biodiversity loss, by contrast, undermines human well-being and economic stability. Effective consultation avoids costly litigation, prevents irreversible harm, and ensures responsible project planning.

Specific Regulatory Concerns

I urge the Services to:
(a) Retain the current definitions of “effects of the action,” “environmental baseline,” and “reasonable and prudent measures,” preserving the Services’ flexibility to require mitigation and habitat replacement;
(b) Retain existing language in 50 C.F.R. Section 402.14 that allows measures to avoid, reduce, or offset incidental take within or outside the action area;
(c) Remove provisions that limit reinitiation of consultation or allow adoption of action agencies’ self-evaluations in place of independent biological opinions;
(d) Reject the assertion that an agency is not responsible for environmental effects merely because it lacks authority over the resulting impact when the effect is a direct consequence of its action; and
(e) Ensure that cumulative and climate-driven impacts are evaluated at biologically meaningful scales during both informal and formal consultations.

Conclusion

Section 7 consultation is the keystone of the ESA’s effectiveness. The proposed rule would erode this foundation, weaken species protections, and conflict with the statute’s purpose, scientific understanding, and decades of precedent. I respectfully request that the Services withdraw the proposed rule and retain strong, transparent, and collaborative interagency consultation requirements that fully protect listed species and their critical habitats.

I am submitting this comment because I care deeply about the health of our environment, which includes healthy ecosystems and biodiversity. I care about science-informed stewardship of the wildlife in this country, and want to see my government continue to uphold the Endangered Species Act.

The ESA works because it centers science and the public interest. This and other proposed changes to the ESA would allow private economic interests to outweigh scientific reality and the public interest. I have the following concerns with the rule changes currently being proposed:
-The Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4) would remove automatic protections from newly listed species. It takes time to write species-specific rules and for recovery efforts to begin to have an impact. The blanket rule provides critical immediate protections to newly listed species so that they are not killed or subjected to further habitat destruction before recovery efforts can begin.
-The proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)) narrows the criteria for critical habitat exclusions and could allow economic interests to override needed habitat protection. Failure to protect essential habitat puts entire ecosystems at risk, not only individual species. Proposed changes that would narrow how “foreseeable future” is interpreted when determining species listing would also hamper the Department’s ability to take into consideration the impacts of climate change on species, undermining the scientific basis of rules. Science tells us that climate change is happening and we know how ecosystems are change and will continue to change as global warming continues, so it is critical that we take those facts into account when determining how to protect ecosystems and species into the future.
-The proposed consultation rule (Section 7) would limit interagency review and consultation, threatening what should be a science-based process that fully assesses the potential impacts of federal projects on endangered wildlife before a project can proceed. A democratic, science-based process requires meaningful review and transparency, which this proposed rule would undermine. Section 7 is the backbone of the ESA, which ensures that federal agencies do not approve projects that would destroy critical habitat or harm threatened or endangered species.

I grew up visiting family in Maine every summer, and I remember when I was younger how seeing a bald eagle flying over the lake was a rare joy. Happily we see multiple eagles every year now, but it still feels like a gift every time. The recovery of bald eagles in the United States is a success story of the Endangered Species Act, and limiting the use of DDT enabled these birds and others to recover without lasting harm to our economy. Without the protections of the ESA, eagles could be extinct, and the symbol of our country could be just a symbol. Salmon are a keystone species, essential to the health of whole ecosystems—feeding animals as diverse as eagles, ravens, wolves, and bears, and bringing nutrients back to the forests that provide multiple benefits to our communities from recreational opportunities to spiritual connection to carbon sequestration. Salmon are incredibly important for the health of ecosystems in our region and culturally significant to many Americans who live here, and it is essential that they continue to be protected over the long term through the ESA.

I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

text:
I strongly oppose these proposed section 7 consultation changes. Please withdraw this proposed rule.

Definition of “Environmental Baseline”:
First species do not exist in a vacuum. I strongly oppose revising the definition of “environmental baseline” and removing it from the definition of “effects of the action”. Species in the wild are subject to a concert of fluctuating environmental variables, all of which must considered to understand the current and reasonably expected range of consequences an action may or will have. This proposed role does not make sense for real-world applications of the ESA. That is, unless you’re working on a controlled laboratory experiment as it’s written, in which all other conditions are controlled, except for the sole variable being tested.

Existing conditions are not separate from the consequences of proposed actions and they should be built into the analysis. The environment is not static but subject to and comprised of multiple pressures in real time. This definition of the environmental baseline renders a species' environment into a static data point, ruling out ongoing processes that are subject to change over time, such as documented and quantifiable changes in weather and temperature and corresponding changes in required resources, such as food item availability in a species’ habitat (not to mention the proposed limits to what may be considered habitat provided in the other proposed section 4(b)(2) exclusions; all of these revisions considered together are not only detrimental to species’ recovery but the negative outcomes will be compounded by each one in an additive fashion).

An environmental baseline is only a point in time snapshot; it is unrealistic to remove the requirement to consult for ongoing indoor worsening environmental pressures that the species is subject to. These must be accounted for and considered as part of the services and agencies work. Second, for the record, let's also stress that this proposed change will codify the concept of "shifting baselines" and should be withdrawn. What we consider today's baseline for an an imperiled species is not the same as the species' healthy or natural baseline prior to its population being subject to current pressures, as well as those pressures leading up to today. Further, we've all heard, 'we don't have the data’ as a reason to not conserve a species when the rich data sets we have today were not available in the recent past, even if the population was documented extensively across multiple formats, such as landing records, photographs, videos, narrower data sets, etc. in previous years.

Shifting baselines also describes the practical loss of knowledge and understanding over time. For instance, when a new conservation manager begins their career in the field, they develop a practical understanding of the health of a species and its habitat based on the current context and conditions. However, a senior conservation manager working alongside them may recall a vastly different set of conditions, population and environmental characteristics at the start of their career. This critical, informative delta between the senior conservation manager and the new conservation manager is lost when the senior conservation manager retires, providing more shifting baselines: the new conservation manager manages to their initial baseline, not their predecessor's baseline when the species was actually healthy enough to be resilient to fluctuating environmental conditions. Thus we inadvertently manage for lesser species population and habitat health over time due to this career-generational loss of knowledge.

And this proposed change would very closely approximate the same negative effects and codify them.

For all of these reasons, I strongly urge the Service to withdraw these proposed rules and instead strengthen the Endangered Species Act.

Finally, these proposed changes will have a substantial impact the protection of our endangered species and their habitat and a 30-day comment period during the holiday season is inadequate and should be extended for 60 days to match other proposed rule changes.

Thank you so much.

title: Comment from feldman, kiara

text:
I am opposed to the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. The four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

Of particular concern is the elimination of the "blanket 4(d) rule" and the changes to critical habitat. There have been several documented cases of threatened species thriving under this rule, particularly plant species. They deserve the same level of protection as the endangered species. It removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

The proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife or if it's designated for "national security" purposes. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery. I have personally seen the devastating harm that destruction of coastal systems has done to the manatee populations, and the destruction of mangroves for development also has a human cost. Those ecosystems protect us from hurricanes.

Introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based. Additionally it introduces significant bias towards corporations and developers that have the funds to lobby for exclusions. Allowing these third parties to provide the data on the species also undercut the core tenet of the ESA which is to use the best available scientific data to determine critical habitat.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Some, like the bald eagle and the Yellowstone wolves, even rebounded. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to rethink and if necessary retract these changes to the rule. It is clear they are driven by private interest and financial gain rather than by science and a care for the long term survival and health of endangered and threatened species.

I strongly oppose the proposed changes to interagency consultation requirements under Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act. These changes would weaken one of the most important preventative safeguards in the ESA and significantly increase the risk of harm to endangered species, including Southern Resident killer whales.

Section 7 consultation exists to ensure that federal actions do not jeopardize the continued existence of listed species or destroy or adversely modify their critical habitat. This process is essential because many of the most significant threats to endangered species arise not from a single action, but from repeated federal decisions that collectively degrade habitat, prey availability, and environmental conditions over time.

For Southern Resident killer whales, federal actions play a central role in shaping their environment. Shipping, port operations, naval activities, dredging, fisheries management, shoreline development, and infrastructure projects all intersect with the whales’ habitat and prey base. Consultation ensures that these actions are evaluated through a science-based lens before harm occurs, not after damage is done.

The proposed changes appear to raise the threshold for when consultation is required, expand agency self-determination of “no effect,” or limit the scope of impacts that must be analyzed. These changes would significantly reduce oversight and allow agencies to proceed with actions that may contribute to cumulative harm without meaningful review. This is especially dangerous for species like Southern Resident killer whales, whose decline is driven by chronic, overlapping stressors rather than isolated incidents.

Weakening consultation also undermines accountability. The ESA does not assume that agencies will always fully evaluate their own impacts without external review. Consultation with expert wildlife agencies exists precisely to prevent conflicts of interest and ensure that species protection is not subordinated to project timelines or institutional priorities.

Additionally, limiting the consideration of indirect and cumulative effects during consultation contradicts decades of scientific understanding. Incremental increases in underwater noise, small reductions in prey, or repeated disturbances may seem insignificant in isolation, but together they can push a fragile population past a biological tipping point. Section 7 consultation is one of the few mechanisms capable of addressing these realities.

The ESA is designed to prevent jeopardy, not merely document it. Weakening consultation shifts the law from a preventative framework to a reactive one, where harm must become severe or irreversible before action is taken. This approach is incompatible with recovery and directly conflicts with the intent of Congress.

I urge the agency to reject the proposed changes in this docket and to preserve strong, enforceable interagency consultation requirements. For Southern Resident killer whales and countless other endangered species, Section 7 consultation is not bureaucratic red tape... it is a lifeline.

title: Comment from Braun, Sarah

text: I respectfully submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) interagency cooperation regulations under Section 7, as published in Docket FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044-0001. The ESA’s Section 7 consultation process is a critical scientific safeguard that helps prevent federal actions from jeopardizing listed species or adversely modifying their habitats. Proposed changes that weaken how consultations assess effects — especially broad, indirect, and cumulative effects — would significantly undermine the law’s biological effectiveness. Section 7 of the ESA directs federal agencies to ensure that actions they authorize, fund, or carry out are “not likely to jeopardize the continued existence” of listed species or result in the destruction or adverse modification of their designated critical habitat, using the best scientific and commercial data available. This interagency consultation process assesses direct, indirect, and cumulative effects — not just immediate and obvious ones — reflecting ecological science demonstrating that species decline through multiple interacting stressors. A peer-reviewed analysis in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that maintaining independent expert agency participation in Section 7 consultations significantly affects outcomes, particularly by reducing incorrect “no effect” determinations. Had agencies been allowed to self-consult without expert review, nearly one-third of actions later found likely to jeopardize species would not have received adequate scientific analysis. This demonstrates that consultation with expert scientific agencies meaningfully improves biological rigor in decision-making. Quantitative analyses of the ESA’s performance have repeatedly shown that science-based protections — including consultation and critical habitat designation — are associated with improved species status trends. By assessing the biological consequences of federal actions before they occur, Section 7 consultations help avoid or reduce impacts that would otherwise push vulnerable populations closer to extinction. The best available quantitative evidence demonstrates that the ESA is effective when implemented promptly and based on sound science. Ecologists agree that species decline not because of single, isolated actions, but because of cumulative and interacting threats such as habitat loss, altered hydrology, invasive species, and climate variability. A biologically robust Section 7 consultation integrates these multiple stressors into the analysis of potential harm. Narrowing definitions or limiting the scope of effects undermines this scientifically essential perspective and increases the risk that species will suffer population declines that go unrecognized until it is too late. Conservation science and practice underscore the importance of coordinated action. Scholarly work on the ESA’s implementation continues to affirm that strong consultation standards — including consideration of direct, indirect, and cumulative effects — are necessary to fulfill the ESA’s dual goals of preventing extinction and promoting recovery. Weakening consultation requirements will impede the ability of federal agencies to make biologically informed decisions about complex environmental impacts.

title: Comment from Hom, Patrick

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival and instead adopt stronger measures to protect wildlife & water quality.

title: Comment from Rice, Janine

text:
I am submitting this comment because biodiversity and healthy ecosystems matter deeply to me.

As someone who lives in Tennessee and regularly sees the effects of habitat loss, I am concerned about weakening protections for imperiled species. I care about science-informed stewardship of the wildlife in this country.

The Endangered Species Act works because it centers science and the public interest—not political pressure or economic influence. Science can tell us what species need to survive; values determine whether we choose to protect them. These rules shift decision-making away from both. The proposed changes would allow industry considerations to outweigh both biological need and scientific reality.

I am Concerned With the Following Proposed Rule Changes:
Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4): Removing automatic protections from newly listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed.
Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)):Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide.
Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)):Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening ecosystem health. If economic interests weigh more than essential habitat, entire ecosystems are at risk, not just wildlife species.
Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7):Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife.

Federal oversight is often the only check on state wildlife systems that are already heavily shaped by industry interests. These rollbacks reduce public accountability at a time when most Americans support stronger environmental conservation protections. A democratic, science-based process requires transparency and meaningful review.

I urge the agency to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s strong, science-based protections. Please strengthen, not weaken, federal safeguards so states and industry cannot sidestep responsibility to protect imperiled wildlife. I ask you to uphold the intent of the ESA: preventing extinction and ensuring future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I support conservation and economic responsibility, and for that reason I implore the Services to reject the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act regulations. These proposals place increased emphasis on economic considerations and agency discretion, yet the core purpose of the ESA has always been to ensure the survival of species before economic tradeoffs are even considered. While economic development is important, the cumulative effect of these rule changes would undermine the ESA’s most efficient and fiscally responsible function: preventing irreversible losses before they become costly, chaotic, and impossible to undo.
The success of the Endangered Species Act lies in its preventative approach. Healthy ecosystems provide indispensable public benefits—clean water and air, pollination, flood mitigation, soil stability, outdoor recreation, cultural continuity, and resilient working lands. These ecosystem services directly support hunting, fishing, tourism, ranching, and farming, all of which are pillars of rural economies across the country. These benefits exist only if ecosystems remain intact, and ecosystems cannot function if species continue to disappear, even under current protections. Weakening the ESA now would accelerate losses that ultimately harm both communities and the economy.

Regarding the proposed change to Section 7, the proposed definition of “environmental baseline” is EXTREMELY DANGEROUS because it does not take into account the ecological function of the species or habitat. The reason for preventing species extinction is to conserve the ecological functions of our lands, rivers, oceans, etc. The American people deserve to live in, experience, and benefit from healthy and functioning ecosystems, many of which are already degraded. According to the proposed definition, an “environmental baseline” would be an already degraded ecosystem. It would be better to consider habitat that could support endangered species and make every effort to ensure those species are protected there, either by allowing them to move in or re-introducing them.
Streamlining consultation can be helpful, but these proposals would limit federal review of agency actions and make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without understanding the immediate and ongoing impacts on endangered wildlife. Clear, science-based consultation upfront protects projects from lawsuits, delays, and costly redesigns later. Predictability is pro-business; weakened safeguards are not.

Please consider the case that Wyoming’s wolf “recovery” numbers are far too low to ensure the species’ survival. If Wyoming gets its way, they will only have roughly 100 wolves and 10 breeding pairs. This can hardly be called an "environmental baseline" given that healthy populations need far more animals to maintain genetic diversity, ecosystem balance, and long-term resilience. The attempt at the functional extirpation of wolves in Wyoming is partially due to former Wyoming Game and Fish Director, Brian Nesvik who oversaw state management policies that allowed hundreds of wolves to be killed and put in place a culture that is leading to this ecocide. Now that he is Director of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, there is serious reason to question whether he can be trusted to prioritize the survival of endangered species over political and economic pressures. Stronger protections are urgently needed to prevent further extinctions, safeguard ecosystems, prevent millions (if not billions) of taxpayer dollars spent on environmental lawsuits, and stabilize outcomes for ranchers, hunters, landowners, and the economy.

Over 84% of all Americans support the Endangered Species Act and are in favor of preventing species extinctions above all else. Please do what is right for all Americans (not just a few greedy ones) and DO NOT adopt ANY of these proposed changes.
title: Comment from Morlas, Ruth

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service,

I am writing to you today as a deeply concerned citizen to express my strongest opposition to the proposed changes regarding interagency cooperation under the Endangered Species Act. The revisions outlined in docket FWS HQ ES 2025 0044 0001 strike at the very heart of the most successful conservation law in our history. For over five decades, the Endangered Species Act has served as a shield for the vulnerable, ensuring that our own government does not become the primary driver of extinction. These proposed changes would effectively shatter that shield.

The most alarming aspect of this proposal is the redefinition of the environmental baseline. By allowing the government to categorize ongoing damage from existing federal facilities, such as aging dams or polluting infrastructure, as part of a fixed baseline, you are essentially grandfathering in the destruction of our natural world. If a federal project is currently responsible for the massive decline of a species, that should be a call to action, not a reason to ignore the problem. Under these new rules, an agency could propose a new project that adds even more harm, yet claim it is insignificant because the previous damage is now considered an unchangeable fact of life. This is a scientific and moral shell game that ignores the cumulative toll on our ecosystems.

Furthermore, the attempt to narrow the definition of what is reasonably certain to occur is a dangerous step backward. We are living through a period of unprecedented environmental change. Science tells us that the impacts of our actions today will ripple through the environment for decades. By demanding a higher and more restrictive threshold of certainty before an agency is required to consider future threats like climate change, you are choosing to be blind to the most significant challenges our wildlife faces. To suggest that we should only care about impacts that are immediate is to abandon the long term survival of species like the salmon and the polar bear. We cannot manage the future of our planet if we refuse to look past a four year political cycle.

I am also deeply troubled by the decision to remove the provisions for offsets and mitigation. In the past, when a federal project caused unavoidable harm to a habitat, there was a mechanism to ensure that conservation work happened elsewhere to make up for that loss. This was a common sense approach that balanced development with responsibility. By stripping away the power to require these offsets, you are giving a free pass to industrial interests and federal agencies to destroy habitat without any obligation to repair the damage. You are essentially stating that the profit margins of a few are more important than the biological diversity that sustains us all.

This proposal repeatedly mentions efficiency and the need to unleash energy production as justifications for these rollbacks. I believe we must ask ourselves what we are being efficient at. Is it efficient to allow a species to vanish forever because a consultation process was deemed too burdensome? Is it efficient to ignore the best available science to speed up a permit? Extinction is the ultimate inefficiency. It is a permanent loss that no amount of industrial growth can ever replace.

The Endangered Species Act was designed to be a check on federal power, ensuring that we look before we leap. These changes would turn a vital safety net into a sieve. I urge you to prioritize the survival of our nation's wildlife over the demands of short term economic gain. Please withdraw these proposed revisions and maintain a strong, science based Section 7 process that truly protects our natural heritage for the generations to come.

Sincerely,

Steven Pilipow

title: Comment from Lauber, HA

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of the Endangered Species Act, erodes legal requirements, and undermines the original intent of Congress for federal agencies to coordinate with each other to ensure federal actions do not jeopardize listed wildlife or degrade their critical habitat.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. This proposed rule narrows definitions for “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” and removes mitigation offset requirements, all of which could allow federal actions to proceed without fully accounting for their impacts on listed species or critical habitat. Weakening these requirements reduces the scope of review and gives agencies greater leeway to approve projects without fully evaluating cumulative or indirect effects. This will leave listed species more vulnerable, accelerate species decline, and undermine the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.
title: Comment from Hartz, Alana

text:
I am strongly against this change. This change would be absolutely catastrophic, making it harder to list species as endangered or threatened and easier to delist a species. These changes would make it more challenging to grant Endangered Species Act protections for species that are impacted by climate change, drought, disease, and other effects. The US Fish and Wildlife Service would also be limited in their ability to designate currently unoccupied wolf habitat as critical, even if those areas are essential for future wolf expansion and recovery.

True endangered species conservation requires forward-thinking and future projections, not a shortsighted narrowing scope of the “foreseeable future”, which hinders our ability to proactively save species before they hover on the brink of extinction. It allows people to leaves species in the dust if it so benefits their business.

True recovery looks at all areas a species did roam, and could roam in the future – not just where they’re currently found. Gray wolves only occupy 10-12% of their historical range but will rely on unoccupied areas if the species is going to truly recover.

FWS and NMFS should reject this proposed rule and rely on the improvements made in 2024.

text:
Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species act is that was passed as a bipartisan effort. It was meant to be an American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage. I am writing to oppose key adverse changes to the Endangered Species Act.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

Please focus agency efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. As stewards of the earth we owe it to wildlie to balance all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change. We need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am strongly opposed to this proposed change to the Endangered Species Act, and I urge you to reject this change. We are living in a time of unprecedented species loss. It is a time when we should be strengthening the protections of rare species, not weakening them.

Interagency consultation is essential to maintaining protections for at-risk species. This proposed change seems like a deliberate attempt to weaken the ESA and like the pockets of those who benefit from actions which harm rare species.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I am writing this to express my strong opposition to the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. The changes would be detrimental to the health of our environment and nation as a whole. As someone who has enjoyed the outdoors, it pains me to think that the decades we have spent in reviving keystone species and restoring some of the most beautiful landscapes in our country should now be threatened and all that work undone.

Since its introduction 51 years ago, the Endangered Species Act has been instrumental and fundamental in our efforts at environmental conservation and the preservation of our wildlands that have been the true great inheritance for all Americans. We cannot weaken it now. We should not question or introduce ambiguity in terms like "recovery" or what constitutes "critical habitats."

By eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule", this increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading - what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

I strongly urge our representatives to oppose these changes as polls have shown that the majority of the public supports wildlife conservation. We all recognize that our future and well-being, as well as those of our posterity, depends on our ability to defend and preserve our wildlands.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
This proposed rule represents a deathly dangerous retreat from the Endangered Species Act’s core mandate to prevent extinction and avoid irreversible harm. Reinstating elements of the 2019 Section 7 regulations while removing critical safeguards adopted in 2024 weakens interagency consultation at a time when listed species face accelerating threats from climate change, habitat loss, and cumulative development pressures. Section 7 was designed to ensure that federal actions do not push species closer to extinction. The proposed changes narrow the scope of effects considered in consultation, weaken the treatment of cumulative and future impacts, and increase the likelihood that harmful actions will be approved based on incomplete or artificially constrained analyses. This is not a neutral clarification of statutory text. It is a substantive rollback of protections that increases extinction risk.

The Service’ reliance on recent executive directives and deregulatory priorities does not relieve them of their statutory obligations under the ESA. The Act is explicit that federal agencies must insure that their actions are not likely to jeopardize the continued existence of listed species or destroy or adversely modify critical habitat. Any regulatory revision that elevates speed, administrative convenience, or development interests over actual, physical, tangible, biological reality violates both the letter and the purpose of the law. The removal of provisions that allowed meaningful consideration of mitigation and offsets, without replacing them with equally protective mechanisms, further undermines conservation outcomes. Ignoring real world ecological impacts because specific terms do not appear verbatim in statutory text reflects an overly narrow and legally risky interpretation of the ESA, particularly given Congress’s clear intent that the Act be precautionary and protective. Ecosystems are already under severe stress, and species are declining at unprecedented rates. Weakening Section 7 consultation standards at this moment is stupid. The consequences of these changes will not only hurt wildlife, but by human communities that depend on healthy ecosystems for clean water, food security, climate stability, and disaster resilience.

I strongly demand an immediate withdraw this proposed rule, retain the stronger 2024 protections, and ensure that Section 7 consultation remains a rigorous, science based safeguard against extinction, as Congress intended.

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

text:
I am opposed to these proposed changes, and any changes that would weaken or limit the enactment of the Endangered Species Act. A vast majority of Americans want a strong Endangered Species Act, want it strongly enacted, and fully funded. I am concerned the proposed changes would weaken key provisions requiring interagency consultations whenever a federal activity could harm threatened and endangered species.

The Section 7 regulations of the ESA currently require the designation of critical habitat for threatened and endangered species in nearly all cases through interagency consultations. Federal agencies are therefore prohibited from funding, permitting, or taking actions that destroy or adversely modify critical habitat. Through consultation with the National Marine Fisheries Service for marine and anadromous species, or the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service for all other species, federal agencies avoid causing serious harm to the recovery of threatened and endangered species by not destroying or degrading critical habitat.

The proposed changes to key provisions including the changes to the definition of “destruction or adverse modification” of critical habitat, will significantly weaken the interagency function of the Act. Also, the narrow definition of "effects of the action" and "environmental baseline" of critical habitat essential for the imperiled species’ recovery will eliminate provisions allowing consideration of important threats, particularly from long-term cumulative climate-driven impacts. Habitat loss and degradation due to climate shifts and other human activities remain the primary cause of species loss and endangerment, so effective protection of adequate critical habitat (including unoccupied habitat) is therefore essential for successful for the recovery of endangered and threatened species.

I feel that this revised definition of adverse modification is fundamentally inconsistent with the intent of the ESA and the will of the majority of Americans for its enactment. The definition should absolutely include cumulative climate-driven impacts to ensure the survival and recovery of imperiled species. I would like this proposed revision to be withdrawn in favor of a definition of adverse modification that incorporates cumulative threats of climate at a biologically meaningful landscape scale in all baseline effect analyses.

I also believe the inclusions of offsets into RPMs should be retained in these sections as appropriate measures for consideration.
title: Comment from Mannweiler, Michelle

text:
I'm strongly opposed to FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044. The proposed weakening of federal interagency consultation under Section 7 of the ESA would directly endanger species whose recovery remains fragile~Grizzly Bears & Gray Wolves. This rule making is occurring in the time of widespread capacity loss across federal wildlife agencies, including firings, defunding affecting the NPS, the Interagency Grizzly Bear Committee & the USFWS.

At the very moment when federal science, monitoring & coordination are being squeezed, the proposal would reduce consultation standards & scope, undermining the ESA's central preventative safeguard. For Grizzlies & Wolves~species brought back from the brink only through rigorous federal oversight~this combo is untenable & dangerous. Weakening it while agencies are being hollowed out is reckless.

Section 7 consultation exists to prevent jeopardy before it occurs. It is a science-based, interagency process designed to catch cumulative impacts, landscape-level threats, & indirect effects that project-by-project reviews routinely miss. This proposal would narrow when consultation is triggered & how effects are analyzed, effectively lowering the bar at the exact moment when agencies lack the staffing & funding to compensate for those cuts.

The reality on the ground matters. Biologists are being let go or stretched beyond capacity; long-term monitoring programs are underfunded; interagency coordination has been weakened. Consultation rollbacks do not occur in a vacuum-they compound existing institutional damage. When the safety net is grayed, removing threads guarantees failure.

Grizzly Bears delisting is not feasible without robust federal consultation & capacity. Grizzlies remain conservation-reliant across much of their range. The ESA & the Service's own recovery framework require post-delisting federal oversight, including a mandatory minimum five-year monitoring period with continued coordination among federal agencies & states. That oversight presumes a functioning consultation regime & staffed federal workforce.
These conditions no longer exist. With the Park Service, the Interagency Grizzly Bear Committee, & the USFWS all experiencing budgetary & staffing strain, it is not feasible-scientifically or administratively-to delist Grizzlies particularly in the N Rocky Mtns. weakening consultation while simultaneously enabling delisting creates a regulatory fiction, it assumed protections & oversight that the federal government is actively dismantling.

Grizzly recovery depends on habitat connectivity, female survival, & low human-caused mortality-all of which are directly affected by federal land management decisions subject to consultation. Curtailing consultation increases the risk of road expansion, recreation pressure, extraction use, & development in linkage habitat. For a long-lived, slow-reproducing species, these cumulative impacts are irreversible.

For Wolves-consultation rollbacks enable predictable state-level overkill. The danger is even more immediate. Weakening federal consultation while relaxing ESA standards hands control to states with documented hostility toward Wolves & management regimes that disregard best available science.

In the N Rocky Mtn states Wolves are already subject to aggressive hunting/killing policies that prioritize population suppression rather than ecological function. Federal consultation is one of the last mechanisms capable of checking cumulative impacts from federal actions (grazing/road building/energy development) that interact with state-sanctioned killing to drive rapid declines.
In Wisconsin & the Great Lakes, the situation is more extreme. WI law mandates a Wolf hunt whenever federal protections are removed, regardless of scientific uncertainty, tribal treaty rights, or recent population data. This statutory trigger is incompatible with adaptive management & makes clear that Wolves will not receive a fair chance post-delisting. Weakening consultation while knowing this outcome is not neutral policymaking-it is knowingly facilitating "harm".

CA illustrates the opposite trajectory. Through strong state protections & continued federal consultation & oversight, Wolves on the Pacific Coast have begun to recolonize fragmented landscapes. Progress there depends on connectivity, tolerance & female establishment, all of which are supported, not hindered, by robust consultation.

The contrast matters. A one-size-fits-all weakening of federal consultation ignores the reality that some states act as partners in recovery while others act as agents of eradication. The ESA was designed precisely because wildlife conservation can't be left solely to states when political pressures overwhelm science.

Narrowing consultation ensures cumulative landscape-scale threats will go unanalyzed & unmitigated.

0044 moves ESA implementation in the wrong direction at the worst time. Weakening federal consultation guarantees increased risk for Grizzlies & Wolves.
